focuses.description: An independent republic enters a new decade with a damaged constitutional partnership, fragmented communal services and an uncertain chain of command. Makarios must preserve sovereignty while addressing the island's divisions.
Clerides and Denktash are negotiating counterparts. Talks began before this start date.
Negotiation, security and constitutional outcomes. Both communities have political agency; foreign players can accept or reject proposals.
Open supervised civilian routes; halve the two starting state construction penalties after an agreed local protocol.
Administrative leverage gives immediate political room, but movement restrictions and enclave penalties remain. Does not reward targeting civilians.

A funded intermediate shared-services stage: south access penalty removed, north construction -3%/positive-growth -4%, national administration friction bureaucracy+2%/police+2.5%. Does not resolve the constitution.
Record abuses and safeguard access to courts; not a magic reconciliation event.
Begin removing divided-command penalties; temporary officer resistance: political_power_factor -0.05 for 180 days.
Retain expertise and external dependence; remove only half the divided-command penalty. Greek officer presence does not make every Greek officer a coup participant.
Complete chain-of-command reform; constitutional reform remains separate.
Government control improves, but outside influence and civilian tension remain. Powers lapse after civilian restoration.
Requires a Turkish Cypriot negotiating acceptance; a CYP focus alone cannot decide the other community's rights.
Majority-rule argument without automatic dissolution of the Turkish Cypriot administration. Rejection preserves deadlock and raises diplomatic pressure.
Replace constitutional breakdown; legitimate decentralisation carries administrative cost.
A revised 1960-style bicommunal republic: tighter veto rules and central services, slower negotiations; replace constitutional breakdown only after acceptance.
The earlier administrative and state relief is replaced, not stacked.
Targets armed organisations on both sides through negotiated/local implementation; Greek mainland resistance can raise coup pressure.
Regime mobilisation with a lasting fragmented-command cost; can unlock a hardline coup route after its formation date.
Judicial orders and civilian protection; can be taken by any ruling party willing to obey them.

Authorise collective punishment rather than distinguish armed opponents from civilians. Unlawful detention, expulsions and killings deepen displacement, destroy livelihoods and invite an international crisis. Accountability and restitution will be required before a durable settlement.
Greece, Turkey, Britain and local community negotiators receive offers; any player can refuse. Available after either security course.
Keep an independent republic. Mutually exclusive with an implemented Enosis agreement, not with merely debating one.
Choose the structure of development: tourism or productive diversification; credit openness or domestic control. No giant free industrial base.
Choose the structure of development: tourism or productive diversification; credit openness or domestic control. No giant free industrial base.
More service income, greater exposure to external demand and a crisis. No anachronistic offshore gas windfall.
Slower service expansion in exchange for agricultural processing and light industry.
Choose the structure of development: tourism or productive diversification; credit openness or domestic control. No giant free industrial base.
Distribute tourism income locally. Compatible with the coastal-hotel project.
One 25% research bonus; no ahead-of-time reduction; the technology must exist in the local 1970 research set.
Boost existing output modestly; does not create a factory if the country has none.
Construction bonus for funded work; not a railway project on an island whose railway closed in 1951.
Famagusta connects the island's productive districts to overseas trade. A port extension requires secure local control, a construction programme and the normal capital and maintenance budget.
Choose the structure of development: tourism or productive diversification; credit openness or domestic control. No giant free industrial base.
No university institution before its historical foundation; no additional research slot.
Choose the structure of development: tourism or productive diversification; credit openness or domestic control. No giant free industrial base.
Investment efficiency is not a transfer of free cash; donors retain their own accept/refuse choice.
Interest effect is -0.15 percentage POINTS, not -15%. Cooperatives are a credible historical institution.
Choose the structure of development: tourism or productive diversification; credit openness or domestic control. No giant free industrial base.
Choose the structure of development: tourism or productive diversification; credit openness or domestic control. No giant free industrial base.
Fuel-use planning and secure purchases; no free oil fields, nuclear plant or modern gas extraction.
Permit a construction programme; a whole factory must be paid/built through the existing economy, not granted for 3% GDP.
Institutional port and services network; no free office building or automatic international tax-haven status.
Remove the narrow-economy construction penalty after sustained development. Does not erase war damage or alter Imperia GDP/productivity by raw writes.
A credible defensive force, external supply choices and civilian authority. Cyprus cannot win a symmetrical arms race with Turkey.
A credible defensive force, external supply choices and civilian authority. Cyprus cannot win a symmetrical arms race with Turkey.
Dispersed defensive preparation, limited offensive capacity.
A more responsive reserve with a modest logistics burden; no gift tank divisions.
A credible defensive force, external supply choices and civilian authority. Cyprus cannot win a symmetrical arms race with Turkey.

Benefits activate only if GRE accepts; tied to bilateral relations, not a free license or automatic alliance.
One 25% artillery research bonus; Soviet/Czechoslovak contacts possible without changing outlook or receiving a free production license.
No free fighter wing; imported weapons use existing purchases and depend on seller approval.
Liaison and casualty evacuation; no modern attack helicopter technology unlock.
Coastal observation, not a blue-water navy.
Evacuation planning and medical stocks; deliberately uses an idea because Imperia shelter buildings cost $0.008bn per level EACH WEEK.
Military readiness diverts civilian capacity.
No generic land-doctrine effect carried over without checking the MD 2.0 doctrine system.
A professional constitutional force. Does not cancel active communal violence or territorial war.
Non-alignment, patron dependence and the Sovereign Base Areas. Offers are bilateral; another player's acceptance is never assumed.
Contacts with Egypt, Yugoslavia and India; no automatic faction or military guarantee.
Non-alignment, patron dependence and the Sovereign Base Areas. Offers are bilateral; another player's acceptance is never assumed.
Trade talks in a pre-EU era; no EU membership, Schengen, euro or instant NATO accession.
Non-alignment, patron dependence and the Sovereign Base Areas. Offers are bilateral; another player's acceptance is never assumed.
Negotiating access is separate from sovereign transfer.
If accepted: joint emergency access and a funded local works agreement. Any payment is a real ENG treasury transfer, never manufactured income.
British refusal remains possible; no automatic annexation or war goal. Slow diplomatic road to negotiated transfer.
Non-alignment, patron dependence and the Sovereign Base Areas. Offers are bilateral; another player's acceptance is never assumed.
Reject automatic political subordination while keeping cultural and commercial ties.
Debating union is not annexation. Community objections, Turkey and Britain are represented in the subsequent conference.
Talk directly and through Turkish Cypriot negotiators; Turkey is not interchangeable with the Turkish Cypriot community.
Revised guarantees need local assent and foreign acceptances. Unilateral withdrawal only changes CYP policy; it does not remove external claims.
Never transfer ENG bases implicitly.
Diplomatic support and mediation, not an automatic foreign army.
Branch remains visible but locked before a real crisis.
Civilian protection reaches Greek and Turkish Cypriots; reduce damage escalation, not an instant end to war.
Temporary regime control with repression, abuses and deepening division; no permanent stability reward.
Controller/occupation follows actual war outcome.
State war damage persists; at war only. This is a military choice, not permission to attack civilians.
Internal displacement uses a separate documented burden; do not inject fictional overseas refugee populations.
Reduces affected-state damage by half after protected return access. Original claims remain documented; housing grants do not extinguish them.

Offsets part of the new displacement-emergency spirit; does not provide extra manpower or erase the right to return. This choice postpones, rather than forbids, restitution; the later accountability focus also contains a funded property-claims stage.
Early investigations and family support can occur before 1981; a formal bicommunal CMP is date-gated to 1981 unless explicitly alternate-history.
Remove repression programme; reopen settlement eligibility after accountability and restitution. Requires legal/institutional steps, not a 35-day moral reset.
Remove only immediate emergency, keep displacement/property claims and affected-state penalties. NCY autonomy/recognition depends on actual negotiated/war result.
Remove half remaining construction damage; remove displacement-emergency only after aid/housing and an agreed durable solution. No magical repair of foreign-held states.

Turkish Cypriot communities live with the legacy of displacement, separate administration and enclave economies. Civilian movement had substantially normalised by 1969, but reciprocal access and a common political settlement remain unsettled.

Fazil Kucuk remains the senior communal/vicepresidential figure until 1973; Rauf Raif Denktas is the negotiating representative and later successor. Neither becomes CYP president merely by being consulted.
Direct dialogue with the communal leadership; the counterpart decides whether to cooperate. Turkish Cypriot community-state is tracked separately from national ruling_party.
Clerides can act for the Makarios government; this does not put Clerides in power. Denktas must obtain a community mandate, not merely accept Ankara's instructions.

Fazil Kucuk, Rauf Denktas, civilian organisations and the emerging CTP are distinct interlocutors. Address enclaves, restrictions, separate administration and political equality; they are not an obedient faction of the CYP ruling party.
Replace access penalties with a lower, defined stage after an implemented agreement. Restrictions were already being eased after 1967; avoid portraying January 1970 as an unchanged 1964 siege.
An OPTIONAL renewed coercive policy, not an assertion of an unchanged 1964siege in 1970. Short-term leverage carries policing expense and hostility; no productivity, tax or manpower reward.
Civilian movement and trade access; removal of army defences is a separate negotiation, not a precondition for medicine.
Fund reliable utilities and treatment across communal boundaries. The same project cannot pay twice if the shared constitution branch has already restored it.
A policy of sustained restriction, not an automatic massacre event; armed incidents can worsen the crisis.
Partial relief without freedom of movement. It cannot unlock the economic-normalisation reward on its own.
Choose between joint services or a negotiated decentralised service arrangement. Hardline governments can open talks here, but receive no access relief until they actually implement safeguards.

Fazil Kucuk, Rauf Denktas, civilian organisations and the emerging CTP are distinct interlocutors. Address enclaves, restrictions, separate administration and political equality; they are not an obedient faction of the CYP ruling party.
Decentralisation gives greater communal control with higher ongoing administrative costs; rights and civilian access remain mandatory.
A modest island-level credit-efficiency effect, not a claim that every Turkish Cypriot supports one economic party.
Supports existing repair and processing capacity; no free factory sector.
Income applies to existing staffed offices only; no invented offshore sector.
Documents ownership and displacement claims, not forced alienation or cancellation of rights.

Fazil Kucuk, Rauf Denktas, civilian organisations and the emerging CTP are distinct interlocutors. Address enclaves, restrictions, separate administration and political equality; they are not an obedient faction of the CYP ruling party.
An offer of plural civilian representation. Turkish Cypriots choose their delegates; CYP cannot install a compliant opposition leader.
Negotiate through established security-linked notables; this preserves patron dependence and may marginalise civilian organisations.
The CTP is not present in January 1970. Its formation and constituency are Turkish Cypriot political developments; a CYP focus only opens dialogue, not control of the party.
Protect lawful organisations, workers and municipal representatives on both sides; do not make rights dependent on supporting the government.
Supervised reciprocal security measures, including armed organisations associated with TMT and Greek Cypriot militias. No forced automatic disarmament of either community.
Rely on existing external patronage; Turkish aid must actually be provided by Turkey. No money is created by this focus.
Community assent is an independently resolved outcome. Cyprus cannot set assent just by completing a negotiation focus.
A federal or power-sharing proposal recognises political equality and safeguards; acceptance requires a real community mandate.
Offer protected rights within a more central republic. Rejection is possible and preserves deadlock; majority voting cannot manufacture Turkish Cypriot consent.
The shared constitutional tree must still ratify and implement the settlement.
A revised central republic needs explicit Turkish Cypriot acceptance, enforceable safeguards and effective freedom of movement.
An audit of implementation, not a second stability prize. Ratification in the shared tree requires this outcome.
Turkish Cypriots can refuse.
Constitutional deadlock and state access penalties remain; threats can provoke external intervention. Reprisals remain a separate explicit policy with damage and displacement consequences.
Post-crisis contact with a de facto administration does not automatically recognise a sovereign state. No 1970 NCY release.

Diplomatic opposition without a free war goal, instant reconquest or mass population transfer. Independent conditional post-partition entry: a government need not have obtained a pre-war community mandate to address an actual post-war administration.
Voluntary return, restitution and compensation options need claimant safeguards and counterpart implementation. They do not absolve perpetrators or erase missing-persons cases.
Aid and family contacts can improve before a final sovereignty settlement. Property claims remain open.
Protect legal claims without manufacturing a victory. This course retains the economic and humanitarian burdens of partition.
Resolve only the obligations actually implemented. Recognition,1983 independence declaration and voluntary reunification remain separate outcomes.

The National Front and other armed opponents challenge the presidency. Mainland officers, the National Guard and the police answer to competing loyalties. The underground and communal distrust are separate political problems.
The 8 March 1970 attempt on Makarios is a conditional historical event; contemporary reports did not establish every perpetrator. No EOKA B label before 1971, no automatic foreign-policy conversion.
Begin replacing divided command with accountable institutions. Request withdrawal/reassignment of outside officers through an actual Greek response; training expertise is not silently replaced.
Keep expertise and political dependence. Existing retained-officer organisation rewards are not granted a second time.
Professionalise police and guard command without suppressing an ethnic population. Reduce underground influence only if disarmament/command outcomes are implemented.
Not every Greek government or officer supports a coup.
Makarios'2 July 1974 letter demanding removal of mainland officers is a historical milestone if the unresolved command dispute still exists; an earlier settlement can avert that confrontation.
Greece can accept, negotiate or refuse. Removing officers by decree does not itself remove a clandestine armed network; provide a command transition.
For a Makarios player this is an opposition/foreign-sponsored threat handled by events. A hardline political route or an explicitly authorised sponsored plot may advance it.
Conditional removal of the armed-underground pressure spirit after sustained lawful disarmament.

A military coup attempt challenges the government. Its sponsors, resistance and outcome determine who governs; an attempted coup does not guarantee either a successful overthrow or a foreign intervention. This milestone is recorded when the corresponding event actually occurs.

Greece, Turkey and Britain can respond to the actual crisis through diplomacy, demands, restraint or actions of their own. One substantive response records that the guarantors have begun to act; the remaining channels remain open. This milestone is recorded when the corresponding event actually occurs.

Historic Turkish approaches to Britain are represented as genuine proposals. Joint action is not assured; a refusal does not mean Britain has accepted unilateral territorial partition. The crisis dossier provides the immediate response; this focus records the completed action.

A confrontational government can reject terms. Turkey still chooses mediation, an ultimatum, limited intervention or a broader operation; no compulsory war. The crisis dossier provides the immediate response; this focus records the completed action.

A coup regime can step down, or resistance can restore constitutional authority. This removes the coup pretext only after real restoration; civilian harms and other disputes remain. This milestone is recorded when the corresponding event actually occurs.

Temporary defensive preparation, not the right to dictate another player's military action. Fast actor-response milestone: events or short decisions resolve this choice independently of the displayed focus duration. The crisis dossier provides the immediate response; this focus records the completed action.

Do not invoke the generic MD territorial ceasefire or 720-day white-peace path blindly. Fast actor-response milestone: events or short decisions resolve this choice independently of the displayed focus duration. The crisis dossier provides the immediate response; this focus records the completed action.

Separate 30 July first-Geneva arrangements from the 8–14 August second conference. Require real negotiations and accept/refuse choices; the first ceasefire is not final ownership or 1983 independence. The crisis dossier provides the immediate response; this focus records the completed action.

A party can reject the proposed settlement, but the second Turkish offensive remains a Turkish decision. Disputes over constitutional models, troop positions and security can sustain a crisis. The crisis dossier provides the immediate response; this focus records the completed action.

Historical second offensive 14–16 August 1974 is distinct from the 20 July landing. No automatic second war after a durable accepted agreement. This milestone is recorded when the corresponding event actually occurs.

Both communities and applicable external parties decide. Any agreed demarcation and withdrawal follows actual terms; no unconsented annexation or property extinguishment. This milestone is recorded when the corresponding event actually occurs.

War outcomes, occupation, atrocities, missing persons and displacement are tracked separately from victory. Capturing a state never grants a productivity, manpower or tax bonus for expelling civilians. This milestone is recorded when the corresponding event actually occurs.
Domestic procurement proceeds immediately; Greek mission benefits require Greek acceptance. No duplicated conditional benefits.
Military posture is independent of civilian-protection policy. Either initial response can lead to a ceasefire or continued defence.
January 1970. The republic is twenty, its leader seventy-six. The Wall stands, the winter has emptied the shelves, and in Bonn Willy Brandt speaks of 'two states in Germany'.
Article 1 of the constitution: the leadership of the working class and its Marxist-Leninist party. The republic stays what it is.
Five parties, four mass organisations, one list: the bloc parties remain allies, not rivals.
Ulbricht's formula: class antagonisms are overcome, the people are one community under the party.
A state that belongs to those who work: the hub from which power can pass to another Emerging current.
After the interregnum the party reclaims what the constitution gave it.
Prague 1968 was crushed - Berlin could finish what Prague began. Moscow will not like it.
The veterans of Spain and the camps take back the party from the managers and the consumers.
When the party falters, the Ministry that knows everything takes over.
The 1968 constitution: the GDR is the socialist state of the German nation. While an Emerging party governs, its programme stands.
The ABI controls the managers: hundreds of thousands of volunteer inspectors against waste and privilege.
Brigades of socialist labour compete for banners and bonuses.
The republic as the western outpost of the socialist world - and its showcase.
Egon Bahr's formula of 1963, answered from the East: if Bonn moves towards us, we can move towards Bonn.
CDU and LDPD rediscover that they were founded in 1945 as independent parties.
No more raids on roof antennas: the evening news from Hamburg is no longer a crime.
Parties, church and the new circles sit at one table with the government - the hub of a democratic opening.
The man who sells the republic's goods to the West now sells its loyalty.
Götting's Union leaves the National Front and claims the Christian heritage of Germany.
Gerlach breaks the bloc discipline twenty years early.
Thirty years after the forced merger, the SPD stands up again in the land of its birth.
The name of the state finally means what it says.
Secret ballot, open lists, no single list of the National Front.
Erhard's recipe for the East: prices, private firms, the Mark - and a social net.

Alt-history: the Kombinat directors and the planners argue for the slow road - prices freed one sector at a time, the plan kept as a frame, Hungary's New Economic Mechanism rather than Erhard's currency reform.
The border opens. The Antifascist Protection Rampart becomes a monument.
The republic is a member of the Warsaw Pact and bound to Moscow by treaty. Before it can go West, someone has to fly to Moscow and ask.
Out of the Warsaw Pact, into the Western camp - if the West will have us.
Neither Moscow's satellite nor Bonn's province: the idea of 1952 and 1956 returns.
Tito showed that a socialist state can stand between the blocs - and that workers' councils can run the factories.
Peace circles and environmental groups meet under church roofs.
Planners, directors and craftsmen agree on one thing: the numbers must be true.
A movement between the blocs - the hub of the Non-Aligned hand-overs.
Schürer's planners govern without the Politburo's slogans.
The church, the only free space in the republic, becomes the mediator of the state.
The general directors stop asking the ministries for permission.
The private craftsmen and family firms return from the nationalisation of 1972.
Bitterfeld's smog has become political.
Goldenbaum's farmers' party leaves the bloc and speaks for the villages.
Harich's platform of 1956: a neutral, democratic, socialist Germany.
The republic between the blocs: its own way, its own rules.
Neutral like Austria, armed like Switzerland.
Hungary tried to leave in 1956 and Soviet tanks answered. The republic asks politely - and offers neutrality instead of the West.
Belgrade, Cairo, New Delhi - and East Berlin.
Prussia, Luther, Frederick - the republic has already rehabilitated half of German history. Why not all of it?
The statue of Frederick the Great returns to Unter den Linden.
1813, Scharnhorst and Gneisenau: the national tradition the NVA already wears on its uniforms.
The nation is older than the class - the hub of the Nationalist hand-overs.
Bolz's National Democrats leave the bloc and preach the nation.
A national-revolutionary underground seizes a collapsing state.
The generals of the NVA decide that the party has failed.
The House of Hohenzollern is invited back to Potsdam.
Not a socialist state of the German nation - the German state.
Order, duty, punctuality - and fewer meetings.
Neither Moscow's oil nor Bonn's credits: self-reliance.

Alt-history: in 1922 at Rapallo the defeated Reich and Soviet Russia broke their isolation together. A national Germany need not be anti-Soviet - Moscow's oil and orders for a German state that keeps its own flag and its own army.
Two states, one nation - and the nation will decide.

Since 1966 Alexander Schalck-Golodkowski's Commercial Coordination has earned the hard currency the plan cannot. Now the MfS officer who keeps the republic's foreign-exchange books runs the republic itself - and every decision is weighed in D-Mark.

In 1970 the republic owes Western banks some two billion Valuta marks, and every machine bought in the West raises the bill. Schalck's line replaces the planners' slogans: every Kombinat earns hard currency first - and the firm takes its cut.
The richest customer lives next door. Inner-German trade knows no customs border, and every West German order is paid in D-Mark - in goods, transit fees and, sooner or later, political goodwill.

Machine tools for India, trucks for Iraq, optics for France, cranes for the Soviet Union: a customer in every market, so that no single customer - least of all Bonn - holds the republic's purse strings.
In 1983 Franz Josef Strauss, the republic's loudest enemy in Bonn, brokered a billion-mark credit with Schalck as his partner. Here the deal is struck a decade earlier (alt-hist).

IMES, Commercial Coordination's arms-trading house (historically founded 1981), sells rifles, ammunition and trucks from a depot at Kavelstorf near Rostock - in the 1980s to both sides of the Iran-Iraq War.

Profit centres instead of ministries, a balance sheet instead of a Five-Year Plan and an MfS officer as managing director: the workers' state becomes a company - with no shareholders' meeting and no elections.

The Intershops sell Jacobs coffee, jeans and Western cigarettes for D-Mark; through Genex, relatives in the West buy Trabants and even prefabricated houses for their families in the East. Whoever holds Western money lives better.
From 1974 every citizen may hold D-Mark and spend it in the Intershop: the republic collects the money Western relatives send. Whoever has an aunt in Hamburg now lives better than a factory director.
Since 1962 the Exquisit boutiques and since 1966 the Delikat shops sell Western-style goods for Marks of the GDR at steep prices. They soak up savings without handing a single citizen a D-Mark.

Since 1963 Bonn has bought political prisoners out of East German jails - in the end some 34,000 people, paid for in oil, copper and coffee delivered through the churches. The republic exports its dissidents and imports hard currency.

From 1973 the state art-trading firm (Kunst & Antiquitäten GmbH) empties attics, manor houses and church lofts for Western dealers; collectors who refuse to sell are assessed for back taxes until they give in.

The managers of Commercial Coordination remain 'officers on special duty' of the MfS, reporting to Erich Mielke. The firm and the Ministry are one - its trading houses in the West double as listening posts.
Schalck cuts the line to Normannenstraße: the firm answers to no ministry, only to its balance sheet. The directors cheer; Mielke keeps the files and waits.

Founded in June 1945 by Andreas Hermes and Jakob Kaiser, purged by the Soviet administration in 1947 and tamed under Otto Nuschke and Gerald Götting, the East CDU rediscovers the Christian democracy it was founded for.
No more single lists: the Union leaves the National Front and stands on its own programme for the first time since 1950.
No more pressure to choose the Jugendweihe over confirmation, no more careers lost to faith: the churches may teach, publish and build again.

The 'Socialist Spring in the Countryside' of 1960 forced the last free farmers into the LPG, and thousands fled west. The Union's economics are Catholic social teaching and Protestant thrift: the family, the workshop and the farm come first.
In September 1989 four East CDU members wrote to their own leadership demanding honesty and reform. Here the letter is written twenty years earlier - and the leadership answers it.

The Federation of Evangelical Churches (1969) is invited into the government's councils, and the state asks forgiveness for the persecution of the Junge Gemeinde in 1953 and the demolition of Leipzig's University Church in 1968.

Since 1964 conscientious objectors may serve unarmed as 'construction soldiers' - and are barred from university for it. The Union offers a real civilian service in hospitals and care homes, as Dresden's church groups proposed.
86 % of the republic's women work, and the state raises the children in crèches. The Union pays mothers and fathers who want to stay at home - more children, fewer hands in the factories.
Every LPG member may leave with his fields, his cattle and his share of the machines. The old farming families return to their yards - and the cooperatives lose their best land.
The LPG stays, but membership becomes voluntary and the members elect their own chairmen. The cooperative farmers keep their security; the countryside changes slowly.

'Property entails obligations', says the Basic Law: private initiative under a Christian social order. Prices are freed step by step, the family firms get credit, and the Kombinate must compete for the first time.
A people's party open to Protestants and Catholics, farmers and engineers: the Union stops being a bloc party and becomes a party of government that must answer the German question.

The sister party leads the opposition in Bonn and will govern again. Christian Democrats on both sides of the border prepare one party, one programme and one Germany - and the West German Union pays for the campaign.
Two German states, both Christian-democratic, both with the West: the republic keeps its own flag and its own seat, as Austria shows a German-speaking state can.

Article 23 of the Basic Law lets 'other parts of Germany' join the Federal Republic. Mecklenburg, Brandenburg, Saxony-Anhalt, Saxony and Thuringia - abolished as states in 1952 - apply to join; the decision lies in Bonn.

Twenty Soviet divisions stand between the Elbe and the Oder. A Christian republic that looks west cannot host them for ever: the government asks Moscow, politely and publicly, to bring its soldiers home.
The party of Wilhelm Külz - of craftsmen, doctors and shopkeepers - called its newspaper The Morning. Manfred Gerlach now promises the republic its liberal morning.
Independent judges, public trials and defence lawyers who actually defend: the state is bound by its own laws - the Ministry for State Security included.

Gerlach's economists rewrite the economic line: prices that carry information, firms that may fail, and a social safety net beneath both. Two blueprints compete for the way there - Erhard's of 1948 and Budapest's of 1968.
The press office of the Council of Ministers stops issuing instructions. Neues Deutschland gets competitors, and the journalists start with the privileges of the functionaries.
The republic never had one: the Volkskammer judged its own laws. Modelled on Karlsruhe, a constitutional court in Leipzig - the old seat of the Reich Court - now guards the citizens' rights.
In 1950 the Waldheim trials sentenced some 3,400 people in minutes each; thousands more were broken in Bautzen and Hohenschönhausen. The new courts reopen the files and rehabilitate the victims.
On 20 June 1948 Ludwig Erhard freed West German prices overnight. The LDPD does the same: the subsidies go, the shelves fill - and the factories that cannot compete close their gates.
Since 1968 Kádár's Hungary has used prices, profits and private plots without leaving the Warsaw Pact. Slower than Erhard - but Moscow can live with it.

In 1972 the SED nationalised some 11,000 semi-state firms, private factories and craft cooperatives within months. The LDPD returns them to their owners - or, if it has not happened yet, stops the nationalisation for good.
The Mark of the GDR trades at one to four on the black market and buys nothing abroad. Gerlach makes it convertible: Western goods and investors arrive - and so does the truth about its value.
The republic has not known open unemployment since the early 1950s; the market reform brings it back. Labour offices, retraining and unemployment pay cushion the blow - at a price.
Every citizen receives a passport valid for all countries. The death strip is cleared and the order to shoot revoked - the Antifascist Protection Rampart has no purpose left.
Courts, press and property are free. Now the liberals must answer the question every German liberal has asked since 1848: unity and freedom - in which order?
Two states, one market, one currency union and a joint council of ministers: unity in steps, with the republic's own institutions intact.
No half measures: the republic applies to join the Federal Republic, its Basic Law and its Mark. The liberals of 1848 would approve; the Kombinat directors and Moscow do not.

On 21 April 1946 the eastern SPD was merged into the SED with a handshake in the Admiralspalast. Friedrich Ebert, son of the first president of the Weimar Republic and a party to that merger himself, now leads the social democrats back out of it (alt-hist).

The Free German Trade Union Federation is free in name only: it hands out holidays and production pledges, not strikes. 17 June 1953 began as a workers' protest against higher norms - the social democrats have not forgotten.

In Bonn Willy Brandt's social-liberal coalition practises 'change through rapprochement'. In East Berlin a social-democratic government finally answers in the same language - and inner-German trade grows.

Social democracy promised more than full employment and cheap bread: decent pensions, shorter hours and a voice for the workers in their own factories. Ebert's economists write it into the economic line.
Free elections for every union post and the right to bargain over wages and norms: the old federation is turned from a transmission belt into a real union.
Let the workers found their own unions, as the shipyard workers of Gdańsk will in 1980. The FDGB loses its monopoly - and its functionaries their power.

Pensions barely cover rent and bread, and pensioners are the only citizens allowed to visit the West - the state does not mind if they stay there. The social democrats raise pensions to a living wage - on credit.
Helmut Schmidt's rule - 'today's profits are tomorrow's investments and the day after tomorrow's jobs' - comes to East Berlin: first the roads, the plants and the export earnings, then the pensions.
Since 1967 the five-day week has had 43 and three-quarter hours. The social democrats bring in the forty-hour week - more life, less output.

The West German coal and steel law of 1951 gave the workers half the seats on the supervisory boards. In the people's own enterprises the works councils now sit beside the director - and share the responsibility for the plan.

Brandt's 'policy of small steps' began with passes for West Berliners at Christmas 1963. The social democrats finish the walk: citizens travel west without permission, and the Rampart's guns are withdrawn.
On 19 March 1970 Erfurt cheered 'Willy, Willy' under the windows of the Erfurter Hof - the wrong Willy, as far as the SED was concerned. Ebert invites Brandt back, this time as a partner.
In 1959 the western SPD renounced Marxism at Bad Godesberg and became a people's party. The eastern party must decide what it is for: a better GDR, or one Germany.
Keep the people's own enterprises, the crèches and the polyclinics, add free elections and free unions: the republic becomes the social-democratic state the Weimar left never built.

Kurt Schumacher's dream of 1946: a united Germany under social democracy. Ebert's party campaigns for unity with Brandt's Federal Republic - the strongest argument against it is quartered in Wünsdorf.
A social-democratic GDR wants friendship with Moscow, not occupation. Ebert proposes a staged withdrawal of the Soviet divisions, guaranteed by a treaty of friendship.
Two parliaments, one treaty: the social democrats in East Berlin and Bonn negotiate a union of equals under a new all-German constitution (Article 146 of the Basic Law) - not an accession.
Robert Havemann - antifascist, chemist, expelled from the party in 1964 for his lectures 'Dialectics without Dogma' - leads Prague's spring in Berlin, two years late.
The Press Office closes; every newspaper, Neues Deutschland included, prints what its editors decide.
Banned from every stage since 1965, Wolf Biermann plays the Friedrichstadt-Palast - live on television.
Forty-three thousand officers go home, the files are opened, the informers lose their power.
The Ministry stays, but a Volkskammer committee reads its files, and decomposition is forbidden by law.
Bautzen and Hohenschönhausen open their gates: dissidents and those jailed for trying to flee the republic walk free.
Like Prague's Action Programme of April 1968: freedom of assembly, rehabilitations, economic reform - adopted by the Central Committee in one night.
Kádár's lesson from Budapest: reform at home, loyalty abroad, and never a word about leaving the Warsaw Pact.
Dubček's road to its end: several parties, free unions, a free press - and the risk of Soviet tanks on Unter den Linden.
A pledge to Brezhnev: the republic stays in the Pact and in Comecon, and Moscow tolerates what happens inside it.
For the first time since 1946 the people choose between parties, not between yes and no to a single list.
The factory combat groups swear to defend the reforms, and Belgrade and Bucharest - who condemned the invasion of 1968 - are asked to stand by Berlin.
The FDGB elects its own leaders and may strike - free unions in the East, ten years before Gdańsk.

Prague's Ota Šik and Budapest's reformers agree on one thing: the enterprise, not the ministry, must decide. The League writes self-management into the economic line - prices that tell the truth, profit as the measure.
Every enterprise elects a workers' council that hires the director and divides the profit - Havemann's 'socialism with freedom' in the factory.
Hungarian style: more consumer goods, private plots and small shops, a refrigerator in every flat - and nobody asks about politics.
Ten years after the Berlin Spring the enterprises belong to those who work in them, and the plan is a contract between free producers - the socialism Havemann lectured about in 1963.
Alfred Neumann fought in the International Brigades. With the old KPD men and the Spain veterans he takes the state back from the managers and the consumers.
Every party member who praised Prague, the market or Western television is called before the control commission.
Back to the fold: every instruction from the Soviet embassy is obeyed, every Soviet adviser welcome - and Soviet oil flows at friendship prices. Moscow likes what it sees.
Bucharest and Tirana show the way: a hard line needs no master - and Brezhnev's détente is revisionism too.
A Soviet adviser in every ministry and every Kombinat, as in 1950 - the Guard asks for them.
No Western machines and no Soviet favours: the republic builds its own plants with its own hands, whatever the shops lack.
Not one Deutschmark of debt: what the republic cannot pay for, it does without. The Guard's economic line is the one of 1950 - heavy industry, sacrifice and no masters.
The private bakers, tailors and carpenters who survived 1972 join the cooperatives - or close their doors. Their workshops and their savings go to the state.
Steel from Eisenhüttenstadt, machines from Magdeburg: the 'first socialist city' sets the pace again, as in 1952 - and the consumers wait, as in 1952.
Closed, armed and pure: the republic as the fortress of the working class on the front line of the Cold War.
Statues, films and pioneer oaths: the KPD leader murdered in Buchenwald in 1944 becomes the patron saint of the republic.
Combat groups in every factory, pre-military training in every school, the reserves called up every year.
Voluntary Saturday shifts, the National Reconstruction Programme, brigades of socialist labour - sweat instead of credits.
Erich Mielke, Minister for State Security since 1957, no longer protects the party - he replaces it. Forty-three thousand officers are now the government.

No arrests, no martyrs: careers broken, marriages poisoned, rumours planted - the quiet method of Directive 1/76, years early - carried out by unofficial collaborators in every brigade, every house community and every parish council.

The method of the 1970s: sign Helsinki, smile at the West - and decompose the enemies of the state in silence. The Ministry's own law college at Potsdam-Eiche trains its officers in 'operative psychology'.
The method of 1950: show trials, death sentences, mass arrests. Fear works faster than decomposition - and the whole world watches.
Former Politburo members confess on television to spying for Bonn. Nobody believes it, and everybody understands it.
A file on every citizen, a microphone in every office, a smell sample in every jar: the state knows everything about everyone.
The Ministry's own army, quartered in Berlin-Adlershof, guards the government quarter - and now the Minister's state.
The SED keeps its congresses, its banners and its First Secretary - all of them reporting to the Ministry.
Two million party members are no longer needed: the apparatus is dissolved and its files move to the Ministry's archive.
Markus Wolf's foreign intelligence - the 'man without a face' - runs agents in Bonn, at NATO and in every West German party.
The foreign intelligence's science sector steals what the COCOM lists will not sell: computer circuits, machine tools, chemical formulas.
Günter Guillaume, an officer of Main Directorate A, works in the Chancellor's office in Bonn. Every paper on Ostpolitik crosses Mielke's desk.

The Ministry already owns firms, guest houses and Schalck's trading empire; its prisons make furniture, tights and camera parts for Western mail-order houses. Mielke makes it the economic line: every enterprise has an officer, every officer a quota.
Bonn pays forty thousand marks a head for political prisoners, IKEA and Quelle buy what Bautzen and Hoheneck produce. The Ministry sells its prisoners twice - their labour and their freedom.
No deals with the class enemy: every prisoner stays, every enterprise gets an MfS liaison officer, and every delivery gap is investigated as sabotage.
The Ministry for State Security becomes the republic's largest enterprise: construction firms, workshops, trading houses and a headquarters in Normannenstraße that grows by a block every year.
Gerhard Schürer, chairman of the State Planning Commission since 1965, takes the government: the plan, not the Politburo's slogans, now decides.

In October 1989 Schürer told the Politburo that the republic lived on Western credit and could not pay. Here the report is written in 1970 - and published, and the economic line is rewritten to fit the numbers.
Comecon's Unified System of Electronic Computers: Robotron in Dresden builds the EC 1040, and the planners finally get machines to count with.
Every Kombinat gets a hard-currency export target. What the West will buy is no longer sold in the shops at home.
Engineers, economists and Kombinat directors replace the party secretaries in the Council of Ministers. The Central Committee's economic departments lose their right to give orders.
Schürer governs with the party, not against it: the SED keeps its seats and its cadre lists, and the planners get the apparatus's loyalty in return - and its habits.
Live within our means: fewer Western imports, no more prestige projects, every surplus Deutschmark goes to pay back the debt.
Borrow now, grow later: Western credits buy the machines, and the machines will earn the hard currency to repay them.
Rents frozen at the level of 1936, bread rolls at five pfennigs: the price subsidies swallow billions every year. Schürer cuts them.
Frankfurt, Vienna and Tokyo lend to the most reliable debtor in the East. The new plants open on time - the interest falls due on time too.
Every district gets a computing centre; the plan figures of thousands of enterprises travel to Berlin on punched cards.
Linear programming on the EC 1040: Kantorovich's mathematics balances what no ministry ever could - and the apparatus's instinct is no longer needed.
The Comprehensive Programme of 1971: the republic builds the machine tools, ships and computers of the socialist camp and is paid in roubles.
Machine tools from Karl-Marx-Stadt, optics from Jena, potash from the Werra - sold for Deutschmarks and dollars, not transferable roubles.
For the first time the plan balances imports and exports in both currencies - roubles and Deutschmarks - and nobody hides the gap.
True numbers, computed plans, no more 'plan fulfilled 101 %': the planners' republic has a budget it can show to anyone.
Bishop Albrecht Schönherr, Bonhoeffer's student, leads a government of the church: not against socialism, not beside it, but within it.
The church runs dozens of hospitals and hundreds of homes for the old and the disabled - the care the state forgot. Now the care becomes the economic line: people before plan figures.
The church's research home in Luther's town publishes what the state statistics hide: the air, the water, the forests. Environmental circles meet in the parish halls.
Since June 1969 the eight regional churches of the GDR stand together in their own federation, separate from the West German EKD.
Action Reconciliation sends young East Germans to work at Auschwitz and in Polish hospitals. The government takes up the work of atonement.
The state hands its polyclinics and care homes to the Inner Mission and the Caritas, and pays for them: nurses, deaconesses and doctors who stay instead of leaving for the West.
The badge shows the Soviet statue in front of the UN - a man forging a sword into a ploughshare. Here it is state policy: arms plants make tractors.

The Conciliar Process of the churches - historically the ecumenical assemblies of Dresden and Magdeburg in 1988-89 - becomes the programme of government: justice for the weak, peace without weapons and an economy that spares creation.
A republic that refuses the logic of deterrence: fewer soldiers, no nuclear weapons on its soil, neutrality as a Christian duty.
The Ten Commandments replace Ulbricht's Ten Commandments of Socialist Morality: confirmation instead of the state youth ceremony, and an open hand to the Christian Democrats in the West.
The churches may run schools again, and Christian pupils may study at university without a party card.
Twenty Soviet divisions stand between the Elbe and the Oder. The Peace Republic asks the Kremlin, politely and in public, to take them home.
The churches of East and West were one until 1969. Now the Christian Republic asks Bonn to fund the church's work openly - and to talk to its government.
Since 1964 young men who refuse the weapon serve with a spade - the only unarmed service in the Warsaw Pact. The church's government honours them.
The Dresden proposal, made law: conscientious objectors serve in hospitals, homes and on the land instead of the army.
Eighteen months of compulsory service end: the NVA becomes an army of volunteers, and the factories get their young men back.
The general directors of the Kombinate - Wolfgang Biermann of Carl Zeiss Jena at their head - stop asking the ministries and start running the state.
A hundred general directors form the real cabinet; the ministers become their clerks.
Seats on the Kombinat boards for district secretaries, hunting lodges and Volvos for the Politburo: the party is bought, not fought.
The industrial departments of the Central Committee and half the ministries are dissolved; the directors answer to their balance sheets alone.
The Kombinate keep what they earn and invest it themselves - Ulbricht's reform of the 1960s, taken to its end and written into the economic line.
The Kombinate become state holding companies: the directors own the management and a share of the profits, the state owns the shares - for now.
Krupp, Siemens and Volkswagen in Zwickau and Jena: half the shares, half the profits - and all the know-how the embargo lists forbid.
Twenty giant concerns swallow the rest of industry - and the last private and semi-state suppliers with it.
Swedish furniture, West German shoes and mail-order catalogue goods are made in Kombinat workshops for Western brands - the best goods leave the country.
The red barons own the republic in all but name: efficient, rich - and every director has his dacha, his car and his hard-currency account.
The directors build new export halls with their own money and keep a share of the hard currency they earn - the workers get the overtime.
Biermann's own house: cameras, microscopes, planetaria and space cameras for Soviet spacecraft - the flagship sells to the whole world and builds the republic's first chip lines.
No single leader: master craftsmen, shopkeepers and the owners of the semi-state firms govern as a council - an alt-hist union of the middle class.
In spring 1972 the SED took the last 11,000 private and semi-state firms - the makers of furniture, toys, textiles and spare parts. The council gives them back.
The firms go back to the families that founded them - some heirs live in Stuttgart and Munich and come back with Western money.
The firms become workers' companies: every employee holds a share, the master craftsman keeps the management.
The Office for Prices stops fixing what a chair, a cake or a car repair may cost: the market sets the price, and the council writes free enterprise into the economic line.
Open the market: private firms may import, export and compete with the Kombinate - and with the West.
The old craft order returns: guilds set standards, train apprentices and protect their members from the Kombinate and from foreign competition.
Since the Middle Ages Leipzig has been the fair between East and West. Now its halls stay open all year, and private firms sign their own contracts.
The master's certificate, the journeyman's years, the chamber's seal: a craft education again worth its name.
Half the republic's workers are employed by firms of fewer than five hundred people - the most Western economy east of the Elbe.
The craftsmen's cooperatives, forced on the trades since 1958, become voluntary: whoever wants to work alone may.
The private baker, butcher and repair shop return to every street - the end of the queue and of goods sold under the counter.
Reimar Gilsenbach and the nature circles of the Kulturbund govern the smog republic - an alt-hist green government long before any in the West.
The Council of Ministers wanted to make every figure on air and water a state secret. The Green League prints them in every newspaper.

In the cellar of the Zion Church, historically from 1986, independent groups print what nobody else may - the government lets them grow into the movement that carries it. Western television reports every word.

The Kulturbund's own Society for Nature and Environment (historically founded 1980) organises the clean-up Saturdays: orderly, under party guidance - and without the angry young people from the church cellars.
Leuna and Buna drain into the Saale, the pulp mills into the Elbe; the fish are dying as far as Hamburg. Sewage plants for the chemical belt.

Two hundred and fifty million tonnes of lignite a year, villages swallowed by the pits, sulphur over every town: the League counts what King Lignite really costs and rewrites the economic line - less power, more life.
Soviet pressurised-water reactors replace the dirtiest pits: clean air - and a new dependence on Moscow's fuel.
No new pits and no reactors: save energy, burn less, build wind and water power - and accept colder winters and slower factories.
The Bruno Leuschner plant at Lubmin grows block by block, Stendal is begun early: half the republic's electricity without smoke.
Insulated prefabricated blocks, district heat from the power stations, wind turbines on Rügen and a Trabant that burns less.
The last open-cast mines close, the briquette factories fall silent, and Leipzig sees a blue sky in winter.
Sulphur from the power stations of Saxony and Bohemia kills the spruce of the Erzgebirge. The League replants and asks Prague for filters.
Bitterfeld, Wolfen and the poisoned Silver Lake: the chemical triangle gets filters, treatment plants and a budget.
Every tonne of sulphur and every litre of phenol in the river now costs the polluting Kombinat a fine.
The clean-up comes out of the state budget: no fines, no quarrel with the Kombinate - just less money for everything else.
Ernst Goldenbaum has led the Farmers' Party since 1948. Freed from the bloc, it speaks for the villages that feed the republic.
The cooperative members elect their chairmen again - not the district party secretary - and the farmers' party writes the village into the economic line.
The LPG stays - but as a true cooperative: the members own it, elect it and share its profit.
The land reform of 1945 gave the land to the farmers, collectivisation took it back. Whoever wants may leave the LPG with his fields.
Bread, milk and meat from the republic's own fields: the farmers' state feeds itself and no longer depends on grain ships.
The planners want to split every village into a crop cooperative and a livestock cooperative. The farmers' government stops it: fields and stables stay together.
Every tonne of grain bought from Canada or the Soviet Union costs hard currency or loyalty. New fields, new silos, new seed.
Pork and beef go to West Berlin and the Soviet Union for hard currency; at home the queues at the butcher grow.
Every pig stays in the republic: sausage on every table - and no hard currency in the till.
Roads, schools, doctors and a culture house for every village: the young no longer have to leave for the cities.
The combine harvesters from Singwitz and the tractors from Schönebeck go to the cooperatives first, not to export.
A long-term contract with the prairie farmers: grain at world prices, delivered every autumn, whatever the harvest at home.
In 1956 Wolfgang Harich wrote a programme for a special German road to socialism and got ten years in prison for it. Now he governs.
Walter Janka, Gustav Just and the other comrades of Harich's circle are freed of their convictions and return to their posts.
Khrushchev's secret speech was read in Berlin in 1956 and then filed away. The Third Way finishes it: no cult, no purges, no leader for life.

Belgrade has run its factories through workers' councils since 1950 and trades with both blocs while belonging to neither. The Third Way asks Tito's men to teach - and rewrites the economic line on their model.
Power to the councils: every factory, district and university elects its council, and the councils elect the republic.
Socialism by the ballot: several socialist parties compete in free elections, and the Volkskammer becomes a real parliament.
The general director answers to the elected council of his workers - Belgrade's model in Leuna and Eisenhüttenstadt.
Every party, union and university may publish its own paper. Socialism has to win the argument now.
Neither Stalin's state nor Bonn's market: a democratic, neutral socialism that trades with everyone and that the rest of Europe watches with astonishment.
Harich's plan of 1956 was a reunification negotiated with the SPD. The Third Way government sends its envoys to Bonn.
Austria bought its freedom in 1955 with neutrality. Both German states leave their blocs, and the foreign armies go home.
Two states, one confederation: a joint council, free movement and a common market - each keeps its own social order.
A socialism that must wall in its people has already lost. The Third Way opens the crossings and bets that people will stay.

Founded in 1948 with the SED's blessing to give former Wehrmacht officers, nominal Nazi party members and the national middle class a political home, Lothar Bolz's NDPD was meant to keep nationalism on a leash. Now it holds the leash.

The NDPD always spoke for the shopkeepers, master craftsmen and small manufacturers. Its economics are simple - German work for German welfare, bought at home where possible - but who pays for the welfare?
Potsdam and Dresden, Frederick the Great and Augustus the Strong: the two great traditions of the republic's lands are restored to honour - palaces, regiments and all.

In the Görlitz Agreement of 6 July 1950 the GDR recognised the Oder-Neisse line as the 'border of peace and friendship'. The Silesians and East Prussians in the NDPD never quite accepted it - the party must now say what it thinks.
Frederick William I, the 'soldier king', left a full treasury and no debts. The NDPD cuts subsidies and administration alike - honest budgets, thinner pay packets.
Cheap bread, cheap rents and a national bonus for every family with three children: the NDPD buys the loyalty of the nation - and the bill comes later.
NDPD members own the bakeries, butcher shops and small factories the state has been squeezing. Their firms get tax relief, credit and the right to hire.

'Deutsche Wertarbeit' was the boast of Saxony's toolmakers and Thuringia's glassblowers long before the Kombinate. The national government stakes the economy on it: fewer, better products, made at home and sold on quality.
Dresden's opera house has stood in ruins since the firestorm of February 1945; historically it was rebuilt from 1977 to 1985. Here it is the first act of a national government - an expensive one.
Every young German serves the nation for a year - in the NVA, in the hospitals or on the building sites. Prussia's 'school of the nation' reopens, without the drill sergeant's cane.
The nation is whole within its borders: the NDPD confirms Görlitz without reservation. Warsaw is relieved, Moscow satisfied, and the expellee associations in the West call it treason.
Bonn has kept the border question open 'pending a peace treaty' - why should East Berlin not? No claim is made and no soldier moves, but the words alone chill Warsaw and alarm Moscow.
Ulbricht's constitution of 1968 called the GDR 'a socialist state of the German nation'. The NDPD drops the adjective and keeps the noun: two states, one nation, one future.
A common citizenship, a joint national assembly and an open inner-German border, each state keeping its own army: the NDPD asks Bonn whether national democrats can be partners.
A council of officers, functionaries and agitators without names seizes the collapsing state. It promises order and national rebirth; it delivers decrees, curfews and fear (alt-hist).
Lists are drawn up in every ministry, Kombinat and barracks. Whoever served the old order must prove his loyalty to the new one - or disappear.

No Western credit, no Comecon delegation, no foreign journalist: the council closes the country more tightly than the Wall ever did. Whatever the republic needs, it must now make itself - the shelves empty first.

The SED's two million members are ordered to hand in their cards; district secretaries are arrested at their desks. The apparatus that ran the republic for twenty years is gone - and with it the people who knew how.

The council fears Mielke's 43,000 officers more than any party. The Ministry for State Security is stormed, its officers interned - and its files and its Guards Regiment handed to the council's own secret police.

Ration cards return for the first time since 1958. Lignite, potatoes and labour brigades are to replace what Comecon and the West no longer deliver; Schwarzheide and Leuna turn brown coal into petrol.
A militia company in every factory, a shooting range in every school, a minefield on every border: the council arms seventeen million people against enemies on all sides - most of them imagined.
Five years behind closed borders: every factory works to a war plan, every field to a ration, and the republic needs nothing from anyone - except the things it can no longer have.

Colonel General Heinz Keßler, Chief of the NVA's Main Staff - a Wehrmacht soldier who crossed over to the Red Army in 1941 - heads a council of generals in Strausberg. The party has failed; the army takes over, 'temporarily'.
Curfews, military tribunals and soldiers at the gates of the Kombinate. The streets are quiet; the queues outside the shops are not.

Explosives from Schönebeck, rifles from Suhl, W50 trucks from Ludwigsfelde, landing ships from Wolgast: the generals take personal charge of the factories that equip them - and write the plan as a staff order.
The Warsaw Pact plans to carry any war to the Rhine within days, with the NVA in its first strategic echelon. The council must decide whether the army exists for the alliance or for the homeland.

The Combat Groups of the Working Class - several hundred thousand men in factory overalls - answer to the SED district leaderships and the Interior Ministry. The council puts them under NVA command as a territorial army.
Colonels replace the state secretaries: the ministries are run like a staff, with orders, deadlines and reports - and no patience for the planners' excuses.
Kalashnikovs from Wiesa, trucks from Ludwigsfelde, patrol boats from Wolgast - sold to Baghdad, Tripoli and Addis Ababa for hard currency. The generals become arms dealers; their own regiments wait.
Every rifle the republic makes stays with the NVA: licence production of Soviet tanks and guns at full speed, and a modern army that the shops pay for.
'Special production' is the plan's word for weapons. The council doubles it: licence-built Kalashnikovs, ammunition and armoured personnel carriers - and fewer washing machines.
The NVA trains to reach the Rhine: two armies of six divisions, ready to cross the inner-German border on the first day. Moscow approves; the West notices.
No divisions for the Rhine: the NVA digs in between the Elbe and the Oder with reservists, fortified towns and the Combat Groups. The West relaxes a little; Moscow's planners do not.
Martial law was declared 'until order is restored', and order is restored. Now the generals must say how long 'until' lasts - and what the army's budget will be.
The council promises to step down within three years and hand the state to an elected civilian government - as Portugal's captains will do after 1974.
There will be no return to the party and no elections. The council becomes the state, and its chairman wears the uniform of an Army General.
Free elections under the army's guard; the winner forms a civilian government, and the generals return to Strausberg with their honour and their budget intact.
Officer schools train the administrators, a general runs every district and the GST is the only youth organisation: the republic is reorganised as one great military district.

Louis Ferdinand, Prince of Prussia - grandson of the last Kaiser, once a worker on Henry Ford's assembly line in Detroit, head of the House of Hohenzollern since 1951 - is invited from Bremen back to Potsdam (alt-hist). Sanssouci, the New Palace and Cecilienhof become the seat of the crown; the open question is what kind of crown.

Duty, thrift and incorruptibility: Frederick William I balanced his budget to the last thaler and hanged a corrupt official at the gate of Königsberg castle. The crown's economics fit on a parade ground - and pinch every household.

'Suum cuique' was the motto of the Order of the Black Eagle; Frederick's Prussia took in Huguenots, Salzburg Protestants and Bohemian weavers. The crown protects the churches, the Sorbs and every honest dissenter.
The NVA's stone-grey uniforms and parade step are already Prussian. Now its regiments take back the old names and colours, and the officers swear an oath to the crown.

The land reform of 1945 took every estate over 100 hectares from the Junkers. The crown returns the manor farms to the old families as model estates - and the cooperative farmers lose their best fields.

Frederick the Great founded the Royal Porcelain Manufactory in Berlin and filled Prussia with silk, glass and cloth works. The crown does the same with state money: new manufactories under royal warrant.
A king who reigns but does not rule: a parliament elected by all and a prime minister responsible to it - the model of London and Stockholm, not of 1914.
The king appoints the government and commands the army; parliament may advise. It is the Prussia of 1850 and its three-class franchise - with few friends abroad and many enemies at home.

The coffins of Frederick the Great and his father have rested at Hohenzollern Castle in Württemberg since 1952; historically Frederick was laid to rest at Sanssouci, as he had wished, only in 1991. The crown asks Bonn to let him come home now.

Frederick the Great founded the Seehandlung in 1772 - a royal trading house that became Prussia's state bank and financed its mills, canals and salt works. The crown revives it: a royal treasury that lends to the estates and the manufactories and runs a surplus.

Proclaimed in the Marble Hall of the New Palace, the Prussian state that the Allies abolished in 1947 returns as a kingdom on the Spree and the Havel. Whether anyone beyond its borders will recognise it is another matter.
2.2 million members, one in eight adults: the SED is the state's skeleton.
The district and county secretaries are the real government of the provinces.
The FDJ trains the next generation of cadres - blue shirts, red ideas.
CDU, LDPD, NDPD and DBD: keep them as transmission belts or give them room to breathe?
The bloc parties organise the middle class for the SED - nothing more.
Give the bloc parties real ministries and a voice in the Volkskammer.
Every cadre passes through the college in Berlin-Kleinmachnow.
Every member hands in his card and is interviewed - a quiet purge of the passive and the doubters.
Every five years the party confirms its line, its leader and its plan in the Palace of the Republic.
Two hundred members, one vote that counts: Moscow's. The Central Committee elects the First Secretary.
The crown prince since 1958, Ulbricht's own pupil - and Brezhnev's choice.
The head of government claims the party.
The secretary for the economy: the plan should rule the party, not the other way round.
The guardian of doctrine steps out of the shadow.
Army General Hoffmann: the Minister of National Defence as head of the party.
The youngest Politburo member, the party's best speaker - and the only one the young people like.
Krolikowski reports to the Soviet embassy - and the Soviet embassy remembers.
The former FDJ chief, born 1937 - the first leader who did not fight Hitler.
The district secretary of Dresden, never admitted to the Politburo, offers a careful reform.
Retired 'for reasons of age', Ulbricht has not forgiven.
Thirteen of twenty Politburo members ask Brezhnev, behind Ulbricht's back, to let the old man go.
Walter Ulbricht has led the party since 1950 and the state since 1960. At seventy-six he still writes the economic theses himself - and still believes the republic can overtake West Germany.

Erich Honecker, secretary for security and cadres since 1958, remains the party's second man. Moscow approves, the apparatus runs smoothly - and Ulbricht's pupil gains a little more of it every month, while the reform economists lose their patron.

Alt-history: Ulbricht moves the cadre department from Honecker to Paul Verner, the Berlin district chief who owes him his career. The crown prince loses his network overnight, the apparatus answers to the founder rather than to Karlshorst - and the Soviet embassy takes note.
Ulbricht's own think tank in the Politburo: Günter Mittag, the economist Wolfgang Berger and the young planners write the theses, and the apparatus is told afterwards.

Ulbricht's formula of 1967: the classes are no longer enemies; workers, farmers, the intelligentsia and even the churchgoers form one community under the party. Since the Bitterfeld conferences writers go into the factories and workers write - 'Pick up the pen, mate!'

The 1965 law on the unified socialist education system: ten years of polytechnic school for every child, one day a week in a factory. Its first full generation enters the workforce in 1970 - skilled workers, not slogans.

Summer 1973: 25,000 guests from 140 countries and eight million visitors turn East Berlin into a 'Red Woodstock'. For nine days the republic looks young, open and confident - and the solidarity with Vietnam and Chile is real.

The New Economic System of 1963 grown up (ÖSS, 1967-70): the Kombinate become accounting units, prices and profit become levers, and science is declared a direct productive force - the Academy reform of 1968 ties the institutes to the plan.

Alt-history: Ulbricht deepens the reform instead of the prestige list. Enterprises keep part of their profit and set part of their prices; the Kombinat directors become managers. Moscow and the apparatus smell market socialism.
1968-70: petrochemistry at Schwedt and Leuna II, electronics, machine tools and automation get every brick and every Mark first - the hard winter of 1969/70 empties the shops.

Georg Klaus's cybernetics and the new Robotron combine promise a plan that calculates itself. Ulbricht orders an automated control system for the whole economy by 1975 - and computing centres for the Planning Commission.
December 1970: the supply crisis is the talk of the Politburo, but Ulbricht refuses to cut the prestige projects. Growth now, the shops later.
Winter 1970/71: butter, meat and coal are bought in the West on credit to calm the shops. The reformers' numbers look worse, the queues get shorter.
The reform's end state: the Kombinate trade with each other by economic contract, not by order from above, and keep a share of what they earn for their own investment.

19 March 1970: Willy Brandt comes to Erfurt. Ulbricht sends Stoph with one demand - recognition under international law - while the crowd outside the Erfurter Hof chants 'Willy, Willy' - until the MfS fills the square with its own people.
21 May 1970: in Kassel Brandt offers twenty points for regulated coexistence. Stoph answers with one - recognition first. Ulbricht's republic negotiates as a sovereign state or not at all.
Summer 1970, before Brezhnev: 'We are not Belorussia, we are not a Soviet republic.' Ulbricht lectures the Kremlin on economics and keeps his own channel to Bonn for credits, licences and trade.
Ulbricht swallows his pride: the German policy is coordinated with Moscow line by line, the economic theses go to Gosplan before they go to the Central Committee - and the Soviet oil keeps flowing.

Alt-history: 21 January 1971 - thirteen Politburo members have asked Brezhnev, behind Ulbricht's back, to let the old man go. Ulbricht refuses. He convenes the Central Committee himself, invokes forty years at the head of the party and dares Brezhnev to depose the founder of the republic.

3 May 1971, after the letter of the thirteen: 'for reasons of age'. Ulbricht hands over the party and keeps the chair of the State Council - the founder leaves with ceremony, not in disgrace. His reformers lose their patron.
Alt-history: Professor Chazov's specialists from Moscow and the government hospital in Berlin-Buch keep the old man at his desk - at the price of half-days and a fortune in Western medicine.
Whoever follows Ulbricht inherits a republic built in his image. The old man wants to name the heir himself - before Moscow names one for him - and to hand over a party in good order.
The pupil inherits the master's chair: Moscow's favourite and the party's organiser, who promises the people more today.
The premier of Erfurt and Kassel: the state administration over the party apparatus.
Alt-history: the youngest star of the Politburo, forty-one, the only leader the young like - the old guard is appalled.
Alt-history: the architect of the reform inherits it - a technocrat at the head of the party.
Ulbricht's grand theory: socialism is no brief transition but a social formation of its own, planned by science and carried by a community - a system that needs no lessons from Moscow.
Erich Honecker: born 1912 in Wiebelskirchen, roofer, Communist youth leader, ten years in Nazi prisons, organiser of the 13th of August. Moscow's choice - and a man who wants the people content.

Günter Mittag keeps - or regains - the economic secretariat: a brilliant, feared technocrat who will make the numbers fit whatever the General Secretary promises, and who squeezes the works councils to do it.

Werner Krolikowski, the Dresden district chief, takes the economic secretariat (as from 1973 to 1976) - coordinates every plan figure with Gosplan - Soviet oil and Soviet licences are secured - and reports every number to the Soviet embassy on Unter den Linden. The general directors distrust him.

Alt-history: Gerhard Schürer, chairman of the State Planning Commission, also gets the economic secretariat - and insists that the plan show what the republic can really afford. The padding goes; so do a few promises.

June 1971, VIII Party Congress: the 'main task' is to raise the material and cultural standard of living of the people. Every gain in production is paid out at once in rents, pensions, wages, the baby year and goods - the investment race of the Ulbricht years ends, and the import bill starts to grow.
The state buys 800,000 pairs of Levi's in the West and they sell out within days. Western goods in Eastern shops calm the young - and drain the hard-currency reserves.

1972-80: the social programme is paid with Western credit - the hard-currency debt rises from 2 to 25 billion valuta marks. The shops are full, the interest bill grows, and Moscow watches the republic drift into the world market.

Alt-history: Schürer's advice is taken in 1972 - the social programme is paid by cutting industrial investment, not by borrowing. Fewer new factories, more new flats, and no debt to the bankers of Frankfurt.
October 1973: 'to solve the housing question as a social problem by 1990'. Three million flats are to be built or modernised - prefabricated estates from Marzahn to Halle-Neustadt, the WBS 70 slab.
The second oil shock and Western interest rates strike in 1979-80, but the subsidies stay: bread at 1950s prices, frozen rents, coffee bought for hard currency. The new credits pay for the old ones.
Alt-history: Honecker listens to Schürer's warning. Subsidies for luxury goods are cut, imports frozen, and the party tells the people the truth: the republic lives beyond its means.
April 1986, XI Party Congress: the housing programme is on schedule, the birth rate is up, full employment holds. Honecker declares the main task a success - and promises more of the same.

From 1971 the answer to Brandt's Ostpolitik is Abgrenzung: contacts with Westerners are reported, Western television is frowned upon, and in 1974 the constitution deletes the 'German nation' - the GDR is a socialist nation of its own, while millions still feel simply German.

13 October 1980, Gera: Honecker demands that Bonn recognise GDR citizenship and fix the Elbe border in mid-river. Days before, the minimum exchange for Western visitors was doubled to 25 DM - hard currency in, relatives out.

1983: the republic is close to insolvency. Schalck-Golodkowski and Franz Josef Strauss, the arch-anticommunist, arrange a one-billion-DM bank credit guaranteed by Bonn. The border mines begin to disappear.
September 1987: Honecker in Bonn - his flag next to the black-red-gold, the anthem, a guard of honour, then a visit to his home town in the Saarland. Recognition in all but name.

December 1988: Honecker answers perestroika with 'socialism in the colours of the GDR'. The Soviet digest Sputnik is banned, Soviet films are pulled - the pupil now lectures Moscow and prepares for a winter without Soviet help.

Alt-history: 'To learn from the Soviet Union is to learn victory' - Honecker takes the old slogan at its word, allows openness in the press, lets Sputnik be read and copies the Soviet law on state enterprises.

The General Secretary is old, ill and convinced he is indispensable. Behind him Krenz, Stoph and Mittag wait - each with his own friends in Moscow. Honecker wants his heir to keep the social programme.
The FDJ chief and security secretary, born 1937: the crown prince of the second generation.
The old premier, who has reported to Moscow behind Honecker's back for years, as a caretaker.
Alt-history: Honecker's closest ally, the economic czar, inherits the party - and its debts.

December 1971: 'If one starts from the firm position of socialism, there can be no taboos in art and literature.' Plenzdorf's 'New Sorrows of Young W.' fills the theatres, and the churches breathe a little easier.
April 1976: on the site of the Hohenzollern palace rises the Palace of the Republic - parliament, theatre, bowling alley and a thousand lamps. Berliners call it 'Erich's lamp shop'.
16 November 1976: after a concert in Cologne the singer Wolf Biermann is stripped of his citizenship. A hundred artists protest; many follow him west. The thaw is over.
Alt-history: the Politburo lets the troublesome singer come home from Cologne. The artists stay, the churches and the young are reassured, the West German press is baffled - and the Stasi fumes.

6 March 1978: Honecker receives Bishop Schönherr. The church gets broadcasting time, new church buildings and access to prisons; the state gets a church that works 'in socialism' rather than against it.
Under Honecker the Ministry for State Security doubles to 91,000 officers and some 170,000 informers. Directive 1/76 replaces open terror with quiet Zersetzung - and the bill for it grows every year.

The republic at forty: new housing estates, full employment, cheap bread, more Olympic medals than the Americans in Seoul - and a hard-currency debt the Planning Commission no longer dares to print. Honecker's socialism exists, really.
Willi Stoph: bricklayer, Wehrmacht artilleryman, first Minister of National Defence, Chairman of the Council of Ministers - the man who shook Brandt's hand in Erfurt now leads the party.
