Horst Sindermann, the Halle district chief who built Halle-Neustadt, takes over the Council of Ministers (as he did in 1973): a calm administrator with a soft spot for housing and social policy - and little patience for the Kombinat barons.
Alt-history: Gerhard Schürer leaves the Planning Commission for the premiership. The government is run like a balance sheet - and the balance sheet is honest, even when the news is bad.

Alt-history: Stoph keeps the Council of Ministers for himself. Party and government meet in one office - and in one overworked man; the Central Committee secretaries lose their posts in the ministries.

The Council of Ministers takes back what the Politburo apparatus took: ministers decide, the Central Committee departments advise, and the plan is run by the state. Stoph has waited twenty years for this.

The branch ministries give orders to every Kombinat: one ministry for chemistry, one for electrical engineering, one for coal. Order and capacity - and a bureaucracy that grows with every new department.

The industrial price reform of 1964-67 is carried on to consumer prices: goods are recalculated from real costs, subsidies stay only for bread and rents - the factories finally see what their goods cost, and the people see it too.
Fewer forms, computing centres in every ministry, ESER mainframes for the State Planning Commission: Stoph cuts the state apparatus by a tenth and makes the rest count.

The plan is tied to deliveries from West Germany: steel, machines and chemicals bought on the interest-free swing of inner-German trade, paid back in goods. Moscow asks why the Five-Year Plan reads like a West German order book.

From 1971 the Five-Year Plans are coordinated line by line with Moscow under the Comecon Comprehensive Programme: secure oil and gas for twenty years, Soviet science - and less room for the general directors.
The Council of Ministers' own Five-Year Plan: drawn up by the ministries, checked by the Planning Commission, approved by the Volkskammer - and only then shown to the Politburo.

Stoph and Brandt met in Erfurt and Kassel in 1970. As First Secretary, Stoph keeps the personal line to Bonn open and writes to the Chancellor as one head of government to another - correct, cool, always with the full title of the German Democratic Republic.

Alt-history: Stoph offers neighbourly relations without demarcation - travel relief, town twinning, joint work against the poisoned Elbe - as one sovereign state to another. Inner-German trade booms; Moscow frowns.

Stoph's other answer: every contact codified, every border post fixed by treaty, every Western visitor counted. Coexistence on paper, separation in practice - and the churches lose their West German partners.
Stoph built the National People's Army in 1956 and still holds the rank of Army General. The officers know him - and he knows what they cost.

As First Secretary Stoph chairs the National Defence Council, the republic's secret war cabinet, and rebuilds it around the ministries: mobilisation plans for every district, paid from the civilian budget.
The administrator turns on his old ministry: the army's budget is audited line by line, and the savings go to the Council of Ministers' investment fund.

Stoph's republic: governed by ministries, administered by experts, recognised by its neighbours - a state like any other, not merely the party's instrument. The party notices that it has become less important.
Stoph was born in 1914. His heir should be a man of the state, not of the apparatus - and the ministries should keep running while the Central Committee decides.
The economic manager of the Council of Ministers' years takes the party.
Alt-history: the modest district secretary of Dresden - an administrator like Stoph, and a careful reformer.
Stoph's ally in the Politburo and Moscow's informant: the Kremlin will approve, and the oil will keep flowing.
Günter Mittag: co-author of the New Economic System, secretary for the economy, the most feared man in the Politburo's corridors. Now he answers to nobody but the balance sheet.
Gerhard Schürer stays at the State Planning Commission - the one man who dares to put the real debt figures on Mittag's desk. The general directors hate his honest balance.
Alexander Schalck-Golodkowski's Commercial Coordination answers to Mittag directly: arms, art, blood plasma and prisoners for hard currency, no questions asked - and no receipts.
Wolfgang Biermann runs Carl Zeiss Jena like a feudal estate and delivers every plan. Mittag makes him the model for all general directors - results first, workers' councils last.
Mittag turns Ulbricht's prestige race into a short list: microelectronics, robotics, computer-aided design, biotechnology. Everything else waits - including the shops.
'Comprehensive intensification' after the Soviet oil cut of 1981: more output from the same machines, the same energy and the same people. Every Kombinat must save energy and materials every year.

From 1982 whatever earns hard currency is exported: furniture for Swedish catalogues, cameras for West German mail-order houses, petrol refined at Schwedt from Soviet crude - even blood plasma. The shops at home stay empty; Moscow notices the oil.
Mittag borrows in the West to modernise for export - the credits will be repaid by the goods the new plants make. In 1981 the banks stop lending; not every plant is finished.
Rolling mills, chemical plants and assembly lines from West Germany, France and Japan, Volkswagen engines for the Wartburg: the West builds, the republic pays in goods and credit.
June 1977: the Politburo decides that the republic will make its own chips. Erfurt and Dresden get the money, ZMD gets the best engineers - and the consumer goods plan gets what is left.
The foreign intelligence service's science and technology sector steals what COCOM will not sell: IBM software, chip masks, Western patents by the suitcase.

1979-80: almost all industry is folded into some 130 centrally run Kombinate, each with its own research, suppliers and export trade - every Kombinat makes its own screws, on the Carl Zeiss model. The general directors report straight to Mittag; the last semi-state suppliers are swallowed.
Alt-history: the Kombinate stay lean - the semi-state suppliers keep their workshops and sell parts to the Kombinate by contract. The general directors lose their empires.
Industrial robots by the tens of thousands - many of them home-made, many of them idle - are meant to replace the workers the republic does not have.

Mittag's republic: one great enterprise of Kombinate and chip works from Erfurt to Dresden, run from one office by numbers - brilliant at the Leipzig fair, efficient on paper, and answerable to no one. The party loses power to the general directors.

Alt-history: the Politburo's Economic Commission under Mittag becomes the real government. The Central Committee departments are bypassed, the general directors sit at the table - and the Nomenklatura is told what has been decided.

Mittag has no friends in the Politburo, only debtors - so he buys some: villas in Wandlitz, Volvos, Intershop allowances and hunting lodges for the district chiefs. The apparatus is loyal, and it knows its price.
The successor must be someone the apparatus will accept and the Kombinate will obey - and someone who will not open the books too quickly.
Alt-history: the Dresden district secretary who backed Robotron and the microelectronics centre.
The FDJ generation: a safe pair of hands for the apparatus - and for Moscow.
Kurt Hager: Spain veteran, professor, the Politburo's guardian of science, culture and doctrine since 1963. Under him the party line becomes the republic's whole horizon.

Otto Reinhold, rector of the party's academy, writes the theory: the GDR exists only as a socialist state - a capitalist GDR would have no reason to exist. His economists plan accordingly, and the last private workshops have no place in it.
Ursula Ragwitz, head of the Central Committee's culture department, reads every manuscript and every stage play before the public does. The young stop reading.
Joachim Herrmann, editor of Neues Deutschland and later secretary for agitation, decides each night which photograph of the leadership opens the front page. The workers read the sports page.

Marxism-Leninism as taught in Moscow, without Prague's human face or Belgrade's self-management - and demarcation pushed as far as it will go: 'German' vanishes from institutions' names, Western guests from conferences.
April 1987, to the magazine Stern: 'If your neighbour puts up new wallpaper, would you feel obliged to repaper your flat too?' Perestroika stops at the Oder - and so does Soviet goodwill.
Hager's economics: the needs of socialist man are shaped by socialism, not by the West German shop window. Thrift is a virtue, imports are a weakness, and a republic without debts is a free republic.

Alt-history: Wandlitz and the special shops for functionaries are closed - the party lives like the workers, and the money saved goes back into the plan. The Nomenklatura is furious; the FDGB is delighted.

Socialist competition in every works and the 'Make our towns and villages more beautiful - join in!' campaign in every street: brigades, banners and Saturday shifts build playgrounds, clubhouses and new roads. More output for the same wages - the red pennant hangs over the lathe, the overtime goes unpaid.

The Academy of Sciences, the universities and the research institutes plan their work with the party - and from 1976 the Academy of Social Sciences at the Central Committee defines what Marxism-Leninism means in practice. What is researched is decided by its use to socialism.
1977: world coffee prices explode. The 'Kaffee-Mix' - half coffee, half roasted rye and chicory - saves 300 million valuta marks. The people call it 'Erichs Krönung' and grumble loudly.
Trucks, machines and advisers for Ethiopian and Vietnamese coffee - solidarity that fills the cups. The bill is paid in IFA trucks the republic would rather have kept.
Alt-history: Hager's republic pays back the West German and Swiss banks and lives on what it makes. No new credits, no new dependence - and a lot less trade.

Printing licences, paper quotas, the publishing office in the Ministry of Culture - and the MfS's Department M opens the letters: whoever writes, paints or sings in the republic does so by permission.

Hager lets the artists breathe: Christa Wolf, Heiner Müller and Volker Braun publish with cuts but publish; the rock bands play; the church youth meets. Loyalty is bought with a little freedom - and the West listens in.
As after the Eleventh Plenum of 1965: banned films, pulped books, expelled writers. In 1979 the Writers' Union expels nine members; the rest learn silence.
The ideologist wants an heir who will keep the doctrine pure - and whom Moscow will trust with it.
Moscow's man in the Politburo: orthodox, loyal, and in daily contact with the Soviet embassy.
The FDJ generation, raised on the doctrine Hager wrote.
Hager's republic: a fortress of doctrine where every school, stage and institute speaks with one voice - secure against the West, loyal to Moscow, and slowly suffocating.
Heinz Hoffmann fought in Spain, trained in Moscow and has run the Ministry of National Defence in Strausberg since 1960. Now the general sits at the head of the party.

Colonel General Heinz Keßler, Chief of the Main Staff since 1967, turns the general's orders into plans for six divisions - and the Central Committee's apparatus learns that Strausberg no longer asks it first.

Fritz Streletz, secretary of the National Defence Council from 1971, ties party, army, Stasi and economy into one chain of command. Every Kombinat gets a mobilisation plan - and a new set of orders from the barracks.
Admiral Waldemar Verner's Political Main Administration puts a party secretary beside every commander: an army that thinks right fights right. The commanders call it supervision.
Eighteen months of service for every young man: the NVA is to teach discipline, technology and class consciousness to a whole generation.
Military instruction becomes a school subject for ninth and tenth graders, as it did in September 1978. The Protestant churches protest; the ministry insists.
The GST trains half a million young people in shooting, gliding, diving and radio - pre-military training dressed up as a hobby.

Everything for defence: a nation in arms with reserve divisions in every district, more arms plants, more exercises - and fewer cars, fridges and oranges in the shops. Moscow counts the divisions and is pleased.
Strausberg gets what it asks for: new arms plants, depots for thirty days of war, hardened command posts and a country that lives on permanent alert.
Fewer divisions, better soldiers: long-serving NCOs, modern equipment, and the conscripts back in the factories where the plan needs them. Moscow counts divisions and is not pleased.
Every NVA general passes through the Frunze and Voroshilov academies in Moscow: the best-trained officer corps of the Pact after the Soviets.
The general's economics: the NVA is the plan's first customer, the shops its second. Arms plants get their steel before the furniture Kombinate do.
The state arms exporter ITA sells rifles from the Erzgebirge, ammunition and W50 trucks to Syria, Ethiopia, Mozambique and Nicaragua - partly for hard currency, partly for coffee and goodwill.

Soviet licences go to the republic's own works - Kalashnikovs from Wiesa, ammunition from Schönebeck, W50 trucks from Ludwigsfelde - and everything they make stays with the NVA. Moscow likes an ally that equips itself.
The Ernst Thälmann works in Suhl and their sister plants turn out small arms, ammunition and spare parts for the NVA and for export.

Whole NVA units are lent to the lignite pits, the harvest and the building sites; in the winter of 1978/79 the army digs out the frozen coal trains. The officers grumble that soldiers are not labourers.
Hoffmann holds the Pact's standard: 85 per cent of the NVA ready for combat at all times. No soldier in the coal pits - and the plan misses the hands.
The Ministry of National Defence becomes the plan's most demanding customer: trucks from Ludwigsfelde, warships from Wolgast, rifles from Suhl - and an arms industry that pays its own way.
In March 1982 the Volkskammer created the rank of Marshal of the GDR and never awarded it. Alt-history: the general takes the baton - and must now name who comes after him.
Heinz Keßler, an officer of the NVA since its founding in 1956, is to follow the general. If the Central Committee balks, the Military Council of the NVA stands ready.
Egon Krenz, the FDJ man, is to inherit: the army keeps its budget, the party keeps its leading role.
The best-armed state per head in the Warsaw Pact: respected in Moscow, feared in Bonn - and tired at home.
Werner Lamberz, born 1929, the youngest man in the Politburo and the party's best speaker, now leads it: a socialism that smiles on television.

Heinz Adameck has run East German television since 1954; with Lamberz's backing the DFF is to win back the evening from ARD and ZDF - with new studios and colour programmes the budget can barely carry.
Paul Markowski's department for international relations knows every liberation movement from Luanda to Aden - and travels wherever Lamberz goes. Washington notices where the GDR's friends are.
Joachim Herrmann, editor of Neues Deutschland since 1971, is told to make the party paper readable: fewer congratulatory telegrams, more news. The district secretaries miss their names on page one.
Western journalists call him the GDR's Kennedy: tall, witty, at ease with steelworkers and foreign presidents alike. The party finally has a face people want to see - and trade partners want to meet.
Ein Kessel Buntes brings Western stars and Eastern hits to the DFF from 1972. If the people watch our channel on Saturday, they watch our news on Sunday. The Western stars are paid in hard currency.
December 1971: 'no taboos' for artists who stand firmly on socialism. How far that breadth may reach is now Lamberz's decision.

The First Secretary himself opens the windows: honest statistics, live phone-ins, readers' letters printed uncut, a government spokesman who answers questions and factory managers who may contradict. Moscow raises an eyebrow.

The message stays the same; only the packaging changes - new studios in Adlershof, a younger Aktuelle Kamera, slick posters for the old certainties. Moscow approves; the young switch over to the West after the news.
Lamberz chairs a Politburo commission for Africa: advisers, trucks, printing presses and security instructors for the new socialist states.
Mengistu's Derg turns to the socialist camp. Lamberz flies to Addis Ababa himself: security advisers and IFA trucks for a country at war in the Ogaden, coffee for the GDR.

FRELIMO's Mozambique needs engineers, teachers and miners; the GDR needs workers and hard coal. A treaty would bring Mozambican contract workers to Saxony - and the engineers for Moatize are paid from Berlin.
FDJ Friendship Brigades of young engineers, nurses and teachers go south. This time Lamberz flies home from his African journeys - no helicopter waits for him in the Libyan desert.
Lamberz the agitator knows that a full shop window convinces better than a banner: colour television, rock records and oranges sell socialism - if the republic can pay for them.

1977-78: IFA trucks, cement works and engineers for Iraqi and Libyan crude outside the Soviet quota - the deals Lamberz was flying to Tripoli to close in March 1978. Moscow dislikes oil it does not deliver itself.

Barter instead of hard currency: Ethiopian and Angolan coffee, Ghanaian cocoa and Cuban oranges for IFA trucks, teachers and printing presses. The shelves fill; the factories that build the trucks earn nothing.
The DFF has broadcast in colour since 1969, but a colour set from Staßfurt costs half a year's wages. Lamberz wants one in every living room before the Western sets get there.
Salamander shoes, Schiesser underwear and Nivea cream are made in GDR factories under Western licence - most of it for the West, some for the Exquisit shops. Money now, and a dependence Moscow notes.
Every Kombinat, even in steel and chemicals, must make consumer goods: saucepans from the rolling mill, tents from the fibre works. The general directors call it a waste of their plants.
Leipzig's fair, Berlin's Alexanderplatz and the department stores of every district town become the republic's shop window - for its own citizens first.
Lamberz is barely fifty, but he knows how quickly a Politburo ages. The next leader must come from his own generation - and know how to talk to the cameras.
Hans Modrow, the modest district secretary of Dresden, shares Lamberz's taste for open debate - and the old guard's distrust of it.
Egon Krenz, the FDJ chief, is young, disciplined and liked in Moscow - continuity with a younger face.
A republic whose young people watch its television, dance to its bands and believe its leader: the dream of 1971, almost within reach.
Werner Krolikowski, Dresden's party chief until 1973 and Politburo member since 1971, reports to the Soviet embassy behind his comrades' backs. Now the Kremlin's confidant runs the party.
Willi Stoph shares Krolikowski's contempt for Mittag's economic conjuring; together they run the government by the book - the Soviet book. Mielke's ministry is told to keep out of the ministries.
Erich Mielke's ministry and the KGB in Karlshorst share files, informers and suspicions: the Stasi becomes Moscow's eyes in every office - including the offices of the comrades.
Every favour from Moscow is paid in national pride: Soviet slogans, Soviet holidays, Soviet orders. How far will the republic bend?
The Soviet Union's most reliable ally: every Comecon vote, every manoeuvre, every line of Pravda followed to the letter. The republic keeps its own state - and loses its Western customers.
Soviet specialists sit in the Planning Commission, the ministries and the Kombinate. Things work - in Russian. The general directors seethe.
Alt-history: Krolikowski proposes what no German communist ever dared - a confederation of the GDR with the USSR. The Kremlin decides; the NVA's generals would serve under Soviet command.
Russian becomes the second official language and Soviet officers sit in the Volkskammer as observers. Many East Germans quietly despair.
Six million members, Russian lessons from the fifth grade, friendship trains to Moscow: the DSF becomes the republic's second party.
Every Politburo protocol reaches the Soviet ambassador before the ink is dry. Moscow is never surprised again - and the comrades never trust each other again.
Krolikowski despises Mittag's conjuring with numbers: plans are drawn up as Gosplan does - balanced in tonnes, checked in Moscow, fed by Druzhba oil at Comecon prices and closed to Western whims.
Moscow decides who builds what: the republic gets ships, rail cars, machine tools and chemicals for the whole bloc - and hands its own car and computer ambitions to its neighbours.

Alt-history: what Krolikowski wrote to Moscow in secret from 1980 becomes policy - no new credit from Bonn's and Vienna's banks, repayment before consumption, and an end to Mittag's embellished statistics.
After the Polish crisis the republic and the Soviet Union build their own bridge: a rail ferry from Mukran on Rügen to Klaipėda, opened in 1986. Soviet goods no longer cross Poland.
Rail cars from Ammendorf, ships from Warnemünde, machine tools from Karl-Marx-Stadt: Moscow's orders come first, are paid in transferable roubles and keep every plant busy for years.
Even Moscow's man counts the debt: what the West pays for in marks goes west first, and the Soviet orders wait.
Joint plans, joint research institutes, joint power grids: the republic's economy becomes a western province of the Soviet one.
The Soviet ambassador lets it be known which comrades Moscow trusts - and which Kombinate can expect Soviet orders. Krolikowski only has to listen.
Egon Krenz is young, loyal and known in Moscow from a hundred FDJ delegations: the Kremlin's choice for the next generation.
Kurt Hager, the chief ideologist, guarantees that nothing will change - which is exactly what Krolikowski wants.
The GDR is now the Soviet Union's most dependable ally - richer in orders, poorer in pride. Moscow will never let this republic fall.
Egon Krenz, born 1937, FDJ chief from 1974 and the first leader who was a child when the war ended: continuity, the party promises, with a younger face.
Günter Schabowski, editor of Neues Deutschland and later Berlin's party boss, becomes the voice of the new leadership - quick, eloquent, occasionally careless. One wrong sentence can open a border.
Wolfgang Herger, Krenz's comrade from the FDJ, heads the Central Committee's security department: army, police and Stasi report through him - and the church groups feel it first.

Eberhard Aurich, Krenz's successor at the head of the FDJ, mobilises two million blue shirts for the leader who once wore theirs - and hundreds of thousands march past the tribune at the Whitsun meeting, at the state's expense.
Former FDJ secretaries take over district offices and ministries: a generation that learned to organise rallies now organises the state. Rallies become ministries.
Krenz's economics are the FDJ's: 'Jugendobjekte' in every Kombinat, youth brigades on every priority site, and a young workforce that is promised flats in return.

The FDJ's demand becomes law: young couples move to the front of the housing queue, the interest-free marriage loan grows and shrinks with every child ('abkindern'), every child gets a crèche place - paid partly on credit.

The FDJ Central Committee assigns whole brigades to the republic's priority sites - power stations, chemical plants, railway lines. The building goes fast; the young builders wait for their own flats.
Youth brigades from every district build Marzahn and Hellersdorf: tens of thousands of flats for the capital - and resentment in the provinces that lose their builders.
Krenz asks Bonn for credit to fill the shops before the next winter, as Schalck-Golodkowski did in the autumn of 1989.
Gerhard Schürer's analysis tells the Politburo what it never wanted to hear - as on 31 October 1989: without cuts the republic cannot pay its Western debts. Krenz publishes it.
The generation that grew up behind the Wall now runs the republic it was raised for - steadier than the old men feared, younger than the West hoped.
'With today's session we will introduce a turn' - Krenz's own words of October 1989. Which turn is the question every comrade asks; the first step is to talk to the church.
A new travel law: every citizen may apply for a passport and a visa to the West. The pressure valve opens - Bonn and Moscow hold their breath.
Schalck-Golodkowski carries the offer to Bonn, as in November 1989: open borders for every citizen, if the Federal Republic pays for the travel currency and a new credit line.
June 1989: the Volkskammer applauds the massacre on Tiananmen Square and Krenz carries the congratulations to Beijing. Alt-history: the republic answers its own streets the same way.
The Stasi's crisis plans list thousands of 'hostile-negative' citizens for internment in an emergency. The plans leave the safe and become orders.
As Central Committee secretary for security Krenz supervised the Stasi, the police, the army and the courts; as First Secretary he keeps the portfolio.
Krenz chaired the commission that announced 98.85 % for the National Front in May 1989. Church groups counted too - and found the lie.
For years Krenz was called the crown prince. Now he must name one of his own - from a generation that has started families of its own.
Hans Modrow, the reformer from Dresden, is to follow - the party's insurance against the street.
Werner Krolikowski, Moscow's man for twenty years, is to follow - the Soviet embassy will not object.
Hans Modrow, Dresden's district secretary since 1973, lives in a rented flat, queues like everyone else and was kept out of the Politburo for sixteen years. Now the party asks the outsider.
Wolfgang Berghofer, the young pragmatist who would run Dresden's city hall, brings managers who measure success in flats repaired, not banners - and sends the banner-makers home.
Christa Luft and the economists of the Berlin-Karlshorst college of economics may finally say aloud what their models have shown for years. The truth unsettles.
Markus Wolf, the spymaster of the HV A, has read the West's files on the republic - and believes in a reformed socialism. His counsel comes with his network; Moscow's old guard frowns.
Modrow ran Dresden for sixteen years with what Berlin left him. Now the district becomes the unit that plans: local budgets, local building plans, local craftsmen.

The fifteen district councils get their own budgets and building plans: Berlin sets the frame, Dresden, Rostock and Suhl fill it. The central apparatus loses its grip - and some district bosses build themselves kingdoms.

The 11,000 semi-state firms, private factories and craft cooperatives nationalised in 1972 are handed back to their owners - as Modrow's government allowed in March 1990, here years early. Prices that cover costs, small trades licensed again.
Robotron's headquarters and the microelectronics centre ZMD make Dresden the 'Silicon Saxony' of the East - with a district secretary who fights for every hall.
Western firms may take stakes in East German enterprises - the joint-venture law of Modrow's 1990 government, here years early.
Robotron builds mainframes for the whole bloc and Dresden trades chips for Soviet raw materials - safe partners, no Western strings, and no Western machines for the general directors either.
Plan where it must, market where it can: the districts build, the craftsmen sell, the Kombinate keep part of their profit.
October 1989 in Dresden: the city meets the 'Group of 20' chosen by the demonstrators. Here the party talks to its critics before they take to the streets.
The SED stays, but changes: secret ballots inside the party, term limits for functionaries, an end to the privileges of Wandlitz.
An extraordinary party congress elects a new Central Committee by secret ballot. Half of the old guard is gone; the members are proud of their party again.

Party, bloc parties, church and the democratic communists of Robert Havemann's circle sit at one table in the Dietrich Bonhoeffer House - as in December 1989, years earlier. Modrow concludes that the SED cannot reform itself.
Modrow steps aside: the League of Democratic Communists forms the government, the SED becomes one party among others.
Every 13 February young Christians gather with candles at the ruins of the Frauenkirche. Modrow sends no police - he goes to talk to Bishop Hempel.
Pensioners already travel west; now family visits, honeymoons and study trips are approved by the district, not by the Stasi. Most come back.
17 November 1989: Modrow offered Bonn a 'treaty community' of the two German states. Here the offer comes while the Wall still stands firm.
The outsider who was never admitted fills the Politburo with district secretaries, scientists and women - and asks who should carry the reform on.
Egon Krenz, the FDJ's former chief, promises to keep the apparatus loyal to the reform - if he inherits it.
Werner Lamberz, the charismatic agitator, would carry the reform onto every television screen in the republic.
Modrow names nobody. When he goes, the Central Committee shall choose freely - the first open succession in the party's history.
A socialist republic that talks to its church, lets its people travel and trades with Bonn as an equal: the Dresden model has become the state.
Since 1965 Gerhard Schürer's State Planning Commission has turned every tonne of coal and every pair of shoes into a plan figure. Whoever governs, the economy of the republic starts at its desks.
The VIII Party Congress of June 1971 buries the prestige projects of the 1960s: fewer showpieces, more flats and goods - the 'main task' is now the people's standard of living.
Some 11,000 private, semi-state and craft-cooperative firms - many with a state share since 1956 - still make furniture, textiles, toys and spare parts. The party asks how long it will tolerate them.
Between February and July 1972 the owners are 'persuaded' to sell: 11,000 firms become people's enterprises and their former owners the managers of what was theirs.
Alt-history: the compromise of 1956 survives. The state keeps its share, the families keep their workshops - and the shops keep their buttons, zips and spare parts.
The IX Party Congress of May 1976 promises more of everything - 750,000 new flats, more cars, more goods - and pays for it more and more with Western credit.
1979-81: the industrial associations are dissolved. Some 130 central Kombinate - each with its own research, suppliers and export trade - answer directly to the ministries.
The X Party Congress of April 1981 orders 'comprehensive intensification': more output from less energy, less material and fewer hands - just as the Western debt falls due.
The formula of the 1980s: growth no longer from new factories but from science, robots and savings - the planned economy's last answer to the world market.
Only the Ministry of Foreign Trade may buy or sell abroad: every rouble of Comecon trade and every Western Mark passes through its hands.
Alexander Schalck-Golodkowski's KoKo, founded in 1966 under the wing of the MfS, earns hard currency by any means - art and antiques, arms, blood plasma and prisoners.
Furniture for IKEA, cameras for Quelle, petrol for West Berlin: whatever the West will buy is sold, even when the shops at home stay empty.
By 1981 the republic owes Western banks more than ten billion dollars, and Schürer warns that it will soon borrow only to pay the interest.

Consortia of Western banks in Vienna, London and Frankfurt roll over the republic's debts - at a price in interest and in Moscow's suspicion. (Government-guaranteed credits from Bonn are an offer in the German Question and in Honecker's tree.)
Alt-history: the Romanian road - imports cut to the bone, every exportable good sold, the debt paid off to the last Mark, whatever the shops look like.
A bread roll costs five pfennigs, as in 1950, and a tram ticket twenty. Every year the gap between price and cost grows - and with it the state's bill.
The promise of 1971: bread, rents, fares and children's clothes will not cost a pfennig more - whatever it costs the budget.
The planners' heresy: let prices tell the truth. Wasteful factories are exposed - and so are the households, after twenty years of fixed prices.
The slogan of the 1958 chemistry programme still hangs over Leuna: a republic without oil fields will build its wealth on coal, Soviet oil and its chemists.
The new petrochemical half of the Leuna works runs on Soviet oil instead of coal: ethylene, methanol and polyethylene for the whole republic.
The Buna works' billboard on the transit motorway promises plastics for every household: PVC, synthetic rubber and carbide chemistry from Schkopau.
Halle, Merseburg and Bitterfeld make a third of the republic's chemicals - and most of its smog.
At the end of the Druzhba pipeline the petrochemical Kombinat on the Oder refines Soviet crude - for the republic's tractors and for West Berlin's petrol stations.
The most profitable trade the republic has: Soviet crude at friendship prices goes out again as diesel and heating oil for Western Marks.
Machine tools from Karl-Marx-Stadt, cranes from Leipzig, printing presses from Radebeul: the republic is Comecon's workshop.
The 'first socialist city' on the Oder finishes its cold rolling mill in 1974: sheet steel for cars, fridges and washing machines from Soviet ore and Polish coke.
Eisenhüttenstadt still has no hot rolling mill: its slabs travel to the Soviet Union and back. Alt-history: the gap is closed in the 1970s, not in 1997.
The Kombinate 'Fritz Heckert' and '7 October' sell lathes and machining centres from Moscow to Milan - the republic's best ambassadors in the West.
Expensive Western machines must never stand still: through the 1970s the Kombinate move ever more workers into round-the-clock shifts.
The Trabant P601 of 1964 is still the people's car - two-stroke engine, plastic body, a wait of twelve years. Zwickau has successors on the drawing board; the Politburo hesitates.
No Western licence, no new car: the P601 is improved bolt by bolt and built until the end of time. The hard currency stays at home.
1984: Volkswagen sells the licence for its Polo engine. The Wartburg 1.3 and the Trabant 1.1 get four-stroke engines - paid for with parts delivered to Wolfsburg.
Trabant, Wartburg, the W50 lorry and the Multicar: the IFA Kombinat builds everything that moves on the republic's roads - and for half of Comecon.
Warnemünde and Rostock build freighters, trawlers and fish-factory ships - most of them for the Soviet Union, paid in oil and timber.
Every second ship from the Baltic yards sails east: the Soviet fishing fleet is the republic's best customer - and its most demanding.
Founded in Dresden in 1969: typewriters, calculators, data processing - the republic's answer to IBM, with almost 70,000 employees by the 1980s.
Twenty thousand researchers in Berlin-Adlershof, Jena and Dresden; since the academy reform of 1969 they work to contracts with the Kombinate instead of to their curiosity.
Comecon's Unified System copies IBM's 360: Robotron's EC 1040 of 1973 becomes the bloc's most successful mainframe, sold from Havana to Novosibirsk.
'Rationalisation by our own means': every Kombinat must build its own robots and automatic lines - tens of thousands of 'industrial robots' by 1985, many of them simple manipulators.
June 1977: the Politburo orders a microelectronics industry built from scratch - billions of Marks and tens of thousands of engineers, all under the Western COCOM embargo.
Every chip designed in Dresden and Erfurt, every machine built at home: slower and dearer, but nobody in the West can switch it off.
The MfS sector for science and technology smuggles Western chips, wafer steppers and machines through front companies - and Dresden copies them transistor by transistor.
From 1980 the Centre for Microelectronics Dresden is the heart of the chip programme - from 16-kilobit to 256-kilobit memory chips.
September 1988: Dresden presents a 1-megabit memory chip - years behind the West, and each one costs 534 Marks to make while the world market pays a few dollars.
From 1985 the KC 85 and later Robotron's school computer enter the classrooms - eight bits, cassette drives and a generation that learns to program.
The optics Kombinat of Jena grinds lenses for planetaria, microscopes, the NVA and the Soviet space programme - and sells them for hard currency.
Night sights, rangefinders, tank periscopes and reconnaissance cameras: Jena equips the Warsaw Pact's front line.
September 1976: Zeiss's multispectral camera photographs the earth from Soyuz 22 and later from the Salyut stations - the republic's eye in orbit.
Lusatia and the Leipzig basin hold the republic's only real raw material: 250 million tonnes of lignite a year, dug by excavators taller than a church.
Near Hoyerswerda the world's largest briquette and town-gas works turns lignite into gas, coke and briquettes for every stove in the republic.
Autumn 1981: Brezhnev cuts the republic's oil from 19 to 17 million tonnes a year - Moscow needs the dollars more than its ally needs the oil.
Heating plants are converted back from oil to lignite, output climbs to 312 million tonnes in 1985 - and the saved Soviet oil is refined and sold to the West.
Alt-history: the republic keeps its oil-fired plants and buys the missing two million tonnes in Rotterdam - with money it does not have.
Every Kombinat gets an energy quota: street lights are dimmed, shop windows go dark and the planners count kilowatt-hours like bread.
From 1971 the lignite giant of Upper Lusatia grows to 3,520 megawatts - the largest power station of the republic.
Six 500-megawatt blocks near Cottbus (1976-89) burn eighty thousand tonnes of coal a day - and the open-cast mines swallow the Sorbian villages around them.
Lignite alone cannot carry an industrial state: the planners look east for natural gas and to the atom for the future.
At Lubmin on the Baltic, Soviet VVER-440 reactors go online from 1973 to 1979 - 1,760 megawatts, a tenth of the republic's electricity.
On the Elbe near Stendal four VVER-1000 reactors are to make the republic's largest power station - if the money and the Soviet parts arrive.
Alt-history: after Chernobyl the church circles ask what the cloud from Kiev would have done over Magdeburg, the planners ask what the reactors cost - and Stendal is halted.
1974-79: from Orenburg to the Soviet western border, built by all of Comecon - the republic's section in Ukraine, the FDJ's 'Druzhba' route, is its largest youth project.
From 1979 Orenburg gas reaches the republic; the lignite town gas of Berlin, Leipzig and Dresden gives way.
Since the 'socialist spring' of 1960 every farmer belongs to an agricultural production cooperative; nearly a million people work the land of a small, crowded country.
From the early 1970s the cooperatives hand their fields to crop units of four to six thousand hectares; the animals stay behind in the village cooperatives.
Fields as wide as the horizon, crop-spraying aircraft, combine harvesters in columns: the farm becomes a factory and the farmer a worker in green.
Eberswalde fattens almost two hundred thousand pigs a year, Ferdinandshof thousands of bulls - meat for the people, for export and liquid manure for the groundwater.
Alt-history: crops and animals are reunited in the village cooperative - smaller, slower, closer to the soil, and the young farmers stay.
The cooperative's general assembly again decides what is sown and when; the Democratic Farmers' Party finally speaks for the villages.
Every year the republic buys millions of tonnes of grain and fodder in the West for hard currency; self-sufficiency would save hundreds of millions.
Ammonia and urea from Piesteritz on the Elbe: new plants in the 1970s double the fertiliser for the cooperatives' fields.
Agrochemical centres spread fertiliser and pesticides by lorry and aircraft - efficient, and fatal for rivers and wells.
Drainage and irrigation on a million hectares: the FDJ drained the great Friedland meadows in the 1950s, now the cooperatives do it on every wet field.
The cooperative farmer's half hectare, the city allotment and the rabbit hutch supply much of the fruit and eggs - bought up by the state above the shop price.
Pork and beef go west for hard currency while the butchers at home sell out by noon.
Every district gets a housing construction Kombinat with its own panel factory; from 1973 they are to solve 'the housing question as a social problem' by 1990.
From 1972 one standard panel system for the whole republic: six storeys, central heating, a bath and a fitted kitchen - luxury for families from crumbling tenements.
The chemical workers' city west of the Saale, begun in 1964, grows to ninety thousand people - the model for every new town of the republic.
Crèche, kindergarten, after-school care and the 'baby year' of 1976: nine in ten women of working age can work - and do.
From 1977 the largest building site of the republic: some sixty thousand flats on the eastern edge of Berlin, a new city in ten years.
July 1988: the party celebrates the three-millionth flat since 1971 in Marzahn - while the old towns of Leipzig and Görlitz crumble behind the cameras.
Bread, rents and brown coal are cheap; tights, car parts and bananas are sold under the counter to friends.
Wages rise and the savings books swell - well over a hundred billion Marks by the 1980s - but the shelves do not fill.
Rents at pre-war levels, bread at 1950 prices, children's shoes below cost: by the late 1980s subsidies swallow a fifth of the budget.
Exquisit for fashion, Delikat for fine food: the republic sells cheap basics and expensive 'luxury' side by side - and soaks up the money that has nothing to buy.
Every heavy-industry Kombinat must also make consumer goods: the chemical works sell garden hoses, the arms factories bicycles.
Order a car at eighteen, collect it at thirty: millions of orders wait in Zwickau and Eisenach, and a used Trabant costs more than a new one.
From 1974 citizens may legally hold Western money - and spend it in the Intershops, where the republic sells Western goods for Western Marks.
After the coffee crisis of 1977 and the hated mixed blend nicknamed 'Erichs Krönung', the republic invests in Vietnamese plantations: from the 1980s GDR experts grow coffee in Dak Lak.
1978: the state imports a million pairs of Levi's for hard currency - the queues outside the department stores are longer than for any party rally.

Founded on 1 March 1956, the NVA is the only Warsaw Pact army whose combat units stand under the Pact's Combined Command even in peacetime - six divisions, an air force and a navy, manned by eighteen-month conscripts.
Every regiment has its political deputy and its party organisation; the Political Main Administration in Strausberg makes sure the army never forgets whose army it is.
Nearly every officer carries a party card. Political schooling eats hours of every training week, and the political deputy watches over every commander.
Alt-history: the generals ask for what every Western army has - command without a political deputy looking over the shoulder. Hoffmann's staff draft a professional officer corps.
The 1982 law confirms eighteen months of service for every man - and, in a state of defence, makes women liable too. 'Women for Peace' circles answer with open letters.
After their service, soldiers stay reservists until fifty; every year tens of thousands are called back for weeks of exercises - in a crisis the NVA can double in days.
October 1970: the armies of the Warsaw Pact manoeuvre on GDR soil, commanded by the republic's own Minister of National Defence, Army General Heinz Hoffmann.
In war the NVA's six divisions advance together with the Group of Soviet Forces in the first wave - the front line of the socialist camp runs through Thuringia and Mecklenburg.
The coalition war plan: answer any NATO attack with a counter-offensive across the inner-German border towards Hamburg, Hanover and the Danish straits within days.
Alt-history: instead of storming the Rhine the NVA digs in at home - territorial regiments and a people's war on our own soil, a doctrine closer to Belgrade than to Moscow.
The plan for West Berlin: NVA units, border troops and combat groups would take the half-city within days of a war. Medals of the Blücher Order, created for wartime only, already lie in the depots.
Alt-history: the Ore Mountains, the Harz foothills and the Elbe crossings become fortified districts held by local regiments.
September 1980: the armies of the Pact manoeuvre again on GDR soil and in the Baltic, while the strikes in Gdańsk are on everyone's mind.
Soviet marshals call the NVA the best-drilled army of the Pact, and NATO staffs agree: goose-step, field-grey uniforms and Soviet tanks - the Red Prussians.
In Dresden the academy trains the general-staff officers of the NVA; the best go on to the Voroshilov Academy in Moscow.
The 1st, 4th, 8th and 11th Motor-Rifle and the 7th and 9th Tank Divisions stand ready in the military districts of Leipzig and Neubrandenburg.
T-55 tanks, BMP-1 infantry fighting vehicles, Mi-24 helicopters: almost every weapon of the NVA comes from the Soviet Union, at Comecon prices.
From 1979 the T-72 arrives from Soviet, Polish and Czechoslovak factories - cheap, reliable and ordered through Moscow.
Alt-history: like Poland and Czechoslovakia, the GDR asks for its own T-72 licence - a tank works in Saxony instead of an order book in Moscow.
T-72M1 tanks, BMP-2s, Su-22 fighter-bombers: in the 1980s the NVA modernises faster than the economy can pay for it.
'Willi Sänger', named after a communist resistance fighter murdered by the Nazis: the NVA's only paratroop battalion trains for raids deep behind NATO lines.
The Volksmarine's combat swimmers train to mine harbours, locks and bridges from Kiel to the Danish straits.
1,378 kilometres of fortified border and the Wall around West Berlin, watched by 47,000 border soldiers.
In 1971 the Border Command leaves the NVA and becomes the Border Troops of the GDR - so that 47,000 men no longer appear in the army's strength at the coming force-reduction talks in Vienna.
A five-kilometre zone along the border where only residents with a special pass may live; 'unreliable' families were deported in 1952 and 1961.
Marienborn, Checkpoint Charlie, the 'Palace of Tears' at Friedrichstraße: the passport controllers are Stasi officers in border-troop uniform.
From 1975 the 'Border Wall 75' replaces the improvised walls: 45,000 L-shaped concrete segments, 3.6 metres high, topped with a smooth pipe no hand can grip.
Signal fences, dog runs, floodlights, a patrol road and a raked 'death strip': technology replaces manpower, and the border costs less every year - but the world's picture of it does not change.
The hardliners want no gaps at all: double fences, more mines, more dogs, more towers - the border as a fortress, whatever the world thinks.
Alt-history: more crossing points, and visits to the West widened from pensioners to working people. The border still stands, but it opens its gates a little - and Bonn notices.
25 March 1982: for the first time a law, not just an order, regulates the border regime - including the use of firearms in its paragraph 27.
No written order uses the word, but every guard knows it: a successful escape on his watch ends his career, a shot 'border violator' earns him a medal and leave.
3 May 1974: Honecker tells the National Defence Council that firearms must be used 'ruthlessly' against anyone who tries to break through. The order stays.
Alt-history: the guards are ordered to fire into the air and arrest, not to kill - no more bodies on the death strip for Western cameras.
From 1971 some 60,000 directional mines are fixed to the border fence - until Michael Gartenschläger dismantles two in 1976 and shows them to the West German press.
From 1972 citizens below pension age may apply to visit the West for weddings, funerals and jubilees - tens of thousands a year, and almost all of them come back.
1983-84: as part of the price for Strauss's billion-mark credits the self-firing devices and the minefields disappear from the inner-German border.
The republic's northern flank is the Baltic coast from Wismar to Usedom; its sky lies minutes from NATO's airfields. The Volksmarine and the Air Forces/Air Defence guard both.
Some 16,000 sailors with headquarters in Rostock: frigates, minesweepers, landing ships and fast attack craft.
The Volksmarine stays what the Pact wants: minesweepers, landing ships and fast boats for the western Baltic and the straits.
Alt-history: frigates for the North Sea, port calls in Luanda and Havana - the flag of the republic seen beyond the Baltic.
On Rügen the 6th Flotilla keeps the fast torpedo and missile boats, ready to strike at shipping in the Danish straits.
From 1983 mobile launchers with anti-ship missiles hide behind the dunes - no landing fleet would reach Rügen unseen.
At Wolgast the Peene shipyard builds the Volksmarine's own warships - in the 1980s its Parchim-class corvettes are even ordered by the Soviet Navy.
In war the Volksmarine, the Polish Navy and the Soviet Baltic Fleet sail as one force under a Soviet admiral - their target is the Danish straits.
The LSK/LV is wired into the Pact's unified air defence: its fighters stand on 'duty system' alert under Soviet command, day and night.
The MiG-21, in a dozen variants, is the backbone of the fighter wings of the 1st and 3rd Air Defence Divisions.
The LSK/LV stays what it was built to be: an air-defence force that keeps NATO bombers out of the republic's sky, interceptors on five-minute alert.
Fighter-bombers join the LSK/LV - first the MiG-23BN, later the Su-22: the air force learns to strike ahead of the tank divisions of the first echelon.
From 1978 the MiG-23 arrives - the first fighter of the republic with variable-sweep wings and a real search radar.
Mi-8 transports and, from 1978, Mi-24 gunships form the combat helicopter wings - flying artillery for the tank divisions.
1988: Fighter Wing 3 at Preschen receives the MiG-29 - a fighter as good as anything NATO flies, bought as the republic's money runs out.
Rings of S-75 Dvina and S-125 Neva batteries cover Berlin, the industrial south and the coast, fed by the radar chain from the Baltic to the Fichtelberg.
Interkosmos: the socialist countries do space science together. In 1976 the MKF-6 multispectral camera of Carl Zeiss Jena photographs the earth from Soyuz 22.
Two air-force pilots, Sigmund Jähn and Eberhard Köllner, train at Star City. If Moscow agrees, the first German in space will be a citizen of the GDR.
Some 400,000 workers in grey-green uniform, organised by factory and commanded by the party - in August 1961 they stood at the Brandenburg Gate.
Every large enterprise has its own combat-group hundred; training happens after the shift, on Saturdays and in summer camps.
The best hundreds become motorised battalions with armoured personnel carriers, mortars and anti-tank guns - a second line behind the NVA.
The combat groups' real task is the home front: guarding plants, securing streets and crushing 'counter-revolutionary' unrest - a party militia against another 17 June.
Alt-history: the combat groups join the NVA's territorial defence - a trained reserve of hundreds of thousands under military, not party, command.
The GST teaches the young to shoot, dive, glide, drive and send Morse code - hundreds of thousands of members preparing for military service.
Apprentices and students spend weeks in GST camps; the NVA receives conscripts who already know how to march and shoot.
1 September 1978: ninth- and tenth-graders get compulsory military lessons. The Protestant churches protest openly - and the peace movement is born.
Alt-history: in 1981 Dresden church circles propose a civilian 'social peace service' instead of arms. The state accepts - and the construction soldiers become nurses and builders.
The Civil Defence Law of 1970 makes protection against air raids and nuclear war a duty of every citizen, every factory and every district.
Secret depots hold fuel, grain, medicines and spare parts for months of war or blockade - one of the republic's best-kept secrets.
Normannenstraße, Berlin-Lichtenberg: 43,000 full-time officers under Erich Mielke in 1970 - 'the shield and sword of the party'.
Markus Wolf's HV A - led by 'the man without a face' - runs some of the best-placed agents in Bonn, at NATO and in the Bundeswehr.
Handsome young officers go west to court lonely secretaries in Bonn's ministries - love letters that end in the HV A's files.
24 April 1974: Günter Guillaume, aide to Chancellor Brandt, is arrested as an HV A officer; Brandt resigns on 6 May. Even Wolf later counts it among his defeats.
The HV A's Sector Science and Technology steals what the COCOM embargo forbids: chip designs, software and machine-tool plans worth billions of marks of saved research.
Some 100,000 unofficial collaborators in 1970, 180,000 by 1975: colleagues, neighbours, pastors and spouses who report to a handling officer.
Directive 1/76: instead of arrests, quiet destruction - Zersetzung: rumours, lost jobs, broken marriages, failed exams. Opponents fall apart without a single trial for the West to see.
Alt-history: the methods of the 1950s return - show trials, mass arrests, open intimidation. The streets fall silent, and the whole world watches.
The remand prison in Berlin-Hohenschönhausen, missing from every city map, and the special prison Bautzen II for the state's most prominent enemies - some of whom Bonn will later buy free.
The MfS's own motorised regiment, named after the founder of the Cheka, guards the Politburo's settlement at Wandlitz, the ministries and - in a crisis - the streets of Berlin.
Main Department II hunts the agents of the BND and the CIA - and turns the ones it catches into double agents.
Bugs, steamed letters, hidden cameras and jars of scent samples for the dogs: the ministry's workshops build the tools of total surveillance.
From 43,000 officers in 1970 to 81,000 in 1982: the ministry grows faster than any other part of the state - and costs more every year.
Alt-history: the Central Committee's security department caps the ministry's growth. Fewer officers, more budget for the plan - and a Mielke who must ask before he acts.
Mielke's eternal question: who is who? By the 1980s the files fill more than a hundred kilometres of shelves - the ministry knows everything about everyone.
Alexander Schalck-Golodkowski, head of Commercial Coordination, is an MfS colonel on special assignment: the ministry protects KoKo's hard-currency deals - and takes its share.
Crèche, Pioneers, FDJ, brigade, trade-union holiday, the queue for a flat: the state accompanies its citizens from the cradle to the pension - and expects loyalty in return.
Blue scarves for the six-year-olds, blue shirts for the fourteen-year-olds: almost every child marches in the Ernst Thälmann Pioneer Organisation and the Free German Youth.
At fourteen, nearly all young people pledge themselves to socialism in a secular ceremony, the Jugendweihe, that has all but replaced confirmation.
July-August 1973: the X World Festival of Youth and Students brings 25,000 foreign guests and eight million visitors to East Berlin - nine days in which the republic looks open and young.
December 1971: Honecker promises 'no taboos' in art for those who stand on firm socialist ground. Plenzdorf's 'The New Sufferings of Young W.' fills the theatres.
Socialist realism or nothing: books are pulled, plays cancelled - and when Wolf Biermann is stripped of his citizenship, a stream of artists follows him west.
The Puhdys, Karat and City fill the stadiums with German-language rock; the state label Amiga presses the records, and the 60/40 rule keeps Western songs to a minimum on the radio.
At the Olympic Games in Munich the GDR team, under its own flag and anthem, wins 66 medals and finishes third - ahead of the hosts.
1974: the leadership secretly makes 'supporting means' state policy. Thousands of athletes, many of them minors, receive anabolic steroids they are told are vitamins.
Alt-history: the doping plan is rejected. The money goes to mass sport - 'everyone, everywhere, once a week' - and the medals come a little more slowly.
Montreal 1976: the republic of seventeen million wins 40 gold medals - more than the United States, second only to the Soviet Union.
With almost nine in ten women at work, the state builds crèches and kindergartens on a scale no Western country matches.
9 March 1972: the Volkskammer legalises abortion in the first twelve weeks - and for the first time in its history, members of the CDU vote against a law.
From 1976 mothers get a paid year off after their second child, marriage loans that shrink with every birth, and priority for a flat.
1971: the Federation of Evangelical Churches in the GDR declares that it wants to be a church 'not alongside, not against, but in socialism'.
6 March 1978: Honecker receives Bishop Schönherr. The churches get airtime, prison chaplains and new church buildings; in return they stay out of politics - for a while.
Every evening at eight the republic switches to the Tagesschau. The party must decide: fight the antennas or live with them.
As in 'Operation Ochsenkopf' of 1961, FDJ brigades climb the roofs and saw off every antenna that points west. Fewer people watch - and everyone resents it.
1973: Honecker concedes that anyone may switch Western television on and off as he likes. The raids stop; the comparison with the West stays.
Every Monday Karl-Eduard von Schnitzler cuts up West German news clips and explains what they really mean - the republic watches the enemy and argues back.
28 October 1969: Willy Brandt tells the Bundestag that there are two states in Germany - without recognising the second one. East Berlin must find an answer.
19 March 1970: Willy Brandt steps off the train in Erfurt. Under the windows of the Erfurter Hof the crowd calls for the Western chancellor - and the MfS clears the square.
21 May 1970: Willi Stoph in Kassel. Protesters tear down the flag of the republic, Brandt offers twenty points, Stoph insists on recognition - and both sides agree on a 'pause for reflection'.
No treaty without full recognition under international law - and, Stoph added in Erfurt, 100 billion marks for the damage done by the open border before 1961.
Post, telephone, transit, trade: settle what can be settled and leave the big words to the communiqués. Moscow suspects East Berlin of running its own German policy.
12 August 1970: Brandt and Kosygin sign the Moscow Treaty. The borders of the republic are declared inviolable - in a treaty nobody asked East Berlin about.
Inner-German trade runs on an interest-free overdraft: the swing lets the republic buy in the West today and pay in goods later - 850 million units of account from 1975.
17 December 1971: Michael Kohl and Egon Bahr sign the first agreement between the two German governments - sealed lorries and buses to West Berlin, no more random searches.

Freikauf - since 1963 Bonn has bought political prisoners free through the lawyer Wolfgang Vogel - some forty thousand marks a head, paid in goods through the Protestant church. The republic sells its own citizens.
Instead of tolls at the checkpoints Bonn pays a lump sum: 234.9 million marks a year at first, 525 million from 1980 - and the MfS watches every lay-by on the transit routes.
21 December 1972: Bahr and Kohl sign in East Berlin. Two equal states and an inviolable border - but permanent missions instead of embassies, because Bonn still speaks of one nation.

Two states, two nations: the socialist nation in the GDR has nothing in common with the bourgeois one in the FRG. Contacts with Westerners are reported, and in November 1973 the minimum exchange for visitors is doubled to twenty marks.
Rapprochement instead of Demarcation: the two German states are foreign countries to each other only on paper. Trade, visits and credits flow - and Moscow starts counting them.
From 1973 a joint commission marks the inner-German border stone by stone. By 1978 it is done - except along the Elbe, where Bonn insists that the border runs on the eastern bank.
13 October 1980: every Western visitor must now change twenty-five marks a day at one to one - pensioners and children included. Visits from the West drop sharply; the treasury does not complain.
June 1983: Franz Josef Strauss, the West's loudest anti-communist, arranges a bank credit of one billion marks with Bonn's guarantee. Schalck-Golodkowski negotiates; Moscow is told afterwards.

6 May 1986: after twelve years of talks the two states sign a cultural agreement - exhibitions, orchestras, art treasures scattered by the war - and Saarlouis twins with Eisenhüttenstadt, the first of some sixty town twinnings.

1985-87: the SED and Bonn's Social Democrats draft a chemical-weapons-free zone, a nuclear-free corridor and a joint paper on 'the dispute of ideologies'. For once the party admits that the class enemy may also want peace.
Since 1955 Bonn has threatened every state that recognises the GDR with the loss of West German aid. In January 1970 barely half a dozen non-socialist capitals have dared.
1969 broke the doctrine: Iraq, Sudan, Syria, South Yemen and Egypt recognised the republic, Algeria follows in May 1970. Now the friendships need treaties.
The Thomanerchor, the Dresden Staatskapelle and the Berliner Ensemble tour capitals that do not recognise the republic - Bach and Brecht open doors that diplomats cannot.
India, the largest democracy of the Third World, keeps a trade mission in East Berlin and a treaty with Moscow. On 8 October 1972 it opens an embassy.
Every spring and autumn Leipzig becomes the republic's shop window: Western ministers and industrialists who cannot be received in Berlin come to the fair.
Between 1972 and 1974 the dam breaks: dozens of states establish relations with the republic, from Bangladesh to Japan and Australia.
9 February 1973: Britain and France, two of the four powers responsible for Berlin, establish diplomatic relations with the republic on the same day.
December 1972 and January 1973: Bern, Vienna, Stockholm and Helsinki recognise the republic - Finland on the same day as the Federal Republic.
The flag of the republic flies over embassies in London, Paris, Rome and The Hague. Recognised at last - and watched at last, because Western embassies talk to dissidents too.
18 September 1973: the General Assembly admits both German states. The GDR becomes the 133rd member of the United Nations, one seat ahead of the Federal Republic.
4 September 1974: the United States, the last of the four powers, establishes diplomatic relations with the republic.
In the General Assembly the republic votes with the liberation movements and the non-aligned: against apartheid, against colonial wars, for a new international economic order.
The republic presents itself as the German state from which no war will ever start: disarmament proposals, conferences and a nuclear-free corridor through Central Europe.

1 August 1975: the First Secretary and Chancellor Schmidt sign side by side. The borders are inviolable - and Basket Three promises freedom of movement. Within a year thousands quote Helsinki in their exit applications.
The Final Act guarantees the border, not the right to cross it. Exit applicants lose their jobs, and the MfS sets up a central group against flight and emigration.
Take the signature seriously: family reunions, visas for journalists, exit permits for those who insist. The pressure valve opens - and the West notices.
January 1988: the head of the republic is received in Paris with full honours, and a GDR diplomat presides over the UN General Assembly. Recognition is complete - legitimacy is another matter.
Twenty Soviet divisions, Soviet oil, Soviet protection: the republic owes its existence to Moscow and never forgets it - nor is it allowed to.
Every summer the First Secretary flies to Brezhnev at Oreanda: a swim in the Black Sea, a long walk, and the year's quarrels settled between two men.
7 October 1975: a new treaty of friendship for twenty-five years. Unlike the treaty of 1964 it no longer speaks of German unity - only of the alliance.
July 1971, Bucharest: Comecon adopts its Comprehensive Programme for socialist economic integration - joint plans, joint research, joint investment.
Builders and machines from the republic go to Siberia: the Ust-Ilimsk pulp combine is paid for with East German work and repaid with pulp and paper for years.
From 1975 Comecon prices follow a moving average of world prices. After the oil shock Soviet crude gets dearer every year - and the republic pays in goods it would rather sell for marks.
Schwedt and Leuna crack Soviet crude into diesel and heating oil for Western customers while the republic heats with lignite. Moscow notices where its cheap oil ends up.
Every tonne of oil is paid in sleeping cars from Ammendorf, ships from Rostock and machine tools from Karl-Marx-Stadt - goods the shops at home will never see.
1 January 1972: an identity card is enough to cross the Oder or the Ore Mountains. Millions travel - and Polish shoppers empty the shelves of Frankfurt on the Oder.
August 1980: the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk strikes and Solidarity is born. On 30 October the republic closes its border to Polish visitors - the contagion must not cross the Oder.
26 November 1980: the First Secretary writes to Brezhnev that Poland is lost without collective action. NVA divisions stand ready for the manoeuvre 'Soyuz-80'.
The republic warns Moscow against a second Prague: the Poles must solve their crisis themselves - and the republic keeps its trade with the West.
November 1983: the Bundestag approves the Pershing II, the Soviet delegation walks out of Geneva, and Moscow announces new missiles for the GDR and Czechoslovakia.
Soviet OTR-22 missiles roll into Saxony and Mecklenburg; later the NVA receives its own OTR-23 launchers. The church's peace groups sew 'Swords into Ploughshares' onto their jackets.
The missiles are 'the devil's work', the First Secretary says, and writes to Chancellor Kohl of a coalition of reason: the damage to German-German relations must be limited.
Whatever the quarrels over oil, Poland or missiles, the republic stands where it was founded: in the first strategic echelon of the socialist community.
Every trade unionist buys solidarity stamps: millions of marks a year for liberation movements and young states, handed out by the Afro-Asian Solidarity Committee.
The republic's most popular cause: medicine, trucks and hospital equipment for Hanoi, Vietnamese students in Dresden and Leipzig, schoolchildren collecting for 'the heroic Vietnamese people'.
Trainees from 1973, contract workers from 1980: tens of thousands of Vietnamese work in the Kombinate for four or five years, live in hostels and send goods home by the crate.
June 1972: Fidel Castro names a small Caribbean cay after the murdered KPD leader. Trucks and machine tools go to Havana, sugar and oranges come back - and from 1978 Cuban apprentices follow.
11 September 1973: Pinochet's coup ends Allende's Chile. Some two thousand Chilean exiles find refuge in the republic, the Socialist leader Carlos Altamirano among them.
19 July 1979: the Sandinistas enter Managua. Teachers, doctors and police instructors follow from the republic; in 1985 the Carlos Marx Hospital opens in Managua.
25 April 1974: the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon ends Portugal's empire. In Mozambique and Angola the movements the republic has supplied for a decade take power.
Printing presses, radio transmitters, FDJ Friendship Brigades and thousands of scholarships: the republic exports teachers and textbooks rather than rifles.
NVA instructors, MfS advisers and rifles from army stocks: the republic builds armies and security services for its allies - discreetly, and in smaller numbers than the Cubans.
February 1979: a treaty of friendship with Samora Machel. The republic is to modernise the Moatize coal mine and train Mozambican workers - coal and labour for machines and know-how.
The ANC's journal Sechaba is printed in the republic and its fighters train in Mecklenburg; from 1979 hundreds of Namibian children of SWAPO grow up in Bellin and Stassfurt.
11 November 1975: Agostinho Neto proclaims independence while the guns of the civil war can be heard in Luanda. The republic sends weapons, instructors and IFA trucks - and takes coffee in return.
1977: Werner Lamberz flies to Addis Ababa. MfS officers build Mengistu's state security, trucks and weapons go to the Ogaden front, and Ethiopian coffee pays part of the bill.
1982: the republic is weeks away from insolvency in the West. In the Politburo someone finally asks what the trucks for Angola and the hostels for Hanoi really cost.
From now on friends pay - in oil, coffee or hard currency. Weapons from army stocks go to Libya, Iraq and Syria; Werner Lamberz's last journey in 1978 was meant to arrange exactly that.
Internationalism is not a business. The stamps are still sold, the ships still sail to Maputo and Haiphong - and the bill goes to the republic's own consumers.
From the Mekong to the Cape the republic's teachers, doctors, advisers and engineers are its real embassies - a small state with a long reach.

Three years after the catastrophe of June 1967, Egypt is a nation at war without a victory to show for it. The Sinai lies under occupation, the Canal is shut, Soviet advisers fill the barracks and Nasser, weary and unwell, still carries the hopes of the Arab world. Every decision of the coming decade will be made in the shadow of the Naksa.

A country that has lost a war cannot win the next one on enthusiasm alone. The Arab Socialist Union, the trade unions and the provincial committees are called upon to keep the factories running, the fellahin loyal and the sacrifice shared. Rationing is tolerated and conscripts are fed, so long as the people believe that the burden is being borne equally.

Nasser's heart is failing, and everyone in Cairo knows it, though few dare say so aloud. Sadat, Sabri, Zakaria Mohieddin and the generals around Mohamed Fawzi each imagine themselves at the head of the republic. Behind the polite fiction of collective leadership, the struggle over who will inherit the Rais's authority has already begun.

Should the best cardiologists of the Soviet Union be flown to Cairo, the Rais might yet be spared. Moscow has every reason to keep the man who anchors its position on the Nile alive, and Nasser, however reluctantly, accepts treatment and rest. The succession is postponed, though not cancelled, and the republic holds its breath with every medical bulletin.

Anwar Sadat, long dismissed as a loyal but colourless Free Officer, is named to carry the presidency after Nasser. To the generals and the party apparatus he looks like a safe transitional figure, a man to be managed rather than feared. His rivals in the Arab Socialist Union's inner circle have underestimated him, and they will come to regret it.

Should the men who built the security state refuse to be sidelined, the succession will be settled in the corridors of the Mukhabarat rather than at the ballot box. Ali Sabri and his allies move before any rival can consolidate, backed by Moscow's quiet approval. The Rais's heir is pushed aside, and the apparatus of Nasserism rules in its own name.

With the old guard discredited and the army wary of open rule, a government of technocrats and elder statesmen is called to steady the ship. Zakaria Mohieddin, once named as Nasser's successor in the dark days of 1967, returns to office promising competence over ideology. Washington notices the change of tone, and so do the exhausted bureaucrats of Cairo.

When politicians quarrel over a dead man's legacy, the officers act. War Minister Mohamed Fawzi, backed by a General Staff that has little patience for party intrigue, assumes the leadership in the name of national survival. The republic remains, but it is now openly a state of soldiers, and the front along the Canal comes before everything else.

In May 1971 Sadat moves against those who thought he would be their puppet. Ali Sabri, Sami Sharaf, Sharawi Gomaa and their colleagues are arrested, and the heart of the Nasserist security state is dismantled almost overnight. The president calls it a corrective movement, and the burning of the intelligence tapes seems to promise a freer, if still firmly governed, Egypt.

However the crisis was resolved, the question of who rules Egypt has finally been answered. The new leader no longer governs in the shadow of Nasser's portrait but under his own authority, with a plebiscite to confirm what the officers and ministers have already accepted. The state can now turn from survival to direction.

Egypt has lived under provisional constitutions since the fall of the monarchy. A permanent text is drafted to give the republic a settled legal order, defining the powers of the presidency, the role of the single party and the rights of its citizens. It is both a promise of stability and a statement of who is meant to hold the pen.

The drafters write that the principles of the Islamic sharia are a principal source of legislation. To the scholars of al-Azhar it is a vindication, to the Coptic minority a cause for unease, and to the president a useful counterweight to the left. Faith, once a matter for the mosque, is written into the foundations of the state.

Egypt, the charter declares, belongs to all its citizens alike, Muslim and Copt, and its laws are made by parliament rather than by scholars. The ulema of al-Azhar protest, but the engineers, lawyers and teachers of the modern state welcome a constitution that looks forward. Religion remains honoured, though it is not to be the source of law.

The Arab Socialist Union has been the only legal political organisation for over a decade, and it is showing its age. Some argue that unity requires a single party, others that pluralism must be allowed to breathe, and still others that the emergency must simply continue. The answer will define how Egyptians are permitted to argue with their government.

The nation is at war and cannot afford the luxury of factions. A single organisation, drawing together peasants, workers, soldiers and civil servants, is declared the only legitimate vehicle of political life. Dissent is not forbidden outright but is expected to find its voice within the Union, and nowhere else.

In a bold experiment, the Arab Socialist Union is divided into platforms, or manabir, representing the left, the centre and the right. Out of these tribunes may grow genuine parties, with their own programmes and newspapers. Egypt's old liberals and leftists sense an opening, while the security services watch to see how far it will go.

The state of emergency, in force since 1967, is extended and given new teeth. Suspects may be held without trial, public gatherings need permission and the press learns where the lines are drawn. The government calls it the price of facing Israel, and the men of the Mukhabarat find themselves rarely idle.

The years since Suez have taught Egypt that it has friends but no certainties. Cairo must now decide whether its future lies with the neutral states of the Third World, with Moscow, with Washington, with the faith of its people or with Egypt alone. The choice made here will shape every treaty and every alliance to come.

Nasser's old creed of positive neutrality, forged at Bandung and Belgrade, is renewed. Egypt will take aid from whoever offers it but will serve no master, and will speak for the nations that refuse to be pawns of the great powers. It is a proud course, and a precarious one for a country at war.

The Soviet Union has rebuilt Egypt's army, financed the High Dam and stationed its crews along the Canal. It seems only natural to complete the journey and to align the republic openly with the socialist camp. Planners, advisers and ideologues arrive in growing numbers, convinced that the Nile's future lies in the East.

Sadat's maxim is that ninety-nine percent of the cards in the Middle East are in American hands. Only Washington can compel Israel to withdraw from Sinai, and only Washington has the capital to lift the Egyptian economy. If Moscow's embrace has brought nothing but dependence, perhaps it is time to turn westward.

Defeat in 1967 discredited the secular promises of the revolution, and many Egyptians now look to the mosque for answers. The idea of a state guided by faith, rather than by slogans of socialism or nationalism, grows in the lecture halls and the poorer quarters of Cairo. The leadership must decide whether to ride this current or be swept aside by it.

Egypt has bled for causes that were never entirely its own, from Yemen to Palestine to the dream of Arab unity. A new voice argues that the nation must look first to its own soil, its own interests and its own five thousand years of history. The army, which has paid the highest price for pan-Arab ambitions, listens with interest.

From its Cairo studios, Sawt al-Arab has long carried the message of the revolution to every café and village square from the Atlantic to the Gulf. Under the new leadership the broadcasts are turned to the cause of independence and non-alignment, challenging the monarchs and rallying the street. The voice of Cairo may be hoarse, but it is still heard.

Algerian fighters, African nationalists and exiled movements from across the Third World have long found shelter in Cairo. By opening its offices, scholarships and training camps to them, Egypt claims a role as the capital of liberation. The cost is considerable, though the prestige repays it in friends who will remember.

At Brioni in 1956, Nasser, Tito and Nehru declared their refusal to join either bloc. That spirit is now revived in earnest, with Belgrade and New Delhi as natural partners in a world that wants to be neither red nor blue. Common projects, trade and diplomatic support give substance to what had been largely a slogan.

Should the non-aligned course be entrusted to the old movement, the Arab Socialist Union is restored as the vehicle of national life. Its committees are revived and its cadres return to the villages and factories. It is the familiar face of the revolution, comfortable and well organised, if somewhat tired.

A strong presidency, above party and faction, is entrusted to a figure of experience and moderation. Zakaria Mohieddin and his circle of administrators promise efficient government without the fervour of ideology. Critics call it a technocratic monarchy, while supporters point to the order it brings.

After years of prison camps and executions, the Muslim Brotherhood emerges into public life. Its veteran leaders, led by the aged Umar al-Tilmisani, offer a moderate programme of piety, social welfare and constitutional rule. Secular Egyptians watch with apprehension as the movement that Nasser tried to destroy takes the reins of government.

Veterans of the Free Officers who broke with the regime have kept alive a socialism that is neither Soviet nor authoritarian.
