Khaled Mohieddin and the National Progressive Unionist Party offer a left-wing government committed to workers' rights, civil liberties and independence from both blocs. It is a democratic experiment few thought possible.

Contractors, importers and well-connected managers have grown rich under the shelter of the state. With the opening of the economy, they now seek to govern directly rather than to buy influence. The business circle of Osman Ahmed Osman promises growth and prosperity, and the poor wonder whether they will share in it.

The government declares that Egypt will join no pact, host no foreign bases and bow to no capital. In the manner of Nasser's old doctrine, Cairo will seek its own path between the blocs. The words are bold, but the ministries must now find the means to make them credible.

The Non-Aligned Movement was born in part from Egyptian initiative, and Cairo now claims its rightful place at the head of it. Summits, delegations and joint declarations carry the voice of the developing world into the councils of the great powers. A seat at the table is useful, even to a country that must still beg for spare parts.

Egypt's armoury has been Soviet for years, but a truly independent state cannot rely on a single supplier. Delegations travel to Paris, Belgrade, Beijing and beyond in search of aircraft, engines and ammunition. A diversified arsenal is harder to blackmail, if rather harder to maintain.

Moscow and Washington are each eager to claim the Nile as their own, and Cairo has learned to turn their rivalry to advantage. Every offer of credit, wheat or weapons from one is carefully shown to the other. It is a delicate and sometimes dangerous game, played with great skill by the diplomats of the Foreign Ministry.

From Addis Ababa to Dar es Salaam, newly independent states look to Cairo as an elder brother. Technical missions, teachers and trade agreements deepen the ties that were first sealed at Bandung. In the United Nations, a solid bloc of African and Asian votes will be there when Egypt needs them.

Egypt has become a spokesman for all those who resent the order imposed by Washington and Moscow alike. The republic speaks for commodity producers, former colonies and small nations demanding fair treatment. Its influence now extends far beyond what its modest wealth would suggest.

The old families of the provinces, the omdas and landed notables who survived the land reforms, see their moment. A cabinet drawn from their ranks promises continuity, respect for property and a government that knows the countryside. Reformers warn that the Egypt of Nasser is being quietly unwound.

Free-market economists and importers argue that the Egyptian economy has been strangled by state control. A government committed to liberalisation promises to dismantle subsidies, open the markets and let private enterprise lead. The bazaar cheers, though the factory floors are anxious.

A new kind of politics emerges around the great river itself. Ecologists, agronomists and engineers warn of the silt held back by the High Dam, the salt creeping into the Delta and the fouling of the Nile. They ask Egypt to measure its progress not by tonnes of steel but by the health of the river that gave it life.

Nasser's Arab socialism was always more instinct than doctrine. Now the ideologues of the Socialist Union argue for something firmer, a scientific socialism taught in the party schools and applied through the plan. Marxist economists, long tolerated on the margins, find themselves invited to the centre of policy.

Soviet specialists already train the army and run the missile batteries on the Canal. Now they are welcomed into the planning offices, the factories and the ministries themselves. Their guidance is invaluable, though some Egyptians mutter that they sit at the desk of every minister.

Inside the Arab Socialist Union, a secret cadre known as the Vanguard Organisation has been quietly recruited from the most committed and trusted militants. Formalised and expanded, it becomes the disciplined core of the revolution, shaping policy from behind the scenes. Loyalty to the cause is rewarded, and doubt is noticed.

Ali Sabri and the Vanguard cadres take command of the state in their own name. The apparatus built over a decade, from the intelligence service to the party committees, is now unmistakably the government. Moscow nods with approval, and the more independent minds of the revolution fall silent.

The Egyptian communists dissolved their party in 1965 to join Nasser's Union, and have long worked within the system. Now their moment appears to have come, as veteran cadres emerge from the prison camps and the underground to claim the leadership. The red flag is raised over a country that has never been ruled by one.

From the textile mills of Mahalla to the shipyards of Alexandria, workers declare that the revolution belongs to them rather than to the officials who speak for them. Councils elected on the factory floor seize the means of production and form the basis of a new government. It is a socialism from below, deeply unsettling to every established authority.

Fearing the chaos of revolution, a coalition of officers, landowners and conservative bureaucrats installs a government of order. They promise to protect property, restrain the radicals and keep the Soviet advisers on a short leash. The language is still that of progress, though the spirit is one of caution.

A radical vision takes hold, in which the revolution is not socialist but Islamic, aimed at the overthrow of both the corrupt state and its foreign patrons. Inspired by events far beyond the Nile, activists and clerics rally to a new front. Their government makes the faith, rather than the plan, the engine of the revolution.

A clerical leadership seizes the state in the name of the revolution, claiming that sovereignty belongs to the guardianship of the jurist rather than to the people or the party. The officers resist and the Azhar scholars are divided, but the new rulers are convinced that they carry a divine mandate. Egypt becomes a very different kind of republic.

All the forces of the left, from Nasserist cadres to Marxist intellectuals and trade unionists, are gathered into a single Progressive National Front. Old disputes are set aside in the name of unity against reaction and imperialism. The Front is meant to be a broad coalition, though its leadership is firmly in the hands of the committed.

A powerful planning committee is empowered to direct industry, agriculture and trade in accordance with the needs of the nation. Five-year plans are drafted with Soviet help, targets are set for steel, cotton and power, and the market is relegated to the margins. Efficiency is hoped for, though bureaucracy is feared.

The trade of Egypt, long dominated by the purchase of cotton by the Eastern bloc, is brought into closer cooperation with the economies of Comecon. Moscow and its allies offer credits, machinery and technical expertise in exchange for lasting economic ties. The Nile valley is drawn further into a planned economic community.

Armed workers' and peasants' militias are raised in the factories and villages, drilled by army instructors and commanded by party loyalists. They guard the Canal towns, watch the streets and remind the regular army that the revolution has its own defenders. For many Egyptians it is the first time they have held a rifle.

Egypt formally takes its place among the nations of the socialist camp. The long courtship with the East ends in an alliance, with all the obligations it carries. Cairo is now a pillar of the anti-imperialist front, rather than a wary guest.

The transformation is complete. From the Aswan Dam to the Delta, posters, plans and slogans proclaim a socialist Egypt, building a new society with the friendship of the socialist world. The pyramids look down on a very different kind of republic, and the Rais would hardly recognise it.

Sadat's famous remark, that ninety-nine percent of the cards in the Middle East are held by America, becomes the guiding principle of foreign policy. Only through Washington can Egypt hope to recover Sinai peacefully and revive its economy. Cairo opens its channels to the State Department, and American diplomats begin to visit more often.

Law 43 invites foreign and Arab capital to Egypt on generous terms, with tax holidays, guarantees against nationalisation and freedom to repatriate profits. The architects of the Open Door hope for factories, hotels and banks. The trade unions, who built the public sector, fear what will become of their jobs.

The censors who once sat in every newsroom are withdrawn, and Egyptian writers speak openly for the first time in years. Newspapers criticise ministers, satirists mock the establishment and political prisoners are quietly released. The government hopes that candour will win loyalty, though it also unleashes a flood of grievances.

The president forms a new ruling party, drawn from the centre of the old Arab Socialist Union and open to businessmen, officials and the rural elite. Disciplined and pragmatic, it is meant to guide the Open Door without losing control of the state. It is a party of government rather than of ideas.

The Wafd, the great nationalist party of Saad Zaghloul and Nahhas Pasha, returns from its long exile. Its elderly leaders, led by Fouad Serageddin, offer a government of liberal constitutionalism, free markets and respect for the law. For some it is a restoration, for others a reminder of the corrupt politics that the officers once overthrew.

A cabinet of liberals comes to office, committed to economic freedom, the rule of law and a prudent foreign policy. Their programme is modest and their ministers experienced, with little patience for slogans. They promise an Egypt governed by reason, not by revolutionary fervour.

Socialist Labour, a loyal opposition drawn from the old left of the Union, forms a government that embraces the West without abandoning the working class. It promises a welfare state, trade union rights and a social market economy. Its leaders hope to prove that openness need not mean inequality.

The Open Door, or Infitah, is proclaimed, and the economy is turned towards private enterprise and foreign capital. The sealed system of Nasserism gives way to imported goods, joint ventures and new fortunes along the Nile. Egyptians will be richer in some respects and more divided in others.

American aid officials open offices in Cairo for the first time in years. Wheat shipments, development loans and technical missions begin to flow along the diplomatic channel, proof of what friendship with Washington may bring. Egyptians ask what price will eventually be named.

To rescue the treasury, Egypt turns to the International Monetary Fund, which offers help on condition that the government cut its subsidies on bread, rice and cooking oil. The economists call it necessary medicine, and the poor of Cairo call it theft. The streets will deliver their own verdict.

Rather than seek a single grand settlement, Egypt entrusts itself to Henry Kissinger's patient diplomacy, in which small withdrawals build confidence for larger ones. The shuttle flights between Aswan, Jerusalem and Damascus become the pulse of regional politics. Each step is modest, but together they might lead somewhere.

Egypt formally takes its place beside the Western democracies. Its markets, its diplomacy and its armed forces are increasingly woven into the Atlantic order, and the slogans of non-alignment give way to the language of partnership. After two decades of confrontation with the West, Cairo has chosen its side.

Washington comes to regard Egypt as the keystone of its policy in the Middle East. Military cooperation, joint exercises and steady financial support follow, reinforced by the personal confidence between the two presidents. The most populous Arab state has become a pillar of the American order.

In the universities of Cairo, Assiut and Minya, Islamic student groups are encouraged to challenge the Marxists and Nasserists who dominate campus life. Backed by the authorities, they win student elections and set new standards of dress and conduct. The movement they build will outgrow its sponsors.

Egyptian teachers, engineers and labourers travel to the Gulf, and return with money, conservative habits and a stricter piety. Saudi donors fund mosques, charities and religious schools along the Nile. Faith and finance have become inseparable partners in the shaping of public life.

The ancient institution of the hisba, by which the community enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong, is revived. Inspectors move through the markets and streets, watching weights, dress and public morals. Supporters see a return to virtue, while others see a licence for self-appointed guardians.

The scholars of al-Azhar, guardians of Sunni learning for a thousand years, are called to govern. The Grand Imam Abd al-Halim Mahmud brings moderation, scholarship and the weight of tradition to the highest office of the state. The mosque and the ministry become one in a more orderly fashion than many feared.

The young militants of the Jama'at, radicalised on campus and hardened in prison, decide that the existing order is beyond reform. Their uprising overthrows the old establishment and installs an Emir in the capital. The army is shaken, the streets are tense, and the revolution devours its elders.

Egypt is proclaimed an Islamic state, and the constitution, courts and schools are to be reshaped accordingly. The government presents the change as a return to the true foundations of the nation, and a repudiation of the failures of secular nationalism. A new republic begins, bound to the law of God.

The religious duty of zakat is made the basis of public welfare, collected in the mosques and distributed to the poor. The state trusts charity and conscience to do what the planners of the socialist era could not. Many welcome the dignity of giving, though the treasury wonders how it will pay for roads and schools.

The banks of Egypt are reorganised on Islamic principles, with interest forbidden and profit shared between investor and borrower. Economists debate whether a modern economy can function in this way, while the devout watch with hope. It is an experiment on a national scale.

The new Egypt looks beyond the Arab world to the wider community of believers. Riyadh, Islamabad and Khartoum receive delegations from Cairo, and the old rhetoric of Arab nationalism is replaced by that of Muslim brotherhood. The ummah, not the nation, becomes the horizon of Egyptian diplomacy.

The liberation of Jerusalem is proclaimed a duty of every Muslim, not merely of the Arabs. Sermons, camps and recruiting posters call the faithful to the defence of the third holiest city of Islam. Israel is no longer merely an enemy of the state but of the faith.

The transformation of Egyptian society is now far advanced. Law, education, commerce and the family are ordered by the principles of the faith, and the state sees itself as the keeper of a house of Islam on the Nile. For better or worse, the old republic is gone.

In the shadow of defeat, the army remains the one institution that Egyptians still believe can redeem the nation. Its officers, drawn from the villages and small towns, are held up as the embodiment of the people's will. Trust in the uniform is restored, and with it, expectations of those who wear it.

Egypt is older than Islam, older than the Arabs and older than any of the nations that have lectured it on unity. Historians, artists and schoolbooks celebrate the Pharaohs as the nation's ancestors, and the monuments of Giza as its birthright. Arab brethren look on with unease at this reorientation of identity.

The officers' clubs of Cairo and Alexandria have long been places for meals, sport and conversation. Now they become the meeting places of a political class, where careers are made and plans are quietly drawn. The army is no longer merely a servant of the republic but its natural guardian.

Field Marshals and Chiefs of Staff assume the government of Egypt in the name of the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces. Generals such as Saad el-Shazly and Mohamed Fawzi bring discipline, planning and a deep suspicion of civilian politicians. The republic is secure in their hands, though few are certain when they will give it back.

The old Misr al-Fatat, once the green-shirted youth movement of Egyptian nationalism, rises from obscurity. Its leaders promise discipline, honour and a rebirth of the nation under a populist banner. The Nile's youth respond to the call, and the old establishment looks on in alarm.

Young colonels, impatient with their senior officers and with the failures of the revolution, form a new Revolutionary Command Council. They denounce corruption and compromise, and promise a harder, purer nationalism. The memory of 1952 hangs over them, for they intend to do it all again.

A surprising turn in the officers' councils brings the question of the monarchy back into the open. Fuad II, the infant king deposed in 1952, is invoked as a symbol of continuity above faction and politics. For some the throne is a relic, for others the only legitimate answer to a generation of revolutionary turmoil.

The republic of the officers is openly declared, and the armed forces take the lead in public life. Governors, ministers and company directors are drawn from the ranks, and the logic of the barracks spreads through the state. Order and duty are the watchwords of the new Egypt.

Martial law is declared, and the military courts, patrols and curfews give the authorities the power to act without delay. Strikes are broken, demonstrations dispersed and troublemakers detained. The streets are calm, at least on the surface.

Egypt reorganises its economy for a long struggle. Factories are turned to military production, consumer goods are rationed, and civilian planning is subordinated to the needs of the army. It is a lean and austere regime, but it keeps the guns supplied.

The army builds its own economic empire. The National Service Projects Organisation takes on the production of everything from bottled water to pasta, using conscript labour and military engineers to supply the state. The generals have discovered that a nation's defence rests as much on its factories as on its tanks.

Egypt above all, say the posters, the speeches and the schoolbooks. Loyalty to the nation is placed before party, class and creed, and the citizen is asked to accept sacrifice for the sake of the whole. It is a stern gospel, but one that a proud and bruised country is ready to hear.

From the schoolchild to the reservist, the whole population is drawn into the national defence. Military training, civil defence drills and the glorification of service become part of daily life. Egypt has become a nation in arms, with its army at the centre.

Since 1962 the Arab Socialist Union has been the single political organisation of the Egyptian revolution, a pyramid of village, district and governorate committees reaching from the Delta to Aswan. Its ranks are swollen with officials, officers and ambitious local men who know that membership opens doors. If it can be made to work as more than a ceremonial machine, it may yet carry the republic through the hard years after the defeat.

The National Congress gathers delegates from the Union's committees in Cairo to approve the line of the leadership and to be seen approving it. Under Nasser such assemblies have been exercises in managed unity, yet they remain the only stage on which the regime must explain itself to its own cadres. A well-staged congress can restore confidence in the party after the shock of 1967.

Elections to the People's Assembly are held with candidates drawn from the Union's lists, half of them workers and peasants by decree. There is no party competition, but the ballot lends the regime a claim to popular consent and gives provincial notables a stake in the system. Critics call it a parliament without opposition; the government calls it democracy suited to a nation at war.

The Institute of Socialist Studies trains the future cadres of the Union, schooling young officials in the theory of Arab socialism and in the art of mobilising villages and factories. Its lecturers argue over what the revolution actually means, and its graduates are expected to answer that question the same way. The Institute is meant to turn enthusiasm into discipline.

Twenty years after the Free Officers seized power, Egyptians are asking whose revolution it has become. Is it the peasants' and workers', as the Charter claims, or that of the officers, bureaucrats and security men who run it in their name? The answer given in these years will determine whether the Union holds fast to Nasser's legacy or breaks with it.

The leadership resolves to defend the Charter without apology: socialism at home, non-alignment abroad and the dignity of the fellah and the factory worker above the comfort of the new rich. Nasser's speeches become the scripture of the party, and doubters are reminded that the revolution gave Egyptians land, schools and pride. It is a path of loyalty to what has already been won.

The Agrarian Reform of 1952 broke the great estates and that of 1961 cut them further, but the village still belongs to the few. A third law lowers the ceiling on private holdings once more and redistributes the surplus to landless families. The big families grumble and the harvest may suffer in the confusion, but the fellah finally sees the revolution reach his own field.

Since the early sixties the state has promised every graduate of Egypt's universities a post in the civil service, and the promise has filled the ministries with clerks and made a generation loyal to the revolution. Renewed and extended, the guarantee keeps young men and women in the system rather than in the streets. The price is a bloated bureaucracy that grows with each graduating class.

The Socialist Youth Organisation takes the revolution into the schools, universities and factories, offering camps, study circles and a path of advancement to those who join. Its founders hope to raise a generation that knows Nasser's Egypt as the only Egypt there has ever been. Its critics say it breeds careerists and informers, but few doubt that it reaches where the old party never did.

From Cairo's microphones the revolution has always spoken to the whole Arab world, and the Union now gives that mission an organisation. Delegations, scholarships, party contacts and broadcasts carry the message of unity to Damascus, Baghdad, Tripoli, Sanaa and Khartoum. Egypt, the argument runs, is not one country among many but the guardian of the Arab cause.

A renewed National Charter is drafted for the new decade, restating the principles of 1962 in the light of defeat, war and a changing world. It speaks more carefully about the role of the state, tolerates some pragmatism and promises that socialism and national dignity can be defended together. Many in the party see it as the revolution's second founding document.

The old formulas of the revolution are put quietly aside as the leadership turns toward a different course. Anwar Sadat, long dismissed as a pliant companion of Nasser, shows that he intends to govern in his own right, balancing the army, the religious establishment and the West against the Soviet-backed old guard. What began as a change of tone becomes a change of direction.

The prison gates open for Muslim Brothers and other detainees who have languished since the Nasser years, and the newly freed carry their stories home to the villages and mosques. For the president it is a way of showing that a new era has begun, and of finding allies against the Marxists and Nasserists. For the Brotherhood it is a chance to return to public life.

Anwar Sadat presents himself as the Believer President, a man who prays before the cameras and speaks of faith and science as the foundation of the state. Al-Azhar is courted and the pulpit becomes a tool of government, while religious feeling is turned against the left. It is a powerful image, though one that may prove difficult to control.

The president announces that the age of the midnight knock is over and that Egypt will be a state of institutions and law. The tapes of the security services are burned on television, the powers of the sequestrators are curbed and the courts are promised independence. Whether this is genuine reform or merely the consolidation of one man's rule, the change is felt in every ministry.

Censorship is relaxed and the newspapers are allowed to publish criticism, argument and foreign opinion that would have been unthinkable before. The editors of al-Ahram and the provincial dailies test the limits of what may be said, and the Cairo cafes buzz with debate. The government hopes that an open press will win over the educated classes, even if some of what they read is unwelcome.

After years of reform, the Arab Socialist Union has become an empty shell, and the president decides to retire it. In its place rises a centrist party of government, the National Democratic Party, more suited to a state that courts Washington and foreign capital. The old Nasserists see the end of an era; the new ruling class sees only the start of one.

The first era of the revolution, one of struggle, mobilisation and war, is drawing to its close. Egypt now looks to consolidate what it has built and to prepare for a succession that must come sooner or later. The party elders, the army and the security services all know that the choice of who leads the Union into the 1980s will decide the character of the state.

The Vice President, a former air force commander admired for his discipline and his silence, is called to lead the party into the new decade. He is no ideologue and has little taste for speeches, but the officer corps trusts him and the bureaucracy finds him predictable. With him, the regime promises stability above all else.

The party's old ideologues, veterans of the Institute and the Charter drafts, move to take the reins themselves. They believe the revolution has been lost to cautious technocrats and corrupt officials and that only a purified Union can restore its mission. To the army and the businessmen this is a return to the dogmatism of the sixties; to the believers it is long overdue.

The constitution is amended and the limit on presidential terms falls away, making the Rais president for as long as he cares to serve. Loyal deputies hail the decision as a mark of the nation's trust, while critics warn that Egypt has acquired a new pharaoh in all but name. The state centres itself ever more firmly on a single man.

Decades after the Free Officers took the Abdin Palace, the revolution seems finally to rest on firm ground. The party is led, the economy turns, the frontiers are guarded and the people have a stake in the order they live in. Egypt can tell itself that the sacrifices of the sixties were not made in vain.

The public sector employs hundreds of thousands, yet no one in Cairo can say precisely what it owns or what it earns. Teams of auditors descend on the mills, ports and ministries, uncovering idle workers, forgotten assets and private enrichment under cover of state ownership. The inquiry offers a first step toward restoring the discipline that the revolution is said to demand.

The leadership resolves that the commanding heights of the economy must remain in public hands. Steel, textiles, power and transport are drawn tighter under ministerial control, and the great works of Helwan are expected to lead the nation toward industrial self-reliance. For the planners the state is the only agent big enough to bring Egypt out of poverty.

A reorganised Ministry of Planning is given the authority to set targets and allocate scarce foreign exchange among competing factories, ports and ministries. Its officials draw up balance sheets that few could have imagined a decade earlier, and they insist that a poor country at war cannot afford to waste a single pound. The plan becomes the language in which the state speaks to itself.

Egypt's leaders have long dreamed of a self-sufficient industrial base, and the steelworks at Helwan are the proof that the dream can be built in concrete. Resources are directed to iron, steel, engineering and chemicals before consumer goods, with Soviet technicians supervising the plant. It is a hard bargain, but it promises independence from foreign suppliers.

Workers' representatives are given seats on the boards of public companies, and a share of profit is set aside for them. The reform is presented as proof that the revolution does belong to the working man and not just to the manager. Foremen and union men learn to read balance sheets, while managers learn to live with their new colleagues.

The second five-year plan is announced with great ceremony, promising new factories, higher output and better wages from the Delta to Upper Egypt. It rests on loans, Soviet machinery and the patience of a nation under arms. If it succeeds, it will show that socialism can build as well as defend; if it fails, it will be remembered as one more promise of the old regime.

After years of sequestration, many families whose property was seized in the sixties are told that their assets will be returned. Landowners, merchants and old industrial houses emerge from the shadows, and the middle class gains new confidence. For the Nasserists it is a betrayal of the revolution; for the pragmatists it is the price of renewing the economy.

After the crossing of the Canal, the president issues the October Paper, a document calling for economic opening and the revival of private investment. Its authors argue that Egypt, having won back its pride on the battlefield, must now win its prosperity in the marketplace. The word Infitah, the opening, enters the political vocabulary and will not leave it for decades.

A new investment law offers foreign companies guarantees against nationalisation, relief from duties and the right to repatriate their profits. Bankers and contractors arrive in Cairo; free zones are planned at the Canal and Alexandria. Supporters see capital and technology flowing in at last, while sceptics fear that Egypt is selling its economic independence.

The oil price rise has made Riyadh, Kuwait and Abu Dhabi rich beyond imagining, and Cairo sends envoys to remind them of Egypt's sacrifices for the Arab cause. In return for political friendship and sound projects, the Gulf states are invited to invest in Egyptian banks, land and industry. It is an uneasy partnership between the Arab world's largest army and its largest bank accounts.

A new class of engineers, importers, managers and civil servants moves into modern flats, buys imported goods and sends its children to private schools. They are the beneficiaries of the opening, and their loyalty is to the order that allowed them to prosper. The state builds for them, sometimes at the expense of those who remain in the old quarters.

At last an economy emerges that serves the many rather than the few, with factories, farms, cooperatives and private enterprises each finding their place. The planners claim vindication and the people see more on the market stalls. The revolution can say it has not merely survived but delivered something tangible to the Egyptian household.

Cotton has been Egypt's wealth and burden since the days of Muhammad Ali, and the state now controls its sale to the world. The Marketing Board buys from the growers at fixed prices and sells at world rates, using the difference to finance the state's other ambitions. The system provides revenue and a degree of control, but the grower often feels he is the one who pays.

Consumer cooperatives open in towns and villages, selling subsidised bread, oil, sugar and tea at prices the poor can afford. The shop with a state sign over the door becomes one of the most visible signs of the revolution in daily life. Queues form, shortages come and go, but few Egyptians would wish to see the cooperatives disappear.

The tax system is reshaped to take more from the wealthy and less from those who work with their hands. Landowners, merchants and the new contractors face higher rates, while wage earners are spared. The measure is defended as a matter of simple justice, and the revenues are earmarked for schools, clinics and the war effort.

Clinics and hospitals are opened in provincial towns and rural districts, where a fellah once had to choose between an expensive doctor and no doctor at all. The state promises treatment without payment, a claim which is not always true in practice but which marks a real change. Bilharzia, trachoma and infant mortality are the enemies the new health service is built to fight.

Egypt must earn foreign exchange if it is to pay for wheat, machines and weapons, and the leadership launches a campaign to sell more of the country's output abroad. Cotton, textiles, rice and processed goods are pushed on Eastern and Western markets alike. Success means a stronger pound and fewer humiliating visits to creditors.

The High Dam, built with Soviet help against fierce Western opposition, now stands as the great monument of the revolution. Its turbines supply electricity to the Nile Valley, its reservoir regulates the river, and its power lines carry light to villages that never knew it. The dividend, long promised, begins to be paid in factories, fields and homes.

From the Sawt al-Arab transmitters, the voice of Cairo reaches coffeehouses and barracks from Morocco to the Gulf. The broadcasts carry news, song and political argument in the accents of Egyptian Arabic, and they have done more to spread the revolution than any army. The Union now seeks to make the most of this extraordinary asset.

The front with Israel runs along the Canal, but Egypt's strategic gaze also turns east, to Damascus, Baghdad and Amman. Cairo works to bind Syria and Iraq to its policy, to steady Jordan and to support the Palestinian cause on the Eastern Front. A united front in the Mashriq might at last make Israel face a threat on more than one frontier.

With Libya under Colonel Gaddafi and Sudan under Nimeiry, both new regimes steeped in Nasser's example, Egypt sees a chance to secure its southern and western flanks. The Tripoli Charter of 1969 pledged the three countries to common cause. Strengthened by their friendship, Cairo can look to the Nile and the desert as allies rather than risks.

The security services are brought within the Union's discipline, with party men set to watch the officers and the officers to watch the party. Informers sit in factories, universities and ministries, and files on the unreliable multiply. To its defenders this is a vigilant guard against conspiracies; to its critics it is the old fear in new clothes.

The leadership resolves that the secret services must answer to the party and to the law, not to ambitious men in the Interior Ministry. Powers of arrest are curbed, committees oversee the files, and officers of the Mukhabarat find themselves summoned to explain their budgets. The change is a quiet one, but many in Egypt remember the long years of fear.

With the revolutionary slogans spent and the treasury empty, Egypt turns to the engineers, economists and administrators who have long kept the state running. Zakaria Mohieddin, a Free Officer with a reputation for cool competence and little taste for rhetoric, is called to head a presidency of experts. The promise is simple: fewer speeches, more results.

The Council of Ministers is reconstituted as a body of specialists, with portfolios allotted by competence rather than by loyalty or revolutionary seniority. Engineers run the power stations, economists the treasury, and diplomats the foreign ministry. The politicians grumble, but the president answers that a country at war has no time for amateurs.

Zakaria Mohieddin has never been a popular figure, yet he is respected as a man who understands how the state works and what it can afford. His course is neither a rejection of the revolution nor a defence of it, but a sober attempt to manage its consequences. The first question before him is whether Egypt needs calm or speed.

The government decides that the first task is to calm the economy: contain prices, restrain spending and rebuild confidence before attempting anything bolder. Subsidies are examined with a sceptical eye, and the Central Bank is given room to breathe. It is an unglamorous programme, but the technocrats believe that a stable pound is worth more than any grand plan.

The technocrats argue that Egypt cannot save its way out of poverty and that the country must grow, even at the cost of some borrowing. Credit is directed to projects that promise returns within a few years, and ministers are told to cut through delays. The risk is a larger debt; the reward, a working economy at last.

Appointments in the ministries have long depended on family, party loyalty or the right word in the right ear. A new regime of examinations and promotion boards seeks to put the ablest candidates in the right posts and to close the door on the idle and the connected. The old guard of the bureaucracy resists quietly, as it always has.

The government sets about the tangled administration inherited from three revolutions, merging overlapping agencies and trimming layers of paperwork that every Egyptian has cursed at some point. Directors are made answerable for results, and files that once took months now move in weeks. A leaner machine is expected to serve a better-governed country.

Power is moved outward from the ministries of Cairo to the governors and local councils of the provinces. Roads, schools and water supplies are planned closer to the people they serve, and provincial officials gain some of the authority they have long sought. The experiment reveals how much of the country has been run from a single desk on the Nile.

As the years pass, the question that no minister likes to raise becomes difficult to avoid: what happens when this government has done its work? A state ruled by experts still needs a source of legitimacy, and the people will in time ask who has the right to govern them. The president must choose between strengthening his office and sharing authority.

The president concludes that a country as fragile as Egypt cannot afford a weak executive, and his office is endowed with wide powers to appoint, dismiss and decree. Ministers answer to him alone, and the assembly is relegated to a modest advisory role. The technocrat becomes something greater than a technocrat, and the stability of the state comes to rest on one man.

The president announces that the government of experts has fulfilled its purpose and that power should now return to the elected representatives of the people. Parties are allowed to organise, the assembly regains its voice, and ministers must justify their decisions before deputies. It is a risky step, but one that offers the republic a more durable foundation.

The treasury insists that Egypt cannot go on spending money it does not have. Ministries are required to account for every pound, the subsidy bill comes under scrutiny, and the budget is balanced on paper before it is balanced in life. The trade unions protest, but the finance minister calmly replies that discipline now is cheaper than a crisis later.

Egyptian officials travel to Washington to negotiate with the International Monetary Fund, cap in hand but with a clear list of what they will and will not accept. A loan promises relief for the exchequer, but the conditions mean tighter budgets and the loss of some cherished subsidies. Whatever the outcome, the streets of Cairo will have a view on it.

The Egyptian pound has for years been held at an artificial rate that favours importers and penalises exporters. The government now allows it to fall, hoping to make cotton, textiles and other goods competitive on world markets. The shopkeeper and the housewife will feel the pinch, and the minister must explain why that pinch is necessary.

Egypt's tax system is a patchwork of exemptions, special cases and unenforced rates that bring in little and irritate many. The ministry of finance replaces it with a simpler code, with clear rates and stricter collection. Merchants who once paid little now find an inspector at the door, and the treasury sees its income grow.

Goods entering Egypt through Alexandria, Port Said and Suez have long been subject to a maze of duties, permits and informal fees. The customs service is overhauled, tariffs are simplified and smuggling is attacked in earnest. Honest traders welcome the change; those who profited from confusion do not.

The National Planning Institute gathers economists, statisticians and engineers to study the country's resources and to suggest where each pound would do the most good. Its reports are dry but pointed, and ministers who ignore them do so at their peril. For the first time the government has a body able to say what the nation actually produces.

State companies are given freedom to set their own prices, hire their own managers and keep part of their profits. The supervising ministries lose some of their power, and factory directors are told that they will be judged on results, not obedience. If the experiment works, the public sector may at last begin to resemble a business.

Petrol, electricity and cooking gas have long been sold at prices that bear no relation to what they cost to produce. The government begins to raise them, gradually and with great care, freeing money for hospitals and schools. Every increase is a risk, for Egyptians remember how quickly bread and fuel have driven crowds into the streets.

Along the shores of the closed Canal, the government plans a zone of ports, warehouses and light industry, ready for the day the waterway reopens. Foreign firms are offered favourable terms, and engineers draw up plans for new quays and offices. The idea is to turn the wound of 1967 into a gateway for the future.

The factories of Helwan and Mahalla are old, worn and often poorly managed, and the technocrats bring in consultants and capital to refit them. New machinery, better training and sound accounting are promised to raise output from what already exists. Modernisation is not glamorous, but it may do more for Egypt than a dozen new projects.

After years of careful management, the Egyptian economy begins to function as its planners intended. Prices are more predictable, factories hum and the treasury can meet its obligations. Foreign visitors note the change, and ordinary families feel that the government finally knows what it is doing.

The government expands technical schools and polytechnics to train the machinists, electricians and draughtsmen that Egyptian industry sorely lacks. For too long the universities have produced lawyers and clerks while factories wait for skilled hands. A better-trained workforce is the surest investment the state can make.

Egypt's population is climbing quickly and the Nile Valley cannot support it indefinitely. A Population Council is formed to promote family planning through clinics and educational campaigns, a policy that the technocrats regard as simple arithmetic. Religious leaders view it with suspicion, and the government treads with great care.

Egypt needs money and cannot afford to be choosy about where it comes from. Envoys visit Moscow, Washington, the European capitals and the Gulf, each time presenting the same case: the country is worth lending to. The skilful borrower, the technocrats believe, is one who owes no single creditor so much that he must obey him.

Cairo declares that its policy will serve Egypt's interests rather than any bloc's. Soviet advisers remain at their posts and American diplomats are received with courtesy, while neither is allowed to dictate terms. It is a delicate balance that demands patience, discretion and a very steady hand.

A mission from the World Bank arrives in Cairo to study the Egyptian economy and to recommend projects worthy of support. Its experts tour irrigation works, roads and ports, and leave behind a thick report and a promise of credit. For the government it is a mark of confidence, and for the Bank, a test of Egyptian seriousness.

The republic has become a state run by managers: competent, cautious and more concerned with results than with slogans. The ministries function, the budgets are balanced and the president can discuss the country's affairs with experts rather than with partisans. Whether this is enough to inspire a nation remains to be seen.

The Society of the Muslim Brothers, once hunted by the revolution, now holds the reins of government. The Guidance Office, which used to meet in secret, advises ministers and its Murshid is received as a statesman. For its followers this is the fulfilment of decades of patience and prayer; for its enemies it is the beginning of a new and unfamiliar order.

The Murshid convenes his council of senior Brothers, men who spent years in the prisons of Nasser and learned to wait. Together they determine how swiftly to move, whom to trust, and how to reconcile the Society's vision with the realities of running a state. Their decisions shape the character of the new Egypt.

Under the leadership of Umar al-Tilmisani, the Brotherhood chooses the path of persuasion over confrontation. Violence is disavowed, the law is respected and the Society presents itself as a patient movement that will reform Egypt from within. Foreign capitals, watching nervously, begin to wonder whether this is a force they can work with.

The writings of Sayyid Qutb, executed in 1966, are read in secret by a younger generation that has no patience for compromise. Milestones calls for a vanguard of true believers to break with a society it declares ignorant of God. Where the Society's elders counsel restraint, the Qutbists demand a revolution of faith.

The Brotherhood decides to contest elections, to campaign in the villages and mosques and to take its message to the ballot box. Its candidates promise honesty, charity and a government that fears God more than it fears its own security service. Whatever the results, the Society is at last in open competition with its rivals.

The syndicates of doctors, engineers, lawyers and pharmacists are the voice of the educated middle class, and the Brothers set out to win them. Their candidates are disciplined, hardworking and well organised, and they offer services as well as sermons. A syndicate lost to the Society is a stronghold gained.

The Brotherhood and the revived Wafd, ancient rivals, discover that they share a common opponent in the establishment. A joint list is agreed, linking the liberal nationalism of the old parties with the religious mobilisation of the Society. It is an awkward marriage, but one that brings both an electoral advantage.

Al-Da'wa, the Brotherhood's monthly magazine, circulates in mosques, student unions and village shops, reaching readers who trust it more than the state press. It publishes sermons, editorials, news from the Muslim world and pointed criticism of those who rule. The printed word becomes the Society's most powerful instrument of persuasion.

Egypt's laws, schools, media and public life are brought into closer harmony with Islamic principles, step by step rather than in a single stroke. The Society's leaders argue that society must be prepared first, and that rushed imposition would breed resentment. Each year brings a little more of the new order, and a little less of the old.

The Special Apparatus, the secret wing that once carried out the Society's operations in the 1940s, is revived in the shadows. Its members are trained, armed and sworn to obey, and they gather intelligence on the regime's enemies. Those who remember the assassinations of old Egypt see in it a warning.

Following Qutb's reasoning, the vanguard declares that the society around it is jahiliyya, a state of ignorance comparable to the age before the Prophet. Cinemas, nightclubs, alcohol and secular schools are denounced and, where power allows, shut down. The ulema watch uneasily as the movement outruns their authority.

The armed forces are to be remade as an army of believers, with chaplains in every unit, prayer in every barracks and officers selected for piety as well as skill. The old professional officers resent the purge, and many fear that discipline will suffer. The Society insists that only a faithful army can defend a faithful state.

The Society's elite, now drawn from the committed, the disciplined and the zealous, becomes the true engine of the state. Its cadres sit in the ministries, in the mosques and in the army, bound by oath and by conviction. They believe they are the vanguard of a movement that will spread beyond Egypt's frontiers.

A committee of jurists, scholars and ministers is charged with drafting a legal code based on the Sharia, replacing the French-inspired statutes of the last century. Al-Azhar welcomes the project, secular lawyers condemn it, and the country's Christians wait anxiously for its details. Few acts could change Egyptian life more profoundly.

The founding generation of the Brotherhood is ageing, its leaders tired by prison and exile, and a new generation of activists comes forward. Raised in the student movements and professional syndicates, they have ideas and ambitions of their own. The Society must decide what kind of movement it will be in the decades to come.

Mustafa Mashhur, who has guided the secret organisation through years of repression, takes the helm. He values discipline, hierarchy and obedience, and he sees in the Society a body that must remain united at all costs. Under his leadership the Brotherhood is tightly run and resolute.

A circle of younger Brothers, headed by Abu al-Ela Madi, argues that the Society should embrace pluralism, democratic politics and a civil state with an Islamic reference. They are impatient with the old hierarchy and its secrecy. If they prevail, the Brotherhood may become a party among parties rather than a movement above them.

Egypt is proclaimed an Islamic state, its institutions, laws and daily life shaped by the Sharia and led by the Society of the Muslim Brothers. For many it is the culmination of a century of struggle against secular rule. For others it is the start of a new test, to show that an Islamic order can feed, protect and unite a nation.

With the backing of Saudi Arabia's Prince Muhammad al-Faisal, an Islamic bank is founded which refuses to deal in interest and instead shares profits and losses with its clients. Pious depositors flock to it, and the Gulf states take notice. It is both a financial institution and a statement about what an Islamic economy might look like.

A national zakat fund collects the alms that every Muslim owes and distributes them among the poor, the orphaned and the sick. Run through mosques and trusted committees, it reaches families that the state has never been able to help. The fund is both an act of faith and a quiet instrument of political loyalty.

Islamic investment companies such as al-Rayan promise returns that no bank could match, all in the name of God and honest profit. Millions of Egyptians, including emigrants returned from the Gulf, hand over their savings. The boom is spectacular, and the shrewd note that it depends on a steady stream of new depositors.

Hospitals and clinics run by the Society's medical syndicate treat the poor for little or nothing, staffed by doctors who see their work as both a profession and a duty. In the slums of Cairo and the villages of Upper Egypt, these hospitals are often better than the state can offer. They also win hearts and votes with every patient treated.

Fellahin have long been at the mercy of moneylenders and village creditors who charge ruinous rates. The Society's banks offer them loans without interest, repaid from the harvest, and tied to cooperative purchase of seed and fertiliser. The scheme makes the Brothers friends in places where the state is distrusted.

The Society's brothers in the Gulf, many of them wealthy merchants and professionals, send money home to build the Islamic economy. Funds flow into banks, land and construction, supported by networks of kinship and faith. It is capital that comes with expectations, and Cairo must take care not to be too grateful.

New enterprises, financed by Islamic funds and run according to Islamic principles, produce food, clothing and household goods for the pious market at home and abroad. A halal seal becomes a mark of trust from Cairo to Kuala Lumpur. The Society's merchants find that faith and profit are not always at odds.

The Society's vision of a moral economy takes shape: no usury, honest weights, charity built into the system and wealth answerable to God. Whether it can compete with the markets of the world is a question that its architects answer with confidence and its critics with doubt. For the time being, the poor of Egypt feel a little less alone.

From the mosques and the schools, the Society's preachers and teachers reach into every neighbourhood. They run lessons, youth clubs, clinics and burial funds, building a web of services that holds communities together. Where the state is absent, the Brothers are present.

Textbooks are rewritten, teachers retrained and Quranic study placed at the heart of the school day. The Society holds that the generation raised in this way will know both the Book and the modern sciences. Secular educators protest, but the schools of the Da'wa Networks are already full.

Egypt's Christians, perhaps a tenth of the population, ask what an Islamic state will mean for them. The Society's moderates reply with a compact between mosque and Church, guaranteeing worship, property and a place in public life. The Coptic Pope is cautious but willing to listen, and the radicals murmur at the concession.

The Society revives the old status of the dhimma, under which Christians and other non-Muslims enjoy protection but not equality. The Copts see in it a return to a second-class citizenship that they thought history had ended. Some of the ulema applaud while many quiet Egyptians fear for the consequences.

The Brotherhood is an international movement with branches and sympathisers across the Arab world. Contacts are renewed with the Brothers of Syria, Jordan, Sudan and Palestine, and delegations exchange letters, students and funds. Egypt, the mother of the movement, begins to see its influence extend well beyond its borders.

In Syria the Brothers have been in open conflict with the Baathist regime, which they regard as godless and sectarian. Cairo's Society gives them money, shelter and a voice in the press. Damascus protests angrily and the diplomatic temperature between the two capitals falls.

The Society declares the liberation of Jerusalem a duty on every believer, not a matter for diplomats alone. Volunteers are called, sermons are preached and the army is told that the cause is holy. The proclamation stirs the street and alarms every chancery in the region.

Rather than war, Cairo takes the diplomatic road and works through the Islamic Conference, bringing together the kings, presidents and emirs of the Muslim world. Riyadh, Islamabad and Tehran are courted as partners in a common cause. Egypt takes its place as the intellectual capital of a community of believers that spans continents.

The National Progressive Unionist Rally, known as the Tagammu, brings together Marxists, Nasserists and left-wing intellectuals under the banner of Khaled Mohieddin. A Free Officer who broke with Nasser's camp yet never with its ideals, he offers an independent left that will neither bow to Moscow nor submit to Washington. The experiment is bold, and its supporters are many and unruly.

Delegates from factories, universities, villages and trade unions meet at the Rally's congress to debate the future of the country. Speeches run long, resolutions are amended again and again, and the tobacco smoke thickens. It is the first time in years that Egyptian leftists have been free to argue in public about what their revolution should be.

Within the Rally two souls struggle for the heart of the movement. One is the Marxist tradition of class struggle and scientific socialism; the other the Nasserist legacy of national dignity and social justice. Khaled Mohieddin must decide which voice to follow, or learn to live with both.

The Marxist wing prevails, and the Rally speaks the language of class, of surplus value and of the historic mission of the working class. Its theorists argue that Nasser's reforms were half-measures that stopped short of true socialism. The communists of the old underground, long forced into silence, find a platform at last.

The Nasserist wing holds that the greatest strength of the left lies not in doctrine but in Nasser's heritage of national pride, social reform and Arab solidarity. It speaks to the fellahin, soldiers and government clerks who still keep the late Rais's picture on their walls. Marx may be admired in the study, but Nasser is loved in the street.

The state-controlled labour federation is loosened and workers are allowed to elect their own leaders and bargain freely. For the first time in many years, textile workers of Mahalla and steel workers of Helwan have unions that speak for them rather than for the ministry. The government loses a means of control, and gains a source of legitimacy.

Al-Ahali, the Rally's weekly newspaper, brings the left's arguments to the kiosks of Cairo and Alexandria. Its pages mix economic analysis, satire, cartoons and sharp criticism of the government. Censors keep a close eye on it, but its readers pass it from hand to hand until the print is worn.

The left rallies against the Infitah, which it regards as a betrayal of the revolution and a gift to speculators and foreign capital. Nasserists of the Union stand alongside Marxists and trade unionists, uniting around the defence of the public sector and the poor consumer. For once, the old divisions of the left are set aside.

The Rally's leaders ask what kind of democracy Egypt should build: one of competing parties, or one in which the people's organisations speak for the nation. The question is as old as the revolution, and neither answer comes without cost. Mohieddin's government must now decide how far to trust the people it claims to serve.

Open elections are held, with parties of the left, the right and the religious movements all free to compete. The ballot is a risk, for the Rally may find that its slogans win fewer votes than expected. Yet its leaders insist that socialism without freedom is a contradiction.

The Rally forms a broad popular front with the Communists and other forces of the left, setting up a state in which progressive parties govern together and opposition to the line is discouraged. Supporters see a bulwark against reaction; critics warn of the one-party model by another name. Unity is purchased at the cost of dissent.

Egypt claims to have found its own road to socialism, one rooted in the Nile Valley rather than in Moscow, Beijing or Belgrade. Its factories, farms and unions are run in the interests of those who work in them, and its politics reflect the character of its people. The left can say that it has built something distinctively Egyptian.

The Rally declares the public sector the foundation of Egypt's independence and the guarantee of its workers' livelihoods. Privatisation is ruled out, and managers are told to improve their factories rather than seek buyers. In the mills of the Delta, workers hear the news with relief.

Following the Yugoslav example, factory workers are given a direct voice in the running of their enterprises, electing councils that share in the management. Foremen, engineers and labourers sit round the same table to plan production. It is an experiment that excites some and frightens others, but no one can call it dull.

Industrial democracy councils are established in the major plants of Alexandria and the Delta, bringing workers, technicians and managers together in the same decision-making bodies. The councils are charged with setting production targets and dividing the bonus. Their critics fear chaos; their supporters see a new kind of factory.

A legal minimum wage is declared for workers in the public and private sectors, guaranteeing a floor beneath which no employer may fall. For the lowest paid it is the first assurance of its kind, and families in the poorer quarters of Cairo feel it immediately. Employers warn of higher costs and fewer jobs.

The new government turns its attention to the contractors, importers and speculators who have grown rich while ordinary Egyptians tighten their belts. Taxes on large fortunes and business profits are raised, and the tax inspectors are given new powers. Whether the wealthy will pay or flee remains to be seen.

In the countryside, fellahin pool their land, tools and labour in cooperative villages, sharing the harvest and the costs of seed, machinery and irrigation. The state offers advice and credit but lets the villagers manage their own affairs. For those who have been tenants and labourers all their lives, it is a new kind of dignity.

Great estates of public housing rise on the outskirts of Cairo, with flats for workers and their families at modest rents. They are not luxurious, but they have running water, electric light and a roof that does not leak. The left's argument that every citizen is entitled to a decent home is finally made concrete.

At last the economy begins to reflect the left's principles: wages are protected, prices are regulated and the profits of enterprise are shared more widely. The experiment has not been easy, and the shops are not always full, but few workers would want to return to the old arrangements. Fairness, the Rally claims, is also good economics.

Education was made free for all by the revolution, and fees later crept back at the margins. The Rally restores the principle in full, so that no child is excluded from school or university by poverty. Teachers are recruited by the thousand and classrooms built in the villages.

The Rally sponsors a national women's union to campaign for equal pay, access to education and an end to the legal disabilities that burden Egyptian women. The traditional clergy objects strongly, while women in the factories and universities rally to its banner. A revolution that overlooks half the nation, its advocates say, is only half a revolution.

Khaled Mohieddin looks to Belgrade, where Tito has shown that a socialist state can stand outside both blocs and still prosper. Yugoslav advisers, engineers and economists are invited to Cairo, and delegations travel to study workers' councils and the market socialism of the Balkans. Egypt, the friendship implies, is another leader of the non-aligned.

Yugoslavia offers Egypt a credit to buy machinery, equipment and technical assistance. The terms are generous and the conditions are few, for Tito remembers the Non-Aligned partnership forged with Nasser. Yugoslav firms begin to build and equip Egyptian plants.

The Rally throws itself into the international struggle against imperialism, aligning Egypt with Algeria, Cuba, Vietnam and the liberation movements of Africa and Asia. Moscow welcomes the solidarity, while Washington notes with displeasure. Egypt reclaims the revolutionary voice it once held at Bandung.

The decade of the Infitah has produced a new class of contractors, importers and middlemen who have grown rich on commissions and connections. They are not bound by the old socialist pieties, and they see no reason to hide their wealth. Now they aspire to rule rather than merely to profit.

Within the new class two interests compete: the contractors who build the new Egypt and the importers who supply it with goods from abroad. Both prosper under the opening, but their needs differ, and the government must favour one or the other. The choice will shape the character of the business republic.

The government favours the builders, men such as Osman Ahmed Osman whose companies have laid roads, bridges and apartment blocks across the country. Their cranes dominate the skyline, and they need no lessons on how to deal with ministers. Egypt is declared to be a building site, and the contractors its masters.

The government favours the importers, who bring television sets, refrigerators, cars and cheap clothing to a public that has long done without. The shops of Cairo fill, and the customers are grateful. Local manufacturers complain that they cannot compete, but the importers answer that the people want to buy.

Cranes rise in every quarter of Cairo and Alexandria as contractors compete for ministry orders. Apartment blocks, hotels and offices appear in months, financed by public funds and private speculation. The boom brings jobs, fortunes and a good deal of dust.

Egyptian contractors follow the petrodollars to the Gulf, building roads, ports and palaces for the emirs and the kings. The work is profitable, and it employs thousands of Egyptian engineers and labourers who send their wages home. In Riyadh and Kuwait City, the name of Egypt is again heard with respect.

Glass and concrete towers rise on the banks of the Nile, housing banks, hotels and the offices of foreign firms. They are monuments to the new wealth, visible from every quarter of the city. Not everyone is pleased to see the horizon of Cairo given over to speculators, and the rents climb with the floors.

Import licences, once reserved for state agencies, are now distributed to friends of the government and their associates. Whoever holds the right paper can earn a fortune on a single shipment. The system rewards loyalty far more than efficiency, and everyone in the commercial quarters knows it.

Port Said, battered by the war, is declared a free city, with low duties and few restrictions on trade. Merchants, smugglers and bargain hunters throng the quays, and goods of every origin pass through its warehouses. It is the Infitah in its purest form, and a standing temptation to every Egyptian trader.

Foreign firms appoint Egyptian agents to represent their products, and the agents become the sole gatekeepers of imported goods. A single well-placed agency, whether for cars, pharmaceuticals or machinery, can make a family rich for a generation. The government is happy to oblige its friends and foreign partners alike.

The state, short of cash and long of enterprises, begins to sell the factories, hotels and trading companies built under the socialist years. Buyers are not hard to find, and many have excellent connections. The workers of the Delta watch with dismay as the revolution's legacy is auctioned off.

Investors are offered years of freedom from taxation if they will build, hire and export. Foreign firms and local entrepreneurs alike rush to take advantage, and new plants rise in the desert beyond Cairo. The treasury loses revenue today in the hope of gaining much more tomorrow.

Private banks, joint ventures and foreign institutions open their doors in Cairo and Alexandria, offering credit on terms the state banks never dared. Businessmen who once begged for ministry loans now choose among competing lenders. Behind the marble counters, a new financial power takes shape.

The Cairo and Alexandria bourses, closed to speculation since the nationalisations, reopen in earnest. Brokers once more shout on the floor, and a new generation of investors watches the boards with fierce interest. The old exchange, which once rivalled the great markets of Europe, comes back to life.

The new class discovers that newspapers can be bought, and their editors, columnists and proprietors turn out to be surprisingly cooperative. Praise for the opening fills the columns, and criticism is scarcer than before. Public opinion, it seems, is a commodity like any other.

Ministers and senior officials find that their salaries are only part of their income, and that consultancies, directorships and gifts from grateful contractors come with the position. The line between public service and private enterprise blurs. Egyptians know the price of everything and the cost of every signature.

Companies of private guards, many of them retired police and army men, protect the villas, offices and shopping arcades of the wealthy. The state police, overstretched and underpaid, make no objection. The republic of the contractors is learning that those who own the property must also defend it.

The business class has built fortunes and political power in a single decade, but the poor of Egypt have noticed. Strikes, bread riots and street anger threaten the fragile peace on which the fortunes rest. The new class must decide whether to buy off its critics or break them.

The business leaders conclude that stability is worth a price, and a portion of their profits is directed to subsidies, wages and public works. Bread stays cheap, rents are held and the slums are quieter. It is a bargain between rich and poor, struck for the sake of a calm in which both can continue as they are.

The factory gates are closed, the strike leaders arrested and the police sent into the working districts. The business class holds that order is the first condition of profit, and that wages cannot be dictated from the street. The workers learn that the republic of the contractors will not bend.

Egypt has become a republic of contractors, in which the men who build and import decide what the government does. The state is stable, the cranes still swing and the money still flows. Whether anyone beyond the business class believes in it is another matter.

With the revolution in retreat, Egypt turns to the old families of the provinces: the great landowners, the village headmen and the heads of the leading clans. They are conservative, local and practical, and they know the countryside as Cairo's officials never will. A government of notables promises order, continuity and a measured pace.

The notables must decide how to rule. They may work through the umdas, the village headmen who answer to the state yet speak for their neighbours, or turn to the elders and councils of the clans. Either way, they promise to bring the countryside back into the political order.

The umdas, the headmen of the villages, are given back the authority they enjoyed before the revolution: to settle disputes, to keep the peace and to speak for the people of their communities. They are reliable, influential and entirely local. The villages of the Delta and the Nile Valley return to the rhythm of their ancestors.

A council of elders, drawn from the oldest and most respected families, advises the government on matters of custom, land and public order. Its members are chosen for their standing rather than their ideology. It is a conservative body, but its word carries weight in the countryside.

An assembly of notables meets in Cairo, bringing together landowners, merchants, headmen and religious leaders from every province. It is not a parliament in the modern sense, but it gives the old elite a voice in national affairs. Its debates are slow, courteous and a little old-fashioned.

The Sufi orders, which count millions of followers in the villages and quarters of Egypt, are given the state's patronage. Their saints' festivals are supported, their shaykhs honoured and their members taught that loyalty to the nation is a form of devotion. In an age of fierce religious politics, Sufism offers a gentler path.

The notables insist that society rests on the family and on religion, and the state is made to reflect it. Marriage, morality and the education of children are held to be matters for the household and the mosque. For many Egyptians, in the villages especially, it is a vision of life that feels familiar.

Rural credit banks bring cheap loans to farmers who have always depended on moneylenders and village creditors. The notables are the guarantors of local loans, and the system strengthens their own standing. The fellah finds the harvest a little less precarious.

The land registry is renewed, so that holdings, boundaries and rights are properly recorded for the first time. Disputes that have simmered for generations can now be settled with deeds and maps. Landowners are reassured, though the tax collectors also find that they now have a means of counting.

Small workshops, mills and presses spring up in the villages, processing local produce and providing work close to home. Young men who might otherwise have left for Cairo find a trade near their fathers' fields. It is development on a human scale, and the notables are proud of it.

The gins and mills of the Delta, which turn the harvest into cotton fibre, are modernised and expanded under the patronage of the notables. The white crop that once made Egypt famous is again processed at home rather than shipped raw. Local prosperity comes slowly, but it is solid.

The notables hold that a household, a village and a state alike must live within their means. Spending is trimmed, subsidies are limited and the debt is brought under control. It is a cautious, thrifty policy of the kind that suits provincial minds and prudent landlords.

The government of notables prefers hospitality to heroics, and its diplomacy is one of courtesy and quiet friendship. Envoys are sent to Khartoum, Tripoli and Amman with gifts and good wishes rather than demands. Egypt asks only that her neighbours treat her as a respected elder.

Each year thousands of Egyptian pilgrims travel to Mecca, and the government turns their journey into an instrument of statecraft. Delegations meet the Saudi princes, and arrangements are made on quotas, transport and trade. Pilgrimage, the notables note, is the oldest road between Cairo and Riyadh.

The country is orderly: the village is at peace, the harvest is brought in, the budget balances and the old families keep watch. The notables have not made a revolution, but they have restored something many Egyptians missed. It is a society that knows its place and is, for the most part, content with it.

The ghafirs, the traditional village watchmen, are put on a regular footing and armed with authority as well as a stick. They know everyone in their villages and every path between the fields. The police of the towns find that the countryside is quieter than before.

In Upper Egypt, feuds between families have lasted for generations, settled by the gun or the knife. The notables use their prestige to convene reconciliation councils where blood-money is agreed and old enmities are laid to rest. The Said, long neglected, begins to enjoy a peace that no army could have imposed.

The notables seek an understanding with the army, offering recruits, loyalty and local order in return for being left to manage their own affairs. The officers, themselves sons of provincial families, find much common ground. Cairo and the countryside reach an accommodation that both can live with.

The older generation of notables cannot rule for ever, and the question of who will inherit their influence grows pressing. Will it pass to the sons of the great landed families, or to the educated city men who have made their fortunes in trade and the professions? The answer will define the character of the order.

The heir is a landowner of the old school, schooled in his father's fields and committed to the rural order. He understands the harvest, the irrigation channels and the ways of the villages, and he distrusts the city. Under him the notables remain what they have always been: the aristocracy of the Egyptian countryside.

The heir is a lawyer, merchant or physician of the provincial towns, educated in the city and at ease in both worlds. He carries the old families' standing into the modern economy and sees the future in commerce and the professions. With him the notables take on the manners of a new middle class.

Born in the merchant houses and customs offices of Port Said, the Free Economy Movement has long argued that Egypt's socialist experiment strangled the very traders who once made the canal cities rich. With its supporters now in government, the promise is a country open to capital and commerce, though the bureaucrats and the unions will not surrender their privileges quietly.

The movement's economists agree that the state must withdraw from the marketplace, but not on how quickly. One camp wants to cut the knot in a single stroke and let the market find its level; the other counsels patience and legal groundwork. Whichever path is chosen will shape how many Egyptians remain loyal to the new order.

Subsidies are slashed, tariffs torn down and the pound is exposed to the market almost overnight. The reformers promise that the pain will be brief and the rewards lasting, but in the bread queues of Cairo and the mill towns of the Delta, patience is in short supply and the old guard is already whispering of unrest.

Rather than risk the streets, the government dismantles controls one ministry and one commodity at a time, drafting new commercial codes and easing licensing rules as it goes. The pace frustrates the purists of the movement, but merchants and civil servants alike can adjust, and the reform is far harder to portray as an act of betrayal.

For two decades the state has decided what a loaf of bread, a kilo of sugar and a metre of cloth should cost. Now the ledgers of the supply ministries are closed and prices are left to the bazaar. Traders rejoice at the freedom to profit, while families on fixed wages count every piastre and wonder who this freedom is really for.

Nasser's great state companies, bloated with clerks and loss-making for years, are put up for sale, merged or simply closed. Investors circle the textile mills and the engineering works of Helwan. The unions denounce what they call a fire sale of the nation's inheritance, but the treasury is relieved of burdens it could no longer carry.

Along the canal and the Mediterranean coast, customs barriers fall and foreign firms are invited to build, ship and trade on generous terms. Planners dream of Suez and Alexandria as great entrepots linking three continents, free of the permits and inspections that have made doing business in Egypt such a trial.

The tangled system of surtaxes and levies inherited from the socialist years is swept away in favour of a simple, low and predictable rate. Accountants and shopkeepers celebrate; the movement argues that honest reporting will follow lower rates. Critics counter that the burden has merely been lifted from the wealthy and shifted onto the poor.

Licensing boards, inspection regimes and sprawling rulebooks are cut back to a bare minimum, on the principle that the entrepreneur knows his business better than any official. Businesses spring up in cramped Cairo workshops and Delta warehouses alike, although safety and labour standards are left to the conscience of the employer.

Egypt turns its face to the world market. Import restrictions are lifted and exporters are no longer bound to state trading agencies, while Western chambers of commerce praise the new openness. Local manufacturers, long sheltered behind tariff walls, must now learn to compete with the goods flooding in through the ports.

The Central Bank steps back, and the Egyptian pound is left to find its own value against the dollar and the pound sterling.
