Exporters of cotton and raw materials welcome the change, but every importer and every household that buys foreign goods feels the swing of the exchange rate in the price of daily life.

The Mugamma, the vast government building overlooking Tahrir Square, has become a byword for queues, stamps and delay. The movement vows to shrink it, cutting posts, merging departments and abolishing whole layers of paperwork. For the thousands of employees whose livelihoods depend on the civil service, the cut is a declaration of war.

Where the state has struggled to keep classrooms and wards open, the government now invites private providers to take over. Fee-paying schools and clinics appear in the better districts of Cairo and Alexandria and standards rise for those who can afford them, while the poor are left to a public system that receives ever less attention.

The pace of reform has produced winners and losers, and the losers are organising. Laid-off clerks, striking mill workers and an uneasy officer corps gather in the cafes and mosques. The movement's leaders must now decide whether to soften their programme or stand firm against a growing tide of resentment.

Recognising that a market economy cannot survive on the goodwill of the comfortable alone, the government quietly builds a modest floor beneath the poorest. Basic support for the unemployed, the old and the sick takes the sharpest edge from the grievances of the street, and the movement's pragmatists claim vindication.

The leadership refuses to bend. Strikes are met with the police, critics are warned that reform is not a matter for negotiation, and those who object are told that the market will repay their sacrifice in time. Order is kept on the streets of Cairo, but the bitterness of those left behind runs deep.

The vision of the movement's founders is within reach. Glass offices rise in Cairo, ships queue at the free ports and foreign banks vie to lend. Whether Egypt becomes a trading city-state in spirit or merely a country of two nations, the old state-run economy has been replaced by something its architects scarcely dared hope for.

The movement holds that a nation of traders has no need for an army that swallows a vast share of the national income. Redundant formations are disbanded, the ranks are trimmed and the officer corps is put on notice that its privileges are no longer sacrosanct. The generals grumble, but Israel's guns remain far away from the trading floors.

Instead of running its own arms factories, Egypt turns to private firms and foreign suppliers to equip its forces. Western defence companies open offices in Cairo and tender for contracts that once belonged to state enterprises. The army is told to buy what it needs on the market, as any business would.

Egypt abandons the politics of blocs and sells to anyone with the means to buy. Delegations from Washington, Bonn, Tokyo and even Moscow find Cairo eager to sign. For the movement, commerce is the best foreign policy, and a country that trades with all can quarrel with none.

Scientists, agronomists and engineers who watched the high dam rise at Aswan have come to fear what it may cost the river that has fed Egypt since the pharaohs. Now their movement holds the reins of government, determined that the Nile be treated as a living inheritance rather than a resource to be spent.

The Friends of the Nile are united in their love of the river but divided about the future. Some insist that Egypt's salvation lies in healing the damage done to the valley and the Delta; others look to the desert sun, remembering the solar engines built beside the Nile at Maadi before the Great War. The choice will define the nation.

The government turns its attention to the fields and the water that feeds them. Irrigation canals are repaired, runoff is controlled and farmers are taught to work with the river's rhythms rather than against them. It is a patient programme, with little of the glamour of heavy industry, but one that speaks to the oldest instincts of the Egyptian countryside.

Half a century ago an American inventor named Frank Shuman built a solar-powered irrigation plant at Maadi, only for the Great War to cut short his dream. The Friends of the Nile resolve to finish what he began, and to make the sun that scorches the desert into the engine of a new Egypt.

Since the dam closed the flood, the fertile silt that once enriched the valley has settled behind the walls at Aswan, and farmers have turned to costly chemical fertiliser. Engineers now draw up plans to release and carry sediment downstream, restoring a little of the natural bounty that gave Egypt its ancient name of the Black Land.

Without the silt to replenish it, the Delta coast is slowly retreating before the Mediterranean, and salt creeps into fields and wells. The government builds barriers and plants shorelines, determined to hold back the sea from Alexandria and the northern farmlands, whose loss would be a wound that the nation could not easily heal.

The lagoons of the northern Delta have long supported fishing communities, now struggling with silted channels and polluted water. By cleaning the shallows, regulating catches and restoring the fish stocks, the government hopes to give thousands of fellahin and fishermen a living, and to show that conservation can feed as well as protect.

In the open desert west of the Nile, the first solar arrays are raised to turn sunlight into power and pumping water. Where Shuman's mirrors once stood in the sand at Maadi, a new generation of engineers breaks ground in the New Valley, convinced that Egypt's brightest resource has been waiting there all along.

On the Red Sea coast, where the wind blows steadily across the barren shore, turbines begin to turn above the dunes. The scheme is bold and unfamiliar, derided by sceptics as a toy for visionaries, yet it promises power without smoke and a measure of independence from imported fuel.

Smoke over Helwan, tanneries fouling the river and chemical works discharging into the canals have made the price of industrial progress painfully visible. The Friends of the Nile impose new standards on the factories, forcing owners to clean up or pay the penalty. Output may suffer, but the health of the nation's children improves.

The capital sprawls ever outward, swallowing the farmland that once fed it under apartment blocks and brick kilns. The government draws a line around the city and plants trees and parks within it, giving the crowded millions of Cairo some room to breathe and a reminder that their city grew from the green valley.

The Nile does not belong to Egypt alone. Envoys travel to Khartoum and Addis Ababa with an unfamiliar message, that the river's waters should be shared by agreement rather than guarded by threats. Whether upstream capitals trust Cairo's sudden gentleness remains to be seen.

As the world's first great conference on the human environment convenes, Egypt arrives with a delegation that is eager to be heard. For a nation long accustomed to speaking the language of revolution and war, the language of rivers, soil and air is a new way to win friends, particularly among the Nordic democracies.

The river that sustained the pharaohs begins to recover its health. Farmers speak of better harvests, the coast holds against the sea and the desert shimmers with new power. The Friends of the Nile have shown that Egypt can modernise without sacrificing its oldest and most precious inheritance.

The Friends of the Nile open the political arena, calling an assembly in which agronomists, doctors, villagers and delegates of the river communities have a voice. It is a strange parliament, closer to a town meeting than a party congress, but it gives a government of scientists the legitimacy it needs to carry out its programme.

The movement turns its philosophy into a national story, one that reminds Egyptians that they are, and always have been, a people of the river. Neither East nor West, this identity belongs to the farmer, the boatman and the townsman alike, and offers a unity that no bloc or ideology has been able to provide.

The high dam stands at the heart of the movement's dilemma. It has brought power and secured the harvest against drought, but it has also altered the river for ever. The Friends of the Nile must now decide whether to embrace the dam as a fact of life or to make it answer for what it has taken.

Pragmatists in the government argue that the dam cannot be undone and should be put to the best possible use. Turbines are refitted, reservoir management is improved and the stored water is released with care. Egypt accepts the dam, with its blessings and its burdens, as part of the modern river.

Others insist that the dam's consequences are too grave to ignore. Teams of scientists and engineers fan out across the valley to tackle salinity, erosion and the loss of silt, while farmers receive aid to restore their exhausted soils. The government commits itself to a long and costly campaign against the unintended harm of the great project.

The solar fields and wind farms of the desert need workers as well as engineers. Young men from overcrowded villages find work building, maintaining and guarding the new plants, and settlements spring up on the edge of the sand. The Friends of the Nile hope that clean power will bring employment as well as light.

The movement is no pacifist society, and Israeli guns still shell the canal towns. Its defence policy is built around protecting the valley, the dam and the farmland, with local militias and well-prepared defences rather than costly offensive forces. Egypt will defend its soil, but it will not squander its wealth on conquest.

Beyond the first water talks, Cairo proposes something bolder: a joint authority with Sudan to manage the river as a shared inheritance. If Khartoum accepts, the old suspicion between upstream and downstream might give way to cooperation, and the Nile could become a bond rather than a source of quarrel.

Ali Sabri has long commanded the machinery behind the throne: the Arab Socialist Union, the security services and the loyalist wing of the army. Now the Centres of Power step into the open. Under the Vanguard, the revolution is to be defended not by charisma, but by an organised and disciplined apparatus.

Delegates from every governorate gather in Cairo for a congress meant to give the new order a founding charter. Speeches praise the revolution and the working masses; behind the scenes, the apparatus hammers out who will speak for the party. From this hall emerges the leadership that Egypt's socialism was lacking.

Sabri's allies are not of one mind. The ideologues of the party want to rule through committees, congresses and mass organisation, while the men of the Interior Ministry and the intelligence services trust in files, informers and the knock at the door. The Vanguard must decide which will be the backbone of the state.

The party becomes the skeleton of the nation. Every ministry, factory, village and university has its branch and its cadres, and no appointment of consequence is made without their blessing. The model is Moscow, adapted to the Nile, and its promise is a government that listens to the people only through a single trusted channel.

Authority flows from the offices of the Interior Ministry and the intelligence services rather than from congresses. Under Sharawi Gomaa, the Mukhabarat becomes the final arbiter of who may speak, travel or be promoted. The revolution is secure, but only because every citizen suspects that someone is listening.

Committees of trusted workers and party members are given the right to inspect offices, factories and cooperatives, and to report on waste and dishonesty. The Vanguard presents them as the people watching over their servants. Bureaucrats see them as spies, and the line between civic duty and denunciation is often hard to find.

Schools, colleges and youth halls fall under the banner of the Arab Socialist Youth. Teenagers are drilled in the speeches of the revolution, sent to summer camps and encouraged to watch their elders for signs of bourgeois deviation. A generation raised in the shadow of defeat is being shaped to become the Vanguard's own.

A single directorate now decides what Egypt reads, hears and watches. Editors submit proofs before publication, film scripts pass through the ministry and even the verses sung at village weddings are listened to. The authorities speak of protecting the revolution from imperialist propaganda, though the silence in the cafes says more.

In the basements of the Interior Ministry, cabinets fill with dossiers on ministers, officers, journalists and shopkeepers alike. Every phone call and every private grievance is potentially a matter of record. The security chiefs know that a regime that knows everything about its citizens has little need to fear them.

After the humiliation of 1967, the Vanguard does not trust the generals, whose loyalty is to the army and to the memory of Nasser rather than to the party. Names are struck from the lists, commanders are retired or arrested and loyal officers rise. The army learns that it serves the apparatus, not the other way around.

The last rivals have been silenced, the last factions absorbed, and the Vanguard speaks with a single voice. Posters bring the leader's portrait to every wall in the land. The cult of unity is complete, and the question of who will lead Egypt after him can no longer be asked aloud.

The state is more tightly organised than ever before, and the thoughts of its leaders turn to the question that haunts every system built around one centre: what comes after? Different wings of the apparatus have their candidates, and each knows that whoever inherits the Centres of Power will hold the whole country.

The Interior Minister, master of the security services, takes the helm. Sharawi Gomaa has spent years collecting the secrets on which the regime depends, and he now rules as he has always worked, quietly, thoroughly and with the file always open on his desk. Egypt becomes a state in which order matters before everything else.

The president's trusted secretary and keeper of the intelligence portfolio, Sami Sharaf, has lived all his career in the shadow of power. Now he steps into the light, carrying the loyalty of the secret services and the confidence of Moscow. His presidency promises continuity with the past and a close embrace with the Soviet Union.

Rather than hand the state to a single man, the Vanguard chooses a council of the party's senior figures, in imitation of the Soviet leadership after Stalin. The arrangement reassures the cadres that no strongman will rise above them, though the cost is slower decisions and quiet rivalries behind the closed doors of the central committee.

The revolution is fully institutionalised. A disciplined party, a loyal army, heavy industry along the Nile and a front of friendly states beyond the frontier have turned Ali Sabri's vision from a faction's slogan into the settled order of the nation. Egypt has become a socialist republic that its builders believe is built to last.

The Vanguard turns to the Soviet model, with its five-year plans, its production quotas and its confidence that scientific planning can overcome backwardness. Advisers from Moscow help draft targets for steel, cotton and electricity. The task is vast, but the planners believe that what Russia achieved in a generation, Egypt can achieve in one as well.

Cranes rise over Cairo and the valley as the state pours resources into heavy industry. New plants for steel, machinery and chemicals are meant to carry Egypt from a cotton-exporting country to an industrial power. Workers march to the sites under banners praising the plan, though the cost of such ambitions weighs heavily on the national budget.

Engineers from the Soviet Union arrive at the great steelworks of Helwan, bringing blueprints, technicians and a fraternal confidence in the future. They teach Egyptian workers to run the furnaces and rolling mills, and leave behind a generation trained in the Soviet manner. Yet the presence of so many foreign experts stirs resentment in some quarters.

What remains of foreign finance in Egypt is brought under the control of the state. Branches of British, French and other banks are taken over in the name of the people, their reserves absorbed into the national treasury. The capitals of the West protest loudly, but the Vanguard answers that economic independence is not for sale.

The state sets the price of bread, fuel, cloth and rent, and enforces it with inspectors and ration cards. For the poor, the system offers security against the cruelties of the market. For the economists, it hides shortages and distorts production, but the Vanguard rejects any suggestion that the people's welfare should depend on supply and demand.

Egypt's cotton, rice and textiles flow east in exchange for machinery, spare parts and military supplies, settled in barter agreements rather than hard currency. The arrangement ties the economy ever closer to the socialist bloc and shields it from the whims of Western markets, even as it binds the country to the plans of its partners.

The great industrial drive reaches its goal. New factories hum across the land, a skilled workforce handles the machinery and the products of Egyptian plants appear in the shops and on the shelves. The Vanguard can point to the smokestacks as proof that the revolution has built what the old regime and the colonial powers never allowed.

The state takes sole control of the purchase and distribution of grain. Village cooperatives deliver their harvest to government depots at fixed rates, ensuring cheap bread for the cities and a steady revenue for the treasury. The fellahin, who work the land, feel the pinch, but the Vanguard asks them to be patient for the sake of the revolution.

Teachers, students and party volunteers fan out through the villages with slates, primers and lanterns, determined to teach the millions who cannot read. Night classes fill with farmers and washerwomen learning the letters of the Quran and of the party newspapers alike. The Vanguard believes that a literate people is a people that can be led to socialism.

On the edge of the old capital rise rows of apartment blocks for factory workers and their families, with schools, clinics and cooperatives close by. The Vanguard presents them as the dawn of a new city built by and for the working class. For families leaving the tenements of Cairo, the new flats are a glimpse of something better.

The friendship pact with the Soviet Union is deepened into a true alliance. Moscow pledges its weapons, advisers and political protection, and Cairo opens its military and diplomatic life to a close partner. For Egypt, it is a guarantee against Israel; for the West, a sign that the country has chosen its camp.

Soviet warships gain the right to use the harbours of Alexandria and Mersa Matruh, bringing the Mediterranean squadron within easy reach of the American Sixth Fleet. Sailors in grey uniforms walk the quays of the old port. The arrangement strengthens the shield over Egypt, but critics at home speak darkly of a foreign base on Arab soil.

Soviet-manned missile batteries and fighters take up positions along the canal and over the Delta, closing the skies that Israeli aircraft once ruled. Pilots and crews who speak no Arabic hold the line side by side with Egyptian gunners. Cairo can breathe again, though the price is a dependence that grows with every new squadron.

Cairo throws open its arsenals and training camps to the Palestinian fedayeen and to revolutionary movements across Arabia and the Horn of Africa. The Vanguard sees a duty to fight imperialism wherever it appears. Money, weapons and advisers flow outward, and the neighbouring monarchs look nervously towards the Nile.

Syria, Libya, Iraq, Algeria and the radical states of Arabia gather behind Egypt in a common front against Israel and its Western friends. Summit communiques ring with defiance, and the capitals of the Arab world are bound together by a shared enemy and Soviet arms. The Vanguard has moved Egypt from the head of one coalition to the leadership of another.

The Vanguard calls on the entire nation to prepare for the great struggle. Factories convert to war production, reservists are enrolled and the party's mass organisations drill in the squares of every town. The Egyptian people are told that victory belongs to those who are ready to give everything, and that the hour is near.

The communists who were jailed and driven underground under Nasser now rule from the presidential palace. The republic is renamed in the people's name, the old order is swept aside and the revolution begins again, this time in earnest. In the mosques and the bazaars, however, there are many who regard the new masters with fear.

Veterans of the prisons of Abu Zaabal and the Kharga oasis take their seats in the Central Committee. Men and women who spent years debating Marx in cells now have to govern a country of thirty million. The committee's task is to turn long-nursed theory into a programme that fellahin and factory workers can recognise.

The founders of Egyptian communism are divided. Moscow offers experience, arms and a settled model of the planned state; Peking offers a revolution built on the peasantry and the spirit of self-reliance. The party must choose which of the two great teachers to follow, knowing that the choice will shape the republic for a generation.

The party looks to Moscow, adopting its institutions, its planning methods and its place in the socialist bloc. Soviet advisers fill the ministries, delegations travel to Moscow for training and the Egyptian economy is reorganised on a pattern proven in Russia. The road is well-trodden, and the rewards are the friendship and the weapons of a superpower.

Impressed by the revolutionary energy of Mao's China, a section of the leadership turns away from Moscow. Egypt, they argue, is a land of peasants, and the revolution must be built in the villages rather than the ministries. The break with the Soviet Union is bitter, but Peking opens its arms to a new ally on the Nile.

A State Planning Committee is established in Cairo, with Soviet economists at its elbow. Production targets are set for every mill and mine, and the traditional bazaar economy yields to quotas and plans. The planners are confident that rational direction will transform the Nile Valley, though the clerks who must meet the targets are less certain.

A new ministry is charged with building the foundations of socialist power: steel, machinery, munitions and the factories that make them. In Cairo and the industrial belt around it, shops and furnaces expand under the supervision of party engineers. The ministry's leaders speak openly of an Egypt that makes its own tanks and guns.

Cairo petitions Moscow for a place in the economic community of the socialist states. Membership would bring planned trade, technical aid and a guaranteed market for Egyptian cotton, but also the obligation to fit the national economy into a wider scheme set by others. The decision rests with the Soviet leadership.

Following the Chinese example, the land of the Delta is organised into great communes in which farmers work, eat and study together under party guidance. Cadres praise the end of the landlord and the moneylender, but the fellahin, who have a long attachment to their own plots, look on the new arrangements with uncertainty.

Egypt resolves to depend on no foreign power. Spare parts are made at home, the workshops are encouraged to improvise, and sanctions and embargoes are treated as a challenge to be met rather than a danger to be avoided. The party's slogan holds that a nation which relies on its own strength can never be starved into submission.

The party's cadres are sent out to live among the people, listening to their grievances and carrying them back to the centre, and then returning with policies explained in the people's own words. It is a method designed to keep the revolution from hardening into a bureaucracy, and to keep the leadership rooted in the fields.

Thousands of village youths are given a few months of medical training and sent home with a satchel of herbs, bandages and simple medicines. They are not true physicians, but for the first time the villages of Upper Egypt have someone to treat their fevers and deliver their babies. The programme becomes a symbol of the republic's care for the poor.

The loose rural cooperatives of the Nasser years are merged into large collective farms under party supervision. The planners promise machinery, efficiency and an end to the fragmentation of the land. Many peasants resent the loss of control over their own fields, and the officials sent to oversee them are not always welcome.

The last pockets of private enterprise, from workshops to import houses, are taken into public ownership. The party declares that the means of production now belong to the people. For the former owners, the result is ruin, and for the state, a vast inheritance that its managers must learn to run.

All foreign commerce is placed in the hands of state trading corporations. Cotton, rice and imports pass through offices in Cairo and Alexandria under the watchful eye of the party. The monopoly shields the economy from foreign speculation and gives the planners control over every shipment, though it also stifles initiative and invites delay.

Following Lenin's maxim that communism is soviet power plus electrification, the party launches a programme to carry power lines to every village and workshop. Pylons march down the valley and new generators rise by the river. For millions who have lived by oil lamp and the sun, the electric light is the clearest proof of the revolution.

From the steelworks of Helwan to the cotton fields of the Delta, the economy now runs to a single plan. Prices, wages, harvests and exports are all set in the offices of the central committee. The planners believe they have mastered the unruly rhythms of the market, and that Egypt has finally taken control of its own future.

A communist government in a land where five times a day the muezzin calls the faithful to prayer cannot avoid the question of religion. The party's thinkers disagree on whether the revolution should seek peace with the mosque or confront it. The answer will decide whether the republic is accepted in the villages or resisted.

The party seeks an understanding with the scholars of al-Azhar. Sheikhs are assured that their faith will be protected, while the leadership argues that Islam's call for justice and its concern for the poor are compatible with socialism. The compromise offends the purists but reassures the believers.

The party declares religion a relic of feudal society. Schools teach the scientific worldview, endowments are seized and sermons are monitored. Some villages comply in silence; others see in the campaign an attack on the faith itself, and the pulpits become centres of quiet resistance. The republic has taken on a struggle it may find hard to win.

Women are called to the factory, the schoolroom and the party congress as equal partners. Laws are rewritten to end child marriage and the veil is discouraged in public offices. For many working women, it is a liberation; for traditional families and conservative clerics, it is a provocation that the revolution has not yet earned the right to make.

The old universities are remodelled, with admission opened to the sons and daughters of workers and peasants, and the curriculum reshaped around science, engineering and Marxist theory. Cairo University and Ain Shams are filled with a new kind of student, grateful to the republic and expected to repay it with loyal service.

In every regiment and every ship, a party commissar stands beside the commanding officer. Orders must be countersigned; politics is taught alongside drill. The generals bristle at the new supervisors, but the party has no intention of letting the army become a state within the state, as it so often has in Egypt's past.

The army is recast as the armed people, drawing its officers from workers' families and its soldiers from the factories and the fields. Its loyalty is pledged to the republic and the party rather than to any individual commander. Cairo hopes the Egyptian soldier will fight with a conviction that the humbled conscripts of 1967 lacked.

The founders are ageing and a new cohort is rising, men and women who were children when the revolution came. They have no memory of the prisons and the underground, and their questions are those of administrators. The party must decide whether to hold fast to the doctrines of its youth or to adapt them to a changed world.

Younger leaders press for a new course, with greater autonomy for managers, incentives for workers and a more open exchange of ideas. The old guard fears that reform will be the first step back towards capitalism, but the reformers insist that a system which cannot change will wither. The republic opens itself, carefully, to its own improvement.

The party closes ranks around the doctrines of its founders. Deviation is denounced, debate is discouraged and the leadership insists that the road has already been charted. Discipline holds the republic together, and the faithful take comfort in the certainty that they are following the path of history, whatever the world may say.

After years of struggle, purge and construction, the republic stands complete. A disciplined party, a planned economy and a people schooled in the new order mark the final achievement of the Egyptian communists. Whatever its flaws, it is the fulfilment of a dream long nursed in prison cells and secret meetings.

From the picket lines of Helwan and Mahalla, from the bread riots that shook the cities, a new idea has spread: that those who work should rule. With the old state shattered, the councils of the workers and peasants now claim the authority that ministers and generals once held, and the people hold power in their own hands.

Scattered councils in the mills, docks and villages are knit into a federation, with delegates chosen and recalled by those who sent them. There is no president and no politburo, only a network of assemblies. It is a fragile and unfamiliar structure, but those who built it believe it to be the purest expression of the revolution.

The revolution has two hearts. The mill workers of the industrial towns see themselves as its vanguard, while the villagers of the Delta and the Said insist that the real wealth of Egypt lies in the soil. The federation must decide where its centre of gravity will lie, and which class will set the pace.

In Helwan, Mahalla al-Kubra and the Cairo workshops, committees elected by the shop floor take over the management of the factories. Engineers answer to workers, and the old managers are made to justify every order. The production lines stumble at first, but the workers take a pride in running their own machines.

Village by village, the landless and smallholding fellahin take collective control of the land. Assemblies of farmers decide what to plant and how to share the harvest, and the mayors and landlords who once ruled the countryside are swept aside. It is a revolution of the soil, rooted in a deep memory of oppression.

Workers seize the plants, lock out the managers and run the machines themselves. Banners hang from the gates, and the sound of music mingles with the clatter of the looms. Production falters in the turmoil, but the occupation shows the world that the factories belong to those who work in them.

With the factories under their command, the councils begin to coordinate their output across the industrial belt, deciding for themselves what is to be made and for whom. Delegates travel between plants with schedules and samples. The effort is clumsy, but production gradually improves as workers find that they know their trade better than any bureaucrat.

The estates of the old landowners are divided among the villagers, who farm them as a common holding. Debts are cancelled and the village assemblies decide who gets water and when. The fellahin, so long the poorest of Egypt's people, now see the land as their own, and defend it with a fierce loyalty.

Bread, the staple of every Egyptian table and the spark of so many riots, is distributed freely from council depots to all who need it. No family goes hungry while the revolution holds. The councils proclaim that a society which cannot feed its people has no right to call itself just, though the cost weighs heavily on the common stores.

With the old trading and credit systems in ruins, the councils exchange goods directly: grain for tools, cloth for fuel, services for supplies. Networks of delegates link village and factory, and the pound loses its hold on daily life. It is a rough and ready system, but one that keeps the economy moving without banks or merchants.

The ministries of Cairo, with their stamps, queues and thousands of clerks, are declared obsolete. Officials return to the shop floor or the field, and their functions are taken over by elected delegates who serve for a short term. The Mugamma falls silent, and many ordinary Egyptians feel relief.

The offices and detention centres of the security services are thrown open, and their files burned in the streets. Prisoners walk free to cheering crowds. The councils swear that no secret police will ever again stand over the people, though others fear that the protection of the revolution against its enemies has been dangerously weakened.

With the old army and police dismantled, the councils arm their own militias. Workers drill after their shifts, and guard posts spring up at the factory gates and village crossroads. They have little training and mixed equipment, but the militias believe a people in arms is a people that cannot be enslaved.

The council movement sends messages across the borders, calling on the workers of Libya, Sudan, Yemen and beyond to rise as Egypt has done. The capitals of the world, East and West alike, regard the appeal with alarm. The council republic is isolated, but its leaders insist that the revolution cannot be confined to one country.

Neither Washington nor Moscow will dictate to the councils. Foreign advisers are turned away, and envoys carrying the offers of great powers meet a polite refusal. The slogan of the new order is that no master, whether native or foreign, has a place on Egyptian soil, and the people take pride in a revolution that has no patron.

Egypt has become a federation of free producers, with no president and no ministry above the councils. Workers run the mills, farmers hold the land and the delegates are accountable to those who sent them. The experiment is unprecedented in the Arab world, and the eyes of every revolutionary and every reactionary are fixed upon it.

Teaching is taken out of the hands of the ministry and entrusted to the councils. Evening classes in the factories teach reading and arithmetic alongside the history of labour, and village schools are run by committees of parents and teachers. The councils believe that education must belong to the people if it is to set them free.

Delegates from every council in the republic assemble in a great congress. Weeks of argument follow in smoky halls, as the revolution tries to settle its own constitution. The question before them is whether the new order will be one of permanent debate and open ballots or of firm direction in the face of enemies.

The congress votes to keep power in the hands of ordinary delegates, subject to recall and open debate. Elections are held in every council and decisions are argued out in the assemblies. The process is slow, noisy and sometimes chaotic, but the people feel that the revolution belongs to them and not to a handful of leaders.

Faced with enemies at home and abroad, the congress hands extraordinary authority to a small committee of trusted revolutionaries. The assemblies continue to meet, but it is the committee that decides. Its members insist that the arrangement is temporary, as every revolutionary government always has.

Founded in the spirit of the centre platform of Mamdouh Salem, the Misr Party of Order offers Egypt what neither the radicals nor the old guard can: stability. Its creed is that of a strong state guiding a national capital, with cautious reform, firm discipline and no patience for ideological adventures. The country, weary after years of war and upheaval, listens.

Mamdouh Salem, the former police chief turned administrator, forms a cabinet of technocrats, loyal officers and seasoned civil servants. They are not revolutionaries, and say so. Their promise is to make the trains run, the ministries function and the nation steady, in the belief that a well-managed state is its own justification.

The party's leaders agree on the need for order but disagree on who is to deliver it. One school holds that only a powerful and unified centre can rein in the provinces and the factions; the other sees the future in Egyptian businessmen and industrialists, shielded and guided by the state. The party must decide where its weight will rest.

Authority is gathered into Cairo. Governors answer to the ministries, the ministries to the cabinet, and the cabinet to the party. Provincial grandees and rival power centres find their autonomy trimmed. Supporters call it national discipline, while opponents see the quiet return of the all-powerful state they had hoped was behind them.

The state turns to the businessmen of Egypt, the cotton merchants, contractors and industrialists who know the market, and gives them favoured access to contracts and credit. The aim is a native capitalist class loyal to the nation and not to foreign banks. Critics suspect that the new champions will prove more loyal to their own fortunes than to the state.

Political activity is permitted, but only through a handful of approved platforms, each with its own manifesto and its own place in the system. Citizens may vote, and the debates are lively, but the party that governs has the means to ensure that it will never lose. It is a controlled pluralism for a country that distrusts disorder.

The Interior Ministry gains new powers to watch, license and discipline the political platforms. Its offices keep a close eye on journalists, student groups and preachers, and the police are quietly granted a wider remit. The party tells the public that this is the price of calm, and many Egyptians, tired of unrest, are inclined to agree.

Newspapers, radio and the new television studios are encouraged to put the nation first. Editors receive friendly guidance on which stories to run and which to leave out, while columnists praise the steadiness of the government. Without any need for a formal censor, the public hears one consistent and reassuring voice.

The governors of the provinces, from Alexandria to Aswan, are carefully chosen from among the party's most trusted servants. They report faithfully to Cairo and carry its policy into every town and village. Local notables who once ruled their districts as private fiefs find that the road to advancement now runs through the capital.

The government nominates a number of great enterprises as national champions, in steel, textiles, cement and engineering, giving them privileges and protection in return for service to the national plan. Managers wear suits rather than uniforms, but they take their direction from Cairo. State capitalism, the party insists, is the surest route to prosperity.

Gulf monarchies, flush with oil revenue and nervous about their own security, are happy to finance Egyptian arms factories in return for weapons and trained men. Cairo sees an opportunity to turn its military expertise into hard currency. The arrangement is profitable and discreet, and raises few questions in the Arab world.

The party resolves that Egypt must never again depend on foreign suppliers for its fuel. Survey teams comb the Gulf of Suez and the western desert, and a national oil company takes shape. The petroleum industry, supported by the state, becomes the backbone of the new order and a source of both revenue and political influence.

The opening of the economy, so long discussed, is carried out on the state's terms. Foreign investors are invited to Egypt, but only on conditions set in Cairo: partnerships with national firms, limits on repatriated profit and the retention of strategic industries. The party believes that it has found a middle course between Nasser's closed doors and unchecked liberalism.

A national fund buys grain, sugar and cooking oil in times of plenty and releases them in times of shortage, so that no sudden surge in prices can reach the bread queues. The measure is unglamorous, yet it keeps the cities calm, and the party is keenly aware how swiftly an unruly price can turn into an uprising.

Cairo declines to choose between its patrons. Soviet advisers stay on the Nile and the Soviet arms continue to arrive, while Saudi money and goodwill flow towards the treasury. The party's diplomats pursue a delicate balancing act, in which Egypt's usefulness to both camps is its best protection against dependence on either.

The party's idea of stability does not stop at the border. Envoys travel to Khartoum and Tripoli offering friendship, advice and assistance in suppressing the unrest that threatens the neighbouring regimes. A region of orderly, cooperative governments, under Egypt's gentle guidance, is the foreign policy goal of the Party of Order.

The party's vision is realised. Governors, ministries, industrial champions and the security services work in concert, and the unpredictable energies of Egyptian politics have been channelled into orderly forms. Critics call it stagnant; supporters insist that the nation, after decades of upheaval, has earned a long period of calm.

The Party of Order has no wish to quarrel with the army. The officer corps is courted with promotions, better pay and a place at the table, with the clear understanding that the army's loyalty belongs to the state that rewards it. The generals, once a source of anxiety, become pillars of the system.

After years of defeat and improvisation, the officers are given the means to professionalise. Modern armour is procured, training schools are reformed and doctrine is rewritten for the lessons of the recent wars. The army that emerges is leaner, better equipped and trusted by the government to defend the nation without meddling in its politics.

The party has built a system, but a system needs someone to run it. As the cabinet's founders age, the question of succession can no longer be postponed. The party and the security services each have their candidate, and the future shape of the Order State will depend on who is chosen.

The mantle passes to a career politician, a product of the party's own committees and congresses. He is a master of consensus, not a man of the barracks, and he promises to rule by the party's procedures. The institution outlasts the individual, and the Order State acquires a respectable constitutional face.

The torch passes to a man from the security apparatus, a veteran of the ministries and the files who knows where every thread leads. He rules without fanfare, trusting the services to guard the order that the party has built. Egyptians sense a change in the atmosphere, quieter and more watchful than before.

Inspired by the stunning events in Iran and by the writings of Fathi Shiqaqi, a coalition of young preachers, students and urban poor has overthrown the old order. They proclaim a revolution of the oppressed against both Washington and Moscow, and a republic ruled by the law of God. Egypt, seat of al-Azhar, is to become the lighthouse of the Muslim world.

A council of clerics, jurists and veterans of the underground takes charge of the state. Its proclamations are issued in the name of God and the people, and its decisions are enforced by committees in every neighbourhood and village. The old ministries remain, but the Revolutionary Council now directs them.

The revolution is united in faith but divided about government. One camp wishes to build an elected assembly in which Muslims deliberate under the guidance of the sharia; the other, inspired by the example of Qom, insists that the rule of the learned must stand above any parliament. The republic must choose its form.

Elections are held, and representatives of the cities and the villages gather to deliberate in the name of the shura, or consultation. Every candidate is vetted for piety and loyalty, but within those limits the debate is genuine and sometimes sharp. The assembly gives the revolution a voice and the people a stake in the new republic.

Supreme authority is placed in the hands of the most learned jurist, who guards the republic against deviation. The ulema of al-Azhar, so long confined to their mosques and lecture halls, now find themselves the arbiters of state policy. For the faithful it is the realisation of an ancient ideal; for the secular minded, a cause for deep dread.

Tribunals sit in schools and mosque halls, trying the officials, police chiefs and profiteers of the fallen regime. Verdicts are swift and sentences severe. The people cheer the punishment of the corrupt, while the lawyers of Cairo watch in horror as the careful machinery of Egyptian jurisprudence is swept aside.

Modelled on the great charitable foundations of Iran, new religious endowments take possession of the confiscated properties of the old elite. Their funds support hospitals, schools and the families of martyrs, and give the revolution a network of loyal beneficiaries. Critics note that no one outside the clerical establishment audits their accounts.

Mill hands in Mahalla and dockers in Alexandria elect councils under the guidance of religious leaders, who preach that honest labour is a form of worship and that the exploitation of the worker is a sin. The councils serve the republic rather than challenge it, and they channel working class anger into the service of the revolution.

The import-export houses of Cairo and Alexandria, so closely linked to the old regime and foreign powers, are seized by the state. Trade in grain, cotton and consumer goods passes under revolutionary control. The republic declares that Egypt will no longer be a market for foreign goods and a source of cheap raw materials for other people's profit.

The new government proclaims an economic order grounded in the dignity of the poor. Charitable funds, zakat and state spending are brought together to provide food, shelter and work, and the profits of the wealthy are directed to the needy. The revolution declares that Islam has its own path, neither capitalist nor communist.

The slogan of the Iranian revolution is adopted on the Nile. Soviet advisers are sent home, American envoys are refused entry, and the republic proclaims that it will accept the patronage of no power but God. Cairo's isolation is the price it pays for a revolution that depends on neither bloc.

On the last Friday of Ramadan, crowds fill the streets of Cairo to demand the liberation of Jerusalem. The republic proclaims the Palestinian cause a sacred duty of all Muslims, and a burning issue of the revolution's legitimacy. The war with Israel is no longer a question of borders, but a struggle for the holy city.

After the upheaval of revolution and the strain of construction, the Islamic Republic of Egypt has found its form. Its courts, its foundations, its principles and its banners are all in place. Whether it becomes a beacon to the Muslim world or a cautionary tale, it has changed Egypt beyond recognition.

Volunteers in green armbands guard the mosques, patrol the markets and enforce the decisions of the revolutionary committees. They are young, devout and armed, and answer to the clerics rather than to any general. Alongside the regular army, a new force grows up whose loyalty is not to the state but to the revolution.

The government chooses to work with the soldiers it has inherited. Chaplains are posted to the regiments, officers are examined for piety, and the army is invited to see itself as the sword of Islam. Many professional soldiers, grateful to be spared a purge, accept the new orthodoxy with cautious relief.

The old army, tainted by defeat and by service to the fallen regime, is dissolved. Its officers are dismissed or imprisoned, and in its place the revolutionary militias become the foundation of a new force. The republic's defenders are zealous, devoted and untried, and the experienced professionals who once led the army are gone.

The great estates and those of the corrupt are redistributed among the landless of the villages, with the mosque committees overseeing the process. The fellahin, who have long toiled for others, receive title to their own fields, and sermons praise the revolution that restored the land to those who work it.

The wells of the Gulf of Suez are placed under revolutionary control, and their output is directed towards the needs of the republic. The leaders of the revolution declare that Egypt's oil belongs to its people and to the Muslim nation, and that no foreign company will profit from it again.

Universities, theatres, cinemas and publishing houses are scrutinised for deviation from Islamic values. Curricula are rewritten, books are withdrawn from the shelves and entertainers learn to tread carefully. The republic proclaims the dawn of an authentic culture freed from imitation of the West, though many of Cairo's artists and academics are less enthusiastic.

The republic's emissaries travel up the Nile and across the Red Sea, preaching the revolution to Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia. Pilgrims, students and relief workers carry the message in Egypt's name. In a region of weak states and ancient faiths, the example of the Islamic Republic carries a considerable appeal.

The first stormy years give way to a more settled routine. The army, the land, the culture and the diplomacy of the republic have all found their shape. The revolution is less turbulent than before, and its leaders speak of the long task of building a state worthy of the faith.

At the summit of the new order stands a single jurist, whose word is final on matters of religion and state. He holds no office, commands no army, and yet every ministry and barracks looks to him for guidance. For his followers he is the guardian of the revolution, answerable to God alone.

The Guardians are of one mind about the sanctity of the revolution but not about its destiny. Some insist that it must be carried abroad before the world's powers snuff it out; others argue that it must first be made invulnerable at home. The jurist's decision will define the republic's character for years to come.

Preachers, agents and arms leave Egypt for neighbouring lands, supporting the oppressed and the faithful against their rulers. Cairo declares that the revolution has no borders and no master. The monarchs of the Gulf follow the news with growing alarm, and the intelligence services of half the world take note.

The revolution turns inward, bolting its doors and fortifying its frontiers. Egypt's leaders reason that a republic of the faithful is safe only if it is beyond the reach of its enemies, and they build walls of vigilance in the press, the barracks and the mosque. Foreign envoys and agitators find the Nile a far less welcoming place.

A corps of devout, politically reliable fighters is raised and given precedence over the army. Their loyalty is to the revolution and to the jurist, and their ranks fill with young men who find in the movement a sense of purpose. The regular officers look on with envy and apprehension as the Guardians accumulate weapons and prestige.

Beyond the elite corps, the government calls on millions of volunteers: schoolboys, shopkeepers, old men with rifles. Drilled in the mosque courtyards and marched through the streets, the mobilised masses embody the revolution's claim that a faithful people cannot be defeated. Their enthusiasm is boundless and their training is limited.

The academies of Cairo and Alexandria are scoured of secular and suspect professors. Lectures are monitored, curricula revised and students investigated for loyalty. The faculties empty, the laboratories fall quiet and the Guardians declare the cleansing of the university complete, though Egyptian science suffers badly for it.

Sanctions, boycotts and the hostility of the great powers are met with defiance. Egypt is to produce what it needs and do without what it cannot make, subordinating comfort to principle. The jurist declares that a nation that refuses to bend can survive anything, and the long years of hardship begin.

In a time of scarcity, the state undertakes to distribute essentials directly. Every household receives coupons for bread, oil, sugar and fuel, exchangeable at the revolutionary cooperatives. The system is rigid, and endless queues form, but no family is left to starve, which wins the Guardians the loyalty of the poorest.

Vast religious foundations take possession of seized estates and factories, answerable only to the jurist. They fund hospitals, mosques and the families of the fallen, but also operate as states within the state, with their own revenue, their own influence and their own opaque dealings. The wealth of the revolution is enormous and ill-accounted for.

The principle of the guardianship is firmly embedded in the structure of the state. Every institution, from the courts to the barracks to the bazaar, acknowledges the authority of the jurist. The Guardians have created something new in the long history of Egypt, a government of the learned, armed with the zeal of the revolution.

In every street and village, committees of the faithful keep watch on morals, loyalty and speech. They are the eyes and ears of the revolution, reporting neighbours who miss prayers or utter doubts. Order returns to the streets, but at the price of a society in which everyone suspects the person beside them.

The families of those who fell in the revolution and the wars are cared for by a dedicated foundation, with pensions, housing and honours. Mothers wearing black are received like queens, and their sons are praised from every pulpit. The cult of martyrdom becomes a central pillar of the republic's legitimacy.

The Guardians establish factories of their own, producing arms, machinery and the necessities of war economy. Run by trusted men of the movement, they are free from the interference of the old ministries, answering only to the jurist. A new industrial sector rises from the revolution, shielded from scrutiny and from rivals.

When the legal avenues of trade are closed by sanctions, other routes open. Dhows cross the Red Sea at night, caravans move through the desert and officials in remote ports learn to look the other way. The Guardians scorn the smugglers in public, but the republic's survival increasingly depends on them.

In workshops guarded by the Guardians, engineers labour to build rockets that can strike the enemy at a distance. Parades display the long, blunt shapes on trucks, accompanied by crowds chanting. The missiles become a symbol of the revolution's defiance, and a source of grave concern to Egypt's neighbours.

From Cairo to Damascus, Tripoli and the camps of Palestine, a chain of friendly forces and governments takes shape, bound together by hostility to Israel and the West. The Guardians are its patrons and arsenal. The alliance is loose and its members have little else in common, but its existence changes the strategic map of the Middle East.

The aging jurist's health is a matter whispered in the corridors. The Guardians, who have governed in his name, must now consider who will govern after him. The pragmatists argue for flexibility and the principlists for steadfastness, and the choice between them will decide whether the revolution lasts or hardens.

The new circle of leaders grasps that a revolution, to survive, must trade, eat and make peace with some of its neighbours. The doors of commerce open a little, factories are given modest freedom and diplomats begin to speak softly. The old zealots mutter about betrayal, but ordinary Egyptians breathe a little more easily.

The faithful of the old guard take command, determined that the revolution shall not be diluted. Any hint of compromise is denounced, the ideals of the founding years are restated and the ranks are closed. The Guardians present themselves as the defenders of purity, and the republic marches on with a hardened sense of mission.

The succession has been settled, the industries built and the allies gathered. The rule of the jurist is no longer a revolutionary experiment but an institution, with its own habits, wealth and loyalists. Whether the Egyptian people accept it or merely endure it, the Guardians are here to stay.

With the Open Door under way, Sadat needs a political vehicle to replace the Arab Socialist Union and its Nasserist baggage. The National Democratic Party gathers technocrats, provincial notables and loyal officials under one roof, promising continuity with stability. Critics note that the line between party and state grows ever thinner, and that patronage follows the party card.

The new party belongs, in every meaningful sense, to the man at its head. Ministers, governors and mayors are drawn to the presidential banner, and the press learns to speak of the party as the natural voice of the nation. Whoever wishes to be heard in Cairo must first be heard within its ranks.

Sadat's state of institutions stands at a crossroads. One path allows opposition parties to exist, so long as they know their place; the other keeps the nation under emergency rule in the name of order. The choice will define what kind of republic Egypt becomes once the Nasserist single party is truly gone.

Opposition platforms, or minbars, are permitted to speak, to publish and to contest elections, though the dominant party keeps a firm hand on the rules of the game. Cairo wins applause from Western capitals for its opening, while the regime's loyalists grumble that licence has been granted to those who would undo the revolution.

The emergency laws are kept in force, justified by terrorism, sectarian strife and the long confrontation with Israel. Police stations multiply and the Mukhabarat grows more confident in its reach. Order is bought at the price of liberties, and few in the ministries believe the exception will ever end.

A consultative upper chamber is created to lend the regime a deliberative face. Its members are appointed or elected in carefully managed contests, and include respected jurists, editors and elder statesmen. The Shura Council advises and polishes legislation, and gives the republic an air of institutional depth that critics doubt it truly possesses.

Newspapers affiliated with the licensed opposition are allowed to sharpen their pens, lampooning ministers and probing the excesses of the Infitah. Editors test the limits of the permissible, and the censors test them in turn. The regime hopes that a safety valve will keep anger from boiling over into the streets.

A sweeping measure against behaviour deemed damaging to the nation's values lets the state prosecute critics for disgracing the country at home or abroad. Under the banner of protecting public morals, writers, preachers and politicians alike discover that dissent may now be treated as a matter of honour, and punished accordingly.

In a single sweep, the security services detain Islamists, leftists, Copts, journalists and old politicians by the hundreds. The president declares that he is defending the state against sectarian strife and subversion, but the cells fill with men of every persuasion, and the grudges they carry will outlast the regime that jailed them.

The regime seeks peace with the religious current it once feared. Preachers are given airtime, al-Azhar is courted, and the Brotherhood is tolerated in return for its restraint. Many in the establishment see a pragmatic accommodation; others warn that Cairo is feeding the very movement that may one day turn on it.

The militant groups of Upper Egypt and the Cairo slums are declared enemies of the state. Security units sweep through the villages of the south, while informers and interrogators work in the cellars of the capital. The government promises that the gunmen will be rooted out, whatever the cost to the rule of law.

No president rules forever, and in Cairo the question of what follows is whispered in every salon and barracks. The party, the army and the civil bureaucracy each hold a claim to the legacy. The decision, once taken, will shape the republic for a generation.

The former air force commander, loyal and cautious, steps from the shadow of the presidency into its centre. Hosni Mubarak promises continuity without adventure, and the officer corps, relieved to see one of its own in the palace, closes ranks behind him. The nation breathes out, and waits to see what manner of ruler he will prove.

The apparatus that Sadat built chooses its own man. Fouad Mohieddin, secretary-general of the party and a master of committees and compromise, takes the presidency as the candidate of the organisation rather than the barracks. Governors and local bosses welcome him, though the generals watch with narrowed eyes.

In a break with the long tradition of officers in the palace, the presidency passes to a civilian. Mustafa Khalil, the experienced prime minister and a favourite of Western governments, promises clean administration and sober diplomacy. The army grumbles at the slight, but foreign capitals are quick to offer their approval.

The constitution is amended so that the head of state may stand for office again and again. Loyalists describe it as a safeguard against instability in dangerous times, while opponents see only a monarchy in republican dress. The new article is passed with little real debate.

Egypt is at last presented as a state of institutions, with a dominant party, a managed parliament, an open economy and a settled place in the world. Whether it is a modern republic or merely an elegant façade remains a matter for the historians, but for now the machinery of government runs smoothly.

Law 43 of 1974 opened the door to foreign capital, and now the government widens it further. Tax holidays, guarantees against nationalisation and simpler licensing are offered to investors from the Gulf and the West. Cairo is betting that private money will do what the socialist state never managed.

Western firms are invited to partner with Egyptian companies in factories and assembly plants along the Nile. German engineers, French manufacturers and American suppliers arrive with capital and technical expertise. The old public sector looks on warily as a new class of managers and middlemen rises beside it.

Foreign and joint-venture banks are licensed to operate in Cairo and Alexandria, financing trade, construction and imports. The bankers bring credit and new methods, along with a new set of interests at the president's table. Nasser's closed financial system is quietly left behind.

Out in the desert, far from the crowded Nile Valley, new towns rise from the sand: the Tenth of Ramadan, Sadat City, the Sixth of October. Planners promise factories, housing and a release for the overcrowded capital. Sceptics point to the cost, and wonder whether anyone will wish to live so far from Cairo.

Special zones are set aside near Suez and Alexandria, where companies can import and export with minimal customs and bureaucratic delay. Investors are drawn by the lighter regulation and the cheap labour of the Delta. For the government, they are a showcase of what a modern, outward-looking Egypt can offer.

With the Sinai wells and the Gulf of Suez fields back in Egyptian hands, foreign drilling consortia arrive in force. Rigs crowd the waters off the coast, and crude begins to flow in earnest. Oil becomes the lifeblood of a state long starved of foreign exchange, though it also breeds a dangerous reliance on a single commodity.

The Infitah has matured into a settled strategy. Imports fill the shop windows, foreign banks and hotels dominate the skyline, and a new bourgeoisie flourishes in the cities. The government declares that Egypt has rejoined the world economy, even as the fellahin ask what has changed in their villages.

A country that cannot feed its own people cannot be master of its own destiny. Cairo turns to American grain under Public Law 480, hoping that wheat shipments and new agricultural measures will keep bread on the table. The price is a deeper dependence on the goodwill of Washington.

The subsidies on bread, oil and sugar, a pillar of the Nasserist social bargain, are becoming unaffordable. International lenders demand cuts and the treasury agrees. But the poor of Cairo remember the riots of 1977, and every price rise is watched anxiously from the palace windows.

The pyramids, the temples of Luxor and the beaches of the Red Sea are Egypt's most reliable assets. The state hands hotels and tourist enterprises to private operators, in the hope that profit will bring investment and visitors. Foreign currency flows in, though the benefits reach some Egyptians more than others.

New campuses rise in the provinces and thousands more students pass through lecture halls built for hundreds. The government promises that a degree will still guarantee a post, though the graduates already outnumber the jobs on offer. Education remains the great promise of the republic, and its greatest source of disappointment.

Jehan Sadat, the president's wife, champions reforms to the personal status laws, giving women greater rights in divorce, custody and the home. Liberals applaud and reformers take heart, but the ulema are scandalised, and critics mock the measures as Jehan's law, imposed by decree on a society not yet persuaded.

In a gesture that stuns the world, the president announces that he is ready to travel to Jerusalem itself and speak before the Knesset. It is a gamble of extraordinary daring, aimed at regaining the Sinai and ending the cycle of war. The Arab world is appalled, but in Egypt, many weary families dare to hope.

Peace brings rewards in its train. Washington opens its arsenals and its treasury to Egypt, and American aid flows toward the army and the economy alike. The president insists that the nation has been repaid for its courage, even as the Arab capitals denounce the bargain.

American and Egyptian troops train side by side in the desert, in exercises that would have been unthinkable a few years before. Egyptian officers learn Western doctrine, and the hardware of the Soviet era is gradually set aside. The army becomes a partner of the United States in everything but name.

Egypt takes its place as the cornerstone of American strategy in the region. Military advisers, aircraft and credit follow, and Cairo is expected to support American interests in return. The alliance provides security and prosperity, though many Egyptians ask who now holds the real power on the Nile.

Years after the break over the peace with Israel, Cairo works to mend its ties with the Arab capitals. Envoys travel to Riyadh, Amman and Baghdad, and the old quarrels are softened by Egypt's size and weight. The Arab League returns to the Nile, and Egypt resumes its place at the centre of the Arab world.

Egypt looks northward across the sea, cultivating friendships in Paris, Rome and Athens. Trade delegations, cultural exchanges and quiet diplomacy build a web of goodwill on the Mediterranean shore. For a regime keen to balance its American ties, these ancient neighbours offer welcome partnership.

A large force of conscript policemen is raised to guard government buildings, quell demonstrations and watch the streets. They are drawn from the poorest villages and housed in cramped barracks. The state gains a loyal truncheon, but this instrument of order depends on men who have little reason to love it.

Recognising that the men of the security forces are the foundation of the regime's security, the ministry raises their wages and improves their housing. The conscripts remain loyal, and the interior ministry gains a reputation for looking after its own. The treasury grumbles, but the streets stay calm.

The security conscripts are kept on a meagre wage and a poor diet, and the ministry puts its trust in discipline over generosity. The savings are welcome, but resentment festers in the barracks. Officers warn that men who are hungry and humiliated may one day turn their weapons on those who command them.

The canal, silent and blocked for years, is reopened and widened for the largest ships of a new age. Dredgers work day and night, and engineers plan for a waterway that will carry the commerce of three continents. Egypt's gateway between East and West becomes once more the pride of the nation and its richest asset.

The fairgrounds of Nasr City fill with exhibitors from across the Mediterranean, the Gulf and beyond. Merchants haggle over textiles, machinery and cotton, while diplomats and ministers hold quiet talks over coffee. For the government, the fair is a shop window displaying an Egypt open for business.

The old party of Saad Zaghlul, banned since the revolution of 1952, returns to the political stage. Fouad Serageddin, the aged Pasha who once served the monarchy, rallies the liberals, landowners and professionals who never forgot the parliamentary years. The New Wafd promises constitutional rule, free enterprise and respect for the law.

With Serageddin at the helm, the Wafd forms a government drawn from the lawyers, merchants and veteran politicians of the liberal age. The ministries fill with men who remember the days of the constitution of 1923. The country watches to see whether the old guard can govern a modern republic.

The party faces a question about itself. Should it rely on the experienced pashas and landed families who kept the faith through the long years of exile, or give way to a new generation of lawyers and engineers eager to modernise? The answer will determine what the Wafd is to be.

The veterans of the pre-revolutionary parliament take charge of the party's direction, bringing with them dignity, land and long memories. Landowners flock to the banner, expecting that the estates seized by Nasser's reforms will receive a kinder hearing. The party gains steadiness, and a reputation for looking backwards.

Younger lawyers, economists and engineers push the old men aside, bringing new ideas and fresh faces to the Wafd. They speak of a modern, European-minded Egypt with a free market and a free press. The pashas mutter about the loss of tradition, but the party gains the energy of a movement that expects to win.

The liberal constitution of 1923 is invoked as the foundation of the new order. Free elections, rights for all citizens and a government answerable to parliament are restored as the nation's guiding principles. The Wafd declares that the revolution has at last come home.

The courts are freed from the control of the executive and the judges are assured of their tenure. Corrupt officials discover that the law now reaches them, and investors, foreign and domestic, begin to trust that contracts will be honoured. Egypt's proud legal tradition is restored to its place of honour.

Censorship is lifted and the press is free to praise or condemn the government as it sees fit. Newspapers of every colour spring up in Cairo, and the coffee houses buzz with argument. Ministers learn the discomfort of being criticised in public, and the nation learns the habit of debate.

Power rests firmly with the elected assembly and the ministers who answer to it. The president is a dignified figure above the fray, and the cabinet rises and falls by the will of the deputies. The Wafd has realised the oldest dream of Egyptian liberalism, though a restive nation must learn how to live with it.

The Wafd was born in 1919 under the banner of the crescent embracing the cross, uniting Muslim and Copt in the cause of independence. Its heirs revive that vision of a national community open to all. The Coptic minority, long uneasy under the revolution, welcomes the pledge of equal citizenship.

The Wafd moves to place civil law above religious jurisdiction, with a single system of national courts for all Egyptians. Lawyers hail a modern reform, but the scholars of al-Azhar protest that the faith is being pushed from public life. The government answers that justice must be the same for all.

The property seized by the revolution, from estates to town houses and factories, is returned to those who lost it. Merchants and shopkeepers rejoice, and a confident middle class emerges. The landless fellahin, who benefited from the old land reforms, look on with unease at the return of the old owners.

Talaat Harb founded Bank Misr to build an Egyptian capitalism free of foreign dominance. The Wafd revives his dream, encouraging the bank and its industries to grow once more. Factories rise in Alexandria and the Delta, and the old ideal of a prosperous national economy gains fresh life.

Egyptian owners and managers are encouraged to take the lead in the nation's industry, with preference given to national firms over foreign ones. Taxes are eased on domestic enterprise, and a class of native industrialists comes into its own. The Wafd insists that a free economy and a national economy need not be opposed.

In Alexandria, the cotton exchange, shuttered during the years of state control, opens its doors once more. Brokers and growers gather in the old trading halls to bargain over the white gold of the Nile. The market returns, and with it the prosperity and cosmopolitan air of the old Mediterranean port.

Alexandria, once the most cosmopolitan city in the Mediterranean, is declared a free port. Ships unload without heavy duty, merchants of every nation set up offices, and warehouses fill along the harbour. The city of the Greeks, Italians and Levantines stirs again, and dreams of its former splendour.

Cooperative societies, backed by credit and technical advice, help the fellahin to modernise their farming. New seeds, machinery and marketing arrangements ease the burden on smallholders. The Wafd hopes to prove that a free economy can serve the peasant as well as the pasha.

Prices, trade and enterprise are freed from the grip of the state, and the economy responds with vigour. Egyptian goods find buyers abroad, investment pours in, and the bazaars thrive. The Wafd points to prosperity as proof that liberalism and national dignity go hand in hand.

The Wafd has always looked toward Europe, and its leaders still count friends in Whitehall and the Quai d'Orsay. Old acquaintances are renewed, loans are discussed, and the memories of the bitter quarrel over Suez are set quietly aside. Egypt takes its place among the liberal powers of the Mediterranean.

The unity of the Nile Valley was a Wafdist ideal long before the revolution, and the party now reaches out to Khartoum in a spirit of friendship. Trade, water and political partnership are on the table. The Sudanese, long wary of Egyptian domination, are cautiously receptive to a more respectful tone.

The parliament sits, the courts rule, the press argues and the markets trade. A generation after the revolution closed it, Egypt's liberal age has returned in a new guise. The task now is to prove that the freedoms of the past can survive the pressures of the present.

The army is placed under civilian authority and trained as a professional national force, free from the intrigues of the officer corps. Barracks politics are discouraged and merit is rewarded. The generals accept the new order with reserve, aware that the Wafd has ended the age of the soldier-president.

Serageddin is old, and the party knows that the time must come when a new leader must take his place. The Wafd has little tradition of handing on power gracefully. The choice of successor will reveal whether the party is a movement of ideas or merely the following of one man.

The party turns to a younger man, a lawyer or economist untouched by the quarrels of the past. His speeches speak of the future rather than the glories of 1919, and the new generation of voters responds. The old pashas bow their heads, persuaded that the party has chosen to survive.

Leadership passes to a scion of the great landed families, a man whose name is known in every village of the Delta. He carries the prestige of the old Wafd and the loyalty of its notables. He is a guardian of the party's heritage, though reform may have to wait.

Mustafa Kamel Murad and his Liberal Socialist allies take office with a bold promise to dismantle the heavy hand of the state and let the market breathe. The ministers speak of competition, enterprise and sound money. After years of socialism, Cairo's business community is cautiously delighted.

The cabinet unveils its programme of free markets, lean government and individual choice. Business leaders applaud, Western economists nod approval, and the trade unions grow nervous. It is a bold vision of a very different Egypt, and the government must now decide how swiftly to pursue it.

The reformers are divided on how fast to move. Some urge a sudden break with the controlled economy, cutting prices, subsidies and tariffs at a stroke; others favour a patient transition that spares the poor. The decision will shape the nation's economy and the government's fate.

Prices are freed, subsidies are slashed and the state steps back at once. The economy convulses, shops empty and fill again at higher prices, and families on fixed incomes suffer. The government insists that the pain is the price of recovery, and asks the nation to endure.

Controls are lifted step by step, with warnings given and cushions provided for the vulnerable. Businesses adapt, workers adjust, and the government keeps a watchful eye on the street. Progress is slower than the zealots wish, but it is less likely to end in riots.

The old exchanges of Cairo and Alexandria, among the oldest in the region, reopen their trading floors. Brokers return in dark suits, and shares in Egyptian companies change hands once more. A new generation of investors discovers that wealth can be made on paper as well as in the cotton fields.

The great state enterprises of the Nasser years, from textile mills to steelworks, are offered for sale to private buyers. Efficiency improves and revenues flow into the treasury, but workers fear for their jobs and the unions threaten to strike. The government presses ahead, convinced that the state is a poor businessman.

Licences are simplified, red tape is cut and inspectors are told to give guidance rather than punishment. Businessmen find it easier to open a shop, hire workers and import goods. Critics fear for safety and fair dealing, but entrepreneurs praise a government that gets out of the way.

Taxes are lowered on households and firms alike, in the belief that money left in private hands will be put to better use than the state could manage. Shopkeepers, merchants and professionals feel the difference at once. The treasury trusts that growth will fill the gap.
