The tangle of official and black-market exchange rates is swept away, and the pound is allowed to find its own level. Exporters and importers can plan with confidence, and foreign investors take note. The change is painful for those who lived off the old distortions.

The state no longer fixes the price of cotton, wheat or rice. Farmers sell to the highest bidder and decide for themselves what to plant. Some fellahin prosper, while others fall into debt, and the villages discover the rewards and risks of the market.

Customs barriers fall, visas are eased and foreign companies are invited to open offices in Cairo and the Nile Valley. Skyscrapers of glass and steel rise beside the old city. The nation that once shut itself behind socialist walls now presents itself as a crossroads of commerce.

The planners and the controllers of the old regime have been replaced by prices, profits and competition. The economy hums with a vitality that surprises even its architects. Egypt has become, in outlook if not entirely in practice, a market society.

A charter of rights guarantees free speech, free assembly and the protection of the courts. Political prisoners are released, and opposition parties emerge from the shadows. The government declares that a free economy requires a free society, and invites the nation to judge its record.

Power is devolved from the ministries of Cairo to the governorates, which receive greater authority over their budgets and local affairs. Provincial governors, long the creatures of the capital, now answer to local councils. Reformers hail the end of the centralised state, though some fear regional rivalry.

Egypt turns toward the nations of the European continent, seeking trade, investment and technology. Delegations are exchanged with Paris, Bonn and Rome, and the cabinet speaks of a Mediterranean future. The relationship is built on shared commercial interest and a common wish for stability.

Negotiators travel to Brussels to discuss a formal association with the European Economic Community. The prospect of tariff-free access to the markets of the Six excites manufacturers and growers alike. Whether Europe will accept is a question of diplomacy, but the ambition itself marks a new direction for Egypt.

The liberal government has remade the republic in its own image, with open markets, decentralised power and close ties to Europe. Egyptians are told that they now live in a modern, competitive nation. Prosperity is uneven, but the direction of travel seems unmistakable.

The cabinet argues that a nation at peace with the market has no need of an enormous standing army. The size of the forces is reduced and funds are directed to training and organisation. The officers resent the cuts, but the finance ministry notes with approval that the army now costs far less.

Out go the ageing Soviet tanks and aircraft, and in come modern weapons from the West. The army's technicians must learn new systems, and the purchases are costly. But the generals admit that Western equipment is the equal of any arrayed against them, and the government wins friends abroad.

The liberal programme has been delivered, and the government must now decide how to carry it forward. Should the party seek partners to share the burden of power, or trust its own majority? The coming choice will determine whether liberalism in Egypt is a consensus or a creed.

The liberals reach out to the New Wafd, and the two parties govern together in the name of constitutional rule and a free economy. The coalition brings stability and a broad base of support, though it also demands compromise on matters the liberals might prefer to settle themselves.

The liberals decline to share power, trusting in their own majority and their own vision. Decisions are made swiftly and the programme is carried forward without dilution. Critics warn that a government accountable to no partner may find itself accountable to no one.

Ibrahim Shukri leads the Socialist Labour Party into government, with a promise to defend the workers and fellahin in an age of change. A former Nasserist minister turned reformer, he speaks of social justice, honest government and a fair share for the poor. The trade unions throw their weight behind him.

The new government sets out its programme of social reform, mixing the heritage of Egyptian socialism with a commitment to political freedom. Welfare, wages and public services are placed at the centre of policy. The party hopes to prove that a left-wing government can be both humane and efficient.

The party faces a question of identity. Is it a secular movement of workers and trade unionists in the tradition of European labour parties, or a movement that grounds its socialism in the moral language of Islam? The answer will decide whom it can speak for.

The party draws on the traditions of the European labour movement, stressing class solidarity, trade unions and the rights of working people. Factory delegates and union officials set the tone of debate. Egyptian socialism is recast as a democratic and secular cause, and Western social democrats take note.

The party presents social justice as a duty ordained by religion, and calls for an economy guided by the Islamic ideals of charity and fairness. The alliance with the Muslim Brotherhood, once unthinkable, brings votes and moral authority. Secular comrades protest that socialism has been handed to the preachers.

The unions are freed from state control and allowed to choose their own leaders and conduct their own bargaining. Long-suppressed grievances find a voice in the factories of Helwan and Mahalla. Workers stand taller, while employers learn to negotiate with men who can no longer be ordered about.

Employers, unions and ministers are brought together around one table to hammer out the terms of the nation's economic life. The council gives the workers a voice and the businessmen a hearing. Compromise, not command, becomes the style of policy, and industrial peace the reward.

The government offers the people a pact: a decent wage, secure employment and basic services in exchange for loyalty and effort. It echoes the promises of the revolution, but without the coercion that came with them. The question is whether the state can afford to keep its word.

A new law guarantees workers a fair contract, a safe workplace and protection against dismissal. Factory owners complain of rigidity, but the men on the shop floor see a sign that their labour is respected. The statute book finally speaks the language of the labour movement.

Those who earn more are asked to contribute more, in a tax system designed to share the burden according to ability. The wealthy of Zamalek and Maadi protest, while the treasury welcomes a reliable stream of revenue. The government calls it simple justice.

Elderly workers and widows are promised a secure income in their retirement, funded by contributions and general taxation. The system is extended to farm labourers and the self-employed, who were long left out. In a country where families have always cared for their own, the state now shares the burden.

Clinics and rural hospitals are built in the villages of the Delta and the Said, where the nearest doctor was once a day's journey away. Nurses and midwives are trained in the thousands. The government says the fellahin built the nation, and now the nation will care for them.

Village banks owned by the farmers themselves offer loans on fair terms, breaking the grip of moneylenders and merchants. Smallholders are able to buy seed and fertiliser without falling into debt. The cooperative movement, long a hope of the left, begins to deliver.

New apartment blocks rise on the edge of the capital, built by the state and let at modest rents. Families long crowded into tenements or the tombs of the Cairo cemeteries receive keys to homes of their own. The programme is costly, but the government considers it a promise of the revolution at last redeemed.

Neither a command economy nor a free-for-all, the new order combines public enterprise, private initiative and cooperative effort. Strategic industries remain in the hands of the state, while the market is trusted to supply the rest. The government hopes to prove that a middle way can work.

Egypt's labour government is welcomed into the company of Europe's social democratic parties. Delegates exchange visits with their counterparts in Stockholm, Bonn and Vienna, bringing advice, sympathy and the hope of investment. The party finds friends who share its ideals, and a legitimacy that Moscow could never confer.

Egypt reaches out to the socialist and social democratic governments of the northern Mediterranean, finding common cause in the defence of workers and the welfare state. Cairo, Paris, Madrid and Athens speak of a shared southern European model. The sea becomes a bridge between old labour movements.

After long effort, Egypt has become a social democracy on the Nile, with free unions, a mixed economy and a welfare state. The model is neither Moscow's nor Washington's, but its own. The nation looks on with pride, and the Arab world watches with interest.

The armed forces are recast as an army of citizens, in which service is a duty of every man and promotion rests on merit. Officers are taught that their loyalty lies with the people and the constitution. The government hopes to build a force that defends the republic rather than rules it.

The men who crossed the canal and fought in Sinai are honoured with pensions, medals and a place in public life. The government pays tribute to their sacrifice, and the veterans in turn become a pillar of support. The memory of the fighting is cherished as the foundation of national pride.

The founding generation of labour leaders is ageing, and the party must settle the course it will follow. Should it remain the organ of the factory floor, or become a broader movement of all Egyptians who work for a living? The decision shapes its future.

The party sharpens its focus on the industrial workers, strengthening its ties with the trade unions and the factory committees. The movement becomes disciplined and class-conscious, and the unions have a government that is truly theirs. The middle classes look on with suspicion.

The party opens its doors to clerks, teachers, farmers and shopkeepers, and presents itself as the voice of the whole people. Its message is broad and its appeal wide. The unions sometimes grumble that the workers are lost in the crowd, but the ballot boxes fill.

The revolution has taken a religious turn, and the highest authority in the land now sits in the great mosque. A council of scholars from al-Azhar, led by Grand Imam Abd al-Halim Mahmud, takes over the guidance of the state. The law of God is to be the law of Egypt, and the ulema its guardians.

The Grand Imam, long the foremost religious figure of the Sunni world, assumes the highest office of the state. Egyptians who once looked to the president for guidance now look to the pulpit. It is an experiment without precedent in the modern age, watched with awe and alarm abroad.

Two models of religious rule beckon. One is the learned, moderate tradition of al-Azhar, rooted in a thousand years of scholarship; the other is the austere pattern of the Arabian kingdom, rich in oil and in conviction. The path chosen will define the character of the Islamic state.

The scholars of the old university govern in the manner of their forebears, with deliberation, tradition and respect for the schools of law. They claim that Egypt's Islam is the Islam of moderation and learning. The state becomes a seminar, and ministers speak the language of the madrasa.

Envoys arrive from Riyadh with advice, funds and preachers of the Najdi school. The religious police patrol the markets, and the ulema are guided by teachings from the Arabian peninsula. Egypt's older, gentler traditions are thrust aside, and many scholars of al-Azhar mutter that the Nile has been made a tributary of the desert.

The civil codes inherited from Napoleonic France are set aside, and the courts apply the law of the Sharia. Judges are learned in religion rather than statute, and punishments follow the classical rules. Supporters say the courts are now incorruptible; critics say they are medieval.

A body of senior scholars is empowered to issue binding opinions on matters of law and public policy. Ministers consult them before they act, and their rulings are read from the pulpits. The state gains moral authority, and the scholars gain a power over government that no cleric has held in generations.

Volunteers and officials patrol the streets, enforcing public morals in the name of commanding the good and forbidding the evil. Shopkeepers close for prayer, and cafes and cinemas are watched with suspicion. The pious applaud, while the secular and the cosmopolitan keep their heads down.

The status of Egypt's Christian minority is raised anew. The traditional protections of the dhimma, with their taxes and restrictions, are debated in the councils of the faithful. The Copts, who have lived on the Nile since before Islam, view the discussion with fear and dismay.

The Islamic alms tax is collected by the state and distributed to the needy, the orphan and the traveller. Charity becomes a pillar of public finance, and the poor look to the mosque rather than the ministry. The government hopes that piety will succeed where bureaucracy has struggled.

The religious endowments seized by the revolution in the 1950s are returned to the care of the scholars. Lands, shops and buildings once again support mosques, schools and hospitals. The ulema regain an independent income, and a power they have not enjoyed in a generation.

Interest is forbidden and the banks of Egypt must operate on the principles of profit-sharing and partnership. Financiers struggle to adapt, while devout depositors welcome institutions they can trust in conscience. The experiment is watched closely in the Gulf, and with some alarm in the West.

Merchants of Cairo and Alexandria find eager partners in the wealthy states of the Gulf, who share their faith and their preferences. Trade in food, textiles and goods certified in accordance with the law grows quickly. Egypt rediscovers its place in the commerce of the Muslim world.

Every year, vast numbers of pilgrims pass through Egyptian ports and roads on their way to Mecca. The state improves the harbours and highways along the Red Sea and offers services to the faithful. What was once a trickle of devotion becomes a steady source of livelihood.

Zakat, waqf and halal trade together form a distinct economic order, built on faith and fairness rather than interest and speculation. The prosperity it brings is modest but widely shared. The ulema proclaim that the blessings of heaven have come to the Nile.

Al-Azhar's colleges multiply across the land, teaching religion and modern subjects side by side. Young men and women from the villages gain access to learning they never had. The old university becomes the foundation of a national school system.

Schools across the republic are directed to teach the Quran, the traditions of the Prophet and the Islamic sciences at the heart of the syllabus. The young are raised in the faith of their fathers. Scientists and engineers worry that modern studies are being squeezed aside.

Egypt's scholars seek a pact with the kingdom of Arabia, pledging to defend the faith and the holy places together. The two great centres of Sunni Islam, one of learning and one of wealth, join in common purpose. The prospect of oil money delights the treasury and unsettles Cairo's secular elite.

Preachers and teachers trained at al-Azhar travel south along the Nile and beyond, to Sudan, Chad, Ethiopia and Nigeria. They open schools, build mosques and spread the message of the scholars. Egypt's old role as the teacher of Africa's Muslims is revived.

The ancient university has become a state, and the state has become a university. Law, finance, education and morals are all governed by the doctrine of the scholars. Egypt stands as the world's greatest experiment in clerical rule, admired by some and feared by many more.

The pamphlet of Muhammad Abd al-Salam Faraj declares that jihad is the forgotten pillar of the faith, and that the rulers of Egypt have forfeited their right to obedience. In its wake the state is overthrown and the men of the underground inherit the republic. The era of revolutionary Islam has begun.

The leaders of the movement gather in secret councils to decide the fate of the nation. They consult one another in the manner of the early Muslim community, answerable to their consciences and their guns. Zeal binds the council together, though its members trust few outside it.

The movement is divided. The conspirators of Cairo, led by Faraj, believe in the lightning strike from within the state, while the militants of Upper Egypt trust in popular mobilisation in the villages and universities. Only one vision can prevail.

Faraj's disciplined cells take control of the state. Small, secret and fanatical, the vanguard sees itself as the only true believers in a sea of apostasy. It governs by conviction, suspicion and the sword, and soon the army and ministries are filled with uneasy faces.

The Gama'a Islamiyya, rooted in the villages of the Said and the student unions of Asyut and Minya, brings the revolution to the people. Its preachers and enforcers command a following among peasants and clerks alike. It governs through the mosque, the clan and the pulpit as much as through the ministries.

Officers suspected of disloyalty or impiety are dismissed, arrested or worse. The barracks fill with whispers, and the cadets are taught the creed before they are taught the drill. The movement trusts only the soldiers it has remade in its own image.

The parties that once crowded the political stage are declared un-Islamic divisions in the community of believers. Their offices are shuttered, their newspapers silenced and their leaders sent to prison or exile. A single movement, claiming to speak for God, now speaks for Egypt.

Judges answerable to the emir apply a stern and swift justice, sweeping aside the delays and bribery of the old courts. Citizens who once despaired of the law find disputes settled in days. Theft is punished harshly and corruption is stamped out, though the price in mercy is high.

The fortunes made during the Infitah by importers, contractors and middlemen are declared ill-gotten and seized by the new authority. The villas of the new rich are emptied and their bank accounts frozen. The poor cheer, while the merchant class flees or goes underground.

Interest is outlawed in every transaction, and the banks are dissolved or reconstituted on Islamic principles. Foreign lenders withdraw in alarm, and the financial world looks on aghast. The emirate declares that it will live by the commandments of God, even if the money markets will not.

Egypt withdraws from the commerce of the infidel world and resolves to rely upon its own fields and workshops. Imports are curtailed, foreign goods are forbidden and ration cards are issued. The emirate calls this purity, and the shops, increasingly empty, call it hardship.

The whole economy is bent to the needs of the holy struggle. Factories turn out weapons and uniforms, farms deliver grain for the fighters and every household is called upon to sacrifice. The nation is on a permanent footing of war, and the emirate demands everything from its people.

Preachers, funds and weapons flow across the borders into Sudan, Libya, Syria and Jordan. The emirate holds that the revolution cannot stop at the Nile, and that every ruler of the region is a tyrant to be overthrown. Neighbouring capitals tremble, and the great powers take note.

The emirate denounces the Saudi royal house as corrupt servants of the West and unworthy guardians of the holy places. Diplomats are expelled, the pilgrimage is disrupted and the oil wealth of Arabia is cut off. The breach is bitter, for Egypt's revolutionaries claim a leadership the kingdom will not yield.

Jerusalem and the lands of Palestine remain, in the eyes of the emirate, the first duty of every believer. Fighters are drawn from across the land, and preachers call for a holy war to liberate the holy places. For Israel, the neighbour on the Sinai frontier has become an implacable enemy.

The republic of Nasser and Sadat is gone, and in its place stands the Emirate of Egypt, ruled in the name of God by the men of the movement. Its achievements and its crimes alike are measured against a standard its founders set themselves. The world waits to see whether the emirate can endure.

Fighters hardened in the underground and the foreign wars of the faith are formed into an army of volunteers. They are inspired by faith and uninhibited by the habits of the old officer corps. Lacking organisation, the mujahidin make up for it in zeal.

Workshops in Cairo and the provinces turn out rifles, rockets and explosives for the holy struggle. Engineers loyal to the movement adapt the arsenal of the old army to new purposes. The emirate will not lack the tools of war, whatever the world may think.

The movement's leaders must decide who will guide it in the years ahead. Two figures stand forth: the venerable blind preacher of the south, and the cold, ambitious physician who dreams of a worldwide struggle. The choice will decide whether the revolution stays on the Nile or sets out to conquer the world.

Omar Abd al-Rahman, the blind scholar of Upper Egypt, takes the helm. His sermons stir the multitudes in the mosques, and his authority is rooted in learning as much as in force. The emirate becomes a theocracy of the pulpit, in which the voice of the old sheikh is the voice of the state.

Ayman al-Zawahiri and his comrades turn the movement outward, building networks of cells and sympathisers from Sudan to Afghanistan and Yemen. Egypt becomes the base of a worldwide jihad against the West and its clients. The emirate no longer has frontiers, only fronts.

With the civilian facade set aside, authority passes to a council of senior officers meeting behind closed doors in Cairo. The generals present it as a temporary custodianship, a war council for a nation under arms, but the men who sit around the table understand that whoever commands the divisions now commands the Republic. The programme of the army becomes the programme of the state.

Portfolios once held by Nasser's political companions are handed to serving and retired generals. Ministries are run like staff sections, with memoranda, deadlines and little patience for debate. Cairo's bureaucrats grumble about barracks manners, but the officers promise that after the humiliation of 1967 only disciplined men can be trusted to deliver results.

The junta is not of one mind. The cautious and methodical war minister, Mohamed Fawzi, believes the nation must be harnessed in its entirety before any new test with Israel. The younger and bolder Saad el-Shazly, hero of the paratroopers, wants a lean professional army and a limited, well-prepared blow. The council must choose whose vision the Republic will follow.

Mohamed Fawzi takes the helm and turns Egypt into a single barracks. Reservists are recalled, factories and schools are drawn into the war effort, and the radio speaks of sacrifice and endurance. It is a heavy burden for a poor country, but Fawzi insists that the road back to Sinai runs through every household on the Nile.

Saad el-Shazly argues that wars are won by trained specialists, not by crowds in uniform. Under his leadership the army shrinks its ambitions and sharpens its skills, with long drills, realistic exercises and officers promoted on merit rather than connections. Soldiers grumble at the pace, but a leaner force begins to take shape along the canal.

Civilians accused of sabotage, subversion or simply of weakening the national will now stand before officers in uniform. The trials are swift and the verdicts rarely surprising. The generals call it wartime necessity, while lawyers and old judges whisper that the courthouse has become another barracks.

The Mukhabarat is placed firmly in the hands of the army. Its informants fill the cafes of Cairo, its files grow thick with the names of officers, students and journalists, and no rumour is too small to be recorded. The junta sleeps more easily, though few Egyptians do.

Troops and police deploy through the villages of the Said, where feuds, smuggling and the angry sermons of zealous preachers have long defied Cairo. Checkpoints appear on the river roads and village elders are summoned to the garrison. The generals promise order, and the south learns once more how far the capital's arm can reach.

The Arab Socialist Union, built to give the revolution a mass voice, is stripped of its committees and its pretensions. Local party offices are shuttered or handed to garrison commanders, and the old apparatchiks are retired with polite letters. The officers insist that Egypt needs deeds, not meetings.

Every junta eventually faces the same question. The emergency, it is said, will end with victory or at least with peace, yet the generals have grown accustomed to the Presidential Palace and the offices that come with it. Within the council, quiet arguments begin over whether power should ever be given back.

The generals announce that the army's duty is to defend the nation, not govern it. A date is set, parties are invited to draw up platforms, and officers return to their units with their medals and a measure of public goodwill. Many Egyptians doubt it will last, but for the first time in years the ballot box is more than a rumour.

The council declares that the emergency has no foreseeable end. Elections are postponed again and again, and the army is proclaimed the permanent guardian of the revolution. The generals grow comfortable in their villas and ministries, and the Republic hardens into a state in which the uniform is the only reliable passport.

Abd al-Ghani al-Gamasy, the quiet planner whose maps shaped every Egyptian operation, is elevated to the presidency and the baton of a field marshal. He rules as he planned, carefully, patiently and with an eye for detail. To the public he is a steady hand and to the council a useful figurehead, though few doubt who his real constituency is.

The army has become more than a service. It feeds its own men, builds the roads, trades abroad and guarantees the borders. Officers speak of a Shield of the Nation, and in schools and barracks alike children learn that the uniform stands between Egypt and its enemies. Whether the shield protects the nation or confines it is left unsaid.

The finance ministry is told bluntly that the army comes first. Bread subsidies and school budgets are trimmed to keep the rearmament on schedule, and civil servants are reminded that the nation cannot eat while the canal is held by the enemy. Few dare to object in public.

The armaments works of Helwan and Cairo are ordered to turn their lathes to peaceful use. Refrigerators, pressure cookers and sewing machines roll off lines built for munitions, giving the army a new trade and the public goods that Egyptian shops have long lacked. Critics say the quality is martial, but the shelves are filling.

Conscripts with spades are sent beyond the Nile to the oases of the New Valley. Wells are drilled, fields are marked out and the army takes up farming as another form of duty. Officers boast of self-sufficiency, and the desert, for once, seems to answer to the chain of command.

The army's engineers, so recently drilled in crossing obstacles, are turned loose on the desert. Ribbons of asphalt reach the oases, the mines and the quarries without a single civilian contractor. It is cheap, fast and remarkably orderly, and every kilometre is a reminder of who is building the nation.

Egyptian-made rifles, ammunition and spare parts begin to leave the warehouses for Baghdad and the capitals of newly independent Africa. The sales bring in hard currency and friends, and the generals discover that a country that once only bought weapons can also sell them. Western diplomats take careful note.

Officers' clubs, army shops and soldiers' cooperatives spread across the garrison towns, selling food and household goods at prices no private merchant can match. Veterans and their families find a measure of security, and the army gains a loyal following. Small traders watch with mounting unease.

Farms, factories, workshops and shops together form a state within the state. The army no longer relies on the treasury alone, and its officers sit on the boards of enterprises that employ thousands. Growth follows, but so does the sense that the economy of Egypt has become the economy of the barracks.

Emissaries of the junta travel to Damascus, Baghdad and Amman proposing what Nasser's diplomacy never achieved, a standing military alliance among the confrontation states. Officers speak to officers, bypassing the quarrelling politicians. If the pact holds, the Arab armies may finally act as one.

Egyptian procurement officers shop wherever the price is right. Soviet tanks, French electronics and whatever else can be had are paid for with cotton, credit and favours, and no single supplier is allowed to hold the army hostage. Moscow frowns, Paris smiles, and the arsenals of Egypt fill steadily.

The lesson of the War of Attrition is plain, that the Israeli air force rules the sky unless it is made to pay dearly. Missile batteries rise in dense belts along the canal and in the Delta, manned day and night by crews trained with Soviet advisers. The generals are certain that whoever controls the sky controls the crossing.

Tank crews drill in the desert west of Cairo until the rhythm of manoeuvre becomes second nature. Fresh deliveries of armour are concentrated into formations that can strike with weight and speed once the missile umbrella is spread. The junta wants a fist that is able to hit hard when the moment comes.

Service obligations are rewritten so that more men are trained for longer, and exemptions once bought by the well-connected are narrowed. Fathers in the villages complain of lost labour in the fields, but the army insists that a nation which wishes to recover Sinai must be willing to train its sons.

A trusted corps of picked officers and men is raised to guard the council, the ministries and the broadcasting house. Its soldiers are paid well, fed well and watched closely. The generals no longer fear a coup from the street, only one from within the army itself, and this force is the answer.

The armed forces journal, once a dry bulletin for the barracks, becomes the voice of the government. Its columns praise the discipline of the soldier, the duty of the citizen and the wisdom of the council. Editors in the civilian press learn to read its tone, and to echo it.

The old Young Egypt movement of the thirties returns from the political wilderness, its green banners dusted off and its slogans fitted to a new era. Veterans of the original movement stand beside embittered young officers, united by contempt for the pashas and a hunger for national dignity after the defeat. Egypt, they declare, shall be reborn by its own sons.

Cairo's squares and Alexandria's seafront fill with columns of marching youth, torches and banners. Speakers promise that the nation will rise as one, and the crowds roar in reply. Whatever the foreign embassies make of it, the government has shown that it can summon the street at will.

The movement has two souls. One looks to the monuments of Giza and Luxor and sees a proud Egyptian civilisation older than any creed. The other sees the minaret and the faith that has bound the Egyptians for more than a thousand years. The leadership must decide which to place at the heart of its nationalism.

Schoolbooks are rewritten to glorify the builders of the pyramids, and the language of the movement turns to blood and soil along the Nile. Copts and secular intellectuals take heart at being counted as heirs of a common past, while the sheikhs of al-Azhar mutter that the nation is being taught to honour idols of stone.

The movement embraces the faith as the soul of the nation. Its rallies open with prayers and its programmes speak of a virtuous Egypt, the guardian of Islam and the heart of the Arab world. Ahmed Hussein's later turn toward religion finds a ready audience in the mosques, though not everyone is comfortable with the new tone.

Young men in green shirts drill in school courtyards and on village squares, sworn to the movement and to one another. Their discipline impresses their elders and alarms their opponents. They are the movement's pride, its fist and, some fear, its future police.

Every young Egyptian is called to serve, in the fields, in the workshops, in uniform and in the ranks of the movement. The camps teach discipline, literacy and loyalty in equal measure. Parents grumble at the interruption to schooling, but many are proud to see their sons marching with purpose.

The movement turns its fury on the old landed class and the foreign firms that still prosper along the Nile. Palaces are denounced, concessions questioned and cosmopolitan Alexandria is warned that its days of easy indulgence are over. The workers and the poor cheer, while bankers and diplomats count the cost.

The old Qirsh appeal of 1931 is revived, asking every Egyptian to give a coin toward national industry. Pennies from shopkeepers, students and fellahin are pooled into funds for new Egyptian factories. It is a modest idea, but it gives ordinary people a stake in the nation's machines.

Shopwindows carry placards urging patriots to buy at home, and foreign wares are taxed and scorned. Small manufacturers and craftsmen, long crushed by imports, find their workshops busy again. Importers complain, and consumers learn that national pride sometimes costs a little more.

The great foreign trading houses, whose offices have handled Egypt's cotton and its commerce for generations, are taken over in the name of the nation. London and Paris protest loudly. In Cairo, crowds cheer as the last relics of the capitulations are finally swept away.

Egyptian capital, Egyptian labour and Egyptian management now run the commanding heights of the country. The plants hum, the ledgers are kept in Arabic, and the movement can point to a young economy that no longer bows to foreign creditors. Whether it can stand without them remains to be seen.

Egypt and the Sudan, the movement insists, are one valley and one people, divided only by imperial map-makers. Posters show the Nile flowing unbroken from Khartoum to the sea. In Khartoum this slogan is heard with deep unease, and the Sudanese government wonders where Egyptian ambition will stop.

The movement tells both Washington and Moscow that Egypt will not be anyone's garrison. Advisers are politely but firmly asked to pack, and the nation is promised independence in fact as well as in name. Egypt's patrons are dismayed, but the street applauds.

Egyptian emissaries, teachers and radio broadcasts fan out across the continent, presenting Cairo as the natural leader of a liberated Africa. In Khartoum, Addis Ababa, Chad and Libya the message finds both admirers and wary rulers. The ambition recalls Nasser's, but without the Soviet bargain behind it.

The dream that began in the cafes of Cairo in the thirties is stated openly, an Egypt reaching beyond the Nile Valley to claim a leading place in the Arab and African world. Soldiers, students and workers march under the same banner, and the leaders speak of destiny. Egypt's neighbours listen with growing alarm.

Boys barely out of school are formed into battalions under the green banner, trained by veterans who still remember the previous war. They are loud, enthusiastic and eager, and the regular officers watch with a mixture of fascination and misgiving. Their passion is plain, and their discipline is yet to be proved.

The founder is ageing and the movement must face what comes next. Rival lieutenants court the youth, the officers and the old guard, each insisting that they alone carry the true flame. Behind the cheering crowds, the question of succession quietly decides everything.

The movement and the state become one. Party cells appear in every ministry, every factory and every classroom, and loyalty to the cause is the surest path to promotion. The leaders speak of national unity, and dissenters learn that there is no room for opposition within a revolution.

The movement chooses to give its nationalism a constitutional form. A republic is declared with elected institutions, a national assembly and a president who answers to the voters. The old militants are uneasy at the compromise, but the public welcomes a state that appears to belong to everyone.

A new Revolutionary Command Council is sworn in, made up of younger and angrier officers who regard Nasser's heirs as tired and compromised. They speak of finishing the revolution that began in 1952 and of purging all who have grown fat on it. The old order in Cairo has reason to be afraid.

On the radio, a colonel reads out the council's proclamation. The old regime is condemned, the war will be fought without compromise, and every Egyptian is summoned to serve. The tone is blunt and the promises are large. In the barracks the junior officers cheer, and in the ministries clerks quietly clear their desks.

The council cannot agree on what kind of revolution it is making. One faction demands ideological purity, with the faithful rewarded and the doubtful removed. Another argues that only competent engineers and planners can rebuild the nation. The choice will shape the character of the new regime.

Loyalty becomes the measure of every man. Committees review the record of officers, officials and teachers, and those with doubtful pasts are removed. The faithful are honoured, and the creed of the revolution is recited in every school. The council grows ever more suspicious of anyone who thinks for himself.

Engineers in uniform are placed in charge of ministries, factories and research institutes. The council trusts the slide rule over the slogan, and the results are measured in tonnes, kilowatts and schedules. Ideologues sulk at the sidelines while the army's technicians quietly remake the state.

Special tribunals are set up to try speculators, saboteurs and corrupt officials. Proceedings are rapid and public, and the sentences are severe. The poor cheer when a notorious profiteer is led away, and the rich begin to wonder whose turn is next.

Every institution takes on a martial tone. Students march, workers drill and civil servants wear uniforms on state occasions. Whole neighbourhoods are organised into units with commanders, and Egypt begins to look like a country preparing for a war that is always about to begin.

A new body of officers and planners is given authority to override ministers, banks and managers. Orders are issued in the name of the revolution, and projects that once languished in committee are suddenly begun. The economy is to be run like a campaign.

The council denounces a new class of contractors, importers and senior officials who have grown rich during the years of defeat. Villas are seized, bank accounts are frozen and the proceeds are poured into the national treasury. The crowds approve, while the middle class lies awake wondering about their own savings.

Workers are enrolled into disciplined battalions and sent wherever the nation needs them, to docks, building sites and canal works. They are fed, housed and paid, and they are not free to leave. Foremen are replaced by officers, and the trade unions learn to call their members comrades-in-arms.

Prices, wages, quotas and investment are decided in the council's planning rooms. Directors of factories receive orders rather than advice, and the market is treated as an enemy to be starved. Output rises and shortages fall, but the clerks of the plan hold more power than the people they serve.

Along the western bank of the canal, concrete casemates and sand ramparts rise under the desert sun, a chain of fortified positions meant to hold the line whatever the cost. Gunners and sappers work day and night under the eyes of enemy aircraft. The council is determined that no Israeli column will cross.

Egypt declares itself the vanguard of the Arab revolution and begins to export it. Agents and broadcasts reach into Libya, the Sudan and Syria in support of like-minded officers, while Washington is denounced in every speech. Friends are few, but the council values loyalty over comfort.

The revolution is finished, or so its architects claim. A state of order, discipline and steel stands where the monarchy and the old parties once did. Citizens salute the flag, heed the radio and expect nothing else. For the council the Iron Republic is the proof that the sacrifices were justified.

A paramilitary guard is raised from the most loyal workers, students and veterans, issued with rifles and sent to patrol the factories and the streets. It stands apart from the regular army, answers only to the council and reminds the generals that they too can be watched.

Picked soldiers are gathered into formations trained for ruthless offence, with the best armour and the youngest, hardest officers. Their motto is attack and their schedule leaves no room for doubt. The council sees in them the spearhead that will smash the enemy's line when the day arrives.

A permanent system of security courts takes over from the improvised tribunals. It has its own prosecutors, its own prisons and its own rules, all in the name of protecting the revolution. The police gain confidence, and the lawyers learn how little their briefs now matter.

Egypt is told to rely on nothing but itself. Imports are curbed, foreign advisers are sent home and every household is urged to make do. Sanctions and embargoes hold little terror for a state that has decided to stand alone. The sacrifice is real, but so is the pride.

As victory over its enemies draws near, the council turns on itself. Rival officers accumulate supporters, ministries become fiefdoms and whispers of conspiracy fill the corridors. Everyone realises that the revolution cannot have two heads for long, and that the next decision of the council will determine who survives it.

One colonel emerges from the quarrels, and the others fall in behind him or fall silent. He becomes the voice of the revolution and the sole interpreter of its will. His portrait appears on every wall, and the council becomes his audience.

The officers agree to rule together, with decisions taken by the council and no single man placed above it. It is a fragile balance of rivals who trust each other only so far, but it spares the Republic the folly of a lone ruler. In the corridors of power, argument is kept alive.

After eighteen years in exile, the former king returns to Egypt. Fuad II, who was only a child when the Free Officers sent his family away, steps onto the quay at Alexandria to the sound of cannon and cheering crowds. For some, it is a restoration of lost dignity and for others a humiliating step back in time.

A council of elder statesmen, loyal officers and men of the old court is gathered around the throne. Surviving ministers of the monarchy, landowners and veteran diplomats advise the young king in whispers. They bring experience and nostalgia in equal measure, and the republic's critics are quick to say that the pashas are back.

The restored monarchy must decide what kind of king Egypt will have. One camp points to the constitution of 1923 and argues that the crown will survive only if it rules with parliament. The other holds that after the chaos of the republic, the people need a ruler with real power. The palace is divided.

The king swears to uphold the constitution, and the doors of parliament are opened once more. Parties are permitted, newspapers print freely and the crown presides above the quarrels of politicians. London and the Western capitals are delighted, though the veterans of the old palace camarilla sigh at the loss of authority.

The crown retains the right to appoint ministers, dissolve assemblies and decide matters of war and peace. Parliament may talk, but the king will decide. The royal court speaks of order and continuity, and the liberal press is told to remember how the last parliamentary age ended.

Deputies file into the chamber for the first time in a generation. The veterans of the New Wafd appear in dark suits, proud and a little surprised to be back in the game. Whatever the limits placed on it, the Parliament of the Kingdom gives the new order a voice and an air of legitimacy.

Handpicked soldiers, resplendent in ceremonial uniforms but armed with modern weapons, are charged with defending the king and his palace. Their loyalty is to the person of the monarch rather than to any general or party. The army's officers watch with mixed feelings.

The great palace in the heart of Cairo, long a museum and a ministry, is cleaned, regilded and returned to the crown. Chandeliers are rehung and the old ceremonies revived. The great landowners return to court, delighted to see the world they knew restored, while the fellahin ask what it means for them.

Lands taken from the royal family in 1952 are returned to the crown, together with the revenues that come with them. The estates are a visible sign of the king's rehabilitation, and a pointed reminder to the peasants who farmed them of how much has changed.

A new company under royal patronage takes up the management of Egypt's most famous export. Long-staple cotton again flows from the Delta through Alexandria's brokers to the mills of Lancashire and beyond. Buyers recall the golden days of the trade, and for the first time in years the ledgers are optimistic.

The king writes to his fellow monarchs of Arabia and the Gulf, inviting them to place their wealth in the rebuilding of Egypt. A fund bearing the crown's name is to channel their money into canals, ports and housing. It is a bold appeal from one throne to others, and the response will show how much loyalty the royal name still commands.

Egypt is presented to the world as a stable, hospitable kingdom where capital is welcome and property is secure. Bankers from Beirut, Kuwait and London visit the offices of the new ministry, and the old arguments against foreign money are put aside. The crown's reputation is the guarantee.

A board of engineers, old hands from the days of the monarchy and young graduates, is charged with the canals, barrages and pumping stations of the Nile Valley. The king's name is attached to every new channel, and the fellahin find that water arrives more reliably than it has for years.

The monarchy discovers an unexpected asset in its heritage. Visitors come to see the pyramids and Luxor, but also the palaces, the royal train and the old courts of Cairo. Hotels reopen, guides polish their English and French, and the restored crown helps to make Egypt fashionable again.

Cotton, tourism, Gulf investment and the improved channels of the Nile together give the kingdom something it has lacked for years, a sense of economic confidence. The treasury is healthier, merchants return and the court proudly attributes it all to the wisdom of the crown.

Fuad II is received with honours by the kings of Arabia, Jordan, Morocco and the Shah of Iran. The old rivalries are put aside, and the monarchs pledge to stand together against revolution wherever it breaks out. For Egypt, so recently the home of the Arab revolution, the change of company is remarkable.

The old connection with Britain, once a source of resentment, is quietly revived. Ministers visit Whitehall and British firms return to the Nile. Egypt's merchants hope for easier trade and the court for the dignified friendship of a fellow crown.

Fuad II's family connection to the Pahlavis, linked by marriage in the previous generation, becomes the basis of a political understanding. The Shah, who wishes to see monarchy defended from Cairo to Tehran, offers the friendship of a rich and ambitious neighbour. A bond between two thrones is a new feature of Middle Eastern politics.

The court revives the old title worn by the grandfather and speaks once more of the unity of the Nile Valley under the crown. The palace is restored, the economy is sound, friends abroad are secured and the succession is settled. Loyalists believe that the dynasty has come home for good, while Khartoum watches with trepidation.

The army is given a royal character, with new colours, new regimental names and honorary colonels from the court. Officers who had assumed that the monarchy would fear them discover that it intends to rely on them. Their loyalty is bought with pride and with tanks.

The question of who will carry the crown into the next generation turns to the education of the heir. Tutors, officers and clerics compete to shape the young prince, and the palace argues about whether he should be groomed for ceremony or for command. In a monarchy, the nursery is also a political arena.

The king agrees to share his authority with a council of trusted advisers. The ministers, the generals and the elder statesmen of the court will govern in his name until the heir is ready. The arrangement is dignified and steady, and spares the crown from risking everything on one man.

The king takes the reins of government himself. Ministers become servants of the crown, and there is no intermediary between the throne and the people. Supporters hail a strong monarch for hard times, while the old parliamentarians recall the lessons of the previous reign with a shudder.

Since 1968 the guns along the Suez Canal have never been fully silent. Artillery duels, air raids and commando strikes bleed both sides while the Bar-Lev Line stands defiantly on the far bank. Nasser calls it a war of attrition, convinced that Egypt's greater numbers and patience will eventually wear Israel down.

As Israeli aircraft strike deep into the Nile Valley, the answer is a belt of surface-to-air missile batteries, rolled forward towards the Canal with Soviet crews and Egyptian sweat. Under their umbrella, the army can at last work without fear from the sky. It is the shield that makes any future crossing possible.

Small parties of Egyptian commandos slip across the Canal at night to ambush patrols, mine roads and strike at the outposts of the Bar-Lev Line. The raids achieve little in terms of ground, but they restore the confidence of an army that has known only retreat. Each returning boat is a small victory over the memory of 1967.

Washington's Secretary of State proposes a ceasefire along the Canal, and a framework for talks under Ambassador Jarring. The offer is fraught with risk, for it offers a pause while Israel remains in Sinai. Egypt must weigh the relief of the cities against the dangers of letting the moment pass.

Egypt accepts the proposal and the guns fall silent along the Canal. The cities of Suez and Ismailia breathe at last, and the missile batteries creep forward under the cover of calm. Hardliners call it surrender, but the president insists it is a pause for breath, not an end to the struggle.

There will be no ceasefire, no negotiation and no recognition while Israeli soldiers stand on Egyptian soil. The Rogers Plan is rejected as a trap that would freeze the occupation, and the war of attrition continues. Cairo has made its choice, and the cost will be paid by its soldiers.

In the offices of the General Staff, planners draw up Granite, a full-scale scheme to cross the Canal, storm the Bar-Lev Line and penetrate deep into Sinai. Ambitious and detailed, it is a plan of the kind that Egypt could not yet carry out. The work, however, builds a habit of thinking that will serve it well.

Chief of Staff Saad el-Shazly argues that Egypt should not outreach its means. A more limited plan, called the High Minarets, would cross the Canal and seize a narrow strip on the far side, remaining under the protection of the missile umbrella. It is a prudent strategy of an army that has learned humility the hard way.

The great sand rampart of the Bar-Lev Line seems to defy the engineers, until a young officer suggests that high-pressure water pumps could wash it away. The idea is tested on sandbanks along the Nile, and the results are startling. A problem measured in days of labour is solved in hours.

Year after year the army stages exercises at the Canal, each of which ends in a stand-down. Israeli intelligence grows accustomed to the pattern, and the reports from the front begin to say that nothing is happening. By the time a real attack comes, nobody believes in it.

The plans are complete, the units are in place and the men are trained to the last detail. Operation Badr, named for the Prophet's first great victory, awaits only the order. When it comes, it will be the culmination of six years of preparation and a lifetime of humiliation.

On a clear afternoon the Egyptian army surges across the Canal, bursting the Bar-Lev Line and raising the flag on the eastern bank. The shock to Israel is profound, and the pride of Egypt is restored. The defeat of 1967, which weighed upon a generation, is lifted at last.

Egypt cannot compel the oil producers to act, but it can ask. Envoys travel to Riyadh, Tripoli, Baghdad and Kuwait to urge them to use their wealth as a weapon against the states that arm Israel. The decision is theirs alone, and Cairo awaits their answer.

At a tent beside the Cairo-Suez road, Egyptian and Israeli officers meet to discuss the exchange of prisoners and the future of the front. It is the first face-to-face encounter between the two armies, and the beginning of a more serious dialogue. The road to disengagement starts at Kilometre 101.

After years of tense negotiation, Cairo and Jerusalem are asked to agree on the phased return of Sinai, in exchange for demilitarised zones and international monitors. The terms are bitter to some and generous to others, but they promise the return of every grain of Egyptian sand. Peace is no longer an abstraction.

Eight years of silence end when engineers and naval divers clear the wrecks and mines that choke the waterway. Ships once again pass between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, and the revenues of the Canal return to the Egyptian treasury. The great artery of world trade flows once more through the heart of Egypt.

Suez, Ismailia and Port Said, evacuated and shelled for years, are left in ruins. Now their inhabitants return to rebuild their homes, their harbours and their workshops. The new cities rise from the rubble with great hope, and a certain pride in having survived.

The sixth of October becomes a national holiday, a day on which Egyptians remember the crossing and the soldiers who made it possible. The shame of the Naksa has been erased, not by the extent of victory but by the proof of courage. The army, and the nation, can hold their heads high again.

The guns along the Canal are silent, but the Sinai is still occupied and the Bar-Lev Line grows stronger every month. Neither war nor peace has returned a single kilometre of Egyptian soil. Cairo concludes that only a limited war can break the deadlock and force the superpowers to take Egypt seriously again.

Our pilots cannot yet beat the Israeli air force in the sky, so our missiles will deny it the sky. A dense belt of SA-2, SA-3 and mobile SA-6 batteries along the Canal will cover the crossing points and let the army advance under a roof of missiles.

In 1967 the air force was destroyed on the ground in a single morning. Never again: hardened shelters, dispersed airfields, new MiG and Sukhoi squadrons and pilots trained for low-level strikes will give the next war an Egyptian air arm that survives the first hour.

Israeli armour counter-attacks will come within hours of a crossing. The infantry that crosses first will carry its own defence: Sagger missiles and RPGs in every platoon, and long-range Scuds to deter strikes deep into Egypt.

Exercises on the Canal will become routine, reservists will be called up and sent home again, and rumours of poor Soviet maintenance will be allowed to spread. When the real attack comes, Israeli intelligence must believe it is just another exercise.

Egypt will not fight alone. Damascus must open a second front on the Golan, and the Arab capitals are asked to send squadrons, brigades and money. Every partner that agrees receives its own war aims and joins the coordinated plan.

The President, the war minister and the chief of staff meet behind closed doors and fix the day and the hour. The objective is limited but clear: cross the Canal, storm the Bar-Lev Line and hold the east bank under the missile umbrella until the world is forced to negotiate.

Cairo has always seen itself as the natural capital of the Arab world, and Nasser as its leader. Even after the defeat, its schools, its broadcasts and its diplomats continue to shape the Arab debate. The mantle of leadership is heavy, but Egypt is not ready to lay it down.

In the autumn of 1970, Jordan's army and the Palestinian fedayeen are locked in a bloody struggle. Nasser, exhausted but still the only figure trusted by both sides, convenes an emergency summit in Cairo. His last act of statesmanship is to bring King Hussein and Yasser Arafat to the same table.

At Khartoum in 1967, the oil-rich monarchies pledged annual aid to the Arab states that bore the brunt of the war. The money is vital to an economy strained by military spending and the loss of Canal revenue. Egypt keeps its patrons reassured that their generosity serves the common cause.

Colonel Gaddafi, young, zealous and admiring of Nasser, offers Libya's wealth and his own devotion to the cause of Arab unity. Together with Sudan's new rulers, Egypt signs a charter of cooperation at Tripoli. It is a bold gesture towards a union that many have dreamed of and none have achieved.

Egypt, Libya and Syria announce the formation of a Federation of Arab Republics, with a shared presidential council and common aspirations. The ceremony is grand, the speeches are long and the declarations are heartfelt. Whether the federation will be more than a name remains to be seen.

Gaddafi insists that unity must be real, not merely symbolic, and calls for a full merger of Egypt and Libya. Marches of Libyan supporters head towards Cairo, and the oil wealth of the desert is dangled before the Nile. The proposal tempts some in Egypt and alarms many others.

Egypt prefers a loose association of sovereign states, with limited powers and few obligations. The enthusiasm of Tripoli cools, and the fervour of the unionists is disappointed. For Cairo, prudence is the better part of brotherhood.

Egypt and Sudan are bound together by the river, by history and by blood. Talk of a joint economic union, with common markets, shared agricultural projects and the integration of the Nile valley, revives an old dream. The brothers of the Nile look to a future in which Khartoum and Cairo face the world as one.

The dream of 1958 is born anew. Egypt, Syria and their partners proclaim the rebirth of the United Arab Republic, a union forged by the experience of failure rather than naive enthusiasm. A flag with three stars rises again, and the Arab world watches with hope and apprehension.

Cairo offers a home to the Palestine Liberation Organisation, with offices, broadcasts and recognition as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people. Arafat's fighters find a patron who shares their cause, if not always their methods. Israel notes the welcome and draws its own conclusions.

The Arab League, whose headquarters have long been in Cairo, becomes an instrument of Egyptian diplomacy. Summits, committees and resolutions are shaped in the corridors of Tahrir. The Arab world speaks, as it often does, with a Cairene accent.

Egyptian engineering, Saudi and Emirati money and Western technology are joined in a great enterprise to build an independent Arab arms industry. Factories rise near Cairo to produce missiles, aircraft and vehicles, freeing the Arab world from the whims of foreign suppliers. The project is costly, but the prize is independence.

Teachers, doctors, clerks and construction workers leave the overcrowded Nile valley to seek their fortunes in the Gulf. The remittances they send home feed families, support the currency and ease unemployment. The country gains money, though it loses many of its best-trained sons.

Egypt stands between two giants, dependent on one for weapons and courted by the other for peace. Every decision, from the purchase of a rifle to the drafting of a communique, is weighed against the reaction in two capitals. Cairo's diplomats must walk a narrow path between them.

As Israeli deep-penetration raids humiliate Egyptian air defences, Nasser flies secretly to Moscow to beg for more help. The Kremlin responds by sending Soviet missile crews and fighter pilots, a deployment of astonishing scale and secrecy. For a time, Russians guard the skies above the Nile.

Egypt anchors its security to Moscow, accepting advisers, missiles and tanks in exchange for political loyalty. The dependence is considerable, but the arsenals of the Soviet Union are formidable and its support has never wavered. The Kremlin's friendship is a refuge as well as a leash.

A secret line opens between Cairo and Washington, carrying messages from Hafez Ismail to Henry Kissinger. The two sides test each other's intentions and explore the possibilities of peace. Moscow, naturally, would not be pleased.

Egypt declines to be the property of either power. It accepts the wheat and the weapons of both blocs while committing itself to neither, and presents itself as the champion of independent states everywhere. The balance is delicate, and a stumble might cost dearly.

In May 1971 Egypt and the Soviet Union sign a treaty of friendship and cooperation, binding the two states in a formal alliance. Moscow promises continued support in the face of Israeli aggression, and Cairo pledges its steadfastness to the common cause. For a decade, it will be the cornerstone of the Egyptian military posture.

With the treaty signed, Soviet industry opens its arsenal. Mobile SAM-6 batteries with their radars, SCUD missiles with their promise of long reach and the technical missions that accompany them appear along the Nile. Egyptian crews learn their craft with unusual speed.

Egypt takes its place within the Soviet sphere, with all that it implies. Its armies, its industries and its diplomacy are tied to the Eastern bloc. The Kremlin welcomes a new ally, the largest in the Arab world.

In July 1972 the Soviet advisers are given a week to leave. Sadat reasons that Moscow offers too little and demands too much, and that Egypt cannot negotiate with Washington while Russian experts fill its barracks. The protection of the missile umbrella vanishes with them, which is a bold gamble.

The American Secretary of State shuttles tirelessly between Cairo, Jerusalem and Damascus, carrying proposals, assurances and warnings. Each journey brings the parties a little closer. Egyptian diplomats, once strangers to Washington, find themselves leading the conversation.

Egypt completes its reorientation by joining the Western camp. Its former reliance on Moscow is replaced by cooperation with Washington and its allies. The change is sweeping, and few of the old comrades are left to mourn it.

With the Soviet Union estranged, the Egyptian air force faces a shortage of engines for its MiG fighters. China, which has its own quarrel with Moscow, offers replacement parts without any political demands. It is a modest but timely friendship.

France, the one Western power that has not forgotten its older ties to the Arab world, is willing to sell fighters and electronics where others will not. Egyptian pilots look at the Mirage with interest. De Gaulle's heirs find in Cairo a customer with deep pockets.

In the cold war's long contest for the Middle East, no state counts for more than Egypt. Its choice of ally has changed the balance of the region, and both camps know it. Whoever holds the Nile holds the key to the East.

Since 1967 Egypt has lived on a war footing. The canal is closed, tourism has dried up and a large part of the national income goes to the army. Ministers speak of the economy of the front, in which every factory, field and workshop is judged by its contribution to the eventual reckoning with Israel.

Egyptians are asked to tighten their belts. Imports of luxuries are curbed, bread and tea remain, and radio announcers urge patience until the day of liberation. Housewives queue and shopkeepers grumble, but most accept that a nation at war cannot expect comfort.

The post-Naksa economy is at a crossroads. Years of state planning have built factories and schools but also queues and bureaucracy. Some voices demand a deeper commitment to Arab socialism, others call for opening the doors to foreign capital, and still others for an economy built on Islamic principles. The choice will define the Egypt of the coming decade.

The state remains the engine of development. Factories, banks and great estates stay in public hands, and the unions are promised a larger voice. The philosophy of Nasser is not abandoned but extended, with the conviction that Egypt's workers and fellahin will win their prosperity through planning rather than the market.

Egypt throws open its doors. Foreign investors, Gulf financiers and importers are welcomed, and the state steps back from the markets it once commanded. New hotels and shopping arcades appear in Cairo, a few fortunes are made quickly, and workers and clerks wonder who will pay for the prosperity.

Economic life is to be ordered according to the principles of the faith. Interest is condemned, charity is organised and trade is conducted in accordance with the law of Islam. The scholars of al-Azhar bless the project, and the economists of the ministries labour to translate old principles into modern accounts.

The state's factories, mills and trading firms are grouped into great holding companies under the guidance of the planners. Directors answer to ministers and ministers to the Presidency. The public sector is large, proud and not always efficient, but it is the foundation of the socialist order.

Every family receives a ration card entitling it to rice, sugar, oil and bread at fixed prices. Inspectors patrol the markets to enforce the ceilings. It is a cumbersome system, but it guarantees that the poor will not starve, and it binds the people to the state that feeds them.

Moscow extends long-term credit for machinery, weapons and development projects, to be repaid in cotton, rice and a share of Egyptian output. The arrangement keeps the economy afloat but ties it ever more closely to the Soviet Union. Egyptian officials visit Moscow's ministries as supplicants and as partners.

At Port Said and Suez, customs barriers are lowered and foreign firms are invited to set up warehouses, assembly plants and banks. Cranes, container yards and bonded storage promise to turn the damaged canal cities into trading hubs. Local people hope for work, and nationalists fear for sovereignty.

Delegations from Kuwait, Riyadh and the Emirates arrive in Cairo with large sums and large ambitions. They are offered contracts for housing, agriculture and tourism, and they are treated as honoured guests. For the first time, the oil wealth of the Gulf flows west to the Nile.

The government reduces the subsidies on bread, fuel and basic goods, arguing that the treasury can no longer carry them. Economists applaud, but the poorest quarters of Cairo and Alexandria are filled with anger. The reform is necessary, and nobody can say whether the people will accept it quietly.

The first Islamic banks open their doors in Cairo, offering profit-sharing accounts and trade finance without interest. Pious savers, who had long kept their money under mattresses, bring it into the system. Bankers from the Gulf look on with approval and a little curiosity.

Visitors return to Egypt's temples, tombs and beaches. Guides reappear at the pyramids, hotels repaint their lobbies and tour operators advertise the Nile once more. Tourism brings foreign currency and also work for thousands, from camel drivers to chambermaids.

The central bank, long a department of the treasury, is given real authority over credit, currency and the banking system. Its economists, trained in London and Washington, bring order to the books and discipline to monetary policy. Inflation is a persistent enemy, and the new governor regards it as such.

After years of improvisation, Egypt arrives at an approach all its own, neither a copy of Moscow nor a transplant from the West. Economists call it the Egyptian model, adapted to the Nile and its people. Whether socialist, open or devout in character, it is homegrown, and that makes it durable.

At Aswan, the great dam that Nasser staked his reputation upon is complete. Lake Nasser stretches far into Nubia, the Nile is tamed, and floods and droughts become memories. Soviet engineers and Egyptian labourers take a justified pride, and the Republic has a monument that can be seen from the stars.

Power lines run from Aswan along the Nile and into the villages that have known only oil lamps. Electric light appears in the evenings, pumps and mills begin to turn, and a radio is soon in every coffeehouse. The fellahin begin to believe that the revolution has something for them.

The vast new lake is stocked with fish, and fishing cooperatives spring up along its shores. Boats and nets appear on the water where villages once stood, and a new industry takes hold in the shadow of the dam. Fish from Nasser's lake begin to appear on dinner tables across Egypt.

The dam brings an unwelcome side. The annual flood that carried fertile silt to the fields is gone, farmers are forced to buy fertiliser, and salt begins to creep into the soil. The Delta coast is eroding and the water table is rising. The gift of the dam must be paid for, and Egypt must now choose how.

Plants at Aswan and in the Delta turn out artificial fertiliser to replace the vanished silt. Villages that once relied on the flood now depend on sacks from the state cooperative. Yields rise, and so does the dependence of the fellah on the factories of the Republic.

Engineers set to work laying thousands of kilometres of clay and plastic pipe beneath the fields. The pipes carry off the salty water and keep the roots dry. It is slow, dull and expensive work, but it keeps the soil alive, and the cultivators of the Delta are grateful.

Villages are organised into cooperatives that share seed, credit, machinery and marketing. Small farmers, once at the mercy of money-lenders and landlords, now sit on the boards of their own societies. The state takes its share, but the peasant at last has a voice, if not always a vote.

The white gold of the Nile again takes pride of place. Fields are devoted to long-staple cotton, which earns the foreign currency needed for machinery and arms. The mills of Mahalla and the brokers of Alexandria prosper, though the cultivators ask what they will eat.

Land is turned over from cotton to wheat, maize and beans. The government decides that a nation which cannot feed itself cannot be independent. Export earnings suffer, but the bread queues grow shorter, and the planners are content that Egypt's fields should serve Egypt's stomachs first.

Pumps and canals push the green back into the desert. New villages rise in the western oases and along the margin of the Valley, settled by young graduates and families from the crowded Delta. It is a gamble against sand and salt, but the dream of a second Egypt is hard to resist.

Clinics, posters and radio campaigns urge Egyptians to have fewer children. Nurses visit villages with advice and supplies, and the government speaks of quality over quantity. The sheikhs object, and many families hesitate, but the planners know that no dam can feed an endless multiplication of mouths.

Egypt's millions are a strength, not a burden, declares the government. Large families are honoured, and the growing population is described as the nation's wealth in labour and in soldiers. Planners worry about housing and bread, but the leadership prefers to count the future conscripts.

The ancient saying that Egypt is the gift of the Nile is made true again in the age of the dam. Water, power, fertiliser and cultivation work in concert, and the fields of the Valley and the desert alike yield harvests that earlier generations could not imagine. The Nile has been mastered, not merely endured.

The great promise of the revolution was that Egypt would be a land of factories as well as of fields. Even in wartime the ministries of industry return to their blueprints, believing that an economy built on cotton alone will always be at the mercy of others. The path to strength runs through the foundry and the mill.

At Helwan, south of Cairo, the blast furnaces and rolling mills are expanded. Soviet technicians and Egyptian engineers work shoulder to shoulder to increase the output of the iron and steel works, the backbone of a modern industrial nation. Every ingot is a small answer to those who said Egypt could never build.

With electricity flowing from the High Dam, Upper Egypt can at last support heavy industry. At Nag Hammadi, a smelter is raised to turn imported ore into aluminium for cables, vehicles and aircraft. The sleepy town in the Said finds itself part of the industrial age.

The El Nasr factories at Helwan assemble trucks, buses and cars under Egyptian management. Workers who once repaired imported vehicles now build their own, and though the models are modest, the symbolism is not. Cairo's streets are beginning to fill with machines made in Egypt.

At Mahalla al-Kubra, the great textile mills spin and weave the cotton of the Delta into cloth for the nation and for export. Tens of thousands of workers have found a living there, and their strong solidarity makes them a force the government does well to heed. The mills give Egypt both its wardrobe and its working class.

Under the waters of the Gulf of Suez lies a promising treasure. Rigs rise at fields such as El Morgan and Ramadan, and foreign and Egyptian companies drill along the coast. For a country long short of foreign currency, the prospect of becoming an oil exporter is intoxicating.

A pipeline from the Red Sea coast to the Mediterranean is proposed to carry Gulf crude around the closed canal. With Arab capital and Egyptian land, the project promises to turn the loss of the canal into an opportunity. Pumping stations and tank farms begin to appear along the desert route.

Natural gas discovered off the coast near Alexandria fuels the thermal plants of the Delta. Pipelines carry it ashore at Abu Qir, and furnaces and fertiliser works begin to burn the new fuel. Egypt's engineers are pleased to find that the sea holds more than fish.

On the Mediterranean coast at El-Dabaa, the long-discussed nuclear power station finally rises from the sand. Egyptian scientists speak of electricity and progress. In Tel Aviv and in Western capitals, the same word is heard with suspicion. Egypt has joined the atomic age.

Conventional power stations burning oil and gas are built at Cairo and Alexandria, quick to construct and well understood. Their chimneys provide the electricity that the factories of the Delta need, without the controversy of the atom. Engineers call it sensible and nationalists call it timid.

The railways laid by British engineers have suffered from war and neglect. Track is relaid, locomotives are overhauled and stations are repainted, and the trains once again run along the Valley. For a poor country, the railway remains the surest way to move people and goods.

Beneath the crowded streets of Cairo, tunnels are driven for an underground railway. The congested capital, long choked by trams, buses and donkey carts, will gain a modern artery. Engineers fear the groundwater and the antiquities, and the city's commuters pray for success.

Asphalt roads stretch across the desert to the oases, the Red Sea and the mines of the south. Lorries now cross in hours distances that once took days by caravan. The roads bind the far corners of the Republic to the capital and bring the desert within reach of the plan.

Smelters, mills, refineries and assembly lines are linked by new roads, rails and cables. Visitors from Africa and the Arab lands come to Egypt to see how an Arab nation can make steel, aluminium and cars. Cairo's planners proudly speak of the industrial heartland of the Arab world.

The Six Day War left the Egyptian army broken, its equipment lost in the Sinai and its pride in ruins. In the years since, a new force has been quietly reassembled under Soviet instruction. Officers now speak of rebuilding from the ground up, in order to fight again, and to win.

The favouritism that placed friends of Field Marshal Amer in command of divisions he never understood is rooted out. Officers are promoted on competence, not loyalty, and the chiefs of the humiliated army are replaced by younger professionals. The purge is painful, but few mourn the old order.

Egypt's schools and universities now supply a new kind of soldier, a high-school or university graduate able to read a technical manual and operate a modern weapon. Graduates in uniform serve for long years, and the army learns to rely on brains as well as on numbers.

Israeli armour terrified the Egyptian infantry in 1967. Now, small teams equipped with Sagger wire-guided missiles and RPG-7 launchers are trained to meet the tanks head on. The soldiers practise until the drill is automatic, and confidence slowly takes the place of dread.

The tank divisions, savaged in the Sinai, are rebuilt with fresh Soviet armour. Crews train to fight as coordinated formations rather than as scattered columns. The army's commanders have studied the lessons of the previous war closely, and they intend to apply them.

Engineers rehearse the greatest obstacle of all, the crossing of the Suez Canal and the breaching of the sand ramparts beyond it. Pontoons, bridging equipment and powerful water cannons are tested on mock canals in the desert. The success of any offensive may depend on these quiet, unglamorous men.

Soviet advisers push for an Egyptian army trained in the manner of the Red Army, with mass, depth and the relentless advance of successive echelons. Staff officers learn the doctrine in Moscow's academies and in Egyptian field exercises. It is powerful, orthodox and closely tied to Soviet supply.

Egyptian planners conclude that they cannot match Israel in the air or in manoeuvre, and decide to fight on their own terms. A limited offensive under an umbrella of missiles, seizing a strip of the east bank and holding it, will be the foundation of their plans. The doctrine is realistic, defensive and distinctly Egyptian.

Egyptian officers attend courses in Western staff colleges and study the methods of NATO armies. Instructors from abroad teach flexibility, initiative and the use of combined arms. The change worries Moscow and intrigues Washington, and a few veterans mutter that it is un-Egyptian.
