Elite units trained for raids behind enemy lines are expanded under the name of the Sa'iqa. They cross the canal at night, ambush patrols and strike at outposts, proving that Egyptian soldiers can fight on equal terms. Their exploits are celebrated on the radio and envied in the regular ranks.

The guard formed to protect the President and the institutions of the Republic is built into a trusted and well-equipped corps. Its officers are chosen for loyalty as much as skill, and in a land that has seen coups before, its presence is reassuring to some and ominous to others.

The air defence forces become a separate service, with their own command, their own academy and their own prestige. Missile batteries and radar stations are knitted into a network, and crews practise relocating, camouflaging and hiding. Israel's pilots, who once flew with impunity, begin to meet resistance.

On 5 June 1967 the Egyptian air force was destroyed on the ground. Now new MiGs arrive in crates from the Soviet Union and fresh pilots are trained to fly them. The commanders vow that never again will the sky be lost in the first morning of a war.

Concrete shelters, built to withstand bombs, now cover the aircraft of the Egyptian air force. Runways have been dispersed and repair crews drilled to fix them in hours. The lesson of the first morning of June 1967 has been learnt in concrete and steel.

At Bilbeis, young cadets are put through a demanding course of instruction. Instructors, both Egyptian and Soviet, teach them to fly, navigate and fight. The programme turns out a generation of pilots who will carry the reputation of the air force into the next war.

In October 1967, small Egyptian missile boats sank the destroyer Eilat, the first ship in history to be sunk by missiles in this way. The navy has taken the lesson to heart. A growing flotilla of fast, heavily armed craft now guards Alexandria and Port Said, and the sailors are proud of their small ships.

Egypt's navy looks beyond the Mediterranean and eyes the narrow strait that guards the southern Red Sea. If Israeli shipping can be stopped at Bab el-Mandeb, the enemy's access to the Indian Ocean will be cut and the strangulation of Eilat will begin. Ships, mines and submarines are readied for the task.

Egypt cannot rely on foreign suppliers forever. The ordnance works of Cairo and Helwan are expanded to make ammunition, small arms and spare parts, and the army's technical corps trains a workforce in the arts of industrial production. A nation that makes its own munitions is harder to bring to its knees.

The supersonic HA-300 project, abandoned in 1969, is brought back from the archives. German engineers are gone, but Egyptian and foreign experts pick up the work at Helwan. Nasser's old dream of a national fighter aircraft lives again, and even partial success would be a source of great pride.

Egyptian scientists and engineers work in secret on ballistic missiles and guided weapons. The work is slow and costly, and Western intelligence agencies watch it closely. Israel regards the programme as a direct threat, and the Egyptian leadership sees it as a necessary deterrent.

After three years of rebuilding, the Egyptian army is no longer the broken host of 1967. It has learned, trained and re-equipped, and it knows exactly what it will do on the day. The soldiers in the sand camps of the west bank wait for the order, certain that the canal will be crossed.

Britain's withdrawal and the growth of oil revenues are changing the balance along the Gulf. Membership in the Gulf Cooperation Council provides a framework for consultation without surrendering our sovereignty. Our administration must now turn the charter's commitments into practical cooperation.

Common principles for economic cooperation can give merchants and ministries a more dependable framework. Each state must prepare its own administration, reconcile the agreement with its laws and bear the continuing cost of implementation.

Rules of origin, customs documentation and more predictable treatment of regional goods can make neighbouring markets easier to serve. Better access rewards local enterprise, while inspection and certification create work for the customs administration.

Engineers, laboratories and ministries can compare technical standards and exchange practical research. Participating countries must establish their own committees and contribute expertise to sustain the exchange.

Industrial partnerships need serviced sites, dependable utilities and firms able to work across national boundaries. Preparing our own economy for those partnerships can raise industrial performance, at the cost of investment and a larger demand for energy.

Central banks and commercial banks can improve settlement, accounting and the handling of cross-border payments. Practical coordination can make trade less cumbersome while each state retains its currency and control of monetary policy.

Road connections and dependable border procedures are more immediate needs than grand schemes for a single regional transport network. Planning, utilities and trained customs staff can support construction and commercial traffic, while heavier activity raises energy demand.

Staff talks and shared exercises can help small armed forces understand their neighbours' capabilities. Our services must assign personnel, prepare useful training and maintain liaison arrangements while retaining their national chains of command.

A limited contribution to a common defensive force can make regional consultation more useful in a crisis. Preparing that contribution requires trained personnel, compatible procedures and a lasting military payroll; national governments retain command of their own forces.

Training places, visiting instructors and exchanges between military schools can spread useful experience. Sending officers abroad and maintaining a professional training cadre require additional personnel expenditure and sustained attention from our military schools.

Liaison officers can compare contingency plans, communications procedures and mobilisation requirements. A permanent liaison staff makes national planning more coherent, while its officers and administration require continuing support.

Compatible equipment, repair standards and coordinated procurement can reduce the waste caused by small and incompatible production runs. Our own factories and workshops must still supply the investment, machinery and power needed to take part.

The Gulf's security depends on national governments being able to coordinate when a crisis arrives. Rehearsed defensive plans and supply procedures can improve our national contribution. Liaison officers must keep those plans current as forces, equipment and regional risks change.

Regular meetings give rulers and ministers a place to discuss disputes before they grow into larger confrontations. Maintaining that channel can strengthen political coordination and diplomacy, while adding continuing duties to the national administration.

Iraq enters the new decade with ministries, party offices and military commands competing for authority. Establishing a common government agenda will give the cabinet a firmer hand without settling the constitutional struggle.
A clear executive can force decisions through rival institutions. Concentrating authority strengthens the government while narrowing the room for provincial and civilian consent.
A civic compact offers provincial and professional interests a stake in the state. A broader settlement frees civilian resources, although decisions will take longer to negotiate.
Provincial agents will bring collections and public records under a common standard. Their salaries are a real expense, but Baghdad will finally receive a more reliable share of provincial revenue.
Local councils can connect provincial works with the people who use them. Paying for a functioning local administration is preferable to funding projects that serve only a distant patron.
Reliable civil records make taxation, schooling and public employment easier to administer. A citizen should not need a party sponsor merely to be recognised by the state.
The security services will receive the authority and money to protect the regime. Their expanded reach deters organised opposition, while political supervision weighs on free inquiry.
Contracts and public decisions need a court that can survive a ministerial telephone call. Judicial review improves confidence in domestic investment but limits the cabinet's freedom to act.
Political prisoners and their families remain part of Iraqi society. A review of detention cases can restore public confidence, even as released opponents recover their ability to organise.
Independent courts need judges, clerks and enforceable rulings. A funded bench will make tax obligations and public contracts more credible than another declaration of good intentions.
Payrolls and procurement accounts conceal networks of privilege. An audit must identify who actually serves the state and ensure that public salaries reach real employees.

A durable northern settlement begins with roads, records and public services as well as political talks. Baghdad can prepare a practical offer while Kurdish representatives decide whether its guarantees deserve their trust.
Overlapping commands waste orders and men. A joint review of army and security responsibilities will improve coordination without pretending that political loyalties can be abolished overnight.
A single set of state accounts will expose arrears, duplicate salaries and off-budget commitments. Ministers will have fewer places to hide the true cost of their promises.
An autonomy agreement has little value without schools, roads and salaries behind it. Delivering the promised provincial investment will test whether Baghdad intends to honour the settlement.
A professional chain of command must connect the ministry, the staff and the formations in the field. Removing parallel orders will improve the army more than adding another political headquarters.

The treasury needs a working register of businesses, property and obligations. A trained collection service can broaden reliable revenue without relying on improvised levies whenever oil receipts fall.

An effective Iraqi state should be able to pay its employees, collect its revenue and carry out its own agreements. The settlement will remain imperfect, but its institutions can finally work together.

The Baath's Regional Command must turn a movement built for conspiracy into an organization capable of governing Iraq. Its appointments will shape the relationship between the party, the ministries and the officers on whom the republic still depends.

The Communists and other organized forces possess expertise that the Baath cannot simply command into existence. A national front could put that experience to work, provided its partners receive guarantees that mean more than a place on the government's letterhead.

The party can reserve the commanding offices of the Iraqi state for its own members. A single chain of authority will make decisions easier to enforce, although those excluded from public life will take some of their knowledge and cooperation with them.

A signature in Baghdad will not settle every dispute between the Front's parties. Ministers, workplace representatives and provincial organizers need enforceable rules if cooperation is to survive the first serious disagreement over appointments or public money.

Our ministries and armed forces contain men whose loyalties reach beyond the Regional Command. Screening appointments will strengthen the leadership's access to information and trusted officers, but political reliability cannot replace professional competence in every post.

A regional congress can bind the party's provincial organizations to a common programme rather than a collection of personal promises. It must also provide a recognized forum for the leadership disputes that otherwise spread through the ministries and barracks.

Workers, students and rural organizers can give the Baath a presence far beyond its original circles. Bringing them into a mass movement will deepen the state's reach, while making employment, services and material support matters of party responsibility.

A smaller party can devote more attention to the training and discipline of its organizers. Iraq would gain a more practiced governing core, but it would have fewer people able to carry the party's demands into every town and village.

The party's associations must offer something to the families they seek to organize. Medical assistance and public services can give these bodies a lasting place in Iraqi society, provided Baghdad accepts the obligations that accompany that influence.

Party schools can prepare provincial organizers for work more demanding than repeating instructions from Baghdad. Technical lessons and administrative training will help them manage public undertakings, although the government must distinguish useful instruction from political ritual.

The boundary between a party undertaking and a public enterprise has become dangerously uncertain. Separate accounts will make Iraqi revenues easier to collect and contracts easier to supervise, while limiting the discretion of officials accustomed to treating both treasuries as their own.

Iraq's public sector is expected to carry much of the country's industrial transformation. Giving it a stronger productive foundation will support that ambition, but investment directed through the state leaves fewer resources available for immediate private consumption.

Public offices must serve Iraq's citizens through a common set of procedures. Reducing competing religious and personal channels of authority can make administration more dependable, even where the party finds that professional officials are less willing to follow informal instructions.

Iraqi women cannot contribute fully to public life while training and paid employment remain closed to them. The unions and ministries can widen those opportunities, but employment must be supported by services that allow families to sustain the change.

Public enterprises need accounts that reveal whether workshops are producing useful goods or merely satisfying a minister's report. Regular inspection will help managers coordinate production and collection, while adding responsibilities that neither the ministry nor the enterprise can evade.

The republic cannot govern indefinitely through separate bargains with every community and local notable. A common citizenship would make public responsibilities more predictable, although officials will have to surrender some of the informal leverage on which party control has relied.

The party asks Iraqi households to place development ahead of immediate comfort. A credible bargain must offer dependable education and medical care in return, and those commitments must remain in the budget after the speeches have ended.

The Baathist republic must outlast individual campaigns and the men who announce them. A governing apparatus able to organize technical instruction, public offices and industrial work would give the party a stronger foundation than personal loyalty alone.

Al-Bakr stands at the meeting point of the party and the military networks that helped bring it to power. His presidency can use those connections to staff the republic, but maintaining their cooperation will require more than issuing orders from Baghdad.

Al-Bakr can give experienced colleagues a greater share in the daily work of government. Collective leadership would draw on a wider pool of expertise, while obliging the presidency to negotiate decisions that a narrower executive might impose.

The president can make himself the final arbiter between competing party offices and commanders. That authority promises a clearer direction for Iraq, but the organizations that accept his arbitration will expect their own positions to be maintained.

The Command Council must do more than ratify decisions already reached elsewhere. A regular division of military and educational responsibilities could make it useful to the republic, provided its members accept procedures that restrain personal intervention.

Al-Bakr's standing among experienced officers is an important part of his authority. Giving trusted men a recognized role in training and mobilization can strengthen the presidency, although too narrow a circle would close the army to other capable officers.

The presidency needs a secretariat that keeps ministries working when senior officials are occupied with party affairs. Reliable records and a settled division of responsibilities will make the state's ordinary business less dependent on the president's personal attention.

The deputy's expanding responsibilities have made the division of authority increasingly uncertain. Al-Bakr can seek a clearer settlement of offices, but effective scrutiny will also limit the freedom of the presidency itself.

Saddam has demonstrated an ability to pursue decisions through the party apparatus. Delegating more of the government's work to him may accelerate development, while placing a larger security and administrative machine under the deputy's influence.

The officers and party veterans who sustain the presidency fear being displaced by a new executive circle. A recognized place for them can make the governing establishment more dependable, at the price of restricting future appointments and reforms.

Development orders pass through too many offices before reaching the people expected to carry them out. A coordinating budget under the deputy could connect public projects with responsible officials, although their cooperation will require concessions from the treasury.

The capital's industrial ambitions depend on roads and public works that can carry materials as well as official delegations. A funded programme around Baghdad will give al-Bakr's development policy a practical foundation that survives changes in the cabinet.

Closer relations with Moscow could provide Iraq with military and technical opportunities. Our own officers must first prepare the stores, training arrangements and negotiating positions needed to use any agreement; Soviet cooperation will still depend on Soviet decisions.

A northern guarantee will be judged by the services and conduct of the state, rather than the wording of a communiqué. Al-Bakr must prepare civilian institutions capable of carrying out promises that can otherwise be undone by a local security office.

A conference with Syria would bring rival claims to Arab leadership into the same room. Iraq needs officials able to examine common projects and responsibilities before asking Damascus to accept a union whose institutions neither side has yet defined.

Iraq can purchase machinery more quickly than it can train the people needed to operate it. Technical missions must therefore build Iraqi engineering and construction knowledge, so that development does not depend indefinitely on specialists recalled by another government.

Al-Bakr's presidency rests on institutions whose interests do not always coincide. A durable compromise would give them dependable civilian channels for their work, while requiring the leadership to accept limits that cannot be withdrawn at the first disagreement.

Arab cooperation needs rules for contracts and public revenue as well as declarations of fraternity. A charter can make Iraqi undertakings easier for partners to understand, without committing Syria or any other government to arrangements it has not accepted.

The presidency should pass through an agreement that the republic's institutions can recognize. Al-Bakr must settle the authority of an eligible successor with those whose cooperation will determine whether government continues to function after his departure.

Saddam's rise from the party apparatus to the presidency will change the balance between civilian organizers and the military establishment. He must turn control over competing offices into a government capable of acting, while confronting the distrust that such concentration of power creates.

The presidency can bring rival offices into a chain of authority centered on Saddam himself. A personal executive will receive information and issue decisions more quickly, but it must sustain the security organizations on which that authority rests.

A cabinet of established party officials and specialists can give the presidency a broader administrative base. Keeping their expertise in public service will require room for professional judgment that a fully personal executive would find uncomfortable.

The presidency needs dependable information about the military, the party and foreign interference in Iraq. A stronger security bureau can supply it, but overlapping surveillance and exceptional powers will burden both the public treasury and relations within the state.

Experienced managers understand problems that cannot be solved by replacing an official with a more loyal party member. Retaining them will improve industrial administration, while limiting the presidency's freedom to use every appointment as a political reward.

Oil receipts allow the government to promise Iraqi households a better material life. Medical provision and access to consumer goods can support the presidency's claim to govern for development, provided these commitments remain affordable when revenues or military demands change.

A presidential guard gives the leadership formations whose readiness and loyalty can be cultivated closely. Preferential training and dependable stores can strengthen the regime's military position, but maintaining that standard places a lasting burden on the army's payroll.

Iraq's military strength cannot rest on privileged formations alone. Investment in the regular army's training and replacement system will give its commanders more dependable forces, while committing the government to a broader permanent establishment.

Favored formations cannot maintain their readiness on political standing alone. Common stores and practical equipment work will support the Guard's place in the army, although privileged supply arrangements must still be staffed and paid for.

The presidency needs officers who can coordinate formations rather than merely command their own battalions. Staff appointments should therefore be supported by serious instruction, even where a trained commander proves less dependent on political supervision.

Iraq's ambitions in the Arab world require a government able to negotiate and sustain military purchases. A more capable diplomatic and procurement service can widen Baghdad's options, while leaving foreign suppliers and neighboring governments free to defend their own interests.

Events in Iran may alter the regional balance without revealing how its armed forces would perform in a war. Iraqi planners need a sober assessment of command and supply before the presidency treats apparent disorder across the frontier as an opportunity.

Presidential projects must leave Iraq with useful production rather than monuments to the officials who commissioned them. A civilian plant in Baghdad can support the wider industrial programme, although its construction will compete with immediate household demands.

A foreign credit line will be easier to negotiate if Baghdad can present accounts that creditors understand. The same work can strengthen domestic collection, while the terms and availability of any Gulf loan remain matters for the lender to decide.

A credible deterrent needs forces able to mobilize and defend Iraqi territory. The presidency can sustain that preparation without treating every frontier dispute as an instruction to begin a war, but readiness will still carry a standing personnel bill.

Imported equipment is only useful while Iraq can maintain and replace its essential parts. Domestic workshops and a more practiced licensing service will reduce exposure to shortages, without pretending that every foreign design can be reproduced at once.

The political value of a credit agreement fades when its repayments fall due. Baghdad needs a revenue authority able to meet obligations without concealing their burden, and creditors must retain the claims they have actually agreed to hold.

The presidency must turn personal loyalties and competing offices into an administration that can carry out its decisions. A clearer executive chain will reduce duplicated work, while concessions to the institutions sustaining the regime narrow the state's revenue base.

An officer government inherits more than the command of the armed forces. Its members must establish authority over a fractured political system without assuming that the methods of the barracks will command the same confidence in civilian life.

The officers can regard their government as a temporary administration charged with restoring dependable public life. Competent civilian departments would make that undertaking more credible, but they would also reduce the council's freedom to decide policy alone.

A permanent military presidency would place command and senior appointments at the center of the state. It could act with greater coherence than a provisional council, while carrying the cost of governing civilian institutions through an expanded military establishment.

Industrial managers and civilian ministers can run services that officers have little experience administering. Giving them a real cabinet role will strengthen Iraq's productive economy, provided the military accepts professional authority outside its own command structure.

Provincial commanders possess the forces to enforce orders where civilian administration is weak. A garrison government can use that presence to support collection and policing, but soldiers assigned to such duties remain an expensive substitute for ordinary public offices.

Military purchases must fit an army that can train crews, obtain spares and understand the equipment it orders. A professional procurement service will make licensed designs more useful, while requiring officials whose responsibilities extend beyond signing a contract.

The army's promotion system should reward officers able to organize their formations under pressure. Advancing such men will improve command, although the government must surrender some of the political leverage that comes with selecting every senior appointment.

An officer government cannot ignore whether its commanders will obey it during a political crisis. Trusted networks can accelerate mobilization and decisions, but personal confidence is a poor substitute for the cohesion that competent leadership builds within a formation.

Iraq needs a staff school that teaches officers to coordinate whole formations and their supporting services. Serious instruction takes men away from immediate duties, but it gives the army experience that cannot be obtained through another round of honorary promotions.

Placing officers in civilian ministries will give the council a clearer view of decisions made outside the barracks. It will also draw experienced commanders away from military work and displace officials who understand the departments they are expected to run.

The defence establishment needs accounts that distinguish useful service from appointments maintained for political reasons. A regular budget can reduce exceptional payroll burdens, provided commanders accept that the treasury must be able to question military expenditure.

Former opponents will not return to ordinary public life on the strength of an officer's assurance alone. A conditional amnesty needs civilian institutions able to administer it, while leaving political organizations free to accept or reject the terms offered.

The army should not have to improvise a new frontier organization whenever relations with a neighbor worsen. Trained border commands and dependable supplies can make defence more credible, but the personnel required must remain on the public payroll.

A promise of civilian government requires a timetable that ministries and prospective representatives can use. Preparing that transition can make public contracts more dependable, even though no constitutional vote is certain to produce the council's preferred result.

Officers employed as political overseers and provincial administrators should return to a regular military establishment. Clear responsibilities will make their service less costly, while narrowing the informal influence that has grown around exceptional appointments.

Different commands cannot sustain themselves indefinitely through separate stores and purchasing arrangements. A unified logistics service will make Iraq's equipment more dependable, provided the government funds the clerks, depots and inspections needed to keep it working.

A future cabinet needs confidence that routine government will continue when the armed forces return to their military duties. Civilian guarantees can reduce exceptional policing and outside political leverage without allowing the council to choose every successor government.

Iraq needs an enduring division between military command and civilian authority rather than another temporary balance of personalities. A recognized establishment will make the army more coherent, but its service and responsibilities must be carried honestly in the budget.

Iraqi Arab socialists must reconcile their commitment to Arab cooperation with the institutions required to govern their own country. A national leadership council can give that programme a practical center without inventing authority for men who have not secured it.

Cairo offers experience in Arab political organization and military procurement, but cooperation cannot rest on fraternity alone. Iraq should develop the officials able to use common contracts and licensed equipment while negotiating the terms Egypt is willing to accept.

An Arab republic need not surrender Iraqi decision-making to another capital. A stronger domestic productive base and institutions resistant to outside pressure would preserve Baghdad's freedom, while leaving it less willing to pursue influence through distant political commitments.

Arab development schemes will fail if participating governments cannot identify who supplies the money, materials and administration. Iraq can begin with its own planning offices and roads, creating a practical basis for projects that partners may later agree to join.

Republican service must offer careers based on the work Iraq needs done. A professional administration can connect public decisions with productive activity, provided ministries are staffed for competence rather than divided among the sponsors of the latest cabinet.

Arab socialism will be judged in Iraqi homes as well as at political meetings. A social charter must provide dependable schooling and medical care, while recognizing that public obligations continue long after a government announces them.

The public sector can lead the industrial development needed to sustain an independent republic. Concentrating capital in state production will give Baghdad a stronger material base, while drawing resources away from immediate civilian consumption.

Public undertakings need not exclude workshops and businesses outside the state sector. A mixed economy could expand Iraqi civilian production more quickly, although the government would have to accept the concessions that persuade private owners to invest.

A public industrial contract should leave Iraq with an operating plant rather than another office responsible for supervising one. Concentrating investment in Baghdad's military production will support the state-sector programme, at a cost that must be met before the project is delivered.

Many Iraqi cultivators cannot obtain machinery or dependable credit on terms their holdings can bear. Cooperative finance can make those resources useful across a wider rural economy, provided the government accepts responsibility for the support it promises borrowers.

A republican state cannot reserve dependable services for those with the right personal connection. Common citizenship would make collection and public security more regular, while limiting the informal bargains through which ministers have secured local cooperation.

Solidarity with the Palestinians requires an administration able to sustain the commitments Baghdad actually makes. Better organized Iraqi support services can make those commitments more effective without sending weapons, money or forces to a recipient that has not agreed to receive them.

Iraq needs technical exchanges that leave knowledge in its own workshops and construction offices. Training engineers to adapt what they learn abroad will make development less dependent on the continuing presence of a foreign mission.

A union conference must define how public money and responsibilities would be shared between participating governments. Iraq's own officials should be able to examine those obligations before inviting partners to accept institutions that could change their sovereignty.

Arab cooperation can be advanced through civilian projects and commercial undertakings as well as political declarations. A practiced diplomatic service will give Baghdad more influence over their terms, while leaving other governments free to judge the proposals for themselves.

Military and civilian establishments both depend on technicians who can teach others to use unfamiliar equipment. Connecting those training networks will help Iraq retain useful knowledge without assuming that imported machinery brings its own permanent supply of instructors.

A partnership cannot survive if its public undertakings keep incompatible books. Iraqi officials must be able to account for business and service revenues before presenting a common budget that another government can reasonably be expected to understand.

An enduring Arab republic must demonstrate that cooperation and Iraqi independence can support one another. Productive civilian institutions and a government able to defend its own decisions would give that claim substance beyond the tenure of a single leader.

The Communist Party carries the experience of repression and years spent rebuilding its organization. A governing congress must turn that experience into a programme for public institutions, rather than allow the habits of clandestine struggle to determine every appointment.

A coalition cabinet can draw on Iraqi political traditions beyond the party's own membership. Its ministers will need agreed responsibilities and dependable civilian offices if cooperation is to mean more than rival party chains of command inside the same government.

The party now carries responsibility for governing Iraq rather than merely opposing those who do. Its committees must learn to organize national institutions without assuming that the discipline of a political movement automatically produces confidence in the state.

Public party offices can reconnect the government with workers and local representatives who endured years of repression. Bringing those networks into legal public life requires accountable organizers and confidence that membership will no longer expose families to arbitrary punishment.

Clandestine organization preserved experienced cadres, but it also separated them from ordinary civilian administration. Reuniting their networks with the governing party will strengthen its reach, provided security habits do not become a substitute for professional public service.

The party cannot govern through the incomplete lists and personal recollections that once protected its members. Dependable records will help local offices find people suited to public work without turning every administrative question into an appeal to the secretariat.

A socialist government can seek cooperation from unions, intellectuals and parties that do not accept every Communist position. Their participation would widen the republic's civilian expertise, while placing real limits on the leadership's freedom to decide alone.

The party can concentrate political direction and industrial priorities in a disciplined governing apparatus. Such a state would be better placed to direct resources toward military production, but Iraqi households would bear the claims that this places on the civilian economy.

Workers need representatives able to raise practical disputes without first obtaining a minister's permission. Independent unions can make production more dependable through negotiated cooperation, even where their demands reduce the output that managers would otherwise require.

Unions can instead be organized around the targets of the national production plan. Clear priorities would support longer and more consistent industrial runs, but workers would have fewer independent channels through which to contest those demands.

The party cannot resolve Iraq's nationalities question by treating every disagreement as a class misunderstanding. A recognized charter must give communities responsibilities that the government respects, while leaving the terms of any northern settlement to those who must live with it.

Workers' councils need functioning industry in which to demonstrate their programme. A civilian plant in Baghdad can give them that foundation, provided technical management and workplace representation learn to work together rather than compete for every operational decision.

Relations with Soviet institutions could offer Iraqi technicians access to useful designs and instruction. Our own reception and licensing services must be able to use those opportunities, while preserving Baghdad's right to negotiate the terms of cooperation.

The rural poor will judge a socialist government by what reaches their holdings and villages. Agricultural advice and dependable credit can give party organizers a productive purpose beyond political mobilization, although promises of support must be honored in difficult seasons as well.

Workplace injuries and neglected machinery impose costs on families as well as production. Inspectors able to enforce practical standards can reduce those burdens, even where taking equipment out of service frustrates a manager's immediate output target.

The party needs technicians and administrators who can explain how a workshop should operate, not merely who should control it. Technical schools will give experienced organizers the knowledge needed to participate in Iraq's industrial development.

Rural credit should support cultivators rather than reproduce their dependence on a different set of intermediaries. A public finance programme can improve agricultural production and bring more transactions into regular accounts, while requiring concessions to borrowers whose incomes remain uncertain.

A socialist republic must give its productive programme a place beyond the next party congress. Public industry can support the state and civilian life together, provided the government continues to carry the social obligations on which its authority rests.

Aziz Muhammad must adapt a party formed through clandestine organization to the demands of national government. The secretariat needs civilian offices that can administer a programme without requiring every local question to be settled personally by its leader.

A cabinet of allies can bring experience into government that the Communist organization cannot supply by itself. Aziz must give those ministers clear responsibilities, while accepting that cooperation requires authority to be shared as well as discussed.

The party's regional congresses can give Aziz a governing mandate extending beyond the capital. Their support will strengthen an independent national apparatus, but delegates will expect their influence over appointments and policy to survive the journey back from Baghdad.

Cooperation is only credible while partners understand which guarantees cannot be set aside for convenience. Aziz should define those limits openly, so that the party can challenge a breach without pretending that every disagreement requires the destruction of the government.

Years of difficult political work created networks able to find people, information and practical assistance under pressure. Bringing that experience into public institutions can broaden Iraq's options, provided informal contacts are made accountable for the responsibilities they acquire.

Delegates cannot supervise a government whose accounts remain private to the ministries. Opening reliable public records to congress scrutiny will make revenue and services more dependable, while forcing the secretariat to defend decisions it once expected simply to announce.

Federal guarantees must connect the northern provinces to the services and routes on which their economy depends. Baghdad can secure cooperation by recognizing those responsibilities, but it must accept that regional institutions will retain part of the revenue they administer.

A unitary socialist government would place collection and administration under a common national direction. It promises a clearer public account, while leaving Aziz responsible for the provincial resentment that stronger central authority can provoke.

A regional compact will mean little to households unless schools and medical services receive dependable support. Aziz must give the provinces a budget they can use without concealing the continuing obligations that those services place on the republic.

Children should not be excluded from useful instruction because the language of the classroom makes it inaccessible. Broader provision will require teachers and materials suited to the communities concerned, making language rights an educational undertaking rather than a ceremonial declaration.

Friendship with Moscow should not require Baghdad to accept every Soviet political expectation. Maintaining room to disagree will encourage a wider range of technical and commercial relationships, although Iraq must still meet the commitments it has actually made.

A new industrial order needs workers able to master unfamiliar machinery and help others use it. Practical training can improve both factory organization and civilian production, while placing demands on the services supporting workers and their families.

A socialist government cannot treat every criticism as an attempt to overthrow it. Parliamentary allies and workplace representatives need a recognized means of challenging ministers without dismantling the institutions through which they must govern together.

Military prestige will not replace medical care or dependable household services. Aziz can direct the state toward civilian welfare and a more regular military establishment, accepting the continuing public commitments that this choice entails.

Workplace delegates can preserve knowledge that disappears when managers reorganize a production line without consulting those who operate it. Their involvement may restrain immediate output demands, but it can make subsequent industrial work more dependable.

Exile scattered Iraqi political experience across neighboring countries and beyond. Returning organizers should be offered useful work in reconstruction and technical instruction, while their appointments must rest on a defined public role rather than a claim to automatic authority.

Villages need access to practical agricultural advice and medical assistance as well as visits from party organizers. Establishing those services will give rural government substance, but it creates obligations that Baghdad must maintain beyond a single political campaign.

A party cannot govern indefinitely through the methods that allowed it to survive in hiding. Aziz must renew its leadership and public accounts together, turning experienced organizers into an administration capable of answering for the work entrusted to it.

Civilian parties must rebuild institutions that have repeatedly been displaced by military and party struggles. Their claim to govern Iraq will depend on public offices able to act predictably without relying on the personal protection of a commander.

A social republic would make public provision part of the ordinary responsibilities of government. Medical care and a stronger civilian economy can support that settlement, provided elected ministers accept the cost of commitments that survive changes of cabinet.

Private undertakings need confidence that contracts and investment conditions will survive a political change in Baghdad. A liberal republic can offer that continuity, while accepting the revenue concessions required to encourage construction outside the state sector.

Social rights must be supported by accounts that connect promises with the services expected to fulfill them. A civilian government can make education and care more dependable by treating their administration as permanent work rather than a succession of ministerial initiatives.

Iraqi businesses cannot rely on contracts whose enforcement depends on a patron inside the ministry. Professional courts and recorded procedures will make obligations more predictable, while challenging officials who profit from uncertainty and personal intervention.

Representative government needs a register that citizens and competing parties can examine with confidence. Building it will require ordinary civilian offices rather than exceptional security supervision, and no party can assume that a properly organized election guarantees its victory.

A federal constitution must give the provinces practical means to exercise the responsibilities it recognizes. Better routes and regular local services can support that settlement, while requiring Baghdad to share revenue rather than merely delegate unpaid duties.

A unitary republic can offer common rules for collection and public administration throughout Iraq. Its supporters must still explain how provincial interests will be heard when the treasury and ministries remain concentrated in the capital.

Neither a central budget nor a regional administration can function on revenue claimed twice. An agreed fiscal settlement should clarify which public bodies collect and retain income, even where that reduces the sums immediately available to Baghdad.

Municipal government needs records of households, services and local economic activity that can be used beyond a mayor's personal circle. Reliable accounts will help collection and public administration without requiring every routine matter to return to a national ministry.

Civilian authority must be able to examine the work and expenditure of the security services. Ending unnecessary exceptional operations can reduce their burden, although oversight will sometimes limit the methods through which officers have gathered information.

Republican schools should prepare Iraqis to participate in public and economic life rather than serve as extensions of a cabinet's patronage. Wider basic instruction requires dependable teachers and administration that continue working when political leadership changes.

Iraq's civilian government should be able to negotiate with several partners without becoming dependent on any one of them. Diversified commercial arrangements and stronger institutions can support that independence, while limiting the resources available for political adventures abroad.

Industrial employers and workers need a recognized way to settle disputes before they interrupt production. A labour bargain will restrain some immediate demands on the workforce, but it can support safer workplaces and a more dependable industrial rhythm.

Universities need room to pursue technical learning without measuring every appointment against a party's immediate political needs. More independent institutions can develop Iraqi computing expertise, provided the government funds their work and accepts conclusions it does not always welcome.

A parliamentary government must explain the obligations it asks future budgets to carry. Transparent credit accounts can improve domestic finance, while leaving foreign lenders free to refuse proposals they consider insufficiently secure.

A durable labour agreement should preserve useful skills when plants change their products or managers. Recognized rights and responsibilities can make those transitions less disruptive, though maintaining the compact requires an administration able to enforce its terms.

Civilian government needs a revenue system that survives the departure of a particular minister. Predictable collection and competent public offices would give elected institutions the means to govern without recreating a patronage machine at every political turn.

A restored crown would need a charter suited to an Iraq transformed since the fall of the monarchy. Its supporters must offer credible public contracts and protections rather than expect the old title alone to secure confidence at home or abroad.

A ceremonial crown would leave the daily work of government to responsible civilian ministers. That separation can make public undertakings easier to trust, while requiring the palace to surrender much of the discretion associated with an executive monarch.

An executive crown would claim a direct role in appointments and national command. It could give the government a stronger center, but Iraq's memory of the monarchy means that concentrated royal authority will face doubts no proclamation can simply remove.

A responsible parliament must be able to question collection and public security without being treated as an obstacle to the crown. Making it useful in ordinary government will require both the palace and the ministries to accept procedures that outlast personal relationships.

The palace needs advisers able to connect military appointments and diplomatic commitments with the practical needs of Iraq. A recognized council can coordinate that work, although its members must justify an establishment that might otherwise become another circle of court patronage.

The treasury must distinguish the expenses of the crown from those of the state. Clear public accounts will strengthen collection and civilian administration, while restricting the palace's ability to resolve every obligation through an informal arrangement.

The crown cannot settle rural grievances by pretending that Iraq's land question ended with the old monarchy. A review should make cultivation and lawful claims more secure, while recognizing the public obligations created by any promise of redress.

Existing owners will be more willing to build if they believe the government will honor established contracts. Such guarantees can provide immediate economic continuity, but they will leave unresolved grievances among those who regard the present distribution of property as unjust.

Competing claims to land can obstruct roads and public works as effectively as a shortage of materials. A funded tribunal should provide a usable settlement of obligations without allowing the palace to decide every case through personal favor.

Rural development requires agreements that cultivators and public authorities can understand and enforce. Clearer contracts will support agricultural work and regular collection, provided their administration reaches beyond the offices of a few influential landholders.

A common crown must offer Iraq's communities more than invitations to a royal ceremony. Shared access to public institutions and instruction can support a national settlement, while limiting the informal privileges through which the palace might otherwise seek support.

Talks with Jordan could open useful commercial and military contacts between the two governments. Iraq should prepare officials able to pursue that cooperation without assuming that family connections entitle Baghdad to a treaty, federation or another country's decisions.

A royal civil service must be able to carry out public work without waiting for an intervention from the palace. Professional appointments and dependable administration can make the restored order more credible than a revival of old offices and titles.

Schools can give citizenship a practical meaning for families that have little direct contact with the capital. The crown should support basic instruction through institutions that serve the public rather than requiring personal loyalty to the royal household.

Commercial partnership depends on the terms under which people can use Iraqi offices, contracts and investment procedures. A more practiced service will make those arrangements easier to use, while leaving private and foreign partners to decide whether they wish to invest.

The crown's public programme should be visible in useful routes and services. Work around Basra can support the commercial life of southern Iraq, provided the treasury meets the obligations involved instead of treating royal sponsorship as a substitute for funding.

A regular budget should reveal whether public commitments are supported by dependable income. Parliamentary and ministerial scrutiny can improve collection and medical administration, while requiring the palace to defend priorities it might prefer to settle privately.

A constitutional crown can endure only if the institutions around it carry the daily work of government. A settled charter would give public and commercial partners clearer terms, while maintaining the offices needed to turn those commitments into ordinary practice.
Oil, borders and the superpower rivalry make diplomacy a practical necessity. A professional foreign service will put Iraqi interests before the rival ambitions of individual ministries.
A dependable partner can provide access to training and technology. Choosing that relationship also gives an outside power greater weight in Iraqi affairs.

Iraq need not place every contract and security calculation in the hands of one bloc. Maintaining alternatives protects room for manoeuvre, but each relationship will have to stand on negotiated terms.
A serious cooperation offer requires trained negotiators and a domestic plan for using imported expertise. Iraq will prepare its industry while the proposed partner considers the agreement.
Different suppliers can meet different civilian needs. Comparing their offers will improve Iraqi construction practice without granting any foreign government an automatic concession.
Agreements must bind the institutions that sign them. A common register of obligations will prevent a minister from selling commitments already made elsewhere.
A defensible frontier does not require a permanent sequence of incidents. Better prepared positions and supply arrangements will give Iraq a stronger hand at the negotiating table.
Negotiations are more credible when the frontier can be held. Iraq will sustain a more expensive defensive posture while accepting the risks that accompany armed deterrence.
Reciprocal border arrangements must survive their signing ceremony. Improving frontier transport will allow Iraq to service the settlement and supply its own border communities.
A direct incident channel can prevent every patrol dispute from becoming a mobilisation. Clear procedures reduce waste while leaving the decision to compromise in Iraqi hands.
Iraq's neighbours are markets, rivals and political partners at the same time. Regional diplomacy should turn that proximity into workable commercial relations.

Relations with Syria carry the weight of rival Baathist claims and shared transport routes. Iraq will improve its own connecting infrastructure while any wider agreement remains subject to Syrian consent.

Trade and finance across the Gulf can support Iraqi commercial life. Strengthening the domestic customs and banking service will make those contacts useful without assuming that Kuwait owes Iraq a loan.
Regional party networks can extend Iraqi influence beyond official diplomacy. Supporting them consumes political attention and may complicate relations with governments that host their opponents.
Rival claims to Arab leadership have repeatedly obstructed practical cooperation. Reconciliation should make trade and diplomacy easier without compelling another state to accept Iraqi leadership.

Iraq needs a treasury capable of negotiating maturity schedules and distinguishing a gift from a loan. Better debt administration can lower financing costs; it cannot cancel another government's claim by declaration.

Political assistance should reach organisations that can actually use it. A disciplined support network will produce more influence from the same commitment rather than multiplying unaccountable intermediaries.
An independent foreign policy rests on institutions capable of remembering their commitments. Iraq will keep access to partners while defending its right to choose among them.

A KDP cabinet governing Iraq must administer a republic larger and more diverse than the movement's original northern base. Its ministers will need ordinary public offices that can serve Arab and Kurdish communities without reducing government to a succession of personal agreements.

Autonomy must give regional authorities responsibilities they can actually administer within Iraq. Recognized public services and regular security arrangements can reduce the burden of permanent confrontation, provided Baghdad continues to honor the settlement it has accepted.

A federal republic would give the regions a more substantial place in national government. Roads and dependable project administration can connect that arrangement to everyday life, while the central treasury must accept the revenues and responsibilities reserved to the provinces.

An autonomous administration cannot provide useful services through political recognition alone. A dependable budget for education and medical care would give the northern settlement practical value, while obliging the state to sustain the commitments it has made.

Federal authority requires a clear account of who collects revenue and who is expected to provide services. Formal regional receipts can support that bargain, but Baghdad cannot count the same income as both a provincial entitlement and money free for central expenditure.

The movement's officials must learn to keep public accounts that can be used beyond their own personal networks. Reliable household records and civilian departments will help a KDP government carry responsibilities that are different from those of a regional political organization.

The Barzani leadership holds relationships built through years of struggle and negotiation. Preserving that continuity can make appointments and mobilization more dependable, although established personal authority must still find a place within the institutions of government.

The KDP can develop into a civic organization whose public work extends beyond the authority of its best-known families. Professional offices and clearer contracts would widen its governing base, while reducing the leadership's freedom to settle every matter through personal influence.

The movement needs a recognized way to transfer leadership without allowing competing claims to paralyze its work. A council of eligible leaders can establish authority through an agreed settlement, rather than leave every public appointment dependent on uncertainty at the top.

Regional councils should be able to supervise services and civilian economic work without constantly appealing to the party leadership. Their participation can make administration more dependable, but the government must accept that useful councils will sometimes disagree with it.

Language rights must be supported by classrooms, teachers and materials that families can use. Broader access to instruction would give the northern settlement a practical foundation, while requiring the treasury to maintain provision beyond the announcement of the policy.

The mountains have protected communities and separated them from markets and public services. Better routes around Erbil can reduce the cost of moving people and supplies, while linking the northern economy more closely to the rest of Iraq.

Kirkuk's status cannot be resolved by treating every political claim as an existing right to its resources. A more capable public administration can improve the handling of Iraqi export receipts while the communities and institutions concerned negotiate a lasting settlement.

Regional fighters and national military institutions cannot cooperate effectively through occasional political understandings alone. Common instruction and recognized service responsibilities can improve their coordination, provided the government carries the personnel obligations involved.

Farmers in the northern uplands need credit and advice suited to holdings that cannot operate like large estates. A supported rural programme can improve production, while requiring officials to maintain the commitments made to cultivators beyond the movement's strongest districts.

Shared revenue should make the northern settlement easier to administer rather than give every office a new claim to the same receipts. Clearer export and agricultural accounts can support public work, provided the central government honors the income reserved for regional responsibilities.

Local police must answer to an agreed public authority rather than competing party and security offices. A recognized charter can reduce exceptional expenditure and outside political leverage, but it must remain part of a settlement the government actually respects.

The republic must honor the terms through which its communities have agreed to govern together. Public services, security responsibilities and revenue should follow that settlement, whether its accepted form is autonomy or a federal constitution.

Jalal Talabani's movement must turn its claim to represent a broader northern society into a programme of government. The work will require trained civilian offices as well as the political networks through which the PUK established itself.

A pluralist Kurdish left can draw on teachers, public servants and organizers beyond a narrow party establishment. Their contribution would strengthen civilian government, while obliging the leadership to accept criticism and shared authority.

The PUK can instead concentrate its effort in a more disciplined party apparatus. That organization may direct production and mobilization more firmly, but it risks alienating people whose support depends on having a real voice in public affairs.

Assemblies will be useful only if they can supervise services and accounts that affect their communities. Funding that work can make collection and public security more regular, while adding responsibilities that party offices cannot administer informally forever.

A progressive cadre needs practical skills as well as a clear political programme. Instruction in production and the organization of training will help the PUK's officials carry public responsibilities, although it requires an educational establishment of its own.

A federal programme must explain how the regions will build and protect the institutions it promises. Better project planning and more resilient public authority can support that aim, while central revenue must reflect the responsibilities retained outside Baghdad.

Cooperation with the KDP could reduce duplicated stores and competing security arrangements in the north. The PUK can prepare a useful joint service, but an enduring pact will still depend on the other movement accepting responsibilities it considers fair.

An independent PUK apparatus can pursue its programme without waiting for a common regional leadership to agree. Stronger production and command offices would support that freedom, while requiring the movement to maintain services that cooperation might otherwise have shared.

Northern communities need public services that do not stop at the boundary between rival organizations. Joint medical and educational provision can give cooperation a practical purpose, provided the participants sustain the public obligations involved.

Municipal networks can connect the movement with the civilian economy of northern towns. Competent offices and recorded service income will give that presence a productive role, although administration must become more than an extension of the local party committee.

A federal constitution requires agreement over authority, revenue and the limits of central intervention. Preparing officials able to administer those terms can strengthen the PUK's case, without allowing it to decide on behalf of the other Iraqi parties.

Sulaymaniyah needs productive employment as well as the public offices expected of a regional center. A civilian plant can give the local economy a stronger foundation, provided its operation is supported by practical management rather than political sponsorship alone.

Regional universities can supply the teachers and technical staff that northern public institutions lack. Supporting computing and professional education will connect those institutions with the wider Iraqi economy, while requiring the government to carry their continuing costs.

A security compact must define who commands, who trains and who pays the forces involved. Common instruction can make cooperation more dependable, but a recognized establishment creates obligations that cannot be left to an informal understanding between party leaders.

Mountain trade needs routes that remain useful when political relationships become strained. Better infrastructure around Sulaymaniyah, supported by competent project offices, can connect communities and commercial undertakings without promising to remove the frontier decisions of neighboring states.

Students sent beyond their home districts should return with skills that public works can use. Construction instruction will support the north's expanding routes and services, while the institutions organizing the exchange must provide more than ceremonial visits.

Security formations cannot become a regular public service while their personnel remain scattered across incompatible lists. A dependable payroll can reduce exceptional expenditure and clarify obligations, provided political offices surrender their control over undocumented appointments.

The PUK's governing mandate must be carried into workplaces and civilian services. A more practiced productive administration would give its federal programme substance, while committing it to social provision beyond the movement's established supporters.

Dawa's social networks can carry a message farther than they can administer a ministry. A civilian government must give those networks dependable public offices, so that political support becomes useful service rather than another channel of personal influence.

An Islamic cabinet can work through a constitutional division of public responsibilities. Better medical and educational administration would give that choice practical value, while requiring the party to accept limits on decisions it might otherwise take alone.

Party-directed rule would concentrate policy in an executive able to mobilize its organizations quickly. That authority offers a clear center of decision, but sustaining exceptional security and political supervision will place demands on the public budget.

Religious legal arguments must be translated into procedures that Iraqi public offices can apply consistently. Clearer accounts and contracts would make government more dependable, while requiring professional administrators rather than another layer of informal approvals.

The party's service network must be able to maintain care after a local organizer moves on. Connecting it to competent public offices will widen its reach, although the treasury will then inherit obligations once carried through personal or charitable arrangements.

Al-Sadr's intellectual influence raises questions about the relationship between faith, economic life and public authority. Studying those questions can strengthen the party's educational foundations without confusing spiritual standing with responsibility for the daily work of government.

An Islamic programme of social justice will be judged by the pressures facing Iraqi households. Better care and relief from immediate consumption burdens can support that commitment, but provision must remain dependable when donations or political enthusiasm decline.

Workshops, commercial offices and endowments can support an economy beyond the ministries' direct control. Encouraging them would broaden civilian production, while requiring the government to accept the exemptions and concessions through which their cooperation is secured.

Welfare funds should be judged by the care they provide rather than the standing of the people who administer them. Regular accounts can reduce waste and make provision more dependable, although inspection and supervision require a public service of their own.

Endowments carry obligations to beneficiaries that cannot be understood through informal promises alone. Recorded income and educational responsibilities will make them more useful to the public, while the state must recognize the exemptions that distinguish them from ordinary enterprises.

A government seeking an Islamic mandate must still administer the rights of all Iraqi citizens. Regular public security and institutions resistant to outside pressure can support that responsibility without making access to the state depend on religious affiliation.

Najaf's educational life can support practical skills as well as religious study. Technical instruction connected with construction and public works would give students a wider role in Iraq's development, provided the government funds teachers and useful facilities.

Dawa must show that a religious political programme can remain an Iraqi one. A wider range of technical suppliers and institutions able to resist outside interference will support that independence without requiring Baghdad to deny every useful relationship with Iran.

Workers' associations need a recognized place in settling conditions inside Iraqi plants. Their involvement can improve safety and production cooperation, while limiting the output that managers might otherwise demand without negotiation.

Community instruction can reach families poorly served by distant public institutions. The government should give that work dependable teaching and administration, so that wider literacy becomes a lasting public achievement rather than an occasional charitable campaign.

Relations with Iran should be conducted through responsibilities both governments understand. Preparing Iraqi border and commercial services will make negotiation more useful, while leaving Tehran to decide whether it will accept the non-interference terms Baghdad proposes.

Community medicine can connect local knowledge with a more dependable public health service. Better organized care will support families and reduce avoidable burdens, but the network must be maintained through public obligations rather than expected to survive on personal devotion alone.

The Islamic cabinet must demonstrate that a religious mandate can sustain competent administration. Education and a stronger civilian productive base will give it the means to govern, while binding the state to the social commitments through which it has sought support.

The experience of exile brings political connections and knowledge of institutions outside Iraq. A council seeking to govern at home must turn that experience into Iraqi public service, rather than assume that relationships formed abroad confer an unquestioned national mandate.

An Iraqi charter should define how a government formed around religious opposition will exercise public authority. Representative offices and dependable contracts can give that settlement substance, while requiring the leadership to share responsibility beyond its own executive circle.

A clerical executive would give the movement a concentrated center of political and military decision. It promises a clearer direction, but the security establishment needed to sustain that authority will carry costs of its own.

A representative cabinet needs ministers who can collect revenue and administer instruction across Iraq. Building that competence will broaden the movement's governing base, while making it responsible for a public administration larger than its original networks.

Courts established under revolutionary authority can become instruments through which the executive secures appointments and enforces its political direction. That choice may strengthen the governing circle, but it also deepens the burden of exceptional policing and the distrust of those subject to it.

Returning families and political organizers bring experience that the new administration cannot afford to waste. Their place in public institutions should be defined through useful civilian work, while the government prepares the services needed to support their return.

A government in Baghdad must answer for its own decisions even where its leaders once relied on Iranian support. More resilient institutions and diversified public contracts can widen its room to act, without pretending that existing obligations have simply disappeared.

Closer alignment with a patron can make technical cooperation and political support easier to organize. Iraq must prepare the services needed to use any assistance it receives, while recognizing the influence that dependence can give the government supplying it.

Border administration should reduce the uncertainties that allow local incidents to become national crises. Iraq can prepare more regular supplies and public security arrangements, while any lasting agreement with Iran will still require Tehran's acceptance.

Assistance offered through personal channels can leave the treasury uncertain about what it owes and what it should receive. Published accounts and clear project terms will make Iraqi reconstruction more dependable, even where a prospective donor chooses not to participate.

Armed authority cannot remain divided indefinitely between civilian ministries and formations sustained through political networks. A common command can improve coordination, but recognized personnel and their responsibilities must be carried on the public payroll.

Southern Iraq needs useful employment and functioning workshops as well as a new political leadership. A civilian plant around Basra can anchor recovery, while better repair services protect the work already invested in the region.

Religious education need not leave students without the technical knowledge public institutions require. Connecting instruction with industrial skills can widen their place in Iraqi society, provided the programme offers professional teaching rather than political approval alone.

The movement must explain how citizens outside its principal constituency will be treated by the state. Dependable guarantees can reduce exceptional policing and outside political leverage, while placing limits on officials who would prefer to govern through communal privilege.

Reliable water services are a foundation of public health and productive life in the south. Improving the infrastructure through which they are administered will support recovery, but political sponsorship cannot replace the practical work of maintaining those services.

Schools must be open to children whose families cannot secure a place through personal or political connections. Wider access will strengthen literacy, while requiring the government to supply teachers and materials after the initial commitment has been announced.

Civilian ministers need the authority to examine the personnel and obligations of the security establishment. A regular review can reduce exceptional expenditure, while forcing the leadership to explain appointments that have previously rested on political standing alone.

A governing mandate must be carried into a common command and a practical reconstruction programme. Those institutions can make the state more coherent, but their personnel and continuing responsibilities must remain visible in the public budget.

The Iraqi Islamic Party must rebuild a public organization capable of more than maintaining its own political circles. Competent civilian offices will give its leadership a governing base without assuming that an old title alone settles who should exercise authority.

Parliamentary Islamism would place the party's programme within institutions that can question ministers and supervise public contracts. That settlement can make administration more predictable, while limiting the leadership's freedom to decide policy through its own organization alone.

A party-directed state would concentrate political initiative and mobilization in a stronger executive. It offers a clear center of action, but sustaining the security arrangements around that authority will require continuing public expenditure.

Religious legal commitments must be made usable by businesses and public offices that need consistent procedures. Clearer corporate accounts and project terms can support that work without requiring every commercial question to pass through an informal political patron.

Professional and charitable associations connect the party with people beyond its formal membership. Supporting useful instruction and recorded service income can make those networks productive, while creating public obligations that cannot be met through voluntary effort alone.

A conservative cabinet must still provide officials able to carry out ordinary public work. Professional service can make administration more dependable, while reducing the leadership's freedom to distribute posts according to political convenience.

A social market would give private workshops and civilian producers more room to expand. The government can support that growth through clearer conditions for construction, while accepting the tax concessions through which cooperation is secured.

A welfare programme needs organizations able to provide care without consuming their resources in duplicated administration. More dependable delivery can ease the household burden, but it must be supported by public instruction and institutions that survive the enthusiasm of an individual organizer.

Small businesses need confidence that permissions and contracts will remain usable after a change of minister. Clearer rules can support civilian construction and investment, although the government will have to carry the revenue cost of the concessions it offers.

Charitable funds should be able to show how their income becomes useful care. Recorded obligations and regular supervision can reduce waste in medical and welfare provision, while requiring an administration that beneficiaries can hold responsible.

A governing party cannot reserve dependable public authority for its own supporters. A citizenship compact can make security more regular and resist outside political leverage, while restricting the informal privileges through which ministers might otherwise secure loyalty.

Community education can reach families that existing institutions have served unevenly. Connecting local instruction with professional teachers will widen literacy, while requiring the party to treat learning as a continuing public responsibility rather than a political meeting.
