The party's commercial and social associations can support a civilian foreign policy with practical economic aims. Better project terms and more practiced diplomacy will give Baghdad options without making its institutions dependent on a single external patron.

Employers and workers need arrangements that preserve useful skills when production changes. A negotiated compromise can reduce disruption and medical burdens, while restraining immediate demands that would otherwise be imposed without consultation.

Public examinations can give capable Iraqis a route into administration beyond personal connections. Better records and civilian expertise will strengthen collection and services, provided political leaders accept the limits that professional appointments place on patronage.

A civilian partnership with other Arab governments should be built around projects they can understand and choose to join. Iraq can prepare the commercial and technical liaison needed for that cooperation without presuming another country's money, forces or political allegiance.

Community welfare must support families through ordinary illness and the demands of raising children. More dependable care can strengthen public health and family life, but it requires obligations that neither occasional donations nor political declarations can reliably replace.

The IIP must turn its social and commercial associations into a durable programme of government. A stronger civilian economy and dependable service income will support that mandate, while the treasury continues to carry the concessions made to secure participation.
Oil receipts must reach the treasury rather than disappear between the company, the ministry and the party. A reliable account of sales is the first step towards control of the national income.
Nationalisation will place the industry under Iraqi authority. Taking ownership also means taking responsibility for marketing, management and the disruption of established commercial relationships.

A revised concession can secure better terms while retaining access to established markets and expertise. Iraq will prepare the terminals and connecting works that any workable agreement will require.
An Iraqi oil company must be able to operate fields and negotiate its own sales. Building that organisation will reduce the technical burden left by the old concession system.
The revised concession will be judged by the facilities and technical skills it delivers. Iraq gains an operating export arrangement while an outside partner retains an agreed stake in the industry.
Wells, pumping stations and maintenance shops need Iraqi engineers and skilled crews. Technical training will make the industry less dependent on emergency contracts when foreign specialists leave.
Oil can finance the state on a scale that ordinary taxation cannot yet match. Expanding export facilities offers immediate revenue, at the price of deepening the treasury's dependence on it.

Part of the oil income will be committed to an industrial base beyond the fields. The return will arrive more slowly, but Iraq will gain productive capacity that an oil-price fall cannot erase overnight.

Oil revenues depend on the ability to move exports through the south as well as on production in the fields. We will improve Basrah's transport infrastructure and the connections serving export handling. Better links will help turn petroleum output into a more dependable commercial flow.

Oil income can finance productive capacity that survives fluctuations in the petroleum market. We will support a new civilian industrial complex and give development outside the fields a firmer base. The country's underground wealth should leave something more durable than a succession of government expenditures.
A common revenue ledger will expose overlapping allocations and promises made against the same oil receipts. The oil budget should support a state programme rather than several competing treasuries.

The northern fields still require careful surveys and investment in extraction. Iraqi crews will identify reserves that can be brought into practical production, rather than counting every underground deposit as available income.

Baiji's technical workforce can support a wider refining and energy economy. Better maintenance and operating practice will reduce waste in the fuel-intensive installations that keep Iraqi industry running.
The state cannot export every available barrel and still guarantee fuel in a crisis. A disciplined reserve policy trades some current sales for a more economical military fuel system.

Dependable spare parts and field maintenance keep the oil economy in operation. Iraqi crews will gain the skills to maintain its machinery, while a nationalised company can finally overcome its remaining technical disadvantage.

New installations are of limited use without operators who understand the machinery entrusted to them. We will expand practical instruction for refinery and maintenance personnel. A stronger technical workforce will help the industry absorb improved methods and make more effective use of its equipment.

Buyers and delivery schedules change even when ownership does not. A commercial review will improve Iraq's access to reliable purchasers without pretending that a new export contract transfers control of the industry.

Sovereignty requires more than a flag over the company office. Iraq will be better placed to defend its commercial decisions once it can operate the industry and negotiate credible alternatives on its own.

Plans for industrial growth must reckon with the power, land and skilled labour actually available to Iraq. We will survey existing capacity and establish a more orderly programme of investment. The resulting commitments will need continued attention from officials who can distinguish a viable project from an impressive promise.
Basic industries will give Iraq a stronger foundation for long production runs and domestic military supply. The programme ties up resources that could otherwise satisfy immediate civilian demand.
Consumer manufacturing can expand the civilian economy more quickly than a prestige heavy-industrial complex. Its factories and skilled workers will support the next round of domestic construction.

Baghdad's industrial districts can support a wider network of workshops and civilian manufacturers. We will establish a new industrial complex to give that expansion a physical foundation. Productive investment in the capital must turn plans and imported machinery into regular work for Iraqi industry.

Provincial workshops cannot meet the growing demand for clothing, household goods and everyday supplies. A new industrial complex in Nineveh will give local manufacturers room to expand and reduce the concentration of production around Baghdad. Provincial development must become a practical part of our industrial policy.
New industrial capacity is useless without dependable connections. The Baghdad power and transport grid must be ready to serve factories rather than force them to operate as isolated projects.
Publicly financed industry will rest on a reliable domestic revenue base. The treasury gains a firmer return, while civilian resources are committed to the state's investment programme.
Credit can bring industrial projects into production before the treasury has accumulated their full cost. Faster construction comes with greater exposure to financing conditions.

Public enterprises need operating accounts that distinguish a viable factory from a permanent subsidy. Reinvestment should reward production and maintenance rather than the influence of an appointed director.
Industrial creditors must be repaid from output rather than another unrecorded promise. Better debt management will reduce financing friction while factories learn to sustain their production runs.
Maintenance periods and common quality standards prevent new equipment from becoming unusable machinery. A small interruption of immediate military output is the price of more dependable production.
Basra needs generating capacity that can keep pace with industrial and urban demand. A new fossil-fuel plant will turn part of Iraq's energy endowment into usable electricity.

Machine tools and precision practice will determine whether Iraqi workshops can reproduce a design or merely assemble imported parts. Skilled tooling is an investment in the next generation of production.

Industry requires accountants, transport brokers and commercial offices as well as machinery. Developing Baghdad's service economy will support enterprises that must buy, sell and keep reliable records.
A working power grid needs trained operators and a disciplined fuel schedule. Better management will make existing thermal generation less wasteful while construction expands around it.

Factories under pressure to meet targets can produce goods that fail long before they should. We will introduce more systematic inspection and help managers correct faults in production. Better standards will take time and resources that cannot be devoted immediately to increasing output.

The commercial economy should contribute to the investment that makes it possible. A specialised tax service will collect a more reliable return from offices and business activity without taxing every sector by the same emergency measure.

The next round of investment should reflect what earlier projects have taught us. Ministers will review the balance between industrial priorities and redirect future commitments where necessary. A credible development programme must be willing to change course without abandoning the productive assets already built.
The land reform has left a patchwork of holdings, claims and unfinished obligations. A practical survey will connect future credit to Iraqi farms that can actually put it to work.
Cooperatives can pool machinery, credit and marketing for farms too small to operate alone. A funded organisation can raise output, although its management will remain a real public expense.

Smallholders need credit, predictable obligations and room to make their own production decisions. The state will support household farming rather than place every investment behind a cooperative manager.

Cooperatives cannot fulfil their purpose if they exist without the machinery and advice needed in the fields. We will support equipment purchases and organise assistance around their members' requirements. Delivering these services will begin to close the gap between agrarian reform and everyday agricultural work.

A smallholder without access to credit remains dependent on poor tools and uncertain harvests. We will guarantee a more useful flow of finance to independent producers and help them improve their farms. The state must accept a financial sacrifice if land reform is to produce viable livelihoods.
Water allocations must correspond to planted fields and working channels. Reliable records will reduce the waste caused by competing claims on the same irrigation supply.

Large irrigation works can serve districts beyond the reach of village improvements. They require a substantial public commitment and construction resources that cannot simultaneously be used for every urban project.
Local channels and pumps can be repaired and extended without waiting for a single grand scheme. Their reach is smaller, but communities can bring useful improvements into operation sooner.

Wasit's cultivators need investment that reaches the productive land rather than ending in the offices of a ministry. We will develop an agricultural district and strengthen the foundation for local farming. The countryside must see tangible results from the government's promises of rural development.
Dhi Qar needs a rural investment programme that reaches actual farms. New agricultural capacity will give local works a productive purpose beyond the ministry's completion reports.
Agricultural extension workers can connect credit and irrigation with the skills needed to use them. The remaining rural bottleneck will shrink only when advice reaches the farm itself.
A harvest that cannot be stored or moved is not a secure food supply. Grain depots and rural roads will connect producers to markets before weather and transport failures consume their return.

Upstream water decisions affect Iraqi farms long before they reach a diplomatic communiqué. Preparing domestic works and technical studies will strengthen Iraq's position while agreements remain subject to its neighbours' consent.

The marsh economy depends on water, transport and the livelihoods of its communities. Support for local production should strengthen those communities rather than treat them as empty land awaiting an administrative plan.

Rural producers and urban consumers both lose when food moves through an unreliable distribution chain. A functioning network will reduce the burden carried by households and complete another part of the rural settlement.
An irrigation system needs inspection after its opening ceremony. A funded technical service will keep channels, pumps and allocation records working as a single productive network.

Mobile clinics can reach communities that cannot support a full urban service network. Coordinating basic treatment and transport will make the rural health budget more effective without removing its cost.

Land reform will be judged by what reaches the countryside: usable credit, maintained waterworks, transport and public services. Completing those obligations can finally remove the last inherited rural bottleneck.

Iraq cannot build a modern administration on an incomplete account of its schools and workforce. A national assessment will direct the first teaching effort towards those excluded from basic education.
A mass literacy campaign can reach adults and children left outside formal schooling. Classrooms, instructors and materials will place a real demand on the education budget.

A school system cannot expand indefinitely without trained teachers. Investing in the profession first will support stronger technical learning, even if the earliest gains in basic literacy arrive more slowly.
Evening classes allow working adults to study without abandoning their livelihoods. Extending teaching beyond the normal school day will turn a national campaign into practical local progress.
Training teachers is only useful if they reach underserved districts. A sustained deployment programme will spread the benefits of professional education beyond the largest cities.

Campaign reports are useful only if they describe what people have actually learned. We will improve the assessment of literacy and make educational authorities answer for the results of their work. Careful records can guide future teaching, although maintaining them adds to the duties of the administration.

Universal services offer the whole population a stake in the state's development programme. The long-term return is a more capable workforce, while the public budget must carry the promise through difficult years.

Scarce public resources can be concentrated where household needs are greatest. Targeting preserves more civilian capacity, although identifying and serving those households requires a functioning local administration.
Basic treatment and dependable local facilities can prevent costly emergencies from becoming the normal form of healthcare. The programme will improve the practical reach of universal provision.
A targeted social policy needs visible investment in the districts it names. Improving Nineveh's public infrastructure will connect local services with the communities meant to receive them.
Public services need a budget that distinguishes useful provision from repeated payments and abandoned contracts. A review will preserve more of the welfare budget for its intended recipients.

Women's education expands the skills available to families, schools and the public service. The programme will make access to learning a practical national commitment rather than a ceremonial promise.
Urban growth has outpaced roads, water connections and basic municipal services. Investment in Baghdad's infrastructure will make new housing districts part of a working city.

Technical colleges will train the surveyors, technicians and workshop staff needed by the development programme. Their value will appear in projects that Iraqi specialists can complete and maintain themselves.
A national education programme cannot end at the edge of the city. Rural schools will sustain the gains of adult teaching and open a route into technical training for the next generation.

Municipalities need dependable revenue and accountable service contracts. A stronger local finance system can support public facilities without repeatedly appealing to Baghdad for an emergency allocation.

Laboratories need maintained instruments and a stable technical staff. Building practical competence in electronics will support Iraqi research without pretending that every field can advance at once.

The public service programme must be able to adapt as needs and resources change. We will review the balance of coverage and funding while preserving the educational progress already achieved. A more durable settlement should rest on commitments the government can continue to meet.

The armed forces need a clear account of their institutions, expenditure and readiness. We will examine how resources move through the military administration and identify the obstacles facing the forces already under arms. A stronger defence policy begins with knowing what the state is actually supporting.
A professional core can give the army formations that train and operate together. Iraq will pay more for each trained soldier in exchange for a more coherent force.
A deep reserve provides replacements and the ability to sustain a long campaign. Its size cannot remove the coordination problems of a force assembled from uneven levels of training.
Staff officers must learn to turn political objectives into orders that formations can execute. More thorough preparation takes time, but reduces the need to improvise doctrine during a campaign.
The reserve needs instructors, refresher courses and a dependable call-up system. Training will make replacement formations useful while adding a real continuing personnel commitment.

The armed forces need common standards for tenders, spares and acceptance trials. A procurement board will connect domestic production with military requirements rather than the preferences of each purchasing mission.
Soviet standards can simplify ammunition, training and spare-parts supply across the army. That efficiency also gives one supplier greater influence over Iraqi military planning.
Different suppliers offer capabilities that no single relationship can provide. Iraq will gain technical options while accepting the extra burden of maintaining several standards.

An advisory agreement is more useful when Iraqi officers know what they need to learn. Domestic preparations will improve staff practice while the Soviet government decides whether to provide the requested cooperation.

Equipment from several suppliers needs translated manuals, trained crews and a dependable repair service. Longer familiarisation will prevent some of the losses caused by operating unfamiliar machines.
Operational plans must reflect the roads and supply columns that support them. Better logistics will allow Iraqi formations to move with fewer avoidable interruptions.

Land-force schools will turn campaign experience into training that survives the transfer of individual commanders. Instructors and permanent courses cost money, but the army will retain what it learns.
Aircraft availability depends on ground crews, spare parts and careful maintenance as much as purchases. Iraq will invest in the skills needed to keep its air force flying safely.
A coastal force needs domestic facilities capable of supporting and repairing its vessels. Basra will provide a modest naval-industrial foundation suited to Iraq's limited frontage on the Gulf.

A domestic armaments plant cannot replace every foreign supplier, but it can support a dependable core of military production. The army will gain an industrial asset rather than another promise of self-sufficiency.
Fuel discipline begins with drivers, maintenance crews and realistic movement schedules. The air-force maintenance programme will be matched by a less wasteful military fuel system.
A small fleet cannot afford to leave repair capacity idle or depend on every overhaul being performed abroad. Improved dockyard practice will make Basra's facilities more productive.
Readiness rests on repeated staff work and the ability to assemble a force before the crisis has passed. A final exercise will test the institutions built throughout the military programme.
Mobilisation exposes weaknesses that a peacetime staff can ignore. Contingency exercises will give the government a clearer understanding of what its army can sustain.
Armed restraint requires a force capable of holding its ground. Iraq will fund prepared positions and defensive readiness while keeping the decision to expand the war under political control.
An offensive option gives the government a credible means of changing the military situation. Preparing it will strain personnel budgets and increase the domestic risks of a failed operation.
Crisis communications can save the expense of reacting to every report with another deployment. Maintaining a channel does not oblige Iraq to accept an unfavourable settlement.

A decision for war must specify who can issue orders and what the army is expected to achieve. Clear authority will help the staff prepare an operation without granting it an unlimited political mandate.

Power, roads and public records must continue to function while resources are diverted to the armed forces. Civil continuity preparations will help restore essential facilities when disruption occurs.
War production will take priority over ordinary civilian demand. The state can obtain more military output, but must accept the economic and personnel commitments that accompany it.

The war cannot consume every part of the civilian economy without undermining the state behind the front. A protected civilian budget sustains productive life while limiting the resources available for military output.
Wartime orders must arrive as usable equipment rather than incomplete contracts. A faster procurement cycle improves production, while emergency purchasing remains more expensive than normal supply.
Wartime public services must cope with disrupted transport and rising demand. Coordinating essential care will reduce waste without pretending that civilian provision has become free.

Emergency spending needs scrutiny before temporary contracts become permanent liabilities. A reliable ledger will recover part of the waste in the equipment budget, without erasing the real cost of war.
Veterans and victims carry the consequences of war long after an offensive ends. Rehabilitation and instruction will preserve experience while committing the state to a real support budget.
Reconstruction must restore productive civilian work as well as damaged monuments. A new industrial undertaking in Basra will provide a concrete foundation for the recovery.

A postwar treasury must distinguish immediate obligations from debts that can be refinanced. Better administration offers some financing relief, but lenders still decide whether to accept revised terms.

Returning soldiers need a place in civilian production, not merely a discharge paper. Training and support can bring wartime skills into workshops and construction while imposing a lasting social obligation.
Recovery contracts should restore equipment and return plants to reliable operation. Paying for competent repair will produce more than a new chain of politically connected intermediaries.

Sanctions expose every weakness in domestic production and commercial access. Iraq will improve the technical capacity it can control while any alternative export or credit arrangement still requires a willing partner.

Peace allows labour and money to return to civilian construction. A smaller readiness commitment eases personnel costs, although the army will need time to recover its former organisation if another crisis begins.
The Iranian frontier connects navigation rights, local communities and the security of the oil economy. A staff assessment will give Iraq a clearer military basis for its demands.
The Shatt dispute gives Iraq a concrete demand to press against Tehran. Sustaining that demand will require military preparation and carries a domestic risk if the confrontation fails.

The claim to Arabistan places Iranian territory at the centre of Iraqi war aims. It is a political commitment to a dangerous campaign, not proof that the province's population will welcome a new government.
A southern command will bring frontier plans, formations and supply priorities under one staff. Iraq gains operational coherence at the price of another sustained military commitment.
Tehran's army must be assessed as it exists, not as Iraqi leaders hope it exists. Reconnaissance and staff work will improve planning while leaving the risks of political miscalculation intact.

The southern war plan must connect objectives with roads, supply and the time available to concentrate forces. Detailed preparation can improve the opening operation without guaranteeing its political outcome.
A short war seeks to turn preparation into a rapid decision. Concentrating resources for that opening also places extra pressure on the supply system if the campaign refuses to end on schedule.
A long campaign requires a war-production base and a reserve that can be replenished. The state will prepare for endurance while diverting specialists and resources from peacetime work.
The opening campaign will consume fuel and spare parts faster than ordinary peacetime routines can supply them. Better preparation reduces waste, while urgent equipment contracts carry a premium.
A war reserve needs more than men on a list. Domestic arms production will support the formations raised for a prolonged campaign and bind the state to maintaining their readiness.

Other Gulf governments may see Iran's power as a danger they would rather Iraq confront. We will seek financial backing and present our preparations as serving a wider regional interest. Assistance can strengthen our position, but money advanced in solidarity may later return as a creditor's demand.
Forward depots and connecting roads will determine how long formations can operate beyond their starting positions. Preparing that network is a tangible investment in the campaign.
Long-war contracts will give producers a more predictable military programme. The treasury accepts lower ordinary receipts in exchange for faster improvements in the output needed at the front.

Foreign equipment remains useful only while the army can obtain the parts and support needed to keep it working. We will approach suppliers about arrangements suitable for a wartime demand. Baghdad must secure their cooperation on terms they accept rather than assume that earlier sales guarantee assistance.
The ultimatum turns a territorial demand into an explicit threat of war. Iraq must now decide whether its preparations justify the consequences of enforcing it.
Executing the plan requires the staff to concentrate what Iraq has actually built. A coherent opening can create an opportunity; it cannot ensure that the war remains limited.
A national mobilisation reaches factories, families and the public-service budget. The state will ask for a larger war commitment while accepting the strain this places on ordinary life.
The first campaign has produced practical lessons as well as bills. The staff will record what formations consumed and what the front actually needed before another operation is approved.

Holding Khuzestan requires secure supply routes and an administration that can function behind the fighting. Territorial control brings obligations that an advance across the frontier cannot settle by itself.
A campaign that survives its promised timetable becomes a different kind of war. Iraqi officers must turn the experience of sustained fighting into a plan for the next phase.

Captured oil installations are not immediately a dependable source of revenue. Restoring roads and facilities will require investment and continuing security before the province can support its new administration.
A civil administration must provide records, revenue collection and enforceable local obligations. Establishing it is a different task from simply maintaining a military presence in the province.
Sustained war demands formations that can be replaced as well as reinforced. A larger reserve strengthens endurance while drawing skilled people and public money away from civilian work.
Another offensive should rest on the lessons of the first campaign rather than a repetition of its assumptions. The staff will prepare the next concentration while the government weighs its cost.
Control of Arabistan changes Iraq's regional position. Turning that gain into durable influence will depend on holding the territory and administering it beyond the end of the campaign.
Victory at any cost binds the state to a war economy whose promises become harder to abandon. Iraq can drive military output higher while its households and treasury carry the consequences.

A provincial settlement must define the obligations of the state after the fighting ends. Civil records and local representation will prepare the ground for the choice between integration by consent and central rule.

Equal citizenship commits Iraq to extending public obligations as well as nationality. Representation and services can deepen integration, but the state must fund the rights it promises to the province.

Central state rule offers Baghdad a tighter grip over the province. Security and administrative enforcement can establish authority more cheaply than broad social guarantees, while leaving deeper resentment unresolved.

Making the province part of Iraq requires the government to complete its chosen settlement and accept responsibility for its people. The final decision will follow actual possession, peace and the institutions built on the ground.

January 1970. Six years after the fall of Khrushchev, the Soviet Union is governed by a troika: Leonid Brezhnev as General Secretary, Alexei Kosygin at the head of the Council of Ministers and Nikolai Podgorny as head of state. Behind the facade of unity, the Politburo balances reformers against the orthodox, Moscow against the republics and the planners against the generals. Whoever holds this balance holds the Union.

On 22 April 1970 the Soviet Union marks one hundred years since the birth of Vladimir Ilyich Lenin. Jubilee medals, mass rallies, new monuments and an endless stream of 'Leniniana' on television and in print turn the anniversary into the greatest propaganda campaign of the decade. The Party presents itself as the rightful heir of the revolution, and every citizen is reminded to whom the future is owed.

Power in the Soviet Union does not flow from elections but from the quiet arithmetic of the Politburo. Every appointment, every retirement and every new regional first secretary shifts the balance between reformers and the orthodox guardians of the system. To rule from the Kremlin, the General Secretary must learn to count votes, reward loyalty and isolate rivals before they can do the same to him.

From 30 March to 9 April 1971 almost five thousand delegates gather in the Kremlin Palace of Congresses for the XXIV Congress of the CPSU. Brezhnev unveils a Peace Programme for relations with the West and the guidelines of the Ninth Five-Year Plan, promising both security and a better life for Soviet citizens. The congress sets the course of the collective leadership for the years to come.

Communism has not yet arrived, but the Party now declares that the Soviet Union has entered the stage of 'developed socialism', a long historical era in which the system perfects itself step by step. The doctrine replaces Khrushchev's bold promise of communism by 1980 with a reassuring message of stability and gradual progress. It gives ideologists such as Mikhail Suslov a firm framework and tells every citizen that the foundations are sound.

The men who rose under Stalin still sit at the summit of the Party. By the middle of the decade the average age of the Politburo exceeds sixty-five, and many regional secretaries have held their posts for twenty years or more. Stability of cadres has bought the leadership loyalty and calm, but it also blocks the path of younger, more capable officials. The Party must decide whether to renew its ranks or honour its veterans.

The generation of 1964 cannot govern forever. By sending veteran ministers and obkom secretaries into honourable retirement and promoting younger engineers, economists and administrators, the leadership can breathe new energy into the state. The old guard will not leave quietly, and the shake-up will cause friction throughout the Party apparatus, but a renewed cadre corps may be exactly what the Union needs to face the decades ahead.

The Party rewards those who have served it longest. Ministers, marshals and first secretaries keep their posts until they die in office, and the nomenklatura enjoys a security unknown since the revolution. The result is calm and predictable government, but also an era that later generations will call the zastoi, the Stagnation, as growth slows, corruption spreads and new ideas wait in vain for a hearing.

Long in preparation, a new Fundamental Law is to replace the Stalin Constitution of 1936. Its sixth article enshrines the Communist Party as the leading and guiding force of Soviet society, while the text proclaims the Soviet people a new historical community of many nations. The Brezhnev Constitution codifies developed socialism, broadens the formal rights of citizens and binds the republics ever more closely to the centre in Moscow.

Where is the Soviet Union heading? Behind closed doors, Party theorists, scientists, economists and patriots offer competing answers: a reaffirmation of the Party's leading role, a cautious opening towards the West, a socialist path independent of both blocs, or a revival rooted in Russian tradition. The leadership must decide which current of thought it will allow to shape the next generation of Soviet politics.

The answer to every question is the Party. Ideological commissions, the Komsomol and the primary Party organisations in every factory and collective farm are ordered to strengthen discipline and political education. Deviations are to be corrected, doubts dispelled and the masses mobilised behind the line of the Central Committee. The Union will march forward as Lenin intended, guided by the vanguard of the working class.

Since 1968 the physicist Andrei Sakharov has circulated his essay 'Reflections on Progress, Peaceful Coexistence and Intellectual Freedom', arguing that capitalism and socialism must converge to save mankind. Instead of silencing the father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb, the leadership now permits an official debate on his ideas. Scientists and intellectuals sense a new thaw, while the guardians of orthodoxy see the first crack in the dam.

Neither the rigid orthodoxy of the apparatus nor the consumer capitalism of the West offers a convincing future. Inspired by Yugoslav self-management, the Prague reformers and the anti-colonial movements of the Third World, a circle of Soviet theorists proposes a socialism of its own: decentralised, pragmatic and open to the non-aligned world. The debate is risky, but it promises fresh answers to old problems.

Writers of the village prose movement, the journal Molodaya Gvardiya and patriotic circles within the Party call for a return to Russian roots: the land, the old churches and the memory of the Great Patriotic War. Elevating the Russian people as the backbone of the Union can rally soldiers and patriots behind the state. For Ukrainians, Balts and Central Asians, however, a Russian revival sounds dangerously like Russification.

Lenin conceived the Bolsheviks as a party of a new type: disciplined, centralised and guided by revolutionary theory. Restoring this spirit means weeding out careerists, raising ideological standards and demanding exemplary conduct from every member. The Communist Party of the Soviet Union would once again lead by example rather than by inertia, and its authority among the people would grow accordingly.

The Komsomol counts tens of millions of young members, many of whom have never felt the enthusiasm of the founding years. Shock construction projects in Siberia, student work brigades and military-patriotic education can mobilise this energy for the building of communism. A generation that lays track across the taiga will also stand ready to defend the motherland.

The Soviet Union calls itself the state of workers and peasants, yet the people on the factory floor often feel far removed from the decisions made in their name. Giving the trade unions a stronger voice, improving working conditions and honouring labour in culture and propaganda can renew the bond between the party and the working class. The ideals of October must be visible in every workshop.

Whatever factions may have risen in recent years, the Communist Party of the Soviet Union claims to be the only true heir of Lenin. Placing power firmly back in the hands of the CPSU under Leonid Brezhnev would restore the familiar order of the Politburo, the Central Committee and the regional committees. The transition will unsettle the ministries for a time, but it promises continuity and a return to the Leninist norms of party life.

What if the old slogan of 1917 were taken literally? The Free Councils of Labour, led by Pyotr Siuda, a veteran of the Novocherkassk strike of 1962, demand that power pass from the party apparatus to elected councils of workers in every factory and town. The experiment would dismantle the nomenklatura and could unleash enormous energy, or plunge the economy into chaos.

For the Neo-Stalinist Platform, the troubles of the Soviet Union stem from the abandonment of Stalin's firm hand. Led by Sergei Trapeznikov, the Central Committee's conservative chief of science and education, the Iron Line promises discipline, ideological vigilance and an end to the half-hearted experiments of recent years. Handing them power would reassure the hardliners in the army and the security organs, but it would chill the intelligentsia and alarm the West.

Alexander Shelepin, former head of the Komsomol and the KGB, has never abandoned his ambition to lead the Soviet Union. His Komsomol Vanguard gathers a younger generation of officials who promise energy, order and a decisive break with the ageing men of the Politburo. Handing them power would be a generational revolution from above, carried out by men known for their authoritarian instincts.

Whatever the course of recent events, the Communist Party remains the leading and guiding force of Soviet society, the nucleus of its political system and of all state and public organisations. Reaffirming this principle, which a new constitution will enshrine in its sixth article, gives the party apparatus a clear mandate to direct the state. It is the foundation on which every further reform or consolidation must rest.

Socialist emulation pits brigades, workshops and factories against one another in comradely competition to exceed the plan. Red banners, honour boards and the title of Hero of Socialist Labour reward the best, while laggards are criticised in the factory newspaper. Freeing the movement from formalism and empty pledges can raise efficiency and morale without abandoning the principles of planning.

The Committee of People's Control, with millions of volunteer inspectors in every factory, office and collective farm, is meant to be the eyes of the working people over the bureaucracy. Giving it real powers to investigate embezzlement, waste and abuse of office would strike at the corruption spreading through the apparatus. The nomenklatura will resent the scrutiny, but honest citizens will welcome it.

From its editorial offices in Prague, the journal Problems of Peace and Socialism brings together communist and workers' parties from around the world. Turning it into a genuine platform for the international movement would carry the Soviet vision of socialism far beyond the bloc and strengthen ties with fraternal parties in the West and the Third World. A shared voice is the first step towards a shared strategy.

Typed on carbon paper and passed from hand to hand, samizdat carries forbidden novels, poetry and the Chronicle of Current Events across the Soviet Union. Instead of hunting down every typewriter, the authorities could simply look the other way. Tolerating the underground presses would win the trust of the intelligentsia and open a channel for honest criticism, though the ideological guardians warn that it is the first crack in the dam.

Every night a vast network of transmitters jams the Russian-language broadcasts of the Voice of America, the BBC and other Western stations. In September 1973, as a gesture of detente, the jamming of several of them was suspended. Ending it for good would save enormous sums, please Western governments and let Soviet citizens hear the world, but it would also break the party's monopoly on information.

In November 1970 Andrei Sakharov, Valery Chalidze and Andrei Tverdokhlebov founded the Human Rights Committee to study how Soviet law could protect the rights of citizens. The KGB regards them as enemies, but recognising the committee as a legitimate voice would demonstrate that Soviet socialism respects its own constitution. Such a step would earn praise abroad and enrage the security organs at home.

Dzhermen Gvishiani, deputy chairman of the State Committee for Science and Technology and son-in-law of Alexei Kosygin, champions management science, systems analysis and computerised planning. His Systems Directorate envisions a Soviet Union governed by experts and data rather than by party dogma. Handing them power would mean leaving the party state behind entirely, a revolution of technocrats that could modernise the country or tear it apart.

For decades the People's Labour Union, known as the NTS, has waged a propaganda war against the Soviet regime from exile, smuggling its journals Posev and Grani into the country. Under Vladimir Poremsky it offers a vision of a national, Christian and solidarist Russia freed from communism. Bringing the émigrés home to power would be an unprecedented break with more than half a century of Soviet history.

The physicist Andrei Sakharov, father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb and now the country's most famous dissident, would lead a government founded on law, human rights and convergence with the West. The Committee for Human Rights promises to free political prisoners, end censorship and guarantee the freedom to emigrate. Such a transfer of power would astonish the world, though the security organs and much of the apparatus would never accept it willingly.

The historian Roy Medvedev, author of a damning study of Stalinism, argues that the Soviet Union can be democratised without abandoning socialism. His Union of Democratic Socialists calls for free debate, competing candidates and an independent judiciary while preserving public ownership. Handing them power would turn the country into a socialist democracy, an experiment that Prague was never allowed to complete.

With the monopoly of the party broken, the Soviet Union must rebuild itself as a democratic state. Freedom of speech and assembly, independent courts and genuine parliamentary institutions are to replace the old structures of control. The transition promises a flowering of science and public life, but it also releases grievances that decades of repression had kept hidden.

For the first time since the Constituent Assembly was dispersed in January 1918, the peoples of the Soviet Union are to choose their representatives freely among competing parties. Regular elections will give the new government genuine legitimacy and open the way for the human rights movement to win popular support. They will also give a voice to nationalists in the republics, who may use it to demand independence.

Central planning has failed to deliver the goods that Soviet citizens want. Private enterprise, free prices and foreign investment are to return after more than half a century of state monopoly, creating a mixed economy in which the state retains only the commanding heights. The reform promises growth and abundance, but in the short term it means rising prices, unemployment and widening inequality.

The Soviet Union, once the leader of the socialist camp, is ready to change sides. Aligning with the United States and Western Europe would end the Cold War on terms no one in 1970 could have imagined, opening access to Western markets, credits and technology. For millions of veterans and party members it would be a bitter betrayal; for the new democrats it is the only path to a normal future.

Josip Broz Tito's Yugoslavia has shown that socialism need not mean Soviet-style central planning. Workers' self-management, decentralised enterprises and a foreign policy independent of both blocs have brought Belgrade prosperity and international prestige. Studying the Yugoslav model, long condemned in Moscow as revisionism, would offer Soviet reformers an alternative that remains socialist without being Stalinist.

Economists, engineers and planners in the research institutes of Moscow and Novosibirsk believe that the Soviet economy can be fixed by expertise rather than ideology. They call for mathematical planning methods, profit incentives and the enterprise autonomy promised by the Kosygin reform of 1965. Giving them a voice would move the country towards a pragmatic course between the dogmas of the party and the models of the West.

Writers such as Valentin Rasputin, Vasily Belov and Vasily Shukshin mourn the dying Russian village, its traditions, its churches and its moral world, destroyed by collectivisation and industrial progress. Their village prose has become a quiet conservative counterculture, tolerated by the censors yet deeply critical of Soviet modernity. Encouraging this current would strengthen a rooted, national alternative to both communist and Western ideologies.

Between the party loyalists and the Western-minded dissidents stands a third force: technocrats, conservatives and environmentalists who want reform without capitulation. Allowing them to organise and to influence policy would broaden the political spectrum and create allies for change within the system. The Politburo's conservatives see a dangerous dilution of the party line, but the reformers see a way out of stagnation.

Nikolai Baibakov has chaired the State Planning Committee since 1965 and knows the Soviet economy better than anyone. His Gosplan Technocracy would govern not through ideology or party congresses but through balances, targets and indicators. Handing power to the planners would put the economy before politics, creating an administrative state run by the men who actually manage the country's resources.

Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, Nobel laureate and chronicler of the Gulag, calls on his countrymen to live not by lies. His followers envision a Russia freed from communist ideology and rooted in Orthodox faith, rural values and the traditions of local self-government. Handing them power would be a moral revolution, but Solzhenitsyn's authoritarian streak and Russian nationalism trouble the non-Russian republics and the Westernisers alike.

The directors of the great factories, combines and ministries are the true masters of the Soviet economy, and they are tired of taking orders from party secretaries. With the backing of Interior Minister Nikolai Shchelokov, the Red Directors propose a government of managers in which the heads of industry hold power directly. Their rule might be efficient, and profitable for many of them, but it risks turning public property into private fiefdoms.

The economist Nikolai Shmelyov argues that the Soviet economy can be saved only by markets, private initiative and honest prices. His Free Enterprise League proposes dismantling the planning apparatus, legalising private business and opening the country to foreign investment. Handing them power would be a leap into the unknown, offering prosperity to the enterprising and hardship to those who have known nothing but the security of the state.

Since the 1960s scientists and writers have fought to save Lake Baikal from the effluent of a giant pulp mill on its shore. Grigory Galazy, director of the Limnological Institute in Irkutsk, now leads the Friends of Baikal, grown into a broader movement against the environmental devastation caused by Soviet industry. A green government would put nature before production targets, a radical departure for a country built on heavy industry.

Alexander Yakovlev, a party ideologist who studied in the United States and warned against Russian chauvinism, has come to believe that socialism needs markets to survive. His Socialist Market Commonwealth proposes combining public ownership with competition, enterprise autonomy and openness to the world. Handing them power would launch a far-reaching reform from within, one that could renew Soviet socialism or unravel it entirely.

Pyotr Shelest, the former first secretary of the Ukrainian party, has long defended the economic and cultural rights of the republics against Moscow's centralism. His Union of Sovereign Republics proposes to turn the Soviet Union into a genuine federation in which each republic controls its own affairs. Handing them power would satisfy national aspirations from Kiev to Tashkent, but it could also loosen the bonds that hold the Union together.

The new Soviet leadership declares that the country will no longer head one bloc in a global confrontation. Neither the old Moscow of the Politburo nor Washington shall dictate the course of the world; instead the Soviet Union will pursue its own interests and keep an equal distance from all camps. It is a dramatic turn that leaves allies bewildered and opens entirely new possibilities for the country.

Between Soviet central planning and Western capitalism lies a third way. Inspired by the Kosygin reform, Yugoslav self-management and the ideas of the Czechoslovak economist Ota Šik, the new economic policy combines planning for key sectors with enterprise autonomy, market prices and trade with the whole world. It is an untested experiment on a continental scale, but its advocates believe it can unleash the potential stifled by decades of rigid planning.

If the Soviet Union no longer leads a bloc, what is the purpose of the Warsaw Pact? Dissolving the alliance would free Eastern Europe to choose its own partners and remove the main justification for NATO's presence on the continent. Each former member will decide its own future, and some will certainly turn west, but the step would mark the true end of the post-war order in Europe.

Founded in Belgrade in 1961 by Tito, Nehru, Nasser and Sukarno, the Non-Aligned Movement brings together states that refuse to join either bloc. Seeking membership would be an astonishing step for a superpower, but it would align the Soviet Union with India and the developing world as an equal rather than a patron. The members will be wary of Moscow's motives, yet its accession would transform the movement overnight.

Published by the Komsomol's own press, the journal Molodaya Gvardiya has become the mouthpiece of the so-called Russian Party: writers and editors who praise village life, Orthodox heritage and the greatness of the Russian nation. Opening its pages wider would give Russian nationalists a respectable platform inside the Soviet system, at the price of unsettling the other republics.

Since 1965, Victory Day is once again a public holiday, and the memory of the Great Patriotic War has become the strongest shared faith of the Soviet people. From the Motherland Calls on Mamayev Kurgan to the eternal flames in every town, twenty million dead bind the nation together. Raising the victory above the revolution itself would make the sacrifice of the Russian people the true foundation of the state.

Beneath the official slogans, a quiet current runs through Soviet Russia: restored churches and monasteries, the village prose of Valentin Rasputin and Vasily Belov, the All-Russian Society for the Protection of Historical and Cultural Monuments. Its followers speak of a vozrozhdenie, a rebirth of the Russian nation after decades of uprooting. Embracing this revival would turn cultural nostalgia into a political programme.

For years the Russian Party worked in the shadows of the Central Committee, in editorial offices and Komsomol cells. Now its patrons step forward openly, promising that Russia will no longer pay for the other nations of the union and will finally be master in its own house. The transfer of power will shake the apparatus, and the republics will watch with deep unease.

In the darkest corner of the Russian Party, radicals dream of more than a reformed union: a Committee of National Rebirth that would sweep away the Marxist creed entirely and rebuild Russia as an ethnic, authoritarian state. What if a deep crisis of the system handed them their moment? Such a seizure of power would break with everything Soviet and could tear the union apart.

The Soviet marshals have always stood just outside the circle of power, mindful of how Zhukov was cast aside in 1957. Should the Party falter and the country slide into disorder, the High Command could step in as guardian of the state, ruling through a council of marshals in the name of order and the great victory. The army's loyalty would then belong to the nation rather than to the Party.

Half a century after Yekaterinburg, the idea seems absurd: a Romanov back in the Kremlin. Yet in emigre circles in France and Spain, Grand Duke Vladimir Kirillovich still claims the throne, and among disillusioned Russian nationalists the old symbols are quietly regaining their pull. What if a collapsing order turned to the crown as the last remaining source of legitimacy?

Why should Russian workers pay for cotton in Uzbekistan and new factories in the Baltic while the villages of the Non-Black Earth region decay? The question is asked ever more openly in Moscow. Putting Russia first means redirecting investment, prestige and political attention to the Russian heartland, even if the other republics see it as a betrayal of the union's promise.

Every Soviet republic has its own Communist Party, its own Academy of Sciences and its own KGB, every one except Russia, whose affairs are run directly by the all-union centre. Russian nationalists have long called this a humiliation. Creating separate Russian institutions would give the largest republic a voice of its own, but also a power base that could one day rival the union itself.

Officially, the Soviet Army belongs to all Soviet peoples, but its officer corps is overwhelmingly Russian and its traditions reach back to Suvorov and Kutuzov. Nationalists want to make that heritage explicit: an army rooted in Russian history, Russian valour and Russian soil rather than in proletarian internationalism. Soldiers who fight for the motherland, they argue, fight harder than those who fight for an abstraction.

Every Russian nationalist must eventually answer the same question: is the Soviet Union Russia's empire, to be held at any cost, or a burden that drains the Russian nation? One camp would keep every republic by force if needed; the other would let the restless periphery go and build a tighter union around the Slavic core. The answer will define the country's borders for generations.

Nearly fifteen million members strong, the Communist Party of the Soviet Union is the spine of the state, the guardian of Lenin's legacy and the source of every career that matters. As the country enters the 1970s, the leadership must decide how the Party presents itself: as a living revolutionary vanguard or as the steady administrator of a mature socialist society. Either way, its authority must remain beyond question.

The nomenklatura lists decide who runs every factory, ministry, newspaper and regional committee in the Soviet Union. Those on them enjoy special shops, dachas and the certainty that their position is safe. Strengthening this system binds the cadres firmly to the Party, but it also breeds a privileged caste that grows ever more comfortable and ever less accountable.

With nearly thirty million members, the Leninist Young Communist League is the Party's school and recruiting ground. Its brigades raise new towns in Siberia, its activists organise every university and factory, and its leaders are the next generation of the nomenklatura. A revitalised Komsomol could bind Soviet youth to the cause, if it can still inspire rather than merely organise.

The 24th Party Congress has decided that every Communist must receive a new party card, and in 1973 and 1974 each member has to appear in person to exchange the old one. Officially it is an administrative procedure; in practice it is a quiet purge, as the passive, the corrupt and the drunk can simply be left without a new card. Done seriously, the exchange could cleanse the ranks without the terror of earlier decades.

Lenin's principle of democratic centralism holds that debate is free until a decision is made, and that afterwards every member must carry it out without dissent. In practice, the emphasis has long fallen on centralism. Reaffirming the doctrine closes the ranks behind the Politburo's line and shields the Party against factions and foreign ideas, though it leaves little room for initiative from below.

A new Soviet constitution, long prepared by a commission under Brezhnev himself, could name the Party outright as 'the leading and guiding force of Soviet society, the nucleus of its political system'. The basic law would enshrine the era of developed socialism and the Party's monopoly in a single article. Written into law, the Party's role would no longer be a matter of practice but of constitutional principle.

Since Khrushchev's programme of 1961, the CPSU no longer calls itself merely the party of the working class but the party of the whole Soviet people. With the dictatorship of the proletariat declared complete, it claims to speak for workers, collective farmers and the intelligentsia alike, and for every nation of the union. Embracing this broad identity widens its base, at the cost of some revolutionary sharpness.

Real power in the Soviet Union lies with a dozen elderly men around a table in the Kremlin Senate. Since Khrushchev's fall in 1964, Leonid Brezhnev has ruled as first among equals, balancing Kosygin's government, Suslov's ideology and the ambitions of younger rivals. Every succession, every change of course and every career is decided here, behind closed doors and by a show of hands.

Alexei Kosygin has headed the Council of Ministers since 1964 and is respected at home and abroad as a capable manager. His economic reform of 1965, however, is being slowly strangled by the Party apparatus. What if the Premier's allies in the ministries and the Central Committee called a plenum to make him General Secretary, placing the government's pragmatism above the Party's ideology?

As Chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet, Nikolai Podgorny is the formal head of the Soviet state and the third man of the collective leadership. A veteran of the Kharkov party organisation and former leader of the Ukrainian Communists, he commands loyalties in the largest non-Russian republic. What if a plenum turned to him, raising the organs of the state above the Party secretariat?

Mikhail Suslov, the Party's chief ideologist, has never sought the top post, preferring to guard doctrine from the shadows, which has earned him the name 'grey cardinal'. Ascetic, dogmatic and feared, he has made and broken careers for more than two decades. What if a plenum asked him to step forward and personally steer the Party back towards ideological purity?

Alexander Shelepin, once head of the Komsomol and later of the KGB, helped topple Khrushchev in 1964 and was soon seen as Brezhnev's most dangerous rival. Since 1967 he has been sidelined to the trade unions, yet 'Iron Shurik' still has friends among the security men and the former Komsomol generation. What if a plenum brought him back to finish what he began, with an iron broom for the cadres?

Yuri Andropov has run the KGB since 1967 and knows more about the Party's secrets, and its corruption, than anyone else in the leadership. Austere, intelligent and patient, he is the candidate of those who believe the country needs discipline and order before anything else. Historically he succeeded Brezhnev in November 1982, but a plenum could bring the Chekist to power much sooner.

Marshal Andrei Grechko, Minister of Defence since 1967, speaks for an army that has made the Soviet Union a military superpower. Blunt and hawkish, he distrusts detente and the civilians who negotiate it. What if the Politburo, fearing weakness abroad and drift at home, handed the Party to a soldier for the first time, with the General Staff standing firmly behind him?

Dmitry Ustinov became People's Commissar for Armaments in 1941, at just thirty-two, and has overseen the Soviet defence industry ever since, from tanks and artillery to missiles and space rockets. As Central Committee Secretary for defence, he is the patron of the military-industrial complex. What if a plenum chose the armourer himself, placing the needs of the defence plants at the centre of the state?

Grigory Romanov, the rising master of the Leningrad party organisation, rules the second city of the Soviet Union with a firm hand and a close eye on the defence factories that fill it. Young by Politburo standards, orthodox and efficient, he is already spoken of as a future leader. What if a plenum skipped a generation and summoned the man from Smolny to the Kremlin?

Konstantin Chernenko has spent his career at Brezhnev's side, rising from propaganda work in Moldavia to head the Central Committee's General Department. He has no power base of his own beyond the apparatus, which is precisely why the old guard trusts him. Historically he succeeded Andropov in February 1984; a plenum could make the loyal apparatchik leader whenever the elders want continuity above all.

Mikhail Gorbachev, the energetic party chief of Stavropol, belongs to a generation shaped by Khrushchev's thaw rather than by Stalin's purges. Powerful patrons such as Andropov and Suslov have marked him as a man of the future. Historically he became General Secretary in March 1985; a plenum could hand power to the new generation earlier, with all the hope and risk that change brings.

Since October 1964, Leonid Ilyich Brezhnev has led the Party, first cautiously, then with growing confidence. After the upheavals of Stalin and Khrushchev, he offers the nomenklatura what it craves most: stability, predictability and respect for its positions. Hailed as 'dear Leonid Ilyich' in official speeches, he now stands ready to shape a whole era in his own image.

Brezhnev built his career in Dnepropetrovsk and Moldavia, and the men he met there have followed him to Moscow: Andrei Kirilenko in the Secretariat, Nikolai Shchelokov at the Interior Ministry, Nikolai Tikhonov in the Council of Ministers. Promoting this circle of old comrades secures the General Secretary's grip on key posts, but it also rewards loyalty above competence.

Every document that reaches the Politburo passes through the Central Committee's General Department, headed since 1965 by Konstantin Chernenko. He controls the agenda, the minutes and the flow of paper to the General Secretary's desk. Turning this office into the nerve centre of the leadership makes the bureaucracy run more smoothly and makes Brezhnev's most loyal aide indispensable.

The collective leadership born in 1964 rests on a careful division: Brezhnev leads the Party, Kosygin the government and Podgorny the state. Each has his own clients and ambitions, and open rivalry would threaten everything. By balancing the troika, giving each man a sphere and none a reason to rebel, Brezhnev keeps the peace in the Politburo while quietly strengthening his own position.

The invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 has shown the world that Moscow will defend socialism in Eastern Europe by force. Now the leadership must decide how to use the strategic parity it has reached with the United States. Should it negotiate from strength and harvest the fruits of detente, or harden the Brezhnev Doctrine and confront the West wherever it challenges the socialist camp?

With nuclear parity achieved, Brezhnev believes the Soviet Union can finally negotiate with the West as an equal. Arms control, trade agreements and summits are not a sign of weakness but proof that the correlation of forces has shifted in favour of socialism. Detente from strength promises Western technology and grain while the Soviet Union keeps its military might intact.

In September 1971, Brezhnev invites West German Chancellor Willy Brandt to his dacha at Oreanda in the Crimea. Between swims in the Black Sea and long conversations, the two men confirm the spirit of the Moscow Treaty and of Bonn's new eastern policy. Courting West Germany opens a door to credit and technology and drives a wedge into the Western alliance.

In June 1973, Brezhnev travels to the United States for a second summit with Richard Nixon, a year after their breakthrough meeting in Moscow. On the table lies an Agreement on the Prevention of Nuclear War, committing both superpowers to consult rather than slide into confrontation. Whether Washington signs depends on its own calculations, but the visit itself is a triumph of Soviet prestige.

In August 1975, thirty-five states sign the Final Act of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe in Helsinki. For Brezhnev, it is the crowning achievement of his career: the post-war borders of Europe, including the division of Germany and the Soviet gains of 1945, are recognised as inviolable. The human rights clauses of the third basket seem a small price to pay, for now.

Prague in 1968 proved that the socialist commonwealth is a single body and that the loss of any part threatens the whole. The hawks around Suslov, Grechko and the General Staff argue that detente is a Western trap and that the Brezhnev Doctrine must guide Soviet policy. Choosing the doctrine means standing firm everywhere and trusting military power over Western goodwill.

The Warsaw Pact and Comecon bind Eastern Europe to Moscow, yet Romania goes its own way, Poland simmers and Hungary experiments with markets. An iron bloc would tighten the reins: joint command structures, deeper economic integration and Soviet advisers in every allied defence ministry. The allies would gain security and lose what little room for manoeuvre they still have.

For every American carrier a Soviet cruiser, for every new missile a Soviet reply. Under this principle, the Soviet Union matches each Western weapons programme step by step, determined never again to suffer the inferiority of the Cuban crisis years. The military-industrial complex welcomes the orders, even as the arms race tightens with every turn.

From Vietnam to Africa and the Middle East, national liberation movements look to Moscow for weapons, advisers and money. Soviet ideologists call it the internationalist duty of the first socialist state to support every people fighting imperialism. Embracing this duty spreads Soviet influence across the Third World, but it also deepens commitments in distant wars with uncertain outcomes.

In January 1977, presenting Tula with its title of Hero City, Brezhnev declares that the Soviet Union does not seek military superiority and wants only a defence sufficient to deter any attacker. The marshals grumble, but the speech is meant to reassure a new American administration and keep detente alive. Words, however, must be matched by deeds to be believed.

Growth is slowing, and the leadership can no longer fund everything at once. The consumer wants flats, cars and full shelves; the marshals want tanks and missiles; and the new oil fields of Western Siberia promise a flood of hard currency. As the five-year plans of the 1970s take shape, Brezhnev must decide where the Soviet Union places its bet for the coming decade.

The Ninth Five-Year Plan is the first to promise that consumer goods will grow faster than heavy industry. Refrigerators, televisions and the new Zhiguli cars from Togliatti are meant to prove that socialism can deliver a good life, not just steel and rockets. Putting the consumer first buys the contentment of the population, though it strains a planning system built for tanks and turbines.

The economist James Millar would later call it the 'little deal': the regime tolerates the black market, private plots, favours and petty theft, and in return the population tolerates the regime. Accepting this unspoken bargain keeps private life supplied and tempers discontent, while corruption seeps ever deeper into the foundations of the state.

Millions of Soviet families still live in communal apartments, sharing one kitchen between several households. The Party has promised every family a flat of its own, and new prefabricated districts are rising on the edge of every city, from Moscow to Novosibirsk. Pushing housing construction even harder would answer one of the people's deepest wishes and turn a promise into concrete.

The marshals and the defence ministries argue that the international situation leaves no room for indulgence. As long as the United States arms itself and China threatens the Far East, every rouble belongs first to the armed forces. Placing guns before butter guarantees the strength of the military-industrial complex, while the queues for meat and shoes grow longer.

The Military-Industrial Commission of the Council of Ministers coordinates the nine defence ministries that build everything from rifles to intercontinental missiles. Giving it greater authority and new factories would turn the defence sector into an even more privileged state within the state. Its output would rise, but so would its claim on the country's best engineers and resources.

Behind barbed wire across the western military districts and Eastern Europe stand vast tank parks, row upon row of T-55s and T-62s, with the new T-64 entering service. Soviet doctrine counts on overwhelming armoured mass to reach the Rhine within days. Expanding these parks and pushing the next generation of main battle tanks would cement Soviet superiority on land.

The discovery of Samotlor and the other giant fields of Western Siberia has turned the Soviet Union into an oil power. Exporting crude and gas for hard currency could pay for Western machinery and grain without painful reforms. Betting on oil is the easy road, but an economy that lives off its wells may lose the will to modernise itself.

Soviet agriculture cannot keep pace with demand, and a single bad harvest, as in 1972, forces Moscow to buy millions of tonnes of grain abroad. Oil money offers a way out: sell crude on the world market and buy wheat, fodder and meat in return. The collective farms gain breathing space and the cities stay fed, as long as oil prices remain high.

In 1970, Moscow and Bonn sign the first gas-for-pipes deal: German steel pipes in exchange for Soviet natural gas delivered over twenty years. Austria already receives Soviet gas, and Italy and France are interested in similar contracts. Long-term supply agreements with Western Europe would bring a steady flow of hard currency and bind the continent's industry to Soviet energy, whether NATO likes it or not.

Two men compete to be the guardian of Soviet order. Yuri Andropov's KGB watches dissidents, foreign spies and, increasingly, corrupt officials; Nikolai Shchelokov's Interior Ministry runs the militia and enjoys Brezhnev's personal friendship. Their rivalry is bitter and personal. The General Secretary must decide whose methods, and whose people, he will trust to keep the country in line.

Andropov argues that corruption and indiscipline are eating away at the state, and that only the KGB has the reach and the integrity to stop it. Backing the Committee for State Security gives it a free hand to investigate economic crimes, even among the protected clients of regional party bosses. Order will improve, though many in the nomenklatura will learn to fear the knock at the door.

Nikolai Shchelokov has modernised the militia, raised its pay and polished its image with popular television detective series. He is also an old friend of Brezhnev from Moldavia and Dnepropetrovsk. Backing the Interior Ministry means a loyal, comfortable police force that keeps the streets calm, and one that looks the other way when the right people are involved.

Under Brezhnev's stability of cadres, the first secretaries of the union republics enjoy unprecedented security: Sharaf Rashidov in Uzbekistan, Dinmukhamed Kunaev in Kazakhstan, Heydar Aliyev in Azerbaijan. In exchange for loyalty and good plan figures, Moscow asks few questions about how they run their domains. Trusting the republican cadres keeps the union quiet, but lets local patronage networks flourish.

In 1978, a slim volume of war memoirs appears under Brezhnev's name, celebrating the small bridgehead of Malaya Zemlya near Novorossiysk as if it had decided the war. Printed in millions of copies, it is studied in schools and honoured with the Lenin Prize for Literature. Together with the ever-growing collection of medals on his chest, it marks a personality cult that the nation increasingly mocks in private.

In May 1976, Brezhnev is made a Marshal of the Soviet Union, a rank far above the one he held in the war, which he ended as a major general and political officer. The new title flatters the army and ties the General Secretary to its glory. The generals salute, even if some privately resent seeing their highest honour bestowed upon a former political commissar.

In June 1977, Nikolai Podgorny is abruptly removed from the Politburo and from his post as head of state, and Brezhnev takes the chairmanship of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet himself. For the first time, one man holds both the leadership of the Party and the formal presidency of the Soviet state. The troika is over; Brezhnev now stands alone at the summit.

Behind the medals and the ovations, Brezhnev's health is failing. Strokes, a dependence on sleeping pills and increasingly slurred speech turn every public appearance into an ordeal watched closely by foreign diplomats and the Politburo alike. The leadership must decide how to handle the decline: hide it and carry on, or prepare for an orderly departure.

Yevgeny Chazov and the Fourth Main Directorate of the Ministry of Health, the Kremlin's own medical service, are tasked with keeping the General Secretary on his feet. With the best physicians, private clinics and constant supervision, they can sustain Brezhnev for years, historically until 1982. The leader stays in office, but the country is governed ever more by his aides.

More than once, a tired and ailing Brezhnev asks his comrades to let him retire. The Politburo has always refused, fearing a destabilising struggle for the succession. What if this time they agreed? A dignified retirement, with full honours and a chosen successor, would give the Soviet Union something it has never had: a peaceful, planned transfer of power at the very top.

Whoever controls the succession controls the future of the Soviet Union. Andropov has the KGB, Chernenko the apparatus, Romanov the Leningrad organisation, and the young Gorbachev the favour of the reformers. By naming an heir while he still can, Brezhnev may spare the country a struggle in the Politburo, or ignite one.

Yuri Andropov is the most capable and the most feared man in the Politburo. Naming him heir promises a successor who will root out corruption and restore discipline, provided the Party is ready for a Chekist at its head. Historically, Andropov succeeded Brezhnev in 1982, after first moving from the KGB back into the Central Committee Secretariat.

Konstantin Chernenko is Brezhnev's shadow, his most loyal aide and the keeper of his papers. Naming him heir guarantees that nothing will change: the cadres keep their posts, the policies continue and the old guard sleeps soundly. What if Chernenko came to power directly, without Andropov's interlude, and continuity became the Soviet Union's only programme?

Grigory Romanov, the strict and efficient master of Leningrad, would bring a younger, harder face to the Kremlin: orthodox in ideology, close to the defence industry and impatient with laxity. Naming him heir skips a generation of tired old men and places the Party in the hands of a technocrat of order. What if the man from Smolny, not Gorbachev, became the Soviet Union's future?

In the late 1970s, Mikhail Gorbachev has only just arrived in Moscow as Central Committee Secretary for agriculture. Naming him heir would hand power to a man not yet fifty, a generation younger than the rest of the Politburo. What if the reformer came to power years before 1985, while the economy and the empire still had reserves to spare?

The Party proclaims that the Soviet Union has entered the stage of developed socialism, a mature society that no longer needs revolutionary leaps, only steady improvement. With the borders recognised, the shelves fuller and the army mighty, the Brezhnev era appears to have reached its summit. Whether this is a plateau or the beginning of stagnation, only time will tell.

For the first time since Khrushchev, the Party and the government are united in one hand, and this time it belongs to a manager rather than an ideologue. Alexei Kosygin brings with him the ministries, the planners and the conviction that the economy, not doctrine, decides the fate of socialism. The apparatus watches warily as the Premier sets out to run the Party like a well-managed enterprise.

Nikolai Baibakov, an oilman who has headed the State Planning Committee since 1965, knows the Soviet economy better than almost anyone. Under Kosygin, Gosplan could become the engine of reform rather than its brake, setting more realistic targets and listening to the ministries. Giving Baibakov a free hand strengthens the planners and the industrial ministries that depend on them.

Jermen Gvishiani, Kosygin's son-in-law and deputy head of the State Committee for Science and Technology, champions systems analysis and modern management. Through him, Soviet scientists build ties with Western research institutes and help found the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis near Vienna. Empowering these systems men brings computers, cybernetics and fresh thinking into the heart of planning.

Kosygin has long been frustrated by Party secretaries who meddle in factory management without understanding production. Placing the government before the Party means letting ministries and enterprise directors make economic decisions while the apparatus confines itself to ideology and cadres.
