Efficiency would gain, but the regional party bosses will not easily surrender their power.

Everyone around Kosygin agrees that the economy needs reform; no one agrees on which. Some look to Hungary's New Economic Mechanism and market prices, others to computers and cybernetic planning that could make the plan truly scientific, still others to a careful revival of the 1965 reform within the existing system. The Premier must choose a path and stake his authority on it.

Inspired by Budapest's New Economic Mechanism, Kosygin's bolder advisers propose that prices, profits and demand rather than plan targets should guide Soviet enterprises. Factories would trade among themselves, compete for customers and keep part of their earnings. Market socialism promises dynamism and better goods, while orthodox Marxists warn that it is the first step back to capitalism.

Soviet prices for bread, meat and rent have barely changed in years, held down by subsidies that cost the budget billions. Letting prices move closer to real costs would ease the endless shortages and dry up the black market, but every official remembers what happened in Novocherkassk in 1962 when meat prices rose. Flexible prices are the hardest reform of all to sell.

A new law on the socialist enterprise would give directors genuine independence: the right to draw up their own production plans, choose suppliers, hire and fire, and reinvest their profits. Ministries would become advisers rather than commanders. Productivity could rise sharply, but the trade unions fear that workers will pay for efficiency with their jobs and their bonuses.

Fiat is already building the giant car plant at Togliatti, and Western companies are eager for more Soviet contracts. Kosygin's reformers propose going further: joint ventures with Western firms on Soviet soil, financed by Western credit and run with Western know-how. Capital and technology would flow in, along with debt and a dependence on the capitalist world that hardliners find intolerable.

Soviet cyberneticists argue that the plan fails not because it is a plan, but because no human bureaucracy can process the millions of decisions an economy requires. Computers can. A cybernetic communism would link factories, ministries and Gosplan in a single information system that balances production in real time. The vision is breathtaking; the cost in money and machines is enormous.

Academician Viktor Glushkov of the Kiev Institute of Cybernetics has designed OGAS, the All-State Automated System for the collection and processing of information. A nationwide network of computing centres would connect thousands of enterprises with Moscow and give planners real data instead of padded reports. The bureaucracy blocked it in 1970; under Kosygin, it could finally be built.

Viktor Glushkov's most radical idea goes beyond planning: abolish cash altogether and settle every wage and purchase electronically through the OGAS network. With every rouble traceable, the black market, embezzlement and the second economy would have nowhere to hide. Officials who live off undeclared income are, unsurprisingly, among the plan's fiercest opponents.

At the Central Economic Mathematical Institute in Moscow, economists under Nikolai Fedorenko are building optimal planning models on the foundations of Leonid Kantorovich's linear programming. Kantorovich, who will become the only Soviet Nobel laureate in economics, has shown that mathematics can allocate resources far better than guesswork. Funding these institutes would put science at the heart of Soviet planning.

Kosygin's own instincts are cautious. Rather than markets or computers, he wants to rescue the reform of 1965, with its sales targets, profit indicators and enterprise incentive funds, from the ministries that have hollowed it out. Reform within the plan keeps central planning intact while giving factories just enough freedom to work better.

In 1962, the Kharkov economist Yevsei Liberman published an article in Pravda titled 'Plan, Profit, Bonus', arguing that enterprises should be judged by their profitability and that workers should share in it. His ideas inspired the 1965 reform before the apparatus watered them down. Reviving them would reward efficient factories and give workers a reason to care about quality.

In 1973, the Central Committee and the Council of Ministers order the merger of enterprises into large production associations, combining factories, design bureaus and research institutes under a single management. Done properly, these associations could cut out layers of ministerial bureaucracy and speed the path from invention to production. Done badly, they simply create bigger monopolies.

Reform threatens the power of the regional party secretaries, the branch ministries and the thousands of officials who live by allocating scarce resources. Once again, as after 1965, the apparatus begins to sabotage the changes through delays, reinterpretations and quiet obstruction. Kosygin must now decide whether to win the Party over with concessions or to break its resistance.

Kosygin knows that no reform survives in the Soviet Union without the Party's blessing. By offering the nomenklatura positions in the new structures, consulting the regional secretaries and wrapping the changes in Leninist language, he can turn opponents into reluctant partners. The reform will move more slowly, but it will no longer be fought at every step.

Kosygin's patience is exhausted. If the apparatus will not reform, it must be removed: obstructive ministers dismissed, regional secretaries retired and the stability of cadres brought to an end. Breaking the apparatus would clear the way for real change, but it means open war with the most powerful class in the country and the risk of a backlash that could cost the Premier everything.

Defence absorbs a far larger share of Soviet output than the official budget admits, starving the civilian economy of steel, engineers and investment. Kosygin argues that strategic parity has been achieved and that every additional tank is a refrigerator or a flat the people will never see. Curbing military spending would free resources, but it will turn the marshals and the defence industry against him.

The defence plants hold the best machine tools and engineers in the Soviet Union. Converting part of their capacity to civilian production could bring quality televisions, washing machines and tractors to the market. Defence directors already make some consumer goods as a sideline; Kosygin would make it a central task, much to the displeasure of the Military-Industrial Commission.

Kosygin believes the future of the Soviet Union lies in commerce with the world, not confrontation. Trade agreements with France, Italy and West Germany, credits from Western banks and an end to costly adventures could do more for the image of socialism than any military parade. Trade, not tanks, would ease tensions and bring in the technology the Soviet economy badly needs.

In June 1967, Kosygin and President Lyndon Johnson met for three days at a small college in Glassboro, New Jersey. The summit produced no treaty, but it showed that the leaders of the two superpowers could talk frankly with each other. A new summit with the Premier could revive that spirit, ease tensions and open the way to trade, if Washington is willing to answer.

In January 1966, Kosygin brought India's Lal Bahadur Shastri and Pakistan's Ayub Khan together in Tashkent and brokered an end to their war. It was a rare triumph for Soviet diplomacy in the role of peacemaker. Renewing this role would raise Moscow's standing in South Asia and win friends in both New Delhi and Islamabad, though balancing the two rivals is never easy.

In March 1979, as the communist regime in Kabul begs for Soviet troops to crush the uprising in Herat, Kosygin answers bluntly that the Soviet Union cannot replace the Afghan people in their own struggle. Holding to this line would keep the Soviet Army out of a war it cannot win, at the cost of disappointing an ally and risking its collapse.

Kosygin's heart is failing. A boating accident in 1976 and repeated heart attacks have weakened him, and historically he died in December 1980, only weeks after resigning. If his reforms are to outlive him, the Premier must choose who will carry them forward: a young reformer from the provinces or the disciplined chairman of the KGB.

Kosygin sees in the younger provincial secretaries, above all Mikhail Gorbachev of Stavropol, the men who could finish what he started. Naming Gorbachev heir would hand the reform course to a generation that believes the system can be renewed from within. What if the Premier's legacy passed directly to the future architect of perestroika?

Kosygin and Andropov share a distaste for corruption and a belief that the economy must work better. Naming the KGB chairman heir would secure discipline and order for the reform course, though Andropov's vision is one of tighter control rather than greater freedom. What if the Premier's experiment passed into the hands of the Chekist?

If the Party cannot be reformed, perhaps it can be bypassed. In this most radical outcome, the planners and engineers of Gosplan take over the state, with Nikolai Baibakov at their head, and govern by data and expertise rather than ideology. The leading role of the Communist Party would end, replaced by a technocracy that answers to efficiency alone.

After years of struggle against the apparatus, the Kosygin reforms finally bear fruit: factories that meet demand, shops with goods on the shelves and growth that no longer depends on ever more labour and raw materials. For the first time since the 1950s, Soviet socialism seems able to compete with the West on its own terms.

For years, Nikolai Podgorny's office as head of state has been largely ceremonial: signing decrees, awarding orders and receiving foreign ambassadors. As General Secretary, he would turn the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet into a real centre of power, governing through the institutions of the state rather than through the Party apparatus. The state, not the Party, would become the face of Soviet power.

The Supreme Soviet of the USSR meets only a few days each year to approve the plan and the budget unanimously. Podgorny would give it real work: standing commissions that scrutinise ministries, deputies who question officials and debates that actually change laws. A living parliament would revive Lenin's call for all power to the soviets, though the Party secretaries will see it as a threat to their monopoly.

Podgorny built his career in Ukraine, from the sugar industry and the Kharkov regional committee to the leadership of the Ukrainian Communist Party in Kiev. His network of Ukrainian cadres, engineers and managers remains loyal. Drawing on the Kharkov connection would strengthen the voice of the second-largest republic in Moscow and win support among those who want the union to be a true partnership of nations.

Podgorny has no strong base in the Party Secretariat, but the branch ministries, chafing under the interference of Party secretaries, are natural allies. By promising the ministers greater autonomy and a voice in the Presidium, he can build a coalition of the state against the apparatus. The industrial ministries would gain power, and the economy a clearer chain of command.

Podgorny must decide what kind of state he wants to build. One path leads to a genuine federation in which the union republics gain real rights and a voice in every decision that concerns them. The other leads to a strong Presidium, a central state presidency that governs the union from Moscow above both the Party and the republics. Either way, the Soviet state will never look the same.

The Soviet constitution already calls the union a voluntary federation of sovereign republics; Podgorny would make the words mean something. Republican governments would gain control over their own economies, languages and cultures, and the republics would have to approve any union decision that affects them. A federal union could win the loyalty of the non-Russian nations, or give them the tools to leave.

Every union republic already has its own Council of Ministers, yet in practice these governments wait on orders from the all-Union ministries in Moscow. Podgorny, who ran Ukraine before coming to the Kremlin, knows how little room the republics truly have. Giving their governments real authority over local industry and services would bind the republics more firmly to the Union, even if it adds another layer of officials to pay.

Under khozraschet, Soviet enterprises are supposed to balance their own books, but the republics themselves still live on allocations handed down by Gosplan. Letting each republic keep part of what it earns and answer for its own costs would reward the efficient and expose the wasteful. Kiev, Minsk and Tbilisi would gain a stake in their own prosperity, and the Union a reason to trust them.

The Supreme Soviet has two chambers, and the Soviet of Nationalities was meant to give every republic and autonomous region an equal voice. For decades it has done little more than applaud. As Chairman of the Presidium, Podgorny can breathe life into it, letting deputies from Tashkent to Tallinn debate the questions that touch their peoples and turning a ceremonial body into a genuine forum of the Union.

Under the Constitution the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet is the collective head of the Soviet state, yet real power has always rested with the Party. Podgorny intends to change that balance. A Presidium that drafts decrees, oversees ministries and speaks for the state would govern more efficiently, but the Party apparatus and the republican leaders will not surrender their prerogatives quietly.

The branch ministries have grown into fiefdoms that answer to Central Committee secretaries and defend their own plans at any cost. If ministers were made accountable to the Presidium and the Council of Ministers rather than to Party patrons, orders could flow through a single chain of command. The industrial ministries would welcome clearer authority, and the planners hope for fewer contradictory instructions.

Between sessions of the Supreme Soviet, the Presidium governs through decrees, the ukazy that carry Podgorny's signature. Used boldly, this instrument can settle questions the Politburo prefers to postpone, from pensions to the rights of the republics. Every decree published in Izvestia reminds the country that the Soviet state has a head of its own, and that his word is law.

Questions of internal security are settled in closed meetings between the KGB chairman and the General Secretary. A State Security Council attached to the Presidium would bring defence, internal affairs and state security together under the head of state. The Lubyanka gains a seat at the highest table of government, while the state gains a firmer grip on the guardians of its ideological order.

As formal head of state, Podgorny receives ambassadors, signs treaties and travels where the General Secretary cannot. A grand tour of Africa and the Middle East, like the journey that historically took him to Tanzania, Zambia, Mozambique and Somalia in 1977, would give Moscow a dignified and personal face in Cairo, Damascus, Addis Ababa and Luanda.

Treaties of friendship are the currency of Soviet influence in the Third World, and the head of state is the natural man to sign them. Historically, it was Podgorny who flew to Cairo in May 1971 to sign the first such pact with an Arab state. Making him the Union's treaty signer would let Moscow bind Egypt, Iraq and India more quickly and present the socialist community as a reliable partner.

The black earth of Ukraine still feeds much of the Union, but its kolkhozes suffer from poor machinery, wasted harvests and low procurement prices. Podgorny, once First Secretary in Kiev, understands the republic's countryside better than anyone in the Politburo. Investment in fertiliser, irrigation and storage could restore Ukraine's role as the breadbasket of the Union and win the loyalty of its villages.

The mines of the Donets Basin powered the first Five-Year Plans and remain the heart of Ukrainian heavy industry. Yet the shafts are deep, the seams are thinning and the miners are growing restless. New power stations and modernised pits would keep the furnaces of the south burning, and a government that looks after the miners can count on the support of the trade unions.

Podgorny's reforms have raised a question the Party has long avoided: what kind of state should the Soviet Union ultimately be? One path leads to a looser union in which the republics stand as sovereign partners. The other leads to a strong Soviet presidency that rules above the Party apparatus. The choice will define the Union for a generation.

What if the Union were refounded as a voluntary association of sovereign republics, bound by treaty rather than by the will of the Central Committee? Pyotr Shelest, Kiev's outspoken defender of Ukrainian interests, would lead the new union as its first head. The republics would welcome the change, yet abandoning the leading role of the Communist Party will shake the foundations of the old order.

Foreign newspapers already call Podgorny the Soviet President, though no such office exists. Turning the chairmanship of the Presidium into a true presidency, with its own staff and powers, would give the state a head who does not depend on the goodwill of the Party apparatus. The General Secretary would remain influential, but no longer the only master in the Kremlin.

The state has finally stepped out of the shadow of the Party. Ministries answer to the government, the republics have their voice in the Supreme Soviet, and the head of state speaks with real authority at home and abroad. Podgorny's vision of a Soviet Union governed by its own institutions has become reality, and the system looks steadier than it has in decades.

For decades Mikhail Suslov has guarded the purity of the Party line from the shadows, shaping every major speech, textbook and Pravda editorial. Now the Grey Cardinal stands at the head of the Party itself. Ascetic, cautious and unyielding, he intends to defend Marxism-Leninism against revisionism at home and abroad, even if innovation and scientific freedom must pay the price.

Ideological work is scattered among the propaganda, culture and science departments of the Central Committee, each guarding its own turf. Suslov proposes a single commission to coordinate them all, from university lecture halls to factory wall newspapers. With one hand on every lever of propaganda, the Party can renew the faith of its members and remind the nomenklatura where their loyalty belongs.

Boris Ponomarev has run the International Department of the Central Committee since 1955, maintaining Moscow's ties with communist parties and liberation movements across the globe. Under Suslov's protection, the department can expand its funding, its party schools and its network of contacts in Havana, Hanoi and Ulan Bator. The socialist community needs a guiding centre, and Ponomarev is eager to provide it.

Sergei Trapeznikov, head of the Central Committee's Department of Science and Educational Institutions, is an old companion of Brezhnev and an open admirer of Stalin. Under his supervision, academic appointments and research topics are screened for ideological reliability. Scholars at the Academy of Sciences grumble about lost freedom, but the neo-Stalinist wing of the Party sees in him a champion of discipline in the institutes.

Every communist knows that the Party line must be followed, but where exactly does it run? Suslov must decide whether to concentrate on guarding the ideological purity of Soviet society at home, or to carry the struggle against imperialism and revisionism abroad. Both paths lead back to Marxism-Leninism, yet they demand very different resources and face very different enemies.

Samizdat manuscripts pass from hand to hand, foreign radio stations are heard in Moscow kitchens, and dissidents demand that the state respect its own Constitution. Suslov's answer is uncompromising: the dissident circles must be broken up, their leaders tried or exiled, and the intelligentsia reminded of its duty. The Party gains calm and order, though the price is paid in creativity and goodwill abroad.

Since 1956, Soviet history books have been torn between Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin and the uneasy silence that followed his fall. The Pravda article marking Stalin's ninetieth birthday in 1969 showed how far the pendulum has already swung. Suslov's historians can go further, portraying the late leader as the organiser of victory, a creeping rehabilitation that delights the conservatives and alarms the reformers.

Glavlit, the Main Administration for Safeguarding State Secrets in the Press, decides what Soviet citizens may read. A tighter regime of censorship would strip questionable passages from literary journals, keep foreign publications out of libraries and silence the liberal editors of Novy Mir for good. Hostile voices will find it harder to reach Soviet readers, although scientists will also lose access to useful works from the West.

Detente has brought Western tourists, journalists, jeans and records into the Soviet Union, and with them dangerous ideas. Suslov insists that peaceful coexistence between states does not mean coexistence between ideologies. Fewer exit visas, fewer exchanges and closer supervision of foreigners would seal Soviet society against bourgeois influence, even if foreign trading partners come to view the Union with growing suspicion.

From Indochina to the Horn of Africa, the correlation of forces in the world seems to be shifting towards socialism. Suslov argues that the Soviet Union must not merely observe this historic process but actively lead it, sending arms, money and advisers wherever peoples rise against imperialism. Such a course is expensive and will alarm Washington, but history, he insists, is on Moscow's side.

The crumbling Portuguese empire, unrest in Ethiopia and the struggle in South Yemen have opened new fronts in the battle against imperialism. The MPLA in Angola and FRELIMO in Mozambique look to Moscow for weapons and training. By supporting these movements systematically, the Soviet Union can win loyal allies in Africa and Arabia before Washington or Beijing does.

The Italian, French and Spanish communists under Enrico Berlinguer, Georges Marchais and Santiago Carrillo are drifting towards a democratic road to socialism, independent of Moscow and openly critical of its methods. To Suslov this Eurocommunism is nothing but revisionism in new clothes. Condemning it will cost friendship in Rome and Paris, but it will remind every loyal party that the movement has only one centre.

In June 1969 delegations from seventy-five parties gathered in Moscow for the International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties. Suslov wants a new conference on the same model, with the CPSU firmly at its centre and a joint declaration against imperialism and revisionism. Even if some parties stay away, the image of a united movement assembled in the Kremlin is worth the effort.

Kosygin's reforms tried to motivate workers with bonuses and enterprise profits, an approach Suslov considers dangerously close to capitalism. He prefers the methods of socialist emulation: boards of honour, red challenge banners, medals and the title of Hero of Socialist Labour. Consciousness rather than money should drive the Soviet worker, though planners fear that productivity will suffer without material rewards.

Collective farm markets, cooperative workshops and private plots have grown into a grey economy where prices follow supply and demand. To Suslov, every kopeck earned outside the plan is a step towards the restoration of capitalism. Closing down the cooperative sector will please the Party orthodox and restore ideological clarity, even if shoppers find the shelves emptier than before.

Party theorists already speak of the Soviet people as a new historical community that transcends nationality. Suslov wants to give substance to this formula through sblizhenie, the drawing together of the nations of the Union: more Russian-language teaching, mixed workforces on the great construction sites and a shared Soviet culture. Moscow hopes that national grievances will fade as a common identity takes root.

Young Soviet citizens learn their Marxism-Leninism from dry textbooks and recite it without conviction. Suslov orders a thorough overhaul of ideological education, from the Young Pioneers to university courses in scientific communism. New curricula, better-trained teachers and compulsory study circles cost money, but a generation raised in the faith of the Party will not stray towards bourgeois temptations.

Despite decades of atheist propaganda, churches are filling again and some intellectuals look to Orthodoxy for answers the Party cannot give. Suslov intends to renew the campaign of scientific atheism, tighten the grip of the Council for Religious Affairs and close parishes that grow too popular. Believers and monarchist dreamers are pushed back to the margins, though the faithful will not forget.

Since the border clashes on the Ussuri in 1969, Moscow and Beijing have exchanged insults in print as fiercely as they once exchanged fire. Mao's China calls the Soviet Union social-imperialist, while Suslov denounces Maoism as a petty-bourgeois deviation. Renewing the polemic in Pravda and across the world movement will rally loyal parties around Moscow, but it pushes any reconciliation with China further away.

Mikhail Suslov was born in 1902, and his health grows weaker every year. The orthodox wing of the Party must decide who will guard the Marxist-Leninist line once the Grey Cardinal is gone. Konstantin Chernenko offers continuity and a steady hand on the apparatus, while Grigory Romanov of Leningrad promises a younger and harder line.

Konstantin Chernenko has spent his career in the Party apparatus, running the General Department of the Central Committee and the flow of paper that keeps the Politburo working. He is no ideologue, but he is reliable, careful and loyal to collective leadership. Naming him heir assures the cadres that nothing will change abruptly when the Grey Cardinal departs.

Grigory Romanov rules Leningrad with a firm hand, keeping its factories, shipyards and restless intellectuals in strict order. Younger than the old guard and admired by the defence industry, he represents a harder and more disciplined variant of orthodoxy. Choosing him as heir signals that the Party's conservatives intend to hold power for another generation.

What if the guardians of orthodoxy decided that collective leadership had grown too soft? The Neo-Stalinist Platform, led by Sergei Trapeznikov, steps forward to claim Suslov's inheritance and govern in the spirit of the old Vozhd. The cult of the Generalissimo is restored, discipline replaces debate, and the CPSU as it existed under Brezhnev becomes a memory.

Suslov's work is complete. The Party line is clear, the censors are vigilant and the schools teach Marxism-Leninism without deviation. The Soviet Union stands as a fortress of orthodox socialism, steady and predictable, though critics whisper that it has also become rigid and slow to adapt to a changing world.

Alexander Shelepin, known as Iron Shurik, has led the Komsomol, the KGB and the Committee of Party-State Control. Brezhnev pushed him aside into the trade unions, but now the former Chekist stands at the head of the Party. He promises to restore order, discipline and honesty to a system grown complacent, and the comfortable nomenklatura has every reason to fear him.

Shelepin's power has always rested on a network of former Komsomol leaders: Nikolai Yegorychev of the Moscow party organisation, Nikolai Mesyatsev of state television and Vadim Tikunov of the police ministry. Brezhnev has scattered them to embassies and minor posts. Recalling the Komsomoltsy to Moscow gives the new General Secretary loyal men in key positions, but the established cadres see a rival clan taking their places.

Vladimir Semichastny succeeded Shelepin as chairman of the KGB in 1961 and lost the post in 1967 after Stalin's daughter defected to the West. Since then he has been sitting in Kiev as a deputy premier of Ukraine. Bringing him back to Moscow would place a trusted friend over the security organs and sharpen their fight against foreign subversion.

Since 1967 Shelepin has chaired the All-Union Central Council of Trade Unions, a post meant to be a political dead end. Instead he has used it to build a following among the millions of workers who depend on the unions for holidays, housing and sanatoriums. As General Secretary he can turn that following into a pillar of his rule.

The Soviet worker is guaranteed a job, but too often he arrives late, leaves early and drinks on shift. Shelepin must decide how to raise productivity: through strict discipline enforced from above, or by giving workers and their unions a greater share in running their factories and their lives. Either way, the relationship between the state and its working class will change.

Absenteeism, idleness and theft from the workplace cost the economy dearly every year. Shelepin intends to tighten labour legislation, tie bonuses to attendance and punish shirkers with transfers and fines. Factory directors welcome the firmer hand, but the trade unions he once led will not easily forgive their former chairman for turning against the workers' privileges.

Militia patrols and volunteer druzhinniki descend on shops, cinemas, barbershops and bathhouses during working hours, demanding to know why able-bodied citizens are not at their posts. The raids are crude and unpopular, but they send a clear message that the working day belongs to the state. Productivity rises, though so does the bill for policing the streets.

Vodka is the curse of the Soviet workplace, responsible for accidents, absenteeism and early deaths, yet it is also one of the state's most reliable sources of revenue. Shelepin is prepared to raise prices, limit sales hours and shut down the taverns near factories. Sober workers will produce more, but the budget will feel the loss and many citizens will resent the new restrictions.

Shelepin's years at the head of the trade unions have taught him that workers want respect as well as wages. He proposes a socialism that places the working class at the centre: more say for labour collectives, a greater share of resources for social needs and an end to the arrogance of managers. The unions rally behind him, and talk of free workers' councils begins to spread.

Factory trade union committees already manage holiday vouchers, kindergartens and housing queues, but they have little influence over production. Shelepin wants union councils at every level to take a real part in decisions on working conditions, safety and the distribution of social funds. Workers feel more secure and more valued, though the expanded welfare system will strain the budget.

Lenin dreamed of workers' control over production, and Shelepin himself led the Committee of Party-State Control under Khrushchev. Reviving that spirit, commissions elected by labour collectives would inspect warehouses, audit accounts and expose managers who steal or falsify their reports. Corruption retreats, but the branch ministries resent ordinary workers poking into their affairs.

Hooliganism, petty crime and public drunkenness have grown in Soviet cities, and citizens complain that the militia does too little. Shelepin promises firm order: more patrols, more volunteer squads and swift punishment for offenders. A country that sees a policeman on every corner feels safer, even if the price of order is paid in watchfulness and fear.

Under Brezhnev's policy of stability of cadres, regional bosses have grown rich on bribes, blat and falsified plan reports. Shelepin intends to unleash the procurators and control commissions against them, from district committees to republican ministries. Honest citizens applaud, but the nomenklatura recognises the threat to its comfortable existence and closes ranks.

Brezhnev's men still occupy the Central Committee, the ministries and the republican party leaderships: the Dnepropetrovsk clan, the Moldavian circle and their many clients. Shelepin is ready to break them, dismissing the corrupt and retiring the old. Ending the stability of cadres will shake the apparatus to its core, but it will leave the General Secretary master of the Party.

The Komsomol has always sent its young volunteers to the great building sites of the Union, from the Virgin Lands to the Siberian hydroelectric dams. Shelepin, who once led the youth league, wants to expand these brigades into a permanent army of young enthusiasts. New towns and factories rise faster, and thousands of young men gain discipline before they enter the armed forces.

Projects like the Baikal-Amur Mainline, planned as a great Komsomol shock construction across the taiga, show what young volunteers can achieve. Shelepin wants the Komsomol to take on a far larger share of such infrastructure work, from roads and railways to power lines. The work is hard and the conditions harsh, but the country gains infrastructure at a fraction of the usual cost.

Shelepin is a hardliner at home, but where should he turn abroad? Some believe he could heal the rift with Beijing, where he is remembered as a man with whom one can talk. Others expect him to confront the West directly, abandoning the compromises of detente. The General Secretary must choose which front matters most to the Union.

In the Chinese capital, Shelepin is regarded as a disciplined revolutionary rather than a revisionist bureaucrat. He proposes direct talks between the two camps of the pure line, setting aside years of polemics and border clashes. Whether Mao's China accepts the offer is uncertain, but even an opening would transform the balance of power in Asia.

Detente, in Shelepin's eyes, has only allowed the imperialists to buy time and spread their influence into the socialist camp. He prefers a harder course: no concessions on human rights, no compromises over Berlin and a firm answer to every American provocation. The armed forces and the patriotic public welcome the new resolve, although the risk of confrontation grows.

Shelepin has reshaped the Party, the trade unions and the security organs, but one question remains: what form should his power take? He could rule openly as a leader standing above the Party, or he could bind his order to the collective leadership and prepare a successor who will carry it forward after him.

What if Shelepin decided that collective leadership was itself the problem? With the Komsomol Vanguard as the new ruling force, Iron Shurik would govern as a Vozhd, a leader whose authority rests on discipline, youth and loyalty rather than on the Central Committee. The old CPSU fades into the background, and the Soviet Union enters an era of personal rule.

Instead of ruling alone, Shelepin chooses to embed his reforms in the collective leadership of the Politburo. Discipline becomes the shared creed of the leadership, and Yuri Andropov, the most disciplined of them all, is named the man to carry the work forward. The Party regains its confidence, and the order Shelepin built is meant to outlast him.

Shelepin's campaigns have transformed Soviet life. Factories run on schedule, officials fear the inspectors and the streets are quieter than they have been in years. The Iron Order brings stability and productivity to a Union that had grown lax, although scientists and artists complain that little room is left for creativity and free thought.

For years Yuri Andropov has led the KGB, gathering information on every corner of Soviet society and on all of its failures. Now the former chairman of state security stands at the head of the Party. Austere, intelligent and well informed, he knows that the system is ailing and intends to cure it with discipline, honesty and carefully measured reform.

Andropov trusts the men he worked with at the Lubyanka. Viktor Chebrikov takes over the KGB, Vladimir Kryuchkov runs foreign intelligence, and Heydar Aliyev, a KGB general who rose to lead Azerbaijan, is brought to Moscow. The security services gain unprecedented influence over the state, and their intelligence networks reach deeper into every institution of the Union.

Andropov surrounds himself with younger, energetic men: Mikhail Gorbachev, the party chief from Stavropol, Nikolai Ryzhkov, the industrial manager from Uralmash, and Yegor Ligachev, the incorruptible first secretary of Tomsk. They are loyal communists, but they share the conviction that the economy needs fundamental change. Their rise brings fresh ideas to the leadership and tilts the Politburo towards reform.

As Soviet ambassador in Budapest in 1956, Andropov watched a socialist state collapse within days and helped crush the uprising that followed. He learned that discontent must be addressed before it explodes, but he also saw how Janos Kadar later rebuilt Hungary with his goulash communism. The Hungarian experience offers lessons in both firmness and flexibility.

Andropov's first great initiative is a campaign against idleness, drunkenness and absenteeism. Militia patrols raid cinemas, shops and bathhouses during working hours, demanding papers from anyone who should be at work. Citizens grumble, but productivity rises, and the KGB gains new authority to investigate even the most powerful officials in the republics.

Andropov knows the Soviet system is in trouble, but his diagnosis allows two cures. He can combine discipline with cautious economic reform, giving managers more independence and the young reformers more influence. Or he can build a Chekist state in which security, control and ideological vigilance hold the Union together. The choice will shape the Soviet future for years to come.

Discipline alone cannot save the Soviet economy. Andropov openly admits that the Party does not truly know the society it governs, and he commissions studies on how to give enterprises more independence and workers more responsibility. Order and reform must go hand in hand, and the reformers of the Politburo find themselves listened to at last.

Andropov launches a bold test of economic reform. Enterprises in five industrial ministries, two all-Union and three republican, are allowed to plan more of their own output, keep part of their profits and reward workers for fulfilled delivery contracts. If the large-scale experiment succeeds, its methods could be extended across the entire Soviet economy.

The Central Committee has never had a department responsible for the economy as a whole, only branch departments that defend their own industries. Andropov creates one and places Nikolai Ryzhkov, former director of the Uralmash works, at its head. With a single team studying the economy, the Party can finally plan reforms rather than simply issue targets.

KGB reports leave no doubt: the Soviet Union is falling behind the West in computers and microelectronics, and the gap grows wider every year. Copying Western designs and smuggling components through third countries can only go so far. Andropov orders a crash programme to build a native computing industry before the technological lag becomes a strategic one.

Andropov concludes that only the security organs remain uncorrupted enough to hold the Union together. The KGB receives wider powers over the economy, the Party and the media, and its officers are placed in key positions across the state. Order is restored and enemies are watched closely, but scientists and intellectuals sense the air growing heavier.

Andrei Sakharov, father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb, has become the most prominent voice of the human rights movement. Rather than put him on trial, the KGB proposes to exile him to Gorky, a city closed to foreigners, where he can be watched and silenced. The dissident movement loses its figurehead, though Washington and the Western press will protest loudly.

Speculators, black-market traders and officials who live far beyond their salaries have built a shadow economy of their own. Andropov sets the KGB on their trail, from the trade networks of Moscow to the fish shops of the Okean affair. Unearned incomes are confiscated, and the nomenklatura learns that its privileges no longer guarantee protection.

Every workplace, apartment block and research institute already has its watchers, but Andropov wants a denser network still. New informants are recruited among students, engineers and pensioners, and reports flow to the regional KGB directorates in unprecedented numbers. Foreign intelligence services find it harder to operate, but citizens learn to guard their words more carefully than ever.

For years the Uzbek SSR has reported cotton harvests that never existed, and Moscow has paid enormous sums for phantom fibre. Under Sharaf Rashidov, the republic's leaders built a vast system of bribery and falsified reports. Andropov sends investigators to Tashkent to expose the pripiski, punish the guilty and remind every republic that the centre is watching.

Nikolai Shchelokov, Brezhnev's old friend and Minister of Internal Affairs since the late 1960s, has turned the militia into his personal domain, riddled with corruption and luxury. Andropov removes him and sends KGB officers to purge the ministry from top to bottom. The militia becomes cleaner and cheaper to run, while Brezhnev's old circle loses one of its most powerful members.

Andropov knows how easily a limited intervention becomes an endless war. Wherever Soviet soldiers are bogged down, as they could be in the mountains of Afghanistan, he prefers a dignified way out through negotiations rather than further escalation. Easing such burdens would calm tensions with the West and let the Union concentrate on its problems at home.

Years of Sino-Soviet hostility have brought nothing but border garrisons and wasted resources. Andropov proposes to resume regular consultations with Beijing at the level of deputy foreign ministers, without preconditions. The Chinese leadership will decide whether to respond, but any thaw would ease the burden on the Far East and weaken American influence in Asia.

Andropov's kidneys are failing, and he spends more and more time connected to a dialysis machine at the Kremlin hospital in Kuntsevo. The Politburo receives his instructions in writing while rumours spread through Moscow. Before his illness ends his rule, the General Secretary must decide who will carry his work forward: a reformer, a guardian of continuity or a fellow Chekist.

Mikhail Gorbachev, the energetic party leader from Stavropol, is Andropov's protege and the youngest man in the leadership. Open to new ideas, he has already taken charge of agriculture and much of the economic agenda. Naming him heir tells the Party that the reforms will continue, and it alarms the old guard who would prefer a calmer succession.

The elderly members of the Politburo do not want another reformer, and they rally around Konstantin Chernenko, Brezhnev's faithful chief of staff. His health is poor and his ideas are few, but he guarantees that no one will lose his post. Choosing him satisfies the cadres and preserves stability, even if the reforms quietly lose their momentum.

Heydar Aliyev rose through the ranks of the Azerbaijani KGB, has led his republic's Communist Party since 1969 and is Andropov's choice for First Deputy Premier in Moscow. As a Muslim from the Caucasus at the summit of Soviet power, he would show the peoples of the Union that the Kremlin belongs to them all. To the KGB, he is simply one of their own.

Andropov's campaigns have left their mark. Officials think twice before taking bribes, workers arrive on time, and the Party has regained some of the authority it lost in the years of stagnation. The Disciplined Union is not yet a reformed one, but it has gained the strength and confidence to face the challenges of the coming decade.

Since Marshal Zhukov was ousted in 1957, the army has been kept away from the summit of power. Now Marshal Andrei Grechko, Minister of Defence and a veteran of the battles for the Caucasus and Kiev, stands at the head of the Party. There is no coup and no junta, only a soldier in the General Secretary's chair, and the armed forces finally have a voice at the top.

The Chief of the General Staff has always carried out the decisions of the political leadership without taking part in them. Grechko gives Viktor Kulikov, and after him Nikolai Ogarkov, a regular voice in the Politburo's deliberations. Military planning becomes faster and better coordinated with the needs of the state, and the General Staff becomes the brain of the Union as well as of the army.

General Alexei Yepishev heads the Main Political Directorate of the Soviet Army and Navy, responsible for the ideological education of every soldier and sailor. His political officers are both a link between the Party and the barracks and a guarantee of loyalty. Strengthening the directorate raises the morale of the troops and reassures the Party cadres that the army remains firmly under their control.

The Defence Council of the USSR brings together the General Secretary, the Minister of Defence, the Chief of the General Staff and the leaders of the defence industry. Under Grechko it becomes the true centre of power, deciding not only military questions but also economic priorities. Decisions are swift and clear, though the civilians of the Politburo feel increasingly sidelined.

Soviet military thinkers have long debated whether the next war will be decided by armoured masses or by strategic missiles. Grechko himself trusts in tank armies and trained reserves, but the rocket designers and the Strategic Rocket Forces argue that nuclear power is the only true guarantee of security. The General Secretary must decide where the Union's resources will go.

Grechko's war was won by millions of soldiers and tens of thousands of tanks, and he sees no reason to change the formula. Conscription is enforced more strictly, reserve divisions are filled and training for reservists is expanded. The Soviet Army becomes larger and harder to defeat in defence, although the economy loses more young men to the barracks.

The Group of Soviet Forces in Germany is the spearhead of the Warsaw Pact, with five armies poised along the inner German border. Grechko wants them equipped with the newest tanks, the T-64 and the coming T-72, and trained for a rapid thrust to the Rhine. NATO planners watch nervously as the breakthrough power of Soviet armour grows.

In the event of war, the Soviet Union must be able to call millions of reservists to the colours within days. Grechko orders mobilisation plans revised, depots stocked and military commissariats modernised in every district. The effort fills warehouses with equipment and supplies that could otherwise reach the shops, but the Union will never again be caught unprepared as in 1941.

Marshal Grechko is persuaded that the decisive weapon of the age is the intercontinental ballistic missile. New generations of heavy rockets, among them the R-36M known in the West as the SS-18, will give the Strategic Rocket Forces the power to deter any aggressor. Behind such a shield, Soviet diplomats can negotiate from a position of strength.

Missiles in silos can be targeted, but submarines hiding in the Barents Sea and bombers on airborne alert are far harder to destroy. Grechko orders the development of all three legs of the strategic triad, from new Delta-class missile submarines to modern long-range bombers. The investment is enormous, and Washington will see it as another escalation of the arms race.

The SALT negotiations promise to limit the strategic arsenals of both superpowers, but many officers believe they would freeze Soviet missile forces just as they are catching up. Grechko lends his weight to the sceptics in the Politburo and the defence industry, arguing that no agreement can replace real military strength. Detente cools, and the arms race continues unchecked.

Since the clashes with China in 1969, dozens of Soviet divisions have been stationed along the Amur and the Ussuri, yet coordinating them from Moscow is slow and inefficient. Grechko proposes a separate high command for the Far East, headquartered in Ulan-Ude, with its own air bases and reserves, to defend Soviet territory against any threat from China or Japan.

Founded during the Great Patriotic War to educate the orphans of fallen soldiers, the Suvorov and Nakhimov schools have become the cradle of the Soviet officer corps. Grechko wants more of them, with better teachers and stricter standards, to produce cadets who are ready to command. The armed forces will gain officers who have worn the uniform since childhood.

Every year young men from all fifteen republics enter the Soviet Army, many of them speaking little Russian. Grechko sees military service as the great melting pot of the Union, where Uzbeks, Lithuanians and Russians learn a common language of command and a shared Soviet identity. The barracks become a school of friendship between peoples and of loyalty to the Union.

Soviet weapons have become the most effective form of diplomacy, from Kalashnikovs in Africa to MiG fighters in the Middle East. Grechko wants arms exports organised on a larger scale, with long-term credits for friendly regimes and cheaper aid packages for liberation movements. The defence industry gains new markets, and every rifle shipped abroad buys influence for Moscow.

In Egypt, thousands of Soviet advisers and air-defence crews helped rebuild the army after the defeat of 1967. Grechko proposes to expand such missions in Egypt and extend them to Syria and Iraq, offering training, staff work and modern doctrine to friendly armies. It is up to Cairo, Damascus and Baghdad to accept, but every adviser they welcome draws them closer to Moscow.

Grechko has passed seventy, and even a marshal's health cannot last forever. The question of succession weighs on the leadership: should another man close to the armed forces continue the course, or should power return to the civilian Party apparatus? The decision will determine whether the army's hour becomes an era or merely an episode.

Dmitry Ustinov has directed the Soviet defence industry since he became People's Commissar for Armaments in 1941. Though not a career soldier, he knows every design bureau and every factory of the military-industrial complex. Naming him heir assures the defence industry that its privileged position will survive the Marshal, and that the armed forces will keep receiving the best the Union can produce.

The Marshal's leadership has strengthened the armed forces, but many in the Party fear that the generals are growing too powerful. Grechko himself accepts that the army should step back once his task is done. Konstantin Chernenko, a quiet man of the Party apparatus, is named heir, reassuring the cadres that the Party will once again command the gun.

What if the marshals decided that the Party had failed the Union? The Council of Marshals takes power, stripping the Central Committee of its authority and placing the country under the direct rule of the High Command. Grechko becomes head of a military government, promising order and strength. Many citizens accept the change in silence, but the shock to the old system is immense.

Marshal Andrei Grechko has run the Ministry of Defence since 1967, and in his hands the party itself begins to resemble a garrison. Officers sit beside obkom secretaries, military-patriotic education reaches every school and factory, and the defence of the motherland becomes the measure of every policy. Critics whisper of a state run from Arbat Square, but the Marshal answers that a besieged camp must be commanded, not debated.

Dmitry Ustinov became People's Commissar of Armaments in June 1941, at just thirty-two, and has managed Soviet weapons production ever since. Now the man who armed the Red Army against Hitler leads the party itself. His course is plain: the defence industry is the backbone of the state, and everything else, from the plan to the consumer, must learn to live alongside it.

Leonid Smirnov has chaired the Military-Industrial Commission of the Council of Ministers since 1963, quietly coordinating ministries, design bureaus and factories across the Union. Under a General Secretary who built this system himself, the commission gains new weight. Its decisions now bind Gosplan as well as the defence ministries, and new armaments plants rise wherever it points on the map.

The names of Tupolev, Sukhoi, Mikoyan, Chelomei and Yangel carry more prestige than those of most ministers. Their design bureaus compete fiercely for state orders, test sites and talent, and every new prototype is a matter of national pride. By granting them new experimental facilities and shielding them from the worst of the bureaucracy, the leadership hopes to keep Soviet engineering a generation ahead of the West.

Nine all-Union ministries, from Medium Machine Building to Aviation, Shipbuilding and the Radio Industry, form the industrial heart of Soviet defence. Insiders simply call them the Nine, and their true budgets are among the best-kept secrets of the state. Binding them more tightly together promises cheaper weapons and shorter supply chains, at the price of an ever larger and more privileged apparatus.

The Soviet armed forces have always relied on numbers, but the West is pulling ahead in electronics, precision and engines. The Armourer must decide where the defence industry's resources go next. One path pours money into cutting-edge research and expensive new systems, while the other keeps the assembly lines of Nizhny Tagil and Kharkov running at full speed in the belief that mass will tell in the end.

A single modern weapon, the argument goes, is worth a dozen obsolete ones. Research institutes receive priority funding, tolerances are tightened and new designs are pushed into service even when they cost far more per unit. The army will field less hardware than its planners might wish, but every tank, aircraft and missile it does field should match or surpass its NATO counterpart.

American F-15s and F-16s are entering service, and the Soviet air forces need an answer. The Mikoyan and Sukhoi bureaus are tasked with a new generation of light and heavy fighters, built around powerful turbofans, pulse-Doppler radar and exceptional agility. The future MiG-29 and Su-27 will be costly and difficult to build, but they are meant to win back the skies over Central Europe.

Ustinov has long championed a tank driven by a gas turbine rather than a diesel. The result, developed in Leningrad and adopted in 1976 as the T-80, is fast, powerful and thirsty, and far more expensive than the T-72 rolling off the lines in the Urals. Backing it fully means accepting that cost for the sake of a spearhead able to race across the North German Plain.

Wars, the Marshal's generation learned in 1941, are won by the side that can still deliver tanks when the first battles are over. New armaments plants are built, proven designs are kept in production instead of being replaced and unit costs are driven down relentlessly. The Soviet Army will field more divisions, more guns and more armour than any opponent can hope to destroy.

Dozens of overlapping designs strain both the supply system and the factories. By standardising calibres, engines, chassis and components across the services, planners hope to cut costs, simplify training and keep production lines running smoothly when one model gives way to the next. It is the unglamorous side of armament, but the generals of 1941 remember well what chaos in the arsenal can cost.

Across Russia and the Urals lie vast hidden depots of fuel, ammunition, spare parts and mothballed equipment, held by the State Reserve for the day of mobilisation. Expanding them ties up resources the civilian economy badly needs, but ensures that a Soviet Army cut off from its factories could still fight for months. In a long war, what has already been stored may decide the outcome.

Valentin Glushko, Vladimir Chelomei and Vladimir Utkin lead the great rocket design bureaus, and their rivalries are as legendary as their engines. Each wants priority for his own missiles and launchers, from heavy silo-based ICBMs to the Proton. Ustinov knows all of them personally and intends to harness their competition, giving the Strategic Rocket Forces and the space programme the very best they can build.

The new RSD-10 Pioneer, known in the West as the SS-20, is a mobile intermediate-range missile with three warheads, able to strike any target in Western Europe within minutes. Deploying it in numbers would modernise the Soviet theatre arsenal at a stroke. It would also alarm Bonn and the other NATO capitals, and may well provoke the Americans into stationing new missiles of their own on European soil.

The American Space Shuttle programme has convinced the military that the United States intends to dominate orbit. Ustinov backs a Soviet answer on a grand scale: the super-heavy Energia rocket and the reusable Buran orbiter, developed under Glushko at NPO Energia. The project will swallow billions of rubles and years of effort, but it promises to keep Soviet spaceflight equal to anything launched from Cape Canaveral.

Arzamas-16, Chelyabinsk-65 and Krasnoyarsk-26 appear on no public map. In these closed cities, scientists and engineers live behind fences and checkpoints, better supplied than most Soviet citizens, and work on nuclear weapons and the materials to build them. Expanding this secret archipelago brings new laboratories and reactors into being and keeps the country's best minds devoted to the needs of defence.

The defence ministries already turn out refrigerators, televisions and washing machines alongside missiles and tanks, and for most Soviet consumers these goods are the only face of the military-industrial complex they will ever see. Formalising such dual-use lines brings new civilian capacity to the armaments plants. Quality remains uneven and the military always comes first, but households from Minsk to Vladivostok will notice the difference.

Since the April Revolution of 1978, the communist government in Kabul has torn itself apart while rebellion spreads across the Afghan countryside. Its leaders beg Moscow for help, and the Politburo must decide how far to go. Some argue that only Soviet troops can save the revolution, while others warn that the army would be walking into a war no outside power has ever won.

In December 1979, Ustinov stood alongside Andropov and Gromyko in pressing for intervention, and now the decision is his alone. The 40th Army crosses the Amu Darya to secure Kabul and the main cities, while the General Staff promises a short campaign. The officers who return will be battle-hardened, but the West sees only Soviet aggression, and the mountains will not be pacified quickly.

Instead of sending Soviet divisions into Afghanistan, Moscow sends weapons, advisers and money. The government in Kabul must fight its own war, backed by Soviet helicopters and armour but not by Soviet conscripts. The same approach is extended to friendly regimes from Angola to Ethiopia and Syria, turning the output of the defence industry into influence and hard currency without the risk of a quagmire.

Ustinov is in his seventies, and even the man who built the Soviet arsenal cannot outrun time. Before he goes, he must decide who will inherit not only the party but also the defence complex he has shaped for four decades. The candidates represent two very different futures: the disciplined technocracy of Leningrad, or the energetic new generation from Stavropol.

Grigory Romanov, the hard-driving first secretary of Leningrad, shares the Armourer's faith in industrial discipline and military strength. His city builds tanks, warships and electronics, and he has never shown the slightest sympathy for reformist experiments. By naming him successor, Ustinov ensures that the defence complex keeps its privileged place and that the course set in the Kremlin continues unbroken.

Mikhail Gorbachev, the young agriculture secretary from Stavropol, is energetic, educated and popular with the reform-minded members of the Politburo. Choosing him is a gamble for the old Marshal, since Gorbachev talks of efficiency and modernisation rather than more tanks. Yet Ustinov may conclude that only a younger man can keep the economy strong enough to carry the weight of Soviet defence.

Under Ustinov, the Soviet Union becomes the arsenal of world socialism. Factories from the Urals to the Volga turn out weapons for the Warsaw Pact and for allies on three continents, design bureaus race to field ever better systems and the whole economy bends to the needs of defence. Whether the people can carry this burden indefinitely is a question for another day.

Grigory Romanov has ruled Leningrad since 1970 with an iron grip and a manager's eye for numbers. Now he brings the Leningrad model to the whole Union: strict discipline in the party, close ties between science and industry and zero tolerance for ideological deviation. The order that made the city on the Neva a showcase of efficiency is to be applied from Kaliningrad to Kamchatka.

Every General Secretary brings his own people to Moscow, and Romanov is no exception. Trusted secretaries and managers from the Leningrad obkom move into key departments of the Central Committee and the ministries, displacing the old networks of the Brezhnev era. The newcomers are capable and loyal, but the established nomenklatura resents losing its comfortable positions to the men from the north.

The Kirov Works, LOMO and the Admiralty Shipyards form Leningrad's belt of heavy and defence industry, building tanks, optics and warships. Romanov knows these plants intimately and considers them the pride of the Soviet working class. Expanding their capacity and channelling new orders their way strengthens the defence complex and binds its managers closely to the new General Secretary.

Leningrad pioneered the science-production association, merging research institutes, design bureaus and factories into a single enterprise so that new ideas reach the assembly line in years rather than decades. Elektrosila, LOMO and Svetlana became models of the approach. Extending it across the Union promises to close the gap between Soviet science and Soviet industry, one of the planned economy's most stubborn weaknesses.

Romanov's Leningrad was known for two things: modern management and an unforgiving hand. As General Secretary, he must choose which of the two will define his rule. He can bet on engineers, computers and automation to make the economy work, or on discipline, ideological vigilance and fear to make people work harder within the existing system.

The Soviet Union will be modernised, but strictly on the party's terms. Engineers and economists receive real authority, scientific management and computerised planning spread from the ministries to the shop floor, and productivity becomes the measure of every official. There is no room for liberal experiments or market reforms, for technocracy here means efficiency under firm party control, not freedom.

For decades, Soviet growth came from adding more workers, more land and more raw materials, and those reserves are running out. The intensive economy aims to grow instead through productivity, better technology and smarter use of existing capacity, as Leningrad's own experiments suggested. Planners will be judged on efficiency rather than gross output, a quiet revolution in the culture of Gosplan itself.

Leningrad's engineers dream of factories run by machines: numerically controlled machine tools, industrial robots and computerised control systems that never drink, never shirk and never miss a shift. Building the microelectronics plants to make this possible is expensive, and Soviet chips still lag behind Western ones, but automation offers a way to raise output without finding workers the country no longer has.

Absenteeism, drinking on the job and falsified reports have become a way of life across the Union. Romanov's answer is discipline: inspections, sanctions, dismissals and the full weight of the KGB behind the party's demands. Republic leaders who inflate their figures will now pay for it, and while the country may grumble, the General Secretary is convinced that order must come before everything else.

Romanov's Leningrad was notorious for its hostility to the underground rock scene, Western fashion and anything else that smelled of bourgeois decadence. Now the same severity becomes national policy. Unofficial concerts are broken up, black-market jeans are confiscated and youth culture is steered back toward the Komsomol, and while foreign influence weakens, young people and dissidents alike take note.

Too many ministers, directors and obkom secretaries have grown complacent during the long years of stability of cadres. Romanov intends to change that. Officials who miss their targets or live off connections are removed regardless of their patrons and replaced with younger, more demanding managers, and the nomenklatura learns that its positions are no longer guaranteed for life.

Leningrad has been Russia's naval capital since Peter the Great, and its yards still build the most advanced ships of the Soviet Navy, including the nuclear-powered Kirov-class battlecruisers taking shape at the Baltic Shipyard. Romanov sees the fleet as a symbol of the Union's global reach and pours resources into the shipyards on the Neva, giving Admiral Gorshkov the ocean-going navy he has long demanded.

Romanov does not believe in detente. To him, every concession at the negotiating table is a sign of weakness that the imperialists will exploit. Soviet diplomats are instructed to hold firm on every issue, from arms control to human rights, and the military is assured that no agreement will cut its strength. Even fraternal allies hoping for softer trade terms find Moscow unbending.

The Leningrad Military District and the Baltic republics guard the Union's northwestern flank against NATO. Romanov turns the region into a fortress, with new garrisons, fortified coastlines and reinforced border troops. A hard line toward Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian national sentiment keeps the republics in check ideologically, but deepens a quiet resentment that Moscow would be unwise to ignore.

Romanov is younger than most of the Politburo, but even a vigorous leader must think about who will follow him. He can gather all power into his own hands and trust that his system will outlive him, or entrust the succession to the defence-industrial technocrats who helped him rise. Either way, the decision will shape the Soviet Union for a generation.

Romanov has no intention of being merely first among equals. He gathers the levers of power in his own office, overriding the collective leadership that has guided the party since Khrushchev's fall in 1964. Decisions are made faster and enforced more strictly, and those who hesitate are swept aside, for the Soviet Union has its strong hand again, for better or worse.

Romanov chooses institutional continuity over personal rule. Dmitry Ustinov, the veteran master of the defence complex and his closest ally in the Politburo, is designated to take over should the General Secretary die or step down. The arrangement reassures the generals and the industrial ministries that the course of efficiency and military strength will survive any change at the top.

Under Romanov, the Soviet Union becomes a disciplined and well-managed machine. Plans are fulfilled honestly, factories modernise, scientists and engineers enjoy respect and the authority of the party goes unquestioned. It is a stern and colourless order with little room for dissent or experiment, but for the first time in years the Union seems to be moving with purpose rather than drifting.

Konstantin Chernenko spent his career not on the front lines of politics but behind them, managing paperwork, appointments and correspondence for Leonid Brezhnev. Now the consummate apparatchik leads the party. He offers no grand vision, only the reassurance that the system will go on functioning as it always has, and for a Politburo weary of upheaval that is exactly the point.

Since 1965, Chernenko has headed the General Department of the Central Committee, the nerve centre through which every Politburo document, decree and secret file must pass. Its archives and procedures are his true power base. By streamlining the department and placing his own people at its desks, he controls what reaches the leadership and when.

Every year, hundreds of thousands of Soviet citizens write to the Central Committee about housing, shortages, injustice and abuses by local officials. Chernenko's department handles these letters, and he regards them as the ear of the apparatus. Taking the complaints seriously, and acting visibly on a few of them, gives ordinary people the sense that someone in Moscow is listening.

Chernenko's instinct is to preserve the system Brezhnev built. Yet the economy is stagnating, the younger members of the Politburo are restless and even loyal apparatchiks admit that something must change. The General Secretary must decide whether to stand firmly on continuity or to permit a careful, limited opening toward the reformers gathered around Gorbachev.

There will be no experiments. Cadres stay in their posts, the ministries keep their privileges and the party line remains what it was under Leonid Ilyich. The nomenklatura breathes a sigh of relief and society enjoys a few more years of predictability, while the question of whether the economy can afford this calm is one the old men in the Kremlin prefer not to ask.

In June 1983, the Central Committee met in a plenum devoted entirely to ideology, with Chernenko delivering the main report. Its message was clear: Soviet culture, education and propaganda must be purged of foreign influence and rededicated to Marxism-Leninism. Implementing its resolutions tightens the party's hold on the minds of the people, at least on paper.

Chernenko is no reformer, but he is pragmatic enough to let younger colleagues experiment. Gorbachev and his allies are given room to test new methods in agriculture and industry, provided they do not touch the foundations of the system. It is a small door left ajar, and many in the apparatus fear that it will be impossible to close again.

In 1984, the Soviet leadership adopts a sweeping reform of general and vocational schooling. Every pupil is to learn a trade alongside the standard curriculum, and secondary schools are tied more closely to factories and collective farms. The reform promises skilled hands for an economy short of labour, though teachers complain about the added burden and the costs.

Brezhnev's Food Programme of May 1982 promised to end the chronic shortages of meat, milk and vegetables by the end of the decade. Chernenko intends to see it through, with more investment in the agro-industrial complex, better storage and transport and higher purchase prices for the collective farms. Grain imports from the capitalist world remain an embarrassment the party hopes to end.

Relations with Washington are at their lowest point in decades. The Euromissile crisis, the downing of KAL 007 and Reagan's talk of an evil empire have poisoned the atmosphere. Chernenko must choose whether to return to the negotiating table in Geneva or to answer American hostility with hostility of his own, beginning with the Olympic Games in Los Angeles.

The Soviet Union proposes to resume arms talks in Geneva, covering strategic weapons, intermediate-range missiles and weapons in space alike. The offer is aimed at European public opinion as much as at Washington, presenting Moscow as the true champion of peace. Whether the Americans accept, and on what terms, now lies with them.

Four years after the Americans boycotted the Moscow Olympics, the Soviet Union answers in kind. Citing security concerns and anti-Soviet hysteria, the National Olympic Committee announces in May 1984 that Soviet athletes will not travel to Los Angeles, and most of the socialist bloc follows. At home the decision is presented as a matter of dignity, while in Washington it confirms that detente is dead.

Chernenko is a sick man. Emphysema leaves him breathless, and he spends ever more time at the Kremlin hospital in Kuntsevo while his colleagues govern in his name. The succession can no longer be postponed, and the Politburo must decide whether the next General Secretary will come from the old guard or from a new generation.

Mikhail Gorbachev already chairs the Secretariat when Chernenko is too ill to attend, and he has quietly built a coalition with Gromyko and the younger members of the Politburo. Naming him heir hands the future to a man of fifty-three who speaks of acceleration and renewal. The old guard is uneasy, but even many of them know the country needs a younger leader.

Viktor Grishin has led the Moscow party organisation since 1967 and is the favoured candidate of the Brezhnev-era veterans. A stolid, cautious administrator, he promises that nothing important will change. Elevating him reassures the nomenklatura that its world is safe, though younger cadres and the reformers around Gorbachev see in him only more of the stagnation they despise.

Grigory Romanov, the former Leningrad chief who now oversees the defence industry from the Central Committee Secretariat, is the hardliners' answer to Gorbachev. Disciplined, technocratic and uncompromising, he would combine the ideological firmness of the old guard with new managerial energy. Naming him heir signals that the party's future will be one of order rather than reform.

Chernenko's rule marks the final chapter of the generation that came of age under Stalin and rose under Brezhnev. They govern with caution, respect for seniority and unshakable faith in the system they built. Their era brings stability and comfort to the apparatus, even as the economy slows and the gap between the leaders and the young grows ever wider.

Mikhail Gorbachev became a full member of the Politburo in October 1980, its youngest by far. Now in power, he represents a generation shaped not by the purges and the war but by the Thaw and the Twentieth Congress. He promises perestroika, a restructuring of the Soviet system, in the belief that socialism can be renewed rather than abandoned.

Nikolai Ryzhkov, the industrial manager from Sverdlovsk, takes charge of the Council of Ministers, while Yegor Ligachev from Tomsk runs the Secretariat as the party's second man. Together they form the backbone of the new team, one tasked with making the economy work and the other with cleansing the apparatus of corruption and inertia. Their partnership will last only as long as reform stays within limits both can accept.

Alexander Yakovlev spent a decade as ambassador in Ottawa, a quiet exile after he criticised Russian nationalism in 1972. Gorbachev met him during his visit to Canada in 1983 and was struck by his ideas. Brought back to Moscow, Yakovlev becomes the intellectual architect of glasnost and the most radical voice in the leadership, convinced that the party must open up in order to survive.

In July 1985, Andrei Gromyko leaves the Foreign Ministry after twenty-eight years, and Gorbachev hands it to Eduard Shevardnadze, the Georgian party chief with no diplomatic experience at all. The choice stuns the world, but Shevardnadze brings flexibility and warmth where Gromyko was known as Mister Nyet. His appointment also signals respect for the non-Russian republics at the highest level of the Union.

Gorbachev agrees that the system must change, but not on where to begin. Some advisers urge acceleration, modernising machine-building and raising investment so that the economy grows faster before politics is touched. Others argue that nothing will move until the truth can be spoken openly, and that openness must come first, so the order of reform may well decide its fate.

At the April Plenum of 1985 and again at the Twenty-Seventh Party Congress, Gorbachev calls for uskorenie, the acceleration of socio-economic development. Massive investment flows into machine-building and new technology, aiming to re-equip Soviet industry within a decade. It is an ambitious but traditional programme of growth from above, and it tests whether the planned economy can still be revived by command.

In May 1985, the Central Committee declares war on drunkenness. Vodka prices rise, opening hours shrink, vineyards are uprooted and party members are expected to set an example of sobriety. Discipline and public health improve, but the budget loses billions in alcohol revenue, moonshine flourishes and sugar vanishes from the shops, and people soon nickname Gorbachev the mineral water secretary.

Adopted in June 1987, the Law on the State Enterprise grants factories a measure of self-financing and the right to elect their own directors. State orders replace part of the rigid plan, and enterprises may keep a share of what they earn. The branch ministries lose much of their power in the process, and the planned economy begins to loosen at its very core.

Gorbachev decides that the country cannot be restructured while it is still afraid to speak. Censorship relaxes, papers such as Moscow News and Ogonyok print what was unprintable a year before, and banned films and novels come down from the shelves. Intellectual life flourishes, but the party also loses its monopoly on the truth, and with it a pillar of its authority.

Soviet history is full of blank spots: the purges, the famine, the secret protocols of 1939, Katyn. Under glasnost, historians and journalists begin to fill them in, Bukharin and other victims of Stalin are rehabilitated and the public learns what the textbooks concealed. The reckoning is cathartic for many, but it shakes the faith of those who believed in the party's infallibility.

Andrei Sakharov, father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb and Nobel Peace laureate, has lived in internal exile in Gorky since 1980. In December 1986, a telephone is suddenly installed in his flat, and the General Secretary himself calls to invite him back to Moscow. His release electrifies the dissident movement and convinces the West that the changes in the Kremlin are real.

The Law on Cooperation of May 1988 allows Soviet citizens to found cooperatives in trade, services, catering and even manufacturing. Overnight, much of the shadow economy steps into the light as cafes, repair shops and small producers appear in every city. The state gains taxes and the shops gain goods, though the new cooperators are soon accused of profiteering and ties to organised crime.

New political thinking holds that in the nuclear age, universal human values must take precedence over the class struggle. Gorbachev and Shevardnadze apply it to foreign policy, seeking mutual security instead of military superiority. Western leaders are cautiously impressed, and relations with partners across the world begin to thaw as the confrontation of the early 1980s gives way to dialogue.

Reagan proposed the zero option in 1981, expecting Moscow to reject it.
