Now the Soviet Union takes him at his word: all intermediate-range missiles in Europe, the SS-20 included, are to be eliminated entirely, removing a whole class of nuclear weapons. The generals are furious at giving up more missiles than the Americans, but the decision now rests with Washington.

Gorbachev has called Afghanistan a bleeding wound. After years of war, thousands of Soviet dead and no end in sight, the Politburo decides to bring the 40th Army home, offering Kabul a withdrawal plan that gives the Afghan government time to stand on its own. The army sees it as a humiliation, but Soviet mothers will be grateful.

The Brezhnev Doctrine is dead. In October 1989, Foreign Ministry spokesman Gennady Gerasimov jokes that Moscow now follows the Sinatra Doctrine, letting the countries of Eastern Europe do it their way, and Soviet tanks will no longer rescue unpopular communist governments. The socialist community saves on subsidies and earns goodwill in the West, but its cohesion can no longer be guaranteed by force.

At the January Plenum of 1987, Gorbachev declares that perestroika requires the democratisation of party and state. Several candidates are to stand in elections, secret ballots will choose party secretaries and workers may elect their managers. The reformers rejoice, but the nomenklatura sees its appointments and privileges threatened, and the balance of power in the Politburo tips decisively.

In March 1989, Soviet citizens vote in the first contested national elections since 1917. The new Congress of People's Deputies brings Sakharov, Yeltsin and many critics of the party onto the national stage, and its sessions, broadcast live, captivate the whole country. Several party bosses lose to unknown challengers, a humiliation that reveals how far the party's authority has fallen.

The Union of 1922 can no longer hold the republics together by force alone. Gorbachev proposes a new Union Treaty that would turn the Soviet Union into a voluntary federation of sovereign republics, sharing defence, foreign policy and a common market while granting each wide autonomy. A Union-wide referendum is to give it popular legitimacy, but the republics and the hardliners must still be won over.

Perestroika has unleashed forces no one fully controls. Elections, a free press and national movements are reshaping the country faster than the party can adapt. Gorbachev must decide how far the reform should go, whether to keep it within the framework of the Communist Party and its leading role, or to accept that the party itself must become something new.

At the Twenty-Eighth Congress in July 1990, the party adopts its programmatic statement Towards a Humane, Democratic Socialism. The Communist Party remains the governing force, but it renounces dogma, accepts political pluralism and commits itself to the rule of law. For Gorbachev, this is the synthesis he has sought since 1985: renewal without rupture, and socialism with a human face at last.

The reformers conclude that the Communist Party cannot be saved in its old form. Gorbachev and his allies break with the hardliners and refound the governing party on social-democratic principles, modelled on the labour parties of Western Europe, while old comrades denounce the betrayal. The Soviet Union enters uncharted territory as a pluralist socialist state.

In March 1990, the Congress of People's Deputies ends the party's constitutional monopoly on power, creates the office of President of the USSR and elects Gorbachev to it. Executive authority shifts from the Politburo to the state. A new Federation Council brings the leaders of all the republics into direct consultation with the President, replacing the old system of party seats.

In Strasbourg in July 1989, Gorbachev tells the Council of Europe of a common European home stretching from the Atlantic to the Urals. The vision imagines a continent where the blocs dissolve into cooperation, trade flows freely and the Soviet Union takes its place as one European nation among others. The Iron Curtain is lifting, and partners in Bonn, Paris and Rome are eager to engage.

The slogan of 1917 returns to the streets: all power to the councils. Workers' councils born in factories across the Union demand that the soviets become again what they were meant to be, organs of self-government rather than rubber stamps of the party apparatus. The Free Councils of Labour now hold power, and the ministries, the planners and the nomenklatura brace for a revolution from below.

In June 1962, workers at the Novocherkassk electric locomotive plant struck against higher food prices and cut wages. Troops opened fire, killing more than twenty people, and the event was buried in official silence, but Pyotr Siuda, a striker and witness, kept the memory alive. Now Novocherkassk becomes the founding myth of the council movement and a rallying cry for the trade unions.

The branch ministries in Moscow have commanded Soviet industry from above for half a century. The councils intend to abolish them and hand control of each enterprise to the people who work there. The transition will be chaotic as supply chains break, production falters and old managers resist, but the councils believe that self-management, once rooted, will prove stronger than any bureaucracy.

The council revolution must decide where its centre of gravity lies. The industrial workers of the cities, heirs of the Petrograd Soviet, demand that factory councils lead the new order. Yet the countryside has its own claim, for collective farmers want land and autonomy rather than new masters, and the choice between them will shape the character of the new state.

Elected councils of workers take over the management of their factories, choosing directors, setting production priorities and sharing the proceeds of their labour. The Yugoslav experience is studied closely, but the Soviet councils aim to go further. Freed from ministerial orders, many enterprises discover unexpected reserves of initiative, and workers see for the first time in decades what it means to own the means of production.

Delegates from councils across the Union gather in Moscow for a Congress of Councils, the first truly elected national assembly of working people since the early days of the revolution. Debates are long, loud and sometimes chaotic, but the Congress gives the new order a face and a voice. Its decrees carry a legitimacy that no Politburo resolution ever enjoyed.

The collective farms were imposed on the peasantry by force, and those who work them have little say in how they are run. The councils propose a different model: rural communes owned and governed by the people who till the land, free to decide what to grow and how to share the harvest. Productivity rises as farmers at last work for themselves and their neighbours.

The land belongs to those who work it. State and collective farms are transferred to the rural communes together with their machinery and livestock, and villages across Russia, Ukraine and Central Asia gain control of their own future. The cities will have to wait longer for consumer goods as resources flow to the countryside, but the peasantry has never been more loyal.

The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was meant to be a free federation of soviet republics, and the councils intend to make that promise real. Power flows upward from local councils to republican congresses and only then to the Union, giving Ukrainians, Georgians, Kazakhs and Balts a genuine voice in their own affairs. Many in the republics find the new federation worth belonging to.

The nomenklatura, the secret lists of posts and of the people entitled to fill them, has been the backbone of party rule since Stalin. The councils abolish it outright: positions are now elected or filled on merit, and special shops, dachas and privileges vanish. Corruption declines sharply, but the displaced elite is bitter and the administrative chaos is felt everywhere.

A council republic needs its own defenders. Workers' militias are formed in factories and districts, armed and trained to protect the revolution against counter-revolution and foreign intervention alike. They swell the pool of available manpower, but professional officers watch with alarm as discipline gives way to elected commanders and the regular army loses its monopoly on force.

The councils see the arms race as a burden imposed on working people by two ruling classes. Defence spending is cut sharply, weapons programmes are cancelled and resources are redirected to housing and consumer goods. The generals are outraged, but tensions with the West ease, and workers in Moscow and Detroit alike may wonder why they were ever enemies.

The Soviet council revolution looks abroad for comrades. Yugoslavia, with its long tradition of workers' self-management, becomes the natural first partner, and appeals go out to labour movements from Poland to Latin America. A new international of councils is founded to support self-managing socialism wherever it emerges, offering a third way between Washington and the old Moscow.

The councils hold power, but the long-term direction of the revolution remains open. Some delegates insist that it cannot stop at the Soviet borders and must keep advancing at home and abroad. Others argue that the time has come to consolidate, to build stable institutions and to show the world that council communism can work in peace.

The revolution must never rest. Reviving the old idea of permanent revolution, the councils commit to continuous mobilisation, spreading their model abroad and challenging every entrenched hierarchy at home, while volunteers and aid flow to movements across the world. The energy is intoxicating, but constant upheaval takes its toll on daily life and on stability.

After years of upheaval, the councils choose consolidation. Procedures are codified, elections become routine and the new institutions settle into the rhythm of everyday government. Workers return to production confident that their councils will endure. The revolution has become a state, and for most citizens that comes as a welcome relief.

The Soviet Union has become what Lenin once described in The State and Revolution: a commune state governed by elected and recallable councils of working people. The ministries and the nomenklatura are gone, factories and farms manage themselves and power flows from below. Utopia or dangerous experiment, the council republic stands as a genuine alternative to capitalism and to the old Soviet model alike.

Sergei Trapeznikov, head of the Central Committee's Department of Science and Education, has long been the voice of those who never accepted the denunciation of Stalin. His Neo-Stalinist Platform now holds power, promising strict discipline, ideological purity and a return to the mobilising spirit of the five-year plans. Intellectuals tremble, but many ordinary people remember the Stalin years as a time of order and greatness.

Since 1956, Stalin's name has been spoken only in whispers or in condemnation. The Neo-Stalinists restore him as the architect of victory and industrialisation: monuments return, textbooks are rewritten and Khrushchev's secret speech is quietly disowned. In the republics, the memory of the deportations makes the move deeply unpopular, but in Beijing, which never condemned Stalin, Mao takes notice.

The Neo-Stalinists revive the economics of the 1930s and the war years: maximum investment in heavy and defence industry, rigid central control and the subordination of every resource to the plan. New armaments plants rise and the workforce is placed on a permanent war footing. Living standards suffer and efficiency declines, but the state's capacity to mobilise grows dramatically.

Stalin once declared that cadres decide everything, yet the Neo-Stalinists are also heirs to the five-year plans and the great construction projects. The leadership must choose its emphasis. It can launch a renewed drive of industrialisation powered by ambitious targets, or forge a new and disciplined cadre corps through purges and promotions that will carry the system forward.

Like the first five-year plans, the new industrialisation sets breathtaking targets: new factories, new cities and new industries built at enormous speed. Investment is concentrated on output, and the slogans of the 1930s reappear on factory walls. Civilian industry expands dramatically, but the strain on workers and the disruption of everyday life breed unrest that the regime must contain.

The Stakhanovites of the 1930s smashed every norm and became heroes of the nation. Trapeznikov's circle wants that spirit back: shock brigades, red banners on the shop floor and public honour for those who overfulfil the plan. The trade unions grumble about speed-ups and raised norms, but the Neo-Stalinists believe socialist emulation can achieve what Kosygin's bonuses never did.

In May 1935 Stalin told the graduates of the Red Army academies that cadres decide everything. The Neo-Stalinist platform takes the slogan literally: the nomenklatura is to be rebuilt as a disciplined, ideologically reliable corps, promoted for loyalty and results rather than seniority. The Central Committee apparatus, long used to Brezhnev's comfortable stability of cadres, is promised a firmer hand and a renewed sense of mission.

Corruption, nepotism and quiet private dealing have spread through the apparatus since Khrushchev's fall. The Neo-Stalinists answer with the oldest remedy they know: a purge of the ranks, carried out by the organs of state security and justified in the language of revolutionary vigilance. Thieves and careerists will fall, but so will many who merely backed the wrong patron, and the whole party will learn once more what fear means.

In May 1970 the country marked twenty-five years since the victory over fascism, and the memory of the Great Patriotic War remains the deepest source of Soviet legitimacy. The platform places the war, and the Generalissimo who led it, back at the centre of public life: new memorials, military-patriotic education in every school and a cult of sacrifice that binds the young to the generation of 1941.

Western credits, Fiat licences and grain deals have made the Union dependent on its rivals, or so the Neo-Stalinists argue. Their answer is autarky: foreign trade reduced to what is strictly necessary, contacts with capitalist firms placed under suspicion and the economy organised to survive any embargo the imperialists might impose. Self-reliance has a price in technology and comfort, but it removes a lever the West could one day pull.

Private plots and market sales have crept back into the countryside, and many kolkhozy survive only on state subsidies. The platform orders a return to discipline: tighter control over private livestock, firm delivery quotas and larger, consolidated farms run by reliable chairmen. Output may rise in the granaries, but the collective farmers will remember who took away the little freedom they had won since 1953.

The clashes on Damansky Island in March 1969 brought the Soviet Union and China to the brink of war. Yet Mao has always despised Khrushchev's revisionism far more than Stalin's legacy, and a Moscow that rehabilitates Stalin might find an unexpected listener in Beijing. The platform proposes to offer the Chinese comrades a common return to the pure line, if they are willing to take it.

Western radio, tourists, jazz records and smuggled jeans corrupt Soviet youth more effectively than any army could. The Neo-Stalinists want the frontier sealed once more: the jamming of the Voice of America and Radio Liberty is intensified, contacts with foreigners are restricted and cultural exchanges are cut back to the bare minimum. Trade with the West will suffer, but the ideological frontier of the Union will finally be secure.

The Neo-Stalinist platform has always been divided on one point: should the restoration produce a new supreme leader, or must power remain with the collective Politburo? Some in Trapeznikov's circle dream of a new Vozhd who stands above the apparatus as Stalin did, while others fear another reign of terror that would devour its own creators. The movement must decide which path the restoration will take.

The decision is made: the Union will once again have a Vozhd. The General Secretary is elevated above the Politburo, his portraits fill the squares and his word becomes the final authority in party and state. Supporters call it the restoration of Leninist order; critics whisper that the country has seen all this before, and remember how it ended for the delegates of the Congress of Victors in 1934.

Rather than create another Vozhd, the leadership chooses Stalinism without Stalin. The cult of the late Generalissimo is restored and many of his methods return, but power remains shared within the Politburo, where no single man can turn the organs against his colleagues. The nomenklatura welcomes a system that offers discipline from above and security for those who already sit at the top.

Stalin's first industrialisation turned a peasant land into a great power within a decade. The Neo-Stalinists now promise a second one: new giants such as the Kama truck works, power stations on the Siberian rivers and whole industrial cities built from scratch in the taiga. Mobilisation, central direction and sacrifice are once again to drive the Soviet economy forward, this time towards the twenty-first century.

Alexander Shelepin, the Iron Shurik who once led both the Komsomol and the KGB, has finally taken power together with his network of former Komsomol functionaries. The comfortable collective rule of the Brezhnev years is over. In its place stands a leader state, built on personal loyalty, youthful energy and a security apparatus that answers to one man rather than to the Politburo.

Shelepin's followers do not hide what they want: a single leader whose authority rests on personal will rather than on the consensus of ageing Politburo members. The principle of the Vozhd is proclaimed openly, and the apparatus is told that loyalty to the leader is loyalty to the revolution itself. Few dare to ask aloud where this road led the last time it was travelled.

The Komsomol, with more than twenty million members, is the largest reservoir of energy in the Union, and Shelepin knows it better than anyone. Its brigades are to become the vanguard of the new order, sent to the great construction sites, to the factories and to the border regions. The young are promised responsibility and rapid advancement in return for unconditional commitment.

Every leader state needs a foundation, and Shelepin's advisers are divided on which one to choose. Some want to build the regime on the organs of state security, which Shelepin and Semichastny once commanded. Others want to rest it on the permanent mobilisation of the masses through the Komsomol and great national campaigns. The choice will define the character of the new order.

The KGB was Shelepin's springboard to power, and it will now be his main pillar. Its directorates are expanded, its informers multiplied and its authority over party members restored to levels unseen since 1953. Every foreign influence and every whisper of dissent is to be detected early, and the Chekists become the guardians not only of the state but of the leader himself.

A security state rests on information, and information comes from people. A vast network of informers is recruited in factories, institutes, dormitories and housing blocks, many of them from the ranks of the Komsomol. Foreign intelligence services find it ever harder to operate, but trust between colleagues, neighbours and friends begins to wither, and the atmosphere in the country grows colder.

Rather than relying on the secret police, the regime builds its power on the masses. Rallies, voluntary labour Saturdays, people's patrol squads and endless campaigns keep society in permanent motion. The Komsomol Vanguard presents itself as the movement of a young and fighting generation, and anyone who stands aside quickly learns that indifference is also a political statement.

In the spirit of the Virgin Lands and the great Komsomol construction projects, the regime launches a new series of national campaigns. Tens of thousands of young volunteers are sent to the taiga, the steppe and the Far North to lay railways, raise dams and found new towns. The work is hard and the living conditions harsh, but the campaigns give the regime both results and legitimacy.

The Politburo of 1970 is a council of elderly men, many of whom have held high office since Stalin's days. Shelepin's young cadres now push them aside: pensions, honourable retirements and, where needed, humiliating dismissals clear the way for a new generation. The principle of stability of cadres that protected the old guard under Brezhnev is abandoned, and the whole apparatus trembles.

The Soviet Army already maintains construction battalions, but the new regime turns them, together with the Komsomol brigades, into a permanent labour force for the great projects. Roads, railways, pipelines and bridges are pushed into the remote regions of Siberia and the Far East at a pace no ordinary ministry could achieve. Discipline replaces wages as the main motivation.

Absenteeism, drinking at work and idle hours have become part of everyday life in Soviet industry. The new regime declares war on slackness: inspection teams patrol the factories, latecomers are named and shamed, and managers are held personally responsible for labour discipline. Productivity rises, but the trade unions lose what little ability they had to protect the workers they represent.

The Brezhnev Doctrine already claims the right to intervene wherever socialism is threatened. Shelepin's regime goes further, promising its allies a firmer hand and its enemies a harder line from the Elbe to the Ussuri. Military aid to revolutionary movements grows, Soviet forces are placed on higher readiness, and the world is reminded that the young generation in Moscow does not fear confrontation.

Ideology has divided Moscow and Beijing for a decade, but two leader states may understand each other better than two parties ever did. Without abandoning Soviet interests, the regime signals to Mao that a pragmatic understanding is possible, building on the talks Kosygin and Zhou Enlai held at Beijing airport in September 1969. Whether China takes the outstretched hand is up to Beijing.

A regime built around one man has no ready answer to the question of what comes after him. Shelepin's circle must decide whether to designate an heir from among the loyal Komsomol cadres or to let power return to the party, where it lay before the leader state was proclaimed. The choice will decide whether the system survives its founder.

Vladimir Semichastny succeeded Shelepin both as head of the Komsomol and as chairman of the KGB, and he has followed his mentor ever since. Brezhnev exiled him to a minor post in Kiev in 1967, but under the leader state he has returned to the centre. Naming him heir ensures that the security organs will stand behind the succession, and that Shelepin's line will continue.

The age of the leader state draws to a close. Rather than handing power to a designated heir, the Komsomol Vanguard returns authority to the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and its Central Committee. A plenum will decide the future course, and the comrades who survived the years of mobilisation must once again find a common line.

The vanguard state has become an established order. The Komsomol generation now holds the key posts in party, state and security apparatus, and a young, disciplined elite governs a society trained in permanent mobilisation. Admirers see a socialism that has rediscovered its fighting energy; critics see a garrison state run by the former youth league. Either way, the Union has changed for good.

Dzhermen Gvishiani, Kosygin's son-in-law and deputy chairman of the State Committee for Science and Technology, has long argued that the Union must be run like one great system. Now the systems men hold power: economists, cyberneticians and managers who speak the language of efficiency rather than ideology. Their rule is authoritarian and technocratic, but it looks westwards for methods and partners.

Together with McGeorge Bundy, Gvishiani has been negotiating an international institute where Soviet and American scientists could jointly study the problems of modern industrial societies. At Laxenburg near Vienna, the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis is set to become a bridge between East and West. For the Directorate it is a window on Western management science and a symbol of its new course.

Party secretaries still meddle in every decision of every factory, and the nomenklatura confuses loyalty with competence. The Directorate puts an end to this: enterprise directors receive real authority, professional managers are trained on the model of Western business schools and promotion depends on measurable results. The old party apparatus watches with alarm as its grip on the economy slips away.

The systems men agree on what they reject, but not on what they want to build. One faction envisions a technocratic state in which scientific institutes and planning bodies govern through models and data. The other dreams of a corporate union in which large industrial associations operate like Western corporations, open to foreign capital and trade. The Directorate must now choose its shape.

The Directorate chooses the path of the technocratic state. Ministries are reorganised according to systems analysis, planning bodies are staffed with mathematicians and engineers, and decisions are justified by models instead of quotations from Lenin. The state becomes more efficient and more powerful, but also more distant from the people it governs and more dependent on a small, closed elite of experts.

The Directorate chooses the corporate path. Large industrial associations are transformed into semi-independent corporations that negotiate with foreign partners, raise credit abroad and compete for markets. Western banks and firms are invited to invest, and Soviet enterprises begin to resemble Fiat or Siemens more than a department of a ministry. Efficiency grows, and so does the foreign debt.

The giant car plant at Togliatti, agreed with Fiat in 1966, showed how quickly Western licences can close a technological gap. The Directorate makes this the rule rather than the exception: licences for production lines, electronics and chemical processes are purchased systematically, and Soviet engineers are sent abroad to learn. Critics warn of dependency, but the systems men see no shame in learning from the best.

Viktor Glushkov's plan for a nationwide automated management system, OGAS, was shelved by the old leadership, which feared what transparent data might reveal. The Directorate revives it under a dedicated ministry for computer technology. New microelectronics plants are built, the Ryad series of computers is expanded and a network linking the planning bodies becomes the backbone of a modern state.

The Soviet Armed Forces swallow a huge share of the nation's resources, yet nobody can say exactly how much security they produce. The Directorate applies systems analysis to defence: redundant divisions are disbanded, procurement is subjected to cost-effectiveness calculations and the bloated officer corps is reduced. The General Staff protests bitterly, but the systems men believe a smaller, modern army is a stronger one.

Since 1949 the Western Coordinating Committee for Multilateral Export Controls, CoCom, has kept advanced technology out of Soviet hands. The Directorate offers Washington a bargain: closer economic cooperation, scientific exchange and political predictability in return for easing the embargo lists on computers and electronics. Whether the Americans accept depends on how far they trust the new men in Moscow.

The Directorate has transformed the Union, but its rule rests on no mandate other than competence. Some systems men want to make their rule permanent and institutionalise technocratic government; others believe the modern society they have created now needs a parliament, elections and the rule of law. The Directorate must decide whether it is a transition or a destination.

The systems men decide that their rule is not a transition. The Directorate becomes a permanent institution of state, its members co-opted on the basis of qualifications and its decisions binding on every ministry. Parliament and parties remain decorative. The Union becomes a managed society in which experts govern, and the citizen's role is to work, consume and trust the system.

The Directorate concludes that its historic task has been fulfilled. A modern economy and an educated society, its members reason, can no longer be governed from closed offices. Free elections are called, the Supreme Soviet is transformed into a real parliament and power is handed to the liberals of the Committee for Human Rights. The technocrats step back, hoping their reforms will outlive their rule.

Gvishiani's dream has come true: the Soviet Union is governed as one great system, its economy steered by data, models and professional managers. Productivity and science flourish, and the Union has become a respected partner of the West in technology and trade. Whether this managed union is still socialism, or something altogether new, is a question its leaders no longer find important.

For forty years the People's Labour Union, the NTS, worked from exile, first in Belgrade and later in Frankfurt, where its Posev publishing house smuggled books and leaflets into the Union. Now the Solidarists return home, not as a hunted underground but as a governing party. Their doctrine of solidarism promises a third way between communism and capitalism, rooted in Russian tradition and Christian ethics.

Since Khrushchev's anti-religious campaign closed thousands of churches, the Russian Orthodox Church has survived as a tolerated but closely watched institution. The NTS restores its freedom: confiscated churches and monasteries are returned, seminaries reopen and the Patriarch of Moscow becomes a respected voice in public life. Some even speak openly of the House of Romanov again, a name that was taboo for half a century.

Solidarism regards private property as the foundation of human dignity and responsibility. Small businesses, workshops, shops and service enterprises are returned to private hands, and citizens may once again own land, a house and the tools of their own trade. The nomenklatura, which controlled all property in the name of the people, loses the very basis of its power.

The NTS leadership is divided over the economy. The old guard of the Solidarists wants an organic, corporate order in which employers, workers and the state cooperate through professional chambers. Younger members, inspired by the West German economic miracle, call for a genuine free market. The decision will shape the new Russia for generations.

The Solidarists choose their original doctrine. Society is organised into professional corporations in which entrepreneurs, employees and the state negotiate wages, prices and working conditions together. Class struggle is to be replaced by solidarity, and the trade unions, freed from party control, become genuine partners rather than transmission belts. Critics fear the system is too slow and too comfortable for those already inside it.

The younger generation of the NTS prevails. Prices are freed, state enterprises are opened to competition and the ruble is set on the road towards convertibility. The model is Ludwig Erhard's West Germany, which rose from ruins within a single decade. The transition is painful and old certainties disappear, but the market promises a prosperity the plan never delivered.

The kolkhozy and sovkhozy were born of Stalin's war against the peasantry, and the NTS regards them as a crime that must be undone. Collective farms are dissolved, their land divided among the families who work it, and the peasant becomes a free farmer once more. The transition will be chaotic, but for the first time since 1929 the Russian village belongs to those who till its soil.

In January 1918 the Bolsheviks dispersed the only freely elected Constituent Assembly in Russian history after a single session. The NTS now convenes a new one. Elected by universal suffrage, it is to give the country a constitution, decide the form of the state and settle the relationship between the peoples of the old Union. It is the long-delayed answer to 1918.

The NTS has always seen Russia as part of Christian Europe, and its leaders spent decades in exile in the West. The new government breaks with the Eastern bloc and seeks a place alongside the Western democracies. In Bonn, where the NTS has long had friends, the decision is greeted with particular relief. The Cold War, at least as the world has known it, is coming to an end.

The Union was held together by the party and the army; without the communist monopoly, its fifteen republics face a fundamental question. Should the new Russia become a nation state that lets the other peoples go their own way, or can the old Union be transformed into a voluntary association of free nations? The answer will redraw the map of Eurasia.

The NTS chooses Russia over empire. The new government offers every union republic the right to determine its own future, while Russia itself is reorganised as a democratic federation. In Kiev, Tbilisi, Vilnius and Tashkent the offer is received with astonishment, and in some places with jubilation. Russia becomes smaller, but it is no longer a prison of nations.

The NTS decides to keep the peoples of the old Union together, but on an entirely new basis. Instead of the dictatorship of a party, a voluntary association of equal nations is to emerge, with common defence, a common market and broad autonomy for each member. Not every republic is convinced, but many leaders see more advantages than dangers in remaining together.

Half a century after the revolution, Russia has found its way back to itself. A free economy, a restored church and a government that grew out of the emigration have created a state the old exiles in Frankfurt and Paris could only dream of. The new Russia is a partner of the West, proud of its past and finally able to look to the future.

In November 1970 Andrei Sakharov, Valery Chalidze and Andrei Tverdokhlebov founded the Committee for Human Rights in the USSR, a tiny circle of scientists defending the constitution against the state. Now this committee governs. Its programme rests on Sakharov's idea of convergence: socialism and capitalism must learn from each other, disarm and cooperate if humanity is to survive.

Thousands of Soviet citizens sit in labour camps and psychiatric hospitals for their opinions, their faith or their national aspirations. The new government opens the gates: political prisoners are amnestied, the special psychiatric hospitals are investigated and the Chronicle of Current Events can finally be published openly. The West applauds, while the KGB watches in disbelief as its opponents walk free.

For half a century the Communist Party has claimed the leading role in Soviet society without any vote ever confirming it. The Committee abolishes this monopoly: new parties may form, candidates may compete and the Supreme Soviet will be chosen in free and secret elections. The nomenklatura sees its world collapse, and many communists face the unaccustomed task of persuading voters.

Sakharov's convergence theory leaves an open question: how far should the economy move towards the market? Some members of the Committee want a mixed economy in which private and state enterprises compete as equals. Others prefer the West German or Scandinavian social market, where a strong welfare state cushions the effects of competition. Both camps agree that the old plan cannot continue unchanged.

The Committee chooses convergence in its purest form. State enterprises are given autonomy, private and cooperative businesses are legalised, and market prices take over where planning has failed. The economy becomes a hybrid of socialist and capitalist elements, just as Sakharov predicted in his 1968 essay. Supporters see the future of both systems; opponents see neither one thing nor the other.

The Committee chooses the social market. Competition and private initiative are permitted, but within a strong framework of social security: guaranteed pensions, free healthcare, unemployment insurance and collective bargaining. The aim is to give Soviet citizens the freedom of the West without taking away the security they have grown accustomed to. It is expensive, but it keeps the country stable.

Valery Chalidze and his colleagues have always insisted that the Soviet constitution is a decent document that is simply never applied. The Committee now makes it binding: courts become independent, the procuracy is placed under legal control, and arbitrary arrests and telephone justice are forbidden. Officials discover, to their surprise, that the law applies to them as well.

For decades the censors of Glavlit have shaped every newspaper, book and film in the Union. The Committee abolishes censorship. Samizdat authors publish openly, new newspapers appear and foreign radio stations are no longer jammed. The state loses its monopoly on truth, and with it much of its ability to steer public opinion, but science and culture flourish in the new freedom.

Sakharov, the father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb, has long warned that the arms race threatens the survival of humanity. The Committee acts on his conviction: defence spending is cut drastically, divisions are disbanded and the Union declares itself ready to make unilateral gestures in nuclear disarmament. The generals are outraged, but the world takes notice of a superpower that disarms of its own accord.

Convergence cannot be the work of one side alone. The Committee proposes a comprehensive treaty to Washington: mutual reductions in strategic arms, joint scientific programmes and a gradual opening of both societies to each other. It would be the greatest step towards lasting peace since 1945. Whether the United States is willing to take the outstretched hand remains to be seen.

Since 1936 the Soviet constitution has guaranteed each union republic the right to secede, a right that was never meant to be used. The Committee, which takes the constitution at its word, must now decide whether to let the republics actually exercise it, or to keep them together in a reformed democratic federation. Neither choice will be easy, and both will be contested.

The Committee honours the constitution to the letter. Every union republic is free to hold a referendum and leave the Union if its people so wish. In the Baltic republics, the Caucasus and Ukraine, national movements prepare to vote. Moscow accepts that a Union held together by force cannot be a democratic one, even if this means the end of the old state.

The Committee seeks to preserve the Union on a democratic basis. A new treaty of union gives the republics broad self-government, their own freely elected parliaments and guaranteed rights for minorities, while foreign policy, defence and currency remain common. The hope is that peoples who suffered together under Stalin will choose to build a free federation together as well.

Having embraced democracy, human rights and the rule of law, the new Soviet Union no longer sees any reason to stand against the West. The Committee leaves the logic of bloc confrontation behind and seeks partnership with the democratic world. For the first time since 1945, Moscow and Washington stand on the same side, and the Iron Curtain begins to lift.

The Soviet Union has become an open society, with free elections, a free press, independent courts and open borders. Sakharov's vision of convergence has become reality, and the country that once frightened the world is now among its most active partners in science and diplomacy. Many problems remain, but they are debated openly rather than hidden behind closed doors.

Roy Medvedev, the historian whose manuscript 'Let History Judge' documented Stalin's crimes, has always believed that socialism and democracy belong together. His Union of Democratic Socialists now governs. It does not want to abolish socialism, but to free it from bureaucracy and dictatorship, in the spirit of the Prague Spring and the reform communists of Western Europe.

Medvedev's central demand is pluralism within socialism. New parties are allowed, provided they accept the socialist foundations of the constitution: social democrats, agrarians, Christian socialists and independent Marxists. The Communist Party must compete for votes like any other. Critics on the right call it a half-measure, while critics on the left call it the beginning of the end.

Medvedev's 'Let History Judge' becomes state policy. The archives are opened, the victims of the purges are rehabilitated by name, and the roles of Stalin, Beria and their accomplices are examined in public. Khrushchev's secret speech of 1956 was only a beginning; now the full truth is spoken. It is painful and unsettling, but the party believes that only honesty can restore its credibility.

Democratic socialism can take many forms, and the government looks westwards for inspiration. Some favour the path of Luigi Longo and Enrico Berlinguer's Italian Communist Party, which combines Marxism with parliamentary democracy and independence from Moscow. Others prefer the Sweden of Olof Palme, a social democracy that has achieved prosperity and equality without revolution. The choice will shape the new Soviet socialism.

The government chooses Rome. Close ties are forged with the Italian and French Communist Parties, which have long sought a democratic road to socialism free of Moscow's tutelage. Together they form a new current within the world communist movement, one that respects elections, civil liberties and national paths. In Western Europe the Soviet Union suddenly appears as an ally of reform rather than its enemy.

The government chooses Stockholm. Following the example of Olof Palme's Sweden, it builds a generous welfare state with comprehensive health insurance, housing programmes, decent pensions and equal opportunities in education. Market mechanisms are tolerated where they serve society, but social justice remains the goal. It is an expensive model, but it creates a broad base of satisfied citizens and social peace.

Socialist democracy must not stop at the factory gates. Workers' councils are elected in every enterprise, with the right to take part in decisions on production, wages and the appointment of managers. The model draws on Yugoslav self-management and West German co-determination. Productivity rises as workers gain a real stake in their enterprises, and the trade unions rediscover their purpose.

The Soviet military absorbs resources that the economy and the consumer urgently need. The government cuts the defence budget, reduces conventional forces in Central Europe and redirects funds to housing, healthcare and consumer goods. The General Staff warns of weakness, but the government is convinced that the greatest threat to socialism is not NATO but the empty shelves of Soviet shops.

Willy Brandt's new eastern policy and Olof Palme's active neutrality show that social democrats in the West are looking for partners in the East. The government offers Bonn and Stockholm a special relationship: political dialogue, trade agreements and cooperation between parties that share the goal of a democratic socialism. The Moscow Treaty of August 1970 could become the start of something much bigger.

The reforms have transformed the Union, but one question remains open. Should socialism stay the fixed foundation of the state, with pluralism only within its boundaries, or should the people be free to choose any path, including a return to capitalism? Medvedev himself is a convinced socialist, but many in his party believe that democracy cannot be limited by any doctrine.

The government decides that democracy will remain socialist. The socialist foundations of the economy stay enshrined in the constitution, and parties that reject them are not admitted to elections. Within these boundaries, debate is free and lively. Supporters see this as the true fulfilment of Lenin's promise of soviet democracy; critics see a democracy with a safety catch.

The government decides that democracy cannot have limits. All restrictions on parties are lifted, including on those that question socialism itself, and the people will decide in free elections which economic and political order they want. It is a bold gamble that could end with the voters rejecting the very socialism the reformers set out to save.

What Alexander Dubcek attempted in Prague in 1968, and what Soviet tanks crushed that August, has now come true in Moscow itself. Socialism has become democratic, open and humane, guided by the will of the people rather than the dictates of a bureaucracy. Eurocommunists in the West look on with admiration, and many in Eastern Europe dare to hope again.

Nikolai Baibakov has led the State Planning Committee since 1965 and knows the Soviet economy better than any member of the Politburo. Now Gosplan itself takes power. The planners have no interest in ideological debates; they want balanced plans, reliable supply chains and efficient investment. The party's political role shrinks, and the country is run like a giant enterprise with Gosplan as its board of directors.

The technocrats have no use for slogans. Marxism-Leninism remains the official doctrine in textbooks and on banners, but it no longer guides decisions. Party secretaries lose their influence over economic questions, ideological commissions are reduced to ceremony and economic necessity becomes the only criterion. Many in the nomenklatura feel the ground slipping beneath their feet.

The method of material balances has been the backbone of Soviet planning since the 1930s: every ton of steel, every kilowatt and every machine must be matched between producers and consumers. Under the technocrats it is refined with computers, input-output tables and the linear programming of Leonid Kantorovich. Shortages and bottlenecks diminish as the plan finally becomes coherent.

The planners must set a long-term strategy. One school wants to make the Union an engineering power that modernises its factories, invests in machine tools and competes on quality. The other wants to exploit the vast oil and gas fields of Western Siberia, discovered at Samotlor and Urengoy in the 1960s, and finance development through raw material exports. Both paths have their price.

The planners choose the path of the engineers. Investment flows into machine building, instrument making, chemistry and electronics, and Soviet industry is equipped with modern machine tools and automated lines. The goal is an economy that lives not from the export of raw materials but from its own technical excellence. It is a long and expensive road, but it promises lasting independence.

The planners choose the path of resources. The oil fields of Western Siberia and the gas fields of the Far North are developed at full speed, pipelines are laid towards Europe and the hard currency they earn pays for imported machinery and grain. The gas-for-pipes agreement signed with West Germany in 1970 is only the beginning. The Union becomes an energy superpower, for better or worse.

The vast territories beyond the Urals hold the Union's future wealth, but they lack roads, railways and towns. The planners launch a series of great Siberian projects: new rail lines, hydroelectric plants on the Angara and Yenisei, and territorial production complexes that combine mining, energy and industry. The costs are enormous, but the planners think in decades rather than five-year plans.

The military-industrial complex consumes the best engineers, materials and factories of the Union, while consumers wait years for a refrigerator. The planners order part of the defence industry converted to civilian production: tank plants turn out tractors, aircraft works build household appliances and missile designers work on consumer electronics. The arms lobby resists, and the transition proves harder than expected.

Ideology has no place in the planners' trade policy. The Union buys and sells wherever conditions are favourable, from West Germany and Japan to the Arab world and Latin America, and perhaps one day even China. Political considerations take a back seat to economic advantage. Foreign trade organisations gain greater autonomy, and Soviet goods appear in markets where they were never seen before.

Gosplan's rule has brought order to the economy, but it rests on neither ideological nor democratic legitimacy. The planners must decide whether to make their rule permanent, as a government of experts without ideology, or to hand political power back to the party, which has kept its structures and members across the whole country. Either way, the planners intend to keep the plan.

The planners decide to stay. Gosplan becomes the supreme organ of state, the party is reduced to a mass organisation for mobilisation and education, and real power rests with economists, engineers and statisticians. The Union becomes a state without ideology, governed by figures and forecasts. It is efficient and stable, but its citizens have no voice in it.

The planners decide that their task is fulfilled. The economy has been put in order, and political leadership returns to the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, which kept its structures and members throughout the technocratic interlude. The new party leadership inherits a stronger economy, and many planners return quietly to their offices in the Gosplan building on Marx Prospect.

The planned society has become reality. Every factory, every city and every resource fits into a coherent system steered from Gosplan, and the old dream of a rationally organised economy has finally been realised. Shortages have become rare and growth steady. Whether this is still the socialism of Lenin or simply the triumph of the engineers is a question the planners do not care to debate.

Alexander Solzhenitsyn, Nobel laureate of 1970 and author of 'One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich', has always demanded one thing above all: never to take part in the lie. His followers now govern the country. Their programme is authoritarian and Orthodox, rejects Marxism as a foreign doctrine and places Russia's spiritual and national recovery above any global mission.

In his Letter to the Soviet Leaders, Solzhenitsyn called on the Kremlin to abandon Marxist ideology, give up the empire, develop the Russian North-East and grant religious and cultural freedom. What was once an unanswered appeal from a persecuted writer is now the programme of government. The party is stripped of its ideological monopoly, and the nomenklatura loses its claim to rule.

Solzhenitsyn believed that Russia's future lay not in foreign adventures but in its own vast and undeveloped North-East. The government turns towards Siberia and the Far East: new settlements, roads and railways open up the land, and its resources are developed carefully for the benefit of the Russian people rather than the arms race. A new frontier opens for a generation in search of purpose.

Solzhenitsyn's followers agree that Russia needs an authoritarian but lawful government for the transition. Some want to build this order on the Orthodox Church as the moral foundation of state and society. Others want to revive the zemstvo, the local self-government created by the reforms of Alexander II, so that Russians learn to govern themselves from the bottom up. The choice will shape the new state.

The government chooses Orthodoxy as the foundation of the new order. The Church becomes the moral authority of the state, religious instruction returns to the schools and the government sees itself as the guardian of Russian spiritual tradition. Firm authority is justified as necessary for a people that must first recover from decades of lies. Dissent, now judged by religious rather than socialist standards, is still not welcome.

The government chooses the zemstvo. Following the model of the 1864 reform, elected local assemblies take over responsibility for schools, roads, hospitals and agriculture in the districts and provinces. Moscow retains authority over the great questions of state, but Russians learn to manage their own affairs locally. The bureaucracy shrinks, and a modest civic life returns to the provinces.

Solzhenitsyn argued that the Union was squandering its strength in Cuba, Vietnam, the Middle East and Eastern Europe while the Russian village decayed. The government ends this policy: aid to distant regimes is cut, military advisers are recalled and the satellites are told they must find their own way. Influence abroad declines, but resources are freed for Russia itself.

The writers of village prose, Valentin Rasputin, Vasily Belov and Vasily Shukshin, have mourned the dying Russian village for years. The government makes its revival a national priority: the Non-Black Earth Zone receives roads, schools and investment, collective farmers gain more freedom over their land, and young families are encouraged to return to the countryside. Russia seeks its roots in its own soil.

In 'Rebuilding Russia' Solzhenitsyn would argue that Russia no longer has the strength to hold the Baltic, the Caucasus and Central Asia against their will. Twenty years earlier, his followers in power reach the same conclusion: better to let these peoples go in peace than to keep spending Russian blood and wealth on an empire that drains its own heartland. Riga, Tbilisi and Tashkent are offered the right to leave.

With the non-Slavic periphery released, a harder question remains: what of Ukraine, Belorussia and the Russian-settled north of Kazakhstan? Solzhenitsyn regards the three East Slavic peoples as branches of a single nation that grew from Kievan Rus. Whether they can be persuaded to stay together with Russia, or whether Russia must learn to stand alone, will define the new state.

Moscow proposes a voluntary union of the Russian, Ukrainian and Belorussian peoples, with Kazakhstan invited to join, bound together by a common faith, history and language rather than by Marxist ideology. Kiev, Minsk and Alma-Ata are free to accept or refuse. If they agree, the old Soviet Union will give way to a smaller and more natural community of kindred nations.

If the Slavic brothers will not come, Russia will not beg. Solzhenitsyn has always insisted that the Russian people must first heal themselves, and a Russia within her own borders, free of imperial burdens, may yet prove stronger than the sprawling Union ever was. The RSFSR turns inward to rebuild its villages, its churches and its conscience.

In his 1973 essay 'Repentance and Self-Limitation in the Life of Nations', Solzhenitsyn called on Russia to acknowledge the crimes of the Soviet era and to turn away from external expansion toward inner development. The state now adopts this creed as its own: modest ambitions abroad, moral renewal at home and a quiet return to the Orthodox faith and the Russian land.

The men who truly run the Soviet economy sit not in the Politburo but in the director's offices of the great combines and ministries. Backed by Interior Minister Nikolai Shchelokov and his MVD, the red directors step out of the shadows and take the reins of government, promising efficiency and prosperity while quietly securing their own share of the people's property.

Underground workshops, unrecorded production lines and networks of blat have kept Soviet shelves from emptying for decades. Instead of hunting the tsekhoviki and speculators, the new leadership brings them into the light and taxes what was once prosecuted. Critics call it the legalisation of theft; the directors call it realism, and the shadow economy has never been so confident.

Nikolai Shchelokov has turned the Ministry of Internal Affairs into a power base to rival the KGB, with its own troops, its own informants and its own share of the shadow economy. Under the directors' rule the militsiya becomes the backbone of the state, guarding order on the streets and the interests of its patrons in the ministries.

Two visions of the directors' state compete. The Moscow nomenklatura wants to convert its offices into ownership, turning ministries into holding companies. The republican clans of Tashkent, Baku and Alma-Ata prefer the old ways of patronage, tribute and family loyalty. The directors must decide whose hands will hold the wealth of the Union.

Ministers become chairmen, departments become concerns, and the officials who once managed state property quietly acquire it. Two decades before it happened historically, the nomenklatura privatises the Soviet economy from within, trading Party cards for share certificates. Productivity may rise, but ordinary citizens begin to ask who now owns the factories they were told belonged to them.

In the republics, power has long rested on networks of kinship and patronage, from Sharaf Rashidov's Uzbekistan to Dinmukhamed Kunaev's Kazakhstan. Rather than fight these clans, Moscow embraces them: loyal republican bosses receive a free hand and a share of the spoils in exchange for keeping their fiefdoms quiet. Corruption deepens, but the Union holds together.

Uzbek cotton and Caspian caviar are worth their weight in hard currency, and both have long been skimmed through padded harvest reports and smuggling rings. The directors stop pretending otherwise and organise these trades for export, channelling the proceeds through friendly hands. The cotton scandal that would historically shake the Party in the 1980s becomes a business model instead.

Gosbank alone cannot serve the needs of the new economic masters. Enterprise funds and ministry accounts are pooled into commercial banks owned by the directors themselves, lending to friends, financing deals and moving money between the official and the shadow economy. Moscow gains its first modern office blocks, and with them a new class of Soviet bankers.

The directors know that what the Party gives, the Party can take away. Through Vneshtorgbank, foreign trade missions and front companies in Vienna and Zurich, hard currency flows quietly into private accounts abroad. It is insurance against the next purge, paid for by the Soviet treasury, and it strengthens the shadow economy at the expense of public trust.

The factories have new masters, the banks new owners and the republics new lords. Now the directors must decide what kind of state will protect their gains: an openly governed corporate republic run by managers and bankers, or a populist order that buys social peace with generous handouts. The answer will settle who really owns the Soviet Union.

The directors drop the pretence that the Party still governs. Enterprise managers, bankers and ministry chiefs take their seats as the true ruling council of the land, and the state is run like a holding company answerable to its largest shareholders. Profits flow upward, and the language of class struggle gives way to the language of balance sheets.

A regime of directors cannot rely on ideology or terror, so it relies on generosity. Higher wages, fuller shops, new flats and better pensions are handed out to keep the workers grateful and quiet while the elite enriches itself. It is an expensive bargain, but the directors calculate that contentment is cheaper than unrest.

The Soviet Union completes its quiet metamorphosis into a corporate state. The great combines, banks and trading houses now form the skeleton of the country, owned by those who once merely managed them, and the hammer and sickle survives mostly on letterheads. Efficient and profitable, the Corporate Union is also a land where wealth and power belong to very few.

A cabinet of young economists around Nikolai Shmelyov, the man who would one day write that the Soviet economy lives on advances and debts, takes office with a radical mandate. Their diagnosis is blunt: the planned economy cannot be repaired, only replaced. Markets, prices and private initiative are to achieve what Gosplan never could, whatever the cost in stability.

For decades the state has fixed the price of everything from bread to tractors, and since 1969 a State Committee on Prices has guarded the system, leaving shortages, queues and a thriving black market. The new government abolishes administered prices in one stroke. Shelves will fill again, but for many families the price of a loaf will rise faster than their wages.

The Soviet rouble has never been a real currency abroad, its official rate a fiction maintained by Gosbank and the foreign trade monopoly. Making it convertible would tie the Union to world markets, open the door to foreign trade and expose every inefficient enterprise to honest prices. Western bankers are intrigued; the old guard of the Ministry of Foreign Trade is appalled.

The reformers agree on the destination but not on the speed. One camp argues for a single decisive leap, liberalising everything at once before the bureaucracy can regroup. The other warns that a society raised on guaranteed jobs and fixed prices cannot survive such a jolt and urges a gradual transition. The cabinet must choose its pace.

Everything at once: prices, trade and enterprises are released in a single blow, as Russia would attempt two decades later in another timeline. The reformers bet that the pain will be sharp but short and that a functioning market will rise from the wreckage of the plan. Factories close, savings evaporate and the streets grow restless, but there is no turning back.

The cabinet chooses caution over speed. Markets are introduced sector by sector, beginning with services, light industry and agriculture, while heavy industry and basic prices remain under state control for now. Much as Hungary's reformers have done since 1968, the transition is meant to grow out of the plan rather than tear it down, buying time and public patience.

Two decades before Russia historically tried it, every Soviet citizen receives a voucher, a paper share in the national wealth that can be exchanged for stock in the enterprises being sold off. The idea is to make the people owners and to break the grip of the nomenklatura on state property. Whether workers keep their shares or sell them to the shrewdest bidders remains to be seen.

Fiat helped build the great car plant at Togliatti; now the whole Union is open for business. Western firms are invited to set up joint ventures, buy into Soviet enterprises and lend to the state, with legal guarantees that their property will not be nationalised. The capital and technology are badly needed, though the foreign debt that comes with them may one day weigh heavily on Moscow.

The planned economy is gone. Prices are set by supply and demand, enterprises answer to owners and customers, and the rouble trades on world markets. The Union that Lenin founded has become something its founders would hardly recognise: a market economy still flying the red flag, prosperous for some, bewildering for many and irreversibly changed.

Scientists, writers and engineers who have spent years defending Lake Baikal against the planners now find themselves in power. Inspired by the limnologist Grigory Galazy of the Limnological Institute in Irkutsk, the new cabinet declares that the Soviet people must stop conquering nature and start protecting it. Every gigantic project of Gosplan will be judged by a new measure: what it costs the land.

Since 1966 the Baikalsk Pulp and Paper Mill has poured its waste into the deepest and oldest lake on Earth, home to the nerpa seal and hundreds of species found nowhere else. Scientists and writers across the Union have protested for years. The new government finally orders the mill closed, placing the purity of Baikal above the plan's demand for cellulose.

Soviet planners dream of reversing the great Siberian rivers, sending the waters of the Ob and Irtysh south through a vast canal to irrigate the cotton fields of Central Asia. Ecologists warn of flooded forests, a changed Arctic climate and drowned villages. The project is cancelled, to the relief of Siberia and the dismay of the Central Asian republics that counted on its water.

The Friends of Baikal must decide what kind of movement they are. Some see ecology as the fulfilment of socialism, a planned economy that finally plans for the planet as well as for output. Others simply want to shield nature from industry, whatever the ideology, through strict laws and vast reserves. The choice will shape the green Union to come.

Planning, the reformers argue, is the perfect tool for ecology if only it aims at the right targets. Gosplan is ordered to account for clean water, forests and air alongside steel and grain, and the Party preaches harmony between man and nature as a socialist virtue. Consumers may wait a little longer for their goods, but their children will inherit a living land.

The Soviet Union already has its strict nature reserves, some dating back to Lenin's time, but they have long been sacrificed to mines and logging. Now conservation comes first: new reserves are founded, mining is bound by tough environmental rules and no project may proceed without an ecological review. Nature, not output, becomes the first concern of the state.

Fed by the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, the Aral Sea is already shrinking as Soviet cotton farms drink up its rivers. Hydrologists warn that within a generation it could become a salt desert poisoning Karakalpakstan and Kazakhstan. By curbing irrigation and restoring river flows, Moscow tries to save the sea and wins the gratitude of the peoples who live along its shores.

Since 1949 the steppe near Semipalatinsk in Kazakhstan has been the main Soviet nuclear test site, scarred by hundreds of explosions whose fallout has sickened the surrounding villages. Closing the Polygon is a gesture of respect to the Kazakh people and a signal of goodwill to the world, though the generals and the weapons designers protest bitterly at losing their proving ground.

The RBMK, pride of Soviet nuclear engineering, is cheap to build and can be scaled to enormous size, and the first units are rising at Leningrad. Yet some physicists warn of a dangerous design flaw that could make the reactor run away under the wrong conditions. Heeding them means slower construction and less power, but it may spare a town called Chernobyl a terrible fate.

The Soviet Union becomes the first great power to place ecology at the heart of its state ideology. Clean rivers, protected forests and renewable power replace gigantomania as symbols of national pride, and Lake Baikal stands as the emblem of a new relationship between people and land. Abroad, the Green Union offers the world an unexpected vision of what socialism can become.

Alexander Yakovlev, acting head of the Central Committee's propaganda department, has long believed that socialism can be both efficient and humane. With his allies in power, the Soviet Union looks to Budapest and Belgrade rather than to its own dogmas, promising markets within a planned framework, more freedom for enterprises and less fear for citizens: socialism with a human face.

Fifteen years before Gorbachev made it a watchword, the government embraces glasnost. The censors of Glavlit loosen their grip, newspapers may criticise mismanagement and banned writers return to the pages of Novy Mir. Scientists and engineers welcome the freer exchange of ideas, while the guardians of ideology warn that once people are allowed to speak, they may never stop.

Instead of prosecuting the shadow economy, the reformers give it a legal form. Citizens may now found cooperatives, small collectively owned businesses running cafes, workshops, repair shops and taxis, as the Law on Cooperation would only allow in 1988 historically. The black market shrinks, services finally appear and a new class of socialist entrepreneurs is born.

Two models of reformed socialism lie to the west. Tito's Yugoslavia entrusts its factories to workers' councils that elect managers and share profits. Kádár's Hungary keeps state ownership but frees enterprises to respond to prices and profits under the New Economic Mechanism of 1968. Moscow must decide which experiment to follow on a continental scale.

Following the Yugoslav example, Soviet enterprises are handed to the people who work in them. Elected workers' councils appoint directors, set wages and decide how to invest their profits, while the trade unions gain real influence for the first time since the 1920s. Belgrade welcomes Moscow's late conversion to its heresy, and the Soviet worker becomes a co-owner in fact as well as in slogans.

Hungary's New Economic Mechanism, designed by Rezső Nyers and launched in 1968, keeps the factories in state hands but lets them trade, set many of their own prices and keep their profits. Moscow adopts the model for the whole Union, replacing thousands of plan targets with a few broad guidelines. Kádár's quiet goulash communism becomes the blueprint for a superpower.

A socialism that can compete need not hide behind walls. Trade barriers come down, joint ventures with Western firms are encouraged and Soviet scientists, artists and tourists travel abroad more freely. Detente gains a new depth as the West discovers a Soviet Union more interested in exchange than in confrontation, and tensions between the blocs begin to ease.

The Union has always been federal on paper and centralist in practice. The reformers take the constitution at its word, transferring real powers over budgets, culture and local industry from the Moscow ministries to the fifteen union republics. National elites gain a stake in the reformed Union, and the old charge of Russian domination loses some of its sting.

Market socialism has transformed the Soviet economy, but its architects disagree on where to stop. One faction wants to keep the commanding heights in public hands, with markets serving a socialist plan. The other argues that half-measures breed stagnation and that private property must be allowed to grow alongside the state. The reformers must decide how far the market may go.

The reform stops at the gates of private ownership. Enterprises compete, prices move and managers answer for profits, but the land, the banks and the great industries remain the property of society. It is a balance that Lenin's New Economic Policy once struck and Stalin abolished, now restored as the permanent foundation of Soviet socialism.

The reformers go further than any socialist state before them. Private businesses may grow beyond family workshops, foreign capital may own shares and the state keeps only the strategic industries in its hands. Purists in the Party denounce a betrayal of October, but the result resembles the mixed economies of Western Europe more than anything Marx described.

The Socialist Market Commonwealth is complete: a voluntary association of reformed republics bound by a common market, shared institutions and a socialism that has learned to trust its citizens. The Soviet Union has become what the Prague reformers dreamed of in 1968, a state where economic freedom and social justice coexist. Whether the world believes it is another matter.

Pyotr Shelest, First Secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine, has long defended the language, culture and economic interests of his republic against Moscow's centralism. With his allies now leading the Union, a new idea takes hold: national communism, in which each republic builds socialism in its own way within a loose union of sovereign Soviet states.

The Treaty of 1922 that created the Soviet Union is to be replaced by a new compact among equals. Each union republic is invited to sign, gaining wider powers over its economy, language and internal affairs while remaining within a common state. It is the bargain Gorbachev would offer too late in 1991, proposed while the Union is still strong enough to make it work.

Named after Shelest's 1970 book 'O Ukraine, Our Soviet Land', this programme celebrates Ukraine as a full partner in the Union rather than a province of Moscow. The Ukrainian language returns to schools, universities and publishing houses, Cossack history is honoured and Kiev gains a greater say over the republic's coal, steel and grain. Ukrainians answer with growing loyalty to the reformed Union.

The national communists disagree on the shape of the new Union. Some want every republic, from Estonia to Tajikistan, to follow its own road to socialism as an equal partner. Others believe the Union needs a new core and look to an axis between Moscow and Kiev, with Ukraine as the second pillar of the federation. Shelest's followers must choose.

Lenin's policy of korenizatsiya, the rooting of Soviet power in each nation's own language and cadres, is revived after decades of Russification. Every republic is free to adapt socialism to its own traditions, from the collective farms of the Baltic to the cotton fields of Uzbekistan. The Union becomes a family of distinct nations rather than a single Soviet people.

Russia and Ukraine together form the heart of the Union, and the national communists propose to make this partnership explicit. Kiev becomes a second capital, Ukrainian cadres take a larger share of leading posts in Moscow and the two largest republics jointly steer the federation. The smaller republics grumble at a new dual hegemony, but the Union gains a firmer core.

Republican governments take control of the enterprises on their territory, much as Khrushchev's regional economic councils, the sovnarkhozy, attempted in 1957. The ministries in Moscow lose their grip, and local planners who know their own resources can finally act without waiting for permission. Productivity rises as each republic competes to show what it can achieve on its own.

During the Great Patriotic War the Red Army fielded national divisions raised in the republics, until they were quietly disbanded after the victory. The national communists revive the idea: each republic raises formations of its own citizens, commanded in their own languages but sworn to the common defence. The army grows, and so does the republics' sense of ownership in it.

The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics gives way to a Commonwealth of Soviet States, a voluntary association of sovereign socialist nations sharing a common defence, currency and market. Unlike the hasty Commonwealth of Independent States of 1991, it is built while trust between the republics still exists. Nationalist passions cool, for every nation now has its own state within the family.

Within the Party apparatus an informal current has grown that values Russian tradition above Marxist internationalism. Its patron is Politburo member Dmitry Polyansky, its voice the journal Molodaya Gvardiya, and its supporters reach from the Komsomol to the Writers' Union. Now the 'Russian Party' steps into the open, determined to put the Russian people first in the state they built.

Under its editor Anatoly Nikonov, Molodaya Gvardiya has printed essays praising the Russian village, the Orthodox heritage and the national spirit, drawing fierce condemnation from Party liberals. Its line now becomes official policy: the press, the publishing houses and the Komsomol are encouraged to promote Russian patriotism, and the guardians of ideology learn to speak of the nation as readily as of class.

The village prose of Vasily Belov and Valentin Rasputin mourns the dying Russian countryside, its churches in ruins and its young people fleeing to the cities. The Russian Party makes the revival of the Non-Black Earth Zone a national priority, pouring money into roads, housing and machinery for the old Russian heartland that collectivisation left behind.

The Russian Party is united in its love of Russia but divided over her past. The red wing honours the Soviet state as the latest form of Russian greatness and seeks to fuse Bolshevism with national pride. The white wing looks further back, to Orthodoxy, old Russia and the faith that sustained the people before 1917. One vision must prevail.

The ideas of Nikolai Ustryalov, who saw in Bolshevism a new incarnation of the Russian state, find fresh followers. The Soviet Union is presented as the heir to a thousand years of Russian history and the Party as its rightful guardian. Communist symbols and Russian patriotism merge into a single creed of red greatness that appeals to soldiers and workers alike.

The white wing of the Russian Party wins out. The persecution of the Church ends, the Moscow Patriarchate gains a voice in public life and restored churches ring their bells again across Russia. Faith is recast as the soul of the nation and the Church becomes a pillar of the state, an arrangement unthinkable to the militantly atheist Party of only a few years before.

Every union republic has its own Communist Party except the largest, Russia, whose affairs are run directly by the all-Union apparatus. The Russian Party demands an end to this anomaly and founds a Communist Party of the RSFSR with its own Central Committee. Russians gain an institution of their own, while the other republics fear it as a rival centre of power.

Russia, Ukraine and Belorussia share a common origin in Kievan Rus, and the Russian Party wants their bond to be closer than that with any other republic. Kiev and Minsk are offered a privileged partnership: deeper integration with Russia in exchange for continued autonomy and respect for their own languages. The Slavic core is meant to become the unbreakable heart of the state.

The Soviet Army is honoured as the heir of Suvorov and Kutuzov, of Borodino and Stalingrad, and its traditions are tied ever more openly to Russian history. Officers are told they defend Russia first and ideology second, and the General Staff welcomes the new prestige and budget. A proud army, the Russian Party believes, is the backbone of a great power.

The Russian Party faces its oldest dilemma. Should Russia hold the Union together as an empire, carrying the burden of the borderlands for the sake of greatness? Or should she shed the periphery and become a compact nation-state, spending her strength on her own people? Imperial patriots and the followers of Solzhenitsyn give opposite answers, and the Party must choose.

Russia chooses greatness. The Union is to be held together at any price, its borderlands bound to Moscow by Russian settlers, the Russian language and Russian bayonets. The patriotic press speaks of a historic mission, and the militsiya grows to keep the realm secure. The empire endures, but its peoples are reminded daily who is the elder brother.

Russia chooses herself. The costly subsidies to the borderlands are cut, the republics are allowed to drift toward independence and the state concentrates on the Russian lands, from Smolensk to Vladivostok. Many imperial patriots call it a betrayal, but ordinary Russians welcome a government that finally spends the nation's wealth at home.

The Russian Party completes its programme.
