Soviet achievement and Russian tradition, the space rockets and the onion domes, the victory of 1945 and the memory of Kutuzov stand side by side in a new national synthesis. Great Russia is confident, patriotic and proud of her thousand-year history, and her people believe once more that they are destined to shape the world.

From the shadows of the Union, a clandestine committee of embittered officers, writers and officials has prepared for this hour. Rejecting both communism and the West, they promise the national rebirth of a Russian people they believe has been betrayed by internationalists and bureaucrats. Their rule begins with emergency decrees, closed borders and a hunt for enemies within.

Power is placed in the hands of a State Committee for the National Emergency, a collective body that answers to no Congress and no Politburo. Ministers are dismissed, Party officials arrested and the old nomenklatura stripped of its privileges overnight. The committee rules by decree, and the fear it inspires in the elite is matched by the hope it awakens among the angry and the dispossessed.

The Committee declares that a reborn nation must be an armed nation. Military spending climbs, reserve call-ups are extended, and schools, factories and youth organisations are reorganised along military lines. Every citizen is told that the motherland faces enemies on every side, and the whole country begins to take on the look of a vast barracks.

The leaders of the Committee agree that Russia has been humiliated, but not on how to restore her pride. One faction wants to seal the borders and build an autarkic fortress, immune to Western influence and self-sufficient in everything. The other dreams of revenge and of reclaiming lost influence by force. The direction of the rebirth must now be decided.

The borders close. Foreign trade is reduced to what is strictly necessary, Western radio is jammed more heavily than ever and unauthorised contact with foreigners becomes a crime. Behind its walls the nation is to produce everything it needs and defend every inch of its soil. Fortress Russia trades prosperity for a security its rulers consider absolute.

The Committee speaks openly of revenge for every retreat and every humiliation the Russian nation has suffered. Troops move toward the frontiers, military doctrine turns to the offensive and the propaganda machine prepares the population for war. The world watches with alarm as Moscow rattles its sabre louder than at any time since the Cuban crisis.

The national rebirth is enshrined as the permanent order of the state. A collective dictatorship of the Committee rules over a disciplined, militarised and inward-looking society in which loyalty to the nation outweighs every other value. Scientists and artists chafe under the new orthodoxy, but the regime has achieved what it set out to do: a Russia remade in its own image.

Defence Minister Marshal Andrei Grechko and the senior commanders of the Soviet Armed Forces have lost patience with the quarrelling civilians of the Politburo. Backed by the military districts and the General Staff, they assume direct control of the state through a Council of Marshals. The Party is not abolished, but for the first time since the Revolution it takes its orders from the army.

The General Staff, long called the brain of the army, becomes the brain of the state. Its officers take over ministries and planning bodies, applying the methods of military staff work to the economy and the administration. Decisions are made faster and orders followed more strictly, but civilian expertise is pushed aside in favour of the soldier's way of thinking.

The marshals bring the values of the barracks to civilian life. Absenteeism, drunkenness at work and petty theft are punished severely, corrupt officials face military tribunals and the black marketeers find their protectors gone. Ordinary citizens grumble at the harsh new rules, yet many admit that the trains run on time and the shops are less empty than before.

The officer corps is split between generations. The old marshals who fought from Moscow to Berlin trust in mass armies, vast reserves and the lessons of 1945. Younger reformers around Nikolai Ogarkov, first deputy chief of the General Staff, foresee a revolution in warfare driven by computers, precision weapons and automated command. The Council must decide whose vision will guide the army.

Ogarkov's vision prevails. Military research institutes receive priority funding for electronics, computers and automated command and control, and the army begins to plan for a war fought with reconnaissance-strike complexes rather than endless waves of tanks. The West will one day call it the revolution in military affairs; the Soviet Union now intends to lead it.

The veterans of the Great Patriotic War keep their grip on the army. Their faith lies in mass, in the deep reserves of the Soviet people and in the armoured fists that once broke the Wehrmacht. Conscription is widened, reserve divisions are filled and the army prepares to fight the next war as it won the last, with numbers, steel and endurance.

The Soviet economy has always served the army first, but under the marshals the defence industry takes direct control of the plan. The Military-Industrial Commission sets priorities for the ministries, new arms plants rise in the Urals and Siberia, and civilian production is subordinated to the needs of defence. Tanks roll off the lines while the shops wait their turn.

The Defence Council of the USSR, once a secretive body chaired by the General Secretary, becomes the supreme organ of state power. Military planning, foreign policy and the economy are now coordinated in a single room by the marshals and their chosen civilians. Decisions that once took months of Politburo bargaining are taken in a single sitting.

The Strategic Rocket Forces, the youngest and most prestigious branch of the Soviet military, receive the full backing of the marshals. New generations of heavy intercontinental missiles are ordered from the design bureaus of Mikhail Yangel and Vladimir Chelomei, and silos multiply across the steppe. The Council intends to negotiate with Washington from a position of overwhelming strength, whatever the cost to detente.

Military rule was meant to be temporary, a remedy for a crisis the civilians could not handle. Now the marshals face the question every junta eventually confronts. Some argue that order has been restored and the army should return power to the Party before politics corrupts it. Others believe the country needs the soldiers' firm hand indefinitely.

Their task complete, the marshals hand power back to the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and return to their headquarters. The army keeps its prestige and a powerful voice in matters of defence, but the principle of Party control over the military is restored. The soldiers have shown that they can rule, and the Party will not forget it.

During the Great Patriotic War the Stavka of the Supreme High Command directed the entire Soviet war effort. The marshals now make it a permanent institution of peacetime government, a supreme headquarters that commands not only armies but ministries and republics. The Soviet Union becomes a state permanently organised for war, whether war comes or not.

The rule of the marshals hardens into a lasting order. Every region is a military district, every factory a potential arsenal and every citizen a soldier in reserve. Shielded by its nuclear arsenal and its vast armies, the Garrison State offers its people security and discipline in place of freedom, and the world must reckon with a superpower ruled by its generals.

Few would have believed it possible: in a Soviet Union shaken by crisis, the head of the House of Romanov, Grand Duke Vladimir Kirillovich, is invited back from exile in Madrid. Born in Finland in 1917 and raised in emigration, he has never seen the Russia he claims. Monarchists, nationalists and many weary citizens now look to him as the symbol of a lost continuity.

For the first time since 1896, a Russian emperor is crowned in the Dormition Cathedral of the Moscow Kremlin. The ancient regalia are brought out of the Armoury, the bells of Ivan the Great ring out and crowds fill Red Square, some in joy, some in disbelief. Whatever the future holds, the coronation of Vladimir Kirillovich marks a break with more than half a century of Soviet history.

Tsar and Patriarch were once the twin pillars of Holy Russia, and the restored monarchy seeks to rebuild that alliance. The Moscow Patriarchate is freed from Soviet supervision, its seminaries and monasteries reopen and plans are drawn up to rebuild the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. The Church in turn blesses the crown and calls on the faithful to support it.

What kind of monarchy will Russia have? Liberal monarchists point to the State Duma of 1906 and to the constitutional crowns of Britain and Scandinavia. Traditionalists insist that only an autocrat, ruling by the grace of God as the tsars once did, can hold the vast country together after decades of upheaval. The Grand Duke and his advisers must settle the question.

The emperor reigns but does not rule. A new State Duma is elected by the people, a constitution guarantees civil rights and the government answers to parliament. Russia picks up the thread of the reforms of 1905 that war and revolution cut short, and Western capitals watch with fascination as the largest country on Earth becomes a parliamentary monarchy.

The old formula of Orthodoxy, Autocracy and Nationality is revived. The emperor rules with full authority, assisted by ministers he alone appoints, and the Soviet instruments of control are turned to the service of the throne. Supporters see a return to the natural order of Russian life; opponents note that the new autocracy relies on the same secret police as the old dictatorship.

In Paris, Berlin, Belgrade, New York and Buenos Aires, the descendants of the White emigration have kept Russian culture alive in exile for half a century. Now they are invited home. Engineers, scholars, priests and businessmen return with knowledge, capital and connections abroad, and Russia rediscovers a part of herself that the Revolution scattered across the world.

The restored monarchy inherits fifteen union republics that owe no loyalty to a Russian tsar. Georgians, Balts and Central Asians watch the coronation with suspicion, and many remember the old empire as a prison of nations. The crown offers the republics broad self-government under the dynasty, but some prefer to drift away rather than kneel before a Romanov.

The Romanovs are bound by blood to nearly every royal house in Europe, and the Grand Duke has lived for years in Madrid. His envoys now call on Buckingham Palace and on Prince Juan Carlos, seeking recognition of the restored crown. For London and Madrid, embracing a Russian emperor would be a remarkable gesture, and a useful wedge between Moscow and its communist past.

The double-headed eagle flies once again over the Kremlin. The Russian Empire, abolished in 1917, has risen from the ruins of the Soviet experiment, with a Romanov on the throne and the Church at his side. It is a different empire from the one Nicholas II lost, shaped by decades of Soviet industry and education, but it claims the same thousand-year inheritance.

Gosplan, the State Planning Committee under Nikolai Baibakov, sets the targets for every factory, mine and collective farm from the Baltic to the Pacific. Millions of products, prices and deliveries must be balanced on paper before a single tonne of steel is poured. Strengthening the authority of the planners and the discipline of the five-year plans is the first step towards mastering the economy.

The Eighth Five-Year Plan, covering 1966 to 1970, is the most successful of the post-war era. Industrial output and real incomes grow at a pace no later plan will match, helped by Kosygin's reforms and the opening of Siberian resources. Now its final year must be completed with honour: unfinished factories commissioned, targets reported as fulfilled and the foundations laid for the next plan.

Since 1965 Premier Alexei Kosygin's reform has judged enterprises by sales and profit rather than gross output, rewarded workers with bonuses and granted managers more autonomy. Since the Prague Spring of 1968, however, the Politburo views any loosening of central control with suspicion, and the ministries are quietly rolling the reform back. Should the Kosygin reform be deepened, or allowed to fade away?

Kosygin and his economists argue that the reform has failed not because it went too far but because it never went far enough. Enterprises should keep a larger share of their profits, draw up more of their own plans and answer to their customers rather than to the ministries. The branch ministries and much of the nomenklatura resist, but the Premier is determined to give Soviet industry the incentives it lacks.

Under full khozraschyot, or economic accounting, Soviet enterprises must cover their costs from their own revenues instead of relying on endless subsidies from the state budget. Profitable factories may reinvest and reward their workers, while loss-making ones face pressure to modernise or merge. For managers it means freedom; for the trade unions it raises the spectre of lost jobs and harder work.

Since 1968 Janos Kadar's Hungary has quietly experimented with its New Economic Mechanism, combining central planning with market prices, enterprise autonomy and a modest private sector. Hungarian shops are full while Soviet shelves stand empty. Instead of viewing Budapest with suspicion, Moscow could send its economists to study what works and adapt the lessons to Soviet conditions, and win the gratitude of a loyal ally in the process.

Behind the facade of the planned economy lies a vast second economy of private tailors, mechanics, builders and traders, tolerated because everyone depends on it. Legalising small cooperatives would bring these activities into the open, generate tax revenue and fill the gaps the state cannot. For the nomenklatura, who profit from the shadows, it means the end of lucrative privileges, and they will not forgive it.

In 1962 the cybernetician Viktor Glushkov proposes OGAS, a nationwide automated system linking every enterprise to regional computing centres and to Gosplan in Moscow. In 1970 the Politburo shelves the plan, wary of its cost and of the transparency it would bring. What if the leadership decides otherwise and entrusts the planned economy to computers and mathematics instead of paperwork and guesswork?

The first regional computing centres are online, and data from the factories begins to reach Moscow in hours instead of months. Now the network must be extended across the Union, connecting thousands of enterprises, ministries and planning offices into a single information system. If Glushkov's vision succeeds, the Soviet Union will possess the most advanced planning apparatus in the world.

Leonid Kantorovich, the father of linear programming, has argued for decades that optimal prices can be calculated mathematically to allocate scarce resources efficiently. His work will earn him the Nobel Prize in Economics, yet at home his ideas remain suspect as a disguised theory of the market. Adopting objectively determined valuations could bring rationality to the arbitrary prices of the planned economy.

From Kiev and Minsk to Tallinn, Tbilisi and Tashkent, each union republic receives its own computing centre and institute of cybernetics. Local engineers and mathematicians train on Soviet machines, process regional statistics and write software for their industries. The project spreads modern skills beyond Moscow and Leningrad and gives the republics a stake in the scientific future of the Union.

Khrushchev's regional economic councils, the sovnarkhozy, have been abolished and the centralised branch ministries restored. Each ministry once again commands its own empire of factories, research institutes and supply networks from Moscow. The ministers regain their power and the apparatus its order, but every ministry guards its own interests, and coordination between the branches suffers.

As the economy grows more complex, new all-union ministries are created for instrument-making, mineral fertilisers, the gas industry and other specialised branches. Each brings expertise, investment and a direct line to the Council of Ministers. Each also brings new departments, new officials and new paperwork, adding further layers to an already formidable bureaucracy.

No plan can foresee every missing bolt or delayed cable. Every Soviet enterprise therefore relies on its tolkachi, the 'pushers' who travel the country with favours, bribes and bottles of cognac to obtain the materials the official supply system fails to deliver. They are illegal in spirit yet indispensable in practice, keeping the factories running at the price of an ever-growing culture of informal deals.

Red banners, honour boards and socialist competition between brigades: the Party mobilises the workforce to fulfil and overfulfil the plan. Shock workers are celebrated in Pravda, model collectives receive medals and the best enterprises are entered in the books of labour glory. The campaigns raise output and morale, even if the reported figures sometimes owe more to creativity than to production.

The Ninth Five-Year Plan, covering 1971 to 1975, is adopted by the XXIV Party Congress. For the first time the planners promise that consumer goods will grow faster than heavy industry, while the armed forces press for their own share of investment. The leadership must decide where the priorities of the coming five years truly lie.

Soviet planners divide industry into Group A, the means of production, and Group B, the consumer goods. The Ninth Plan promises for the first time that Group B will grow faster, bringing more clothing, furniture, shoes and household goods to Soviet families. Turning this promise into reality demands investment and attention that the defence industry would rather keep for itself.

The five-storey Khrushchyovka is giving way to a new generation of prefabricated housing. Panel blocks of nine to sixteen storeys, with lifts, larger kitchens and separate bathrooms, rise in vast new districts on the edges of every Soviet city. Millions of families leave their communal apartments for flats of their own, and the housing programme becomes one of the most visible achievements of the era.

A refrigerator in the kitchen and a television in the living room: for Soviet families of the 1970s these are the symbols of a modern life. Factories in Minsk, Moscow and Lvov expand their output of household appliances, and the first colour sets begin to replace black and white. Every new appliance proves that socialism can deliver comfort as well as steel.

The classic Soviet doctrine is clear: heavy industry first, for without machines, steel and energy there can be no consumer goods tomorrow. The planners direct investment towards new plants, power stations and metallurgical combines, accepting that the shop shelves will remain sparse for now. It is the proven path of the first five-year plans, and many in Gosplan see no reason to abandon it.

Magnitogorsk in the Urals, built around a mountain of iron ore during the first five-year plans, remains the symbol of Soviet metallurgy, while the Cherepovets works near the Rybinsk Reservoir is among the most modern steel plants in the country. Expanding both secures the steel on which every other branch of industry depends, from the shipyards of Leningrad to the tractor plants of the Volga.

Machine-building is the heart of every industrial economy, yet Soviet factories still work with ageing lathes and outdated equipment. Prioritising machine tools, precision engineering and automation would raise productivity across all sectors and reduce dependence on imports from the West. Engineers and designers receive new resources, and the factories of Leningrad, Kharkov and Sverdlovsk lead the way.

With the strategic balance against the United States at stake, the Military-Industrial Commission demands absolute priority for the defence sector. New arms plants, design bureaux and test ranges receive the best engineers and the scarcest materials. The marshals and the defence industry welcome the decision, while Soviet consumers once again learn to wait.

The Soviet defence industry is organised into nine ministries, from Medium Machine-Building, which builds the nuclear arsenal, to aviation, shipbuilding, radio and electronics. Each runs its own closed cities, schools, hospitals and research institutes, forming a state within the state. Coordinating them more tightly under the Military-Industrial Commission promises to make the Soviet arsenal cheaper and more efficient to produce.

Tank plants that build refrigerators, missile factories that turn out vacuum cleaners and aircraft works that produce washing machines: the defence industry is ordered to dedicate part of its capacity to civilian goods. The quality is often poor and the designs plain, but the products do reach the shops. It is an imperfect answer to chronic shortages, yet better than none at all.

On 19 April 1970 the first VAZ-2101 rolls off the assembly line in Togliatti, built under licence from Fiat on the banks of the Volga. The Zhiguli, sold abroad as the Lada, is meant to bring the private car within reach of ordinary Soviet families. Completing the giant Volga Automobile Plant would turn the dream of a car of one's own into reality for millions.

In Naberezhnye Chelny on the Kama River, a vast new truck plant is rising, equipped with machine tools bought from the United States, West Germany, France and Italy. Once completed, the KamAZ works will produce heavy lorries for the national economy and the army alike, replacing the ageing vehicles that slow down Soviet transport. It is one of the great construction projects of the decade.

Soviet retail prices have barely moved in years, while production costs keep rising and the state subsidises meat, bread and milk at ever greater expense. Economists warn that artificial prices feed shortages and the black market. Yet the memory of the bloody strikes in Novocherkassk after the price rises of 1962 still haunts the leadership. Should the state dare to touch prices again?

Honest prices would close the gap between what goods cost to produce and what citizens pay for them, draining the black market of its lifeblood and filling the state budget. The reform will be deeply unpopular: queues may turn into protests, and the trade unions will bristle. But without it, the Soviet economy cannot hope to balance supply and demand.

Stable prices are part of the unwritten social contract between the Party and the people. A loaf of bread is to cost the same in 1980 as it did in 1955, whatever the burden on the state budget. Shelves may be empty and queues long, but no Soviet citizen will see the price of essentials rise under this leadership.

Soviet computing stands at a crossroads. One option is to copy IBM's System/360, gaining instant access to Western software and a common standard for the entire Eastern Bloc. The other is to keep developing indigenous architectures such as Sergei Lebedev's BESM series, slower to mature but independent of Western designs. The decision will shape Soviet computing for decades.

The leadership decides to build the Unified System of Electronic Computers, known as Ryad, as a functional copy of the IBM System/360. Together with Comecon partners in East Germany, Hungary, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Bulgaria, Soviet factories can quickly produce compatible machines and run Western software. The price is the gradual withering of the original Soviet design schools.

Sergei Lebedev's Institute of Precision Mechanics and Computer Engineering has created the BESM line, among the most capable computers outside the United States. Instead of copying IBM, the Soviet Union continues to invest in its own architecture, its own software and its own engineers. Progress will be slower and more expensive, but Soviet computing will remain independent and original.

Zelenograd, a new town on the outskirts of Moscow, is the centre of Soviet microelectronics, home to research institutes and plants such as Mikron and Angstrem. Investing in its laboratories and production lines could narrow the gap with the integrated circuits of Silicon Valley. Without modern chips, neither computers nor missiles can keep pace with the West.

The Tenth Five-Year Plan, covering 1976 to 1980, is proclaimed the Plan of Efficiency and Quality. Instead of new factories and ever greater volumes, the emphasis shifts to productivity, technical progress and better products. The XXV Party Congress sets new priorities for the planners, but whether the ministries can change their habits remains to be seen.

At the Shchekino chemical combine near Tula, an experiment begun in 1967 allows management to reduce its workforce while keeping the wage fund unchanged, distributing the savings as higher pay to the remaining workers. Productivity soars. Extending the method across Soviet industry could free hundreds of thousands of workers for new plants, but the trade unions fear the end of guaranteed employment.

The State Quality Mark, a pentagon bearing a stylised letter K, is awarded to Soviet products that meet the highest standards. Factories compete for the right to stamp it on their goods, and those that earn it gain bonuses and prestige. A strict certification system could improve the reputation of Soviet goods at home and in the markets of the socialist community.

In July 1979 the Central Committee and the Council of Ministers adopt a decree on improving planning and the economic mechanism. Net output replaces gross output as the key indicator, stable long-term norms are introduced and enterprises are judged on fulfilling their delivery contracts. It is the last major attempt of the Brezhnev era to make the planned economy more efficient.

For years the Party has proclaimed that the scientific-technical revolution will carry socialism past capitalism. Now the promise must be fulfilled: computers, automation, new materials and modern management are to transform every branch of the economy. If science truly becomes a direct productive force, the Soviet Union can enter the twenty-first century as the most advanced society on earth.

Agriculture is the Achilles heel of the Soviet economy. A quarter of all investment flows into the countryside, yet harvests swing wildly from year to year, collective farms remain inefficient and city dwellers still queue for meat. From the black earth of Ukraine to the virgin lands of Kazakhstan, the leadership searches for a lasting solution.

The orthodox answer to the agrarian crisis is more money: higher procurement prices, debt write-offs, and new barns, roads and housing for the collective and state farms. Under Brezhnev, investment in agriculture reaches unprecedented levels. The farmers welcome the funds, even if critics ask whether capital alone can cure a system that rewards plan figures rather than good harvests.

Soviet fields need more fertiliser, more tractors and more combine harvesters. New chemical plants produce mineral fertilisers in vast quantities, while the tractor works of Volgograd, Kharkov and Minsk deliver modern machines to the countryside. Mechanisation and chemistry, the planners believe, will finally raise Soviet yields to the level of the West.

The great land melioration programme, adopted in 1966, aims to transform Soviet agriculture through drainage and irrigation. Swamps in Belorussia and the Baltic are drained, while canals bring water to the dry steppes of the south. The works are costly and often poorly executed, but they promise to add millions of hectares of reliable farmland.

The leadership launches a programme to revive the Non-Black-Earth zone, the historic Russian heartland stretching from Pskov to the Urals. For decades its villages have emptied while investment has gone to Ukraine and Kazakhstan. Now roads, houses, drainage and machinery are to bring the old Russian countryside back to life, even if the other republics resent the shift in priorities.

In the 1960s the agronomist Ivan Khudenko runs an experiment in Kazakhstan with small autonomous teams, the links, which work their land independently and are paid according to results. Output soars and costs fall, yet the experiment is shut down and Khudenko is destined to die in prison. What if the leadership embraces his ideas instead and gives Soviet farmers responsibility for their own harvests?

The private household plots of collective farmers cover only a tiny share of Soviet farmland, yet they produce around a quarter of the nation's food: potatoes, vegetables, eggs, milk and meat. Enlarging the plots and easing the restrictions on private livestock would quickly improve supply at little cost to the state. Orthodox ideologists grumble, but hungry cities care little for doctrine.

In every Soviet city, the kolkhoz markets offer what the state shops cannot: fresh produce at prices set by supply and demand. Lifting the remaining restrictions on these markets would allow farmers to sell their surplus freely, improving supply and drawing trade out of the shadows. It is a small step towards the market, but a visible one.

Instead of rigid plan targets dictated from above, collective farms and their teams sign contracts with the state to deliver fixed quantities at agreed prices. Whatever they produce beyond the contract, they may sell or keep. The system rewards initiative and efficiency, but it also loosens the grip of the district Party committees on the countryside.

The summer of 1972 brings disaster. After a winter of bitter frosts, drought scorches the fields of the Volga region and Ukraine, and the grain harvest falls far short of the plan. The cities face shortages of bread and the farms a lack of fodder for their livestock. The leadership must decide whether to spend precious hard currency on imports or to ask the people to endure.
Exportkhleb sends its buyers to the grain exchanges of the West. The shops stay full; the gold reserve shrinks.

Hard currency is too precious to waste on foreign grain. Those who have lived through the war know real hardship, and they can bear this too. Livestock herds are slaughtered, rationing quietly returns to the provinces and the queues grow longer. The state preserves its reserves and its pride, but the patience of the population is not unlimited.

Khrushchev's Virgin Lands campaign has ploughed up millions of hectares of steppe in Kazakhstan and Siberia. Erosion and dust storms have since taken their toll, and yields remain unpredictable. A renewed effort with shelterbelts, crop rotation and modern machinery could restore the virgin lands as a reliable granary of the Union.

Cotton is the white gold of Soviet Central Asia. The Uzbek SSR alone grows most of the Union's crop, and its leader Sharof Rashidov promises ever higher harvests to Moscow. But cotton monoculture consumes vast amounts of water and labour, and behind the record figures lie inflated reports and corruption. How far should the Union push its cotton fields?

The waters of the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya are diverted into a vast network of canals, among them the Karakum Canal, to turn the deserts of Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan into cotton fields. The harvests grow and Central Asia prospers, but the rivers no longer reach the Aral Sea. Its shores begin to recede, and future generations will pay the price.

The Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake on earth, is shrinking year by year as its rivers are drained for irrigation. Fishing towns such as Muynak and Aralsk watch the water retreat from their harbours, while salt storms spread over the fields. Reducing water consumption and modernising irrigation could save the sea, even at the expense of the cotton harvest and the patience of Tashkent.

Soviet engineers dream of reversing the flow of the great Siberian rivers. Under the project known as Sibaral, part of the waters of the Ob and the Irtysh would be channelled southwards through a canal more than two thousand kilometres long to the thirsty fields of Central Asia. It would be the most ambitious water project in history, and scientists warn of unforeseen consequences for climate and nature.

The Central Committee adopts the Food Programme of the USSR, a comprehensive plan to secure the nation's food supply by the end of the decade. Agriculture, processing, storage, transport and trade are to be integrated into agro-industrial complexes under unified management. After decades of half-measures, the leadership promises to solve the agrarian problem once and for all.

Discovered in 1965 among the swamps of the Tyumen region, Samotlor is the largest oil field in the Soviet Union and one of the largest in the world. Drilling crews, pipelines and new towns spring up in the West Siberian taiga, and production climbs year after year. Siberian oil is set to become the lifeblood of the economy and its most valuable export.

West Siberia holds not only oil but also enormous deposits of natural gas. Developing them requires roads, railways, power lines and entire cities in a land of permafrost, bogs and winters far below freezing. The Tyumen oil and gas complex becomes one of the largest construction sites on earth, drawing workers from every corner of the Union.

Soyuznefteexport negotiates with Ruhrgas and Mannesmann over an unprecedented deal: West German large-diameter pipes on credit, repaid with deliveries of Soviet natural gas from 1973. Such an agreement would bind the Federal Republic to Soviet energy and open a lasting channel of trade across the Iron Curtain. Moscow makes its offer, and the decision now lies with Bonn.

Discovered in 1966 beyond the Arctic Circle, Urengoy is the largest gas field in the world. Bringing it into production demands drilling rigs, compressor stations and thousands of kilometres of pipeline across the tundra. Once tapped, Urengoy gas can heat Soviet cities, power industry and flow westwards to European customers who pay in hard currency.

The oil crisis of 1973 quadruples world prices, and every barrel of Soviet oil sold abroad now brings in a fortune in hard currency. Petrodollars pay for American grain, Western machinery and generous aid to friendly regimes across the Third World. The windfall makes reform seem less urgent, and the economy grows ever more dependent on the price of oil.

Since the Obninsk plant began supplying the grid in 1954, the Soviet Union has seen itself as a pioneer of peaceful atomic energy. The Ministry of Medium Machine-Building and the Ministry of Energy now draw up plans for dozens of new reactors in the European part of the Union, where fossil fuels are scarce. The key question is which reactor design to build.

The RBMK is a large graphite-moderated channel reactor, derived from the military plutonium reactors. It is cheap, can be built with existing industrial capacity and can be scaled up to enormous outputs. It lacks a full containment structure and hides dangerous design flaws known only to a few specialists, but the planners value speed and size above all else.

The VVER is a pressurised water reactor, similar in principle to Western designs and housed within a containment structure. It is more expensive and demands advanced heavy engineering, but it is safer, more reliable and suitable for export to the socialist countries. Choosing the VVER means slower expansion, but a sounder foundation for the Soviet nuclear industry.

On the shores of the Gulf of Finland at Sosnovy Bor, the Leningrad Nuclear Power Plant takes shape, with its first unit due to go online in 1973. It is to become the flagship of Soviet nuclear energy, supplying power to the second city of the Union and its industries. Its success will set the pace for the reactors that follow across the country.

Nuclear power should not remain a privilege of the Russian heartland. New stations in Ukraine, Armenia, Lithuania and Kazakhstan can supply electricity to the growing cities and industries of the republics and reduce their dependence on distant coal and gas. Each new plant also binds the republics more closely to the scientific might of the Union.

On the Yenisei and the Angara, Soviet engineers are building some of the largest hydroelectric dams in the world. The Krasnoyarsk station nears completion, while the Sayano-Shushenskaya project, under construction since 1968, promises even greater output for the aluminium smelters and industries of Siberia. Ecologists worry about flooded valleys and lost villages, but the turbines keep turning.

The Baikal-Amur Mainline is proclaimed the construction project of the century: more than four thousand kilometres of railway through taiga, mountains and permafrost, north of Lake Baikal to the Pacific. Komsomol volunteers from every republic answer the call. The line will open up the resources of the Far East and provide a second route to the Pacific, safely distant from the Chinese border.

After years of labour in some of the harshest conditions on earth, the Baikal-Amur Mainline opens to regular traffic. Trains now roll from Taishet to Sovetskaya Gavan, carrying timber, coal and ore from the Far East and supplies to the garrisons along the Amur. The project of the century has become reality, and the Soviet Far East no longer depends on a single railway.

The Kuznetsk Basin in Western Siberia and the open-pit mines of Ekibastuz in Kazakhstan hold some of the largest coal reserves in the world. Their coal fires the power stations and steelworks of the Urals and Siberia. New mines, power plants and high-voltage lines can turn these coalfields into the energy backbone of the eastern Union.

The Unified Energy System links the power grids of the Soviet republics into a single network, while the Mir interconnection extends it to the Comecon partners in Eastern Europe. Electricity can flow from Siberian dams to Ukrainian factories and from Soviet power plants to Budapest and Prague. It is socialist integration in the most literal sense.

The Academy of Sciences of the USSR, led by its president Mstislav Keldysh, presides over hundreds of institutes and tens of thousands of researchers. Soviet scientists rank among the best in the world in mathematics, physics and space research, yet much of their work never reaches the factories. Strengthening the Academy and its links to industry could turn scientific excellence into economic strength.

Near Novosibirsk, among the birch forests on the shores of the Ob Sea, stands Akademgorodok, the science town of the Academy's Siberian Branch. Its institutes of mathematics, nuclear physics and computing attract the brightest young minds, drawn by a freedom of debate unusual in the Soviet Union. Expanding the town strengthens Soviet science and computing far from the bureaucracy of Moscow.

Arzamas-16, Obninsk, Dubna and dozens of other science cities are missing from public maps, yet they form the backbone of Soviet nuclear, rocket and weapons research. Their residents enjoy better supplies and housing in exchange for secrecy and loyalty. Expanding the naukograds strengthens both science and defence, behind the fences and checkpoints of the KGB.

For decades, Trofim Lysenko's pseudo-science has dominated Soviet biology, while genuine geneticists have been dismissed, imprisoned or worse. Since his fall in 1965, the discipline has slowly been recovering. A decisive rehabilitation of genetics, with new institutes and modern breeding programmes, could bring Soviet agriculture and medicine back to the frontier of world science.

Soviet and American scientists agree to found the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis in Laxenburg near Vienna, a meeting place for researchers from East and West. Joint commissions on space, medicine, the environment and energy follow. Opening Soviet laboratories to Western contacts accelerates research, but ideologists fear that foreign ideas will cross the border along with the data.

The Americans have planted their flag on the Moon, and the Soviet lunar programme is in crisis after repeated failures of the giant N1 rocket. Should the Union continue the costly race to land a cosmonaut on the Moon, or shift its efforts to long-duration orbital stations and robotic exploration? The decision will define Soviet spaceflight for the next two decades.

On 17 November 1970 Lunokhod 1, delivered by the Luna 17 probe, rolls onto the surface of the Sea of Rains. Steered from a control centre in Crimea, it becomes the first remote-controlled vehicle to explore another world. Robotic explorers allow the Soviet Union to claim triumphs on the Moon without risking the lives of its cosmonauts.

On 15 December 1970 the Venera 7 probe descends through the crushing atmosphere of Venus and transmits data from its surface, the first successful landing on another planet. Further Venera missions are to send back the first images from the Venusian surface. The exploration of the planets offers the Soviet Union a field in which it can lead the world.

Sergei Korolev's giant N1 rocket is meant to carry Soviet cosmonauts to the Moon, but every launch so far has ended in an explosion, and the programme faces cancellation. What if the leadership refuses to give up? With Nikolai Kuznetsov's improved engines and patient ground testing, the N1 could yet fly and restore the prestige of the Soviet space programme.

The N1 finally works. A lunar orbiter and the LK lander carry a Soviet cosmonaut to the surface of the Moon, where the red flag is planted not far from the footprints of the Americans. The world press is stunned, Moscow celebrates, and the space race is suddenly far from over. Socialism has proven that it can match any achievement of the West.

In April 1971 Salyut 1 is set to become the first space station in history. Long-duration flights aboard orbital laboratories allow Soviet cosmonauts to conduct experiments, observe the Earth and learn to live in space for months at a time. It is a field in which the Soviet Union can lead the world, with the military Almaz stations never far behind.

An American Apollo and a Soviet Soyuz are to dock in orbit, and their crews are to shake hands in space. The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project would become a powerful symbol of detente, proof that the superpowers can cooperate even in the most prestigious field of the Cold War. Moscow proposes the joint mission to Washington, and the Americans must decide whether to accept.

The Americans are developing a reusable Space Shuttle, and Soviet military analysts fear it could be used to deploy weapons in orbit or even to snatch Soviet satellites. Ignoring it is not an option for a superpower. The leadership must decide how to answer, and whether to match the American programme in capability and prestige at enormous cost.

NPO Energia, under Valentin Glushko, designs a super-heavy launch vehicle and a reusable orbiter of its own. The Energia rocket can lift a hundred tonnes into orbit, while the Buran spaceplane is designed to fly fully automatically. The programme is the most expensive in Soviet space history, but it gives the Union a capability to rival anything the Americans possess.

The era of short-lived Salyut stations gives way to a modular, permanently crewed outpost in orbit. Mir, a name meaning both peace and world, is assembled module by module and will host cosmonauts and international guests for years on end. A permanent presence in space crowns the Soviet orbital programme and demonstrates the scientific maturity of socialism.

Since 1962, Zenit reconnaissance satellites based on the Vostok spacecraft have photographed the territory of the United States, NATO and China, returning their film capsules to Earth. Better cameras, longer missions and new generations of satellites give the General Staff an ever clearer picture of enemy forces. In the nuclear age, knowledge from orbit is a strategic weapon in itself.

From the laboratories of Akademgorodok to the launch pads of Baikonur, Soviet science has become a pillar of national power. The Union trains more engineers and scientists than any other nation and competes with the United States in every field from physics to spaceflight. Science is no longer merely a tool of the state but the proud face of socialism before the world.

The Soviet Army is the most powerful land force in the world: well over a hundred divisions, tens of thousands of tanks and a doctrine shaped by the experience of the Great Patriotic War. Its groups of forces stand guard in East Germany, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary, while new divisions reinforce the border with China. Maintaining its readiness is the first duty of the state.

Marshal Andrei Grechko, Minister of Defence since 1967, is a veteran of the battle for the Caucasus and a firm believer in massive conventional forces. Under his leadership the armed forces receive new tanks, missiles and infantry weapons, and the military gains a stronger voice in the Politburo. Grechko's ministry is a guarantee of strength, and a constant demand on the resources of the Union.

Since Marshal Sokolovsky's 'Military Strategy' appeared in 1962, Soviet planners have assumed that any war with NATO would turn nuclear within days. A younger generation in the General Staff now argues that massed armour could reach the Rhine before the West dares to escalate. Should the Soviet Army prepare to fight beneath the mushroom cloud, or to win so quickly that the warheads never leave their silos?

Rehabilitated along with its author after the purges, Marshal Tukhachevsky's theory of deep operations is returning to the lecture halls of the Frunze Academy. Instead of grinding through NATO's forward defences, successive echelons of tanks and motor rifles would strike across the entire depth of the enemy position at once. By the middle of the decade the idea is once again the guiding star of Soviet operational art.

Sokolovsky's school holds that no war in Europe can stay conventional for long, and that the Soviet Army must be built accordingly. Divisions will train to advance through contaminated ground in sealed vehicles, while the rocket troops open the way with tactical warheads. It is a grim doctrine, but one that refuses to pretend the nuclear age never arrived.

Marshal Nikolai Ogarkov and his staff propose a sharper blade for the deep battle: operational manoeuvre groups, powerful tank formations that slip through the first breach and race into NATO's rear before reserves can be committed or nuclear release authorised. Headquarters, airfields and missile sites would fall before the enemy understands what has happened. Speed itself becomes the decisive weapon.

A war against NATO and China would be fought on several fronts at once, too many for the General Staff in Moscow to direct alone. In 1979 permanent high commands are created for the Western, South-Western, Southern and Far Eastern theatres, each able to control several fronts and fleets in wartime. Command is pushed forward, closer to the battle it must win.

Kharkov's T-64 is the most advanced tank in the world, but it is expensive, temperamental and difficult to build in the numbers a war with NATO would demand. Nizhny Tagil offers a simpler, sturdier machine derived from the same ideas. The defence industry must decide whether the Soviet Army fields a single main battle tank or tolerates two parallel lines of production.

Alexander Morozov's design bureau in Kharkov has given the Soviet Army a machine years ahead of anything in the West, with composite armour, a powerful smoothbore gun and an automatic loader. Committing fully to the T-64 means accepting its high cost and a complicated engine that keeps the mechanics busy. The elite divisions facing NATO in Germany will receive the finest tank the Union can build.

Uralvagonzavod in Nizhny Tagil has produced a tank built for the realities of mass war: robust, simple to maintain and cheap enough to equip reserve divisions and allied armies alike. The T-72 will never be the most sophisticated machine on the battlefield, but it can be built in vast numbers and sold across the socialist world. In a long war, quantity has a quality all its own.

The Kirov Plant in Leningrad proposes a radical solution: a tank powered by a gas turbine, giving it the acceleration of a sports car and the thirst of an aircraft. Dmitry Ustinov is an enthusiastic patron, and the T-80 promises a mobility no NATO formation could hope to match. Whether its engines can survive a long winter campaign is a question the engineers must still answer.

The BMP-1 has changed the meaning of infantry. For the first time riflemen can fight from inside an armoured vehicle carrying its own gun and anti-tank missile, keeping pace with the tanks even across contaminated ground. Building tactics and production around the infantry fighting vehicle will give every motor rifle regiment the protection and firepower the modern battlefield demands.

The Kalashnikov has armed half the world, but its heavy cartridge is a relic of the Second World War. Izhmash has developed a lighter weapon firing a small-calibre, high-velocity round that is more accurate at range and lets each soldier carry more ammunition. Adopted in 1974, the AK-74 will become the standard rifle of the Soviet Army for decades to come.

The conscript army turns over every two years, and the gap between raw recruits and their officers has long been filled by no one. In 1972 the rank of praporshchik is introduced: long-serving professional warrant officers who manage stores, vehicles and discipline at company level. They cost more than conscripts, but they give the Soviet Army a backbone of experience it has always lacked.

In the barracks, second-year conscripts, the so-called 'grandfathers', rule over the newcomers through beatings, extortion and humiliation that officers prefer not to see. Breaking this unwritten hierarchy means prosecuting the tormentors, punishing commanders who look away and admitting that the problem exists at all. The generals resent the interference, but an army that preys on itself cannot fight well.

General Vasily Margelov has turned the Airborne Troops into an elite force, with their striped vests, blue berets and air-dropped armoured vehicles. Soldiers already call them 'Uncle Vasya's Troops'. Raising the airborne divisions to a strategic reserve of the High Command would give Moscow a force able to seize capitals, airfields and bridgeheads anywhere within reach of the transport fleet.

Military intelligence maintains its own special purpose brigades, small teams trained to parachute deep behind enemy lines, locate NATO's tactical nuclear weapons and destroy them before they can be used. Expanding the Spetsnaz of the GRU would give every front a hidden sword in the enemy's rear. Their very existence remains a closely guarded secret, even within the Soviet Army itself.

Mil's design bureau has created something without parallel: a heavily armoured gunship that can also carry a squad of infantry into battle. The Mi-24 combines rockets, cannon and anti-tank missiles with the speed to strike anywhere along the front. Soldiers already call it the 'flying tank', and its silhouette will soon become one of the most feared in the world.

The legacy of the wartime Katyusha lives on in the Grad, a truck-mounted launcher able to saturate an entire grid square in seconds. Its heavier successor, the Uragan, is already being designed to strike targets far behind the front. Massing rocket artillery would give Soviet commanders the crushing firepower needed to blast open NATO's defences ahead of the armoured breakthrough.

The 1967 Law on Universal Military Duty shortened service to two years but made it truly universal, backed by pre-conscription training in schools and by the volunteer society DOSAAF. Every young Soviet man is meant to arrive at his unit already able to shoot, drive and read a map. The army gains a deep pool of trained reserves, and society learns to see service as a debt owed to the Motherland.

In 1976 the death of Marshal Grechko brings Dmitry Ustinov to the Ministry of Defence, a lifelong manager of the armaments industry rather than a field commander. Ustinov knows every factory and design bureau personally, and under him weapons will flow faster and cheaper than ever before. The professional soldiers grumble that an industrialist, not a general, now runs the Soviet Army.

A generation after Victory, the Soviet Army stands as the largest and most powerful land force on earth, with divisions deployed from the Elbe to the Amur. Its officers are well trained, its arsenals full and its doctrine studied by friend and foe alike. Now it must prove that it is more than a parade on Red Square: a force ready to win any war the Motherland may be forced to fight.

Created by Khrushchev in 1959, the Strategic Rocket Forces have become the senior service of the Soviet military, guardians of the missiles that can reach any point on the globe. Their silos stretch from Belorussia to the Siberian taiga. Investing in new generations of intercontinental missiles will ensure that the Soviet Union can never again be blackmailed by American nuclear superiority.

For the first time in history, the Soviet Union possesses as many intercontinental missiles as the United States. The humiliation of Cuba in 1962 has been answered by a decade of relentless construction, and Washington must now negotiate with Moscow as an equal. Parity brings confidence to the Kremlin, but also a new and dangerous temptation to believe that any confrontation can be won.

The Yuzhnoye design bureau in Dnepropetrovsk is preparing the R-36M, a missile so large that it can carry ten warheads or a single devastating charge. In the West it will be called the SS-18 'Satan', and its accuracy threatens the American Minuteman silos themselves. Deploying it would give the Soviet Union a genuine first-strike capability, and Washington will see it exactly that way.

Fixed silos can be targeted, and every year American missiles grow more accurate. Some designers argue that survivability matters more than sheer numbers: several independently targeted warheads on every missile, and launchers that roam the roads and railways where no satellite can follow them. A smaller arsenal that cannot be destroyed in a first strike may deter more effectively than a larger one that can.

The ageing missiles aimed at Western Europe can be replaced by the RSD-10 Pioneer, a mobile and accurate weapon carrying three warheads. NATO will call it the SS-20, and it can hold every capital from London to Rome hostage without ever threatening America itself. It would give Moscow a powerful lever over Europe, but it may also provoke Bonn and its allies into a dangerous response.

Unlike any Western nation, the Soviet Union treats the defence of its own airspace as a separate branch of the armed forces. PVO Strany commands the radars, interceptor regiments and missile batteries stretching from the Baltic to the Pacific coast. Strengthening it will ensure that no American bomber or spy plane crosses the Soviet border without paying for it, as Gary Powers learned in 1960.

Around the capital the A-35 anti-ballistic missile system is finally entering service, with enormous radars and interceptors designed to destroy incoming warheads high above the atmosphere. It cannot stop a full American attack, but it can protect the leadership against a limited strike or an accidental launch. Completing the shield will be expensive, and it may yet become a bargaining chip in future arms control talks.

Frontal Aviation is the air arm that fights alongside the ground forces, clearing the skies above the tank columns and striking NATO airfields, bridges and nuclear launchers. Its regiments in East Germany and Czechoslovakia stand only minutes from the inner German border. Refining its tactics and training will turn the air force into a true partner of the deep operation rather than a separate war fought overhead.

Variable-geometry wings promise the best of both worlds: short take-offs from rough forward airfields and high speed at low level. Mikoyan's MiG-23 is set to become the workhorse fighter of the Warsaw Pact, while Sukhoi's Su-24 can penetrate deep into Western Europe at treetop height, by night and in any weather. Together they will carry Frontal Aviation into a new decade.

Designed to catch an American supersonic bomber that was never built, the MiG-25 can race at nearly three times the speed of sound at the edge of the stratosphere. No Western fighter can catch it and few missiles can reach it. Pressing it into service as an interceptor and reconnaissance aircraft would give the air defence forces a weapon that truly lives up to its legend.

The strategic bombers of Long-Range Aviation have long lived in the shadow of the rocket forces. Tupolev's Tu-22M, known in the West as the 'Backfire', promises to change that: a supersonic swing-wing bomber able to strike carrier groups at sea and targets across Europe and Asia. Whether it could also reach America will become a fierce question at every arms control table.

The American F-15 and F-16 have set a new standard in the air, and Soviet designers are determined to answer them. Sukhoi's Su-27 promises long range and extraordinary agility, while Mikoyan's MiG-29 will be a nimble frontline fighter for the whole Warsaw Pact. Accelerating both programmes would give the Soviet Air Force aircraft capable of matching, perhaps surpassing, anything the West can field.

Civil Defence of the USSR teaches every schoolchild to put on a gas mask and every factory to prepare its shelters. Deep metro stations double as bunkers, and evacuation plans exist for every major city. Expanding the programme reassures the population that the state has prepared for the worst, and signals to Washington that the Soviet Union intends to survive even a nuclear war.

At the Twenty-Fifth Party Congress in 1976, Brezhnev declares that the correlation of forces in the world has shifted decisively in favour of socialism. Nuclear parity, the American defeat in Vietnam and revolutions across Africa all seem to prove him right. Embracing this confidence turns caution into assertiveness, but the West may well read Soviet optimism as a threat to be countered.

Admiral Sergei Gorshkov has commanded the Soviet Navy since 1956, and he has a vision: a fleet able to sail every ocean and show the red flag wherever the Americans go. Coastal defence is no longer enough for a superpower. Under his guidance new cruisers, submarines and replenishment ships are turning a navy built for home waters into a true ocean-going fleet.

In April 1970 the Soviet Navy stages Okean, the largest naval exercise since the Second World War. Ships of the Northern, Baltic, Black Sea and Pacific Fleets manoeuvre simultaneously across the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Mediterranean, rehearsing the destruction of American carrier groups. The message to Washington is unmistakable: the oceans no longer belong to the West alone.

Admiral Gorshkov preaches that a superpower needs a balanced fleet, yet resources are finite and the admirals are divided into two camps. One side wants submarines above all, cheap to hide and deadly against carriers and convoys. The other dreams of carriers and great surface ships able to project Soviet power to distant shores. The Party must decide what kind of sea power the state requires.

Submarines are the great equaliser of the Soviet Navy. Hunter-killer boats can stalk American carriers and convoys, while missile submarines carry a share of the nuclear deterrent that no enemy can find and destroy. Concentrating the shipyards on the underwater fleet will give the Soviet Union the largest submarine force in the world and a nuclear arsenal hidden beneath the waves.

Rather than sending missile submarines into the open Atlantic, where American hunters lie in wait, the Navy can keep them close to home. The Barents Sea and the Sea of Okhotsk would become protected bastions, guarded by surface ships, aircraft and attack submarines. From these sanctuaries new long-range missiles could still reach the United States, while the boats themselves remain safe.

Project 705, which NATO will call the Alfa, is a submarine unlike any other: a titanium hull, a liquid-metal reactor and a crew so small that automation replaces most of its sailors. It can outrun almost any torpedo in the Western arsenal and dive deeper than its pursuers. The cost is staggering and the reactor temperamental, but no other navy on earth could build such a vessel.

The Rubin design bureau proposes the largest submarine ever built: Project 941 Akula, which the West will call the Typhoon. With a hull broad and strong enough to break through Arctic ice, it could surface near the North Pole and launch its missiles at America. Building such giants will strain the yards of Severodvinsk, but they would make the naval deterrent virtually invulnerable.

Submarines can sink a fleet, but they cannot show the flag or support allies in distant waters. A balanced fleet of aircraft-carrying cruisers and heavy missile cruisers would let the Soviet Union project power from the Mediterranean to the Indian Ocean. The yards of Nikolaev and Leningrad stand ready, if the Party is willing to pay for a true ocean-going surface navy.

The Black Sea Shipyard in Nikolaev is preparing a new type of warship: the heavy aircraft-carrying cruiser. The Kiev class combines vertical take-off jets and helicopters with heavy anti-ship missiles, and as a 'cruiser' it can legally pass through the Turkish Straits. It is not yet a true aircraft carrier, but it is the first step toward one.

Project 1144, the Kirov class, would be the largest surface combatant built anywhere since the Second World War: a nuclear-powered battlecruiser bristling with anti-ship and anti-aircraft missiles. Its purpose is to lead surface action groups against American carriers and to shield Soviet submarines on their way to sea. Its sheer size announces that the Soviet Navy has come of age.

The Fifth Operational Squadron keeps Soviet warships permanently in the Mediterranean, shadowing the American Sixth Fleet and showing support for Arab allies. To stay at sea it needs friendly harbours for supplies and repairs. Moscow will ask Damascus for a naval supply point at Tartus, an arrangement that could give the Soviet Union a lasting foothold on the Mediterranean coast.

Naval Missile Aviation is the long arm of Gorshkov's fleet: regiments of land-based bombers armed with heavy anti-ship missiles. Their task is to find American carrier groups far out at sea and overwhelm them with massed missile strikes before their aircraft can threaten the Soviet coast. Expanding this force is the most economical way to challenge American dominance of the oceans.

A global navy needs global harbours. Berbera in Somalia and Aden in South Yemen overlook the gateway between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean, while Cam Ranh Bay in Vietnam looks out over the South China Sea. Moscow will offer its partners aid and protection in exchange for port rights, but no ally will be forced to accept the offer.

Every ship of the ocean-going fleet must first be built, and the great yards are already working at the limit of their capacity. Severodvinsk on the White Sea launches the nuclear submarines, while Nikolaev on the Black Sea produces the large surface ships. Expanding both will ensure that the ambitions of the admirals are not frustrated by a simple shortage of slipways.

Where once the Soviet Navy hugged the coastline, its ships now sail every ocean on earth. Squadrons patrol the Mediterranean, the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, and Soviet flags fly in harbours from Havana to Aden. Gorshkov's dream has become reality: a true blue-water navy, the equal of any fleet that sails the seas.

Since 1967 Yuri Andropov has led the Committee for State Security, and he has transformed it. Gone are the crude terror methods of the Stalin years; in their place stands a modern, professional service relying on surveillance, informers and the quiet pressure of 'prophylactic' conversations. Andropov is intelligent, ambitious and trusted by Brezhnev, and his KGB is becoming a pillar of the state.

Created on Andropov's initiative in 1967, the Fifth Directorate of the KGB is tasked with combating 'ideological subversion'. Its officers watch writers, churches, national movements and anyone who listens too closely to foreign radio. Expanding its reach will help the Party detect dissent before it can spread, though every new file deepens the silence that hangs over Soviet intellectual life.

Since the trial of Sinyavsky and Daniel in 1966, a small but stubborn dissident movement has taken shape. Samizdat manuscripts circulate from hand to hand, Andrei Sakharov speaks out for human rights, and Solzhenitsyn's novels reach the world through foreign publishers. The state must decide whether to crush these voices, expel them, or quietly allow them a space to exist.

If opposing Soviet power is a sign of madness, then dissidents belong in hospitals rather than prisons. Psychiatrists of the Serbsky Institute have developed a convenient diagnosis, 'sluggish schizophrenia', that can be applied to anyone who refuses to conform. The special psychiatric hospitals will silence the troublemakers, but the West will condemn the practice as a grotesque abuse of medicine.

Neither prison nor tolerance: the most troublesome voices can simply be removed. Solzhenitsyn, after the publication of 'The Gulag Archipelago' abroad, can be stripped of his citizenship and put on a plane to the West, while Sakharov can be banished to the closed city of Gorky. The dissidents lose their audience at home, though they gain a far louder one abroad.

What if the Party decided that typewritten manuscripts and private poetry readings posed no real threat to socialism? Tolerating samizdat would let new ideas circulate among scientists and intellectuals and soften the hostility of Western opinion. The KGB warns that tolerance is the first step toward another Prague Spring, but reformers argue that a confident socialism need not fear mere words.

Since the Six-Day War, thousands of Soviet Jews have applied to emigrate to Israel, and many have been refused, losing their jobs and becoming 'refuseniks'. In Washington, Senator Henry Jackson seeks to link American trade benefits to the freedom to emigrate. The Kremlin must decide whether to open the gates for the sake of detente or to hold on to the specialists it has trained.

Letting those who wish to leave depart would remove a constant irritant from relations with the United States and unlock the trade and credits the economy needs. It also means watching engineers, doctors and scientists board trains and planes for Vienna and onward to Israel. The Politburo weighs the loss of talent against the benefits of detente, and chooses to let them go.

In August 1972 the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet decrees that emigrants must repay the cost of their state education before they may leave. For a university graduate the sum can equal many years of wages. The measure brings in hard currency and discourages the drain of talent, but it provokes outrage in the West and threatens the trade deals of detente.

The First Chief Directorate of the KGB runs Soviet intelligence abroad. Its officers work under diplomatic cover in embassies, trade missions and news agencies, recruiting sources in governments, armies and laboratories around the world. Expanding its networks and its codebreakers will give the Kremlin the secrets it needs to stay one step ahead of its rivals.

Service A of the First Chief Directorate specialises in 'active measures': forged documents, planted newspaper stories and quiet support for peace movements and friendly politicians in the West. Its aim is not to steal secrets but to shape opinion, sow distrust between Washington and its allies, and make the Soviet cause appear to be the cause of peace itself.

The most valuable agents carry no diplomatic passport at all. The illegals live for years under false identities in the West as shopkeepers, engineers or academics, waiting for the moment they are needed. Training them takes years and losing one is a disaster, but a well-placed illegal can reach places no embassy officer ever could, and vanish without a trace.

The KGB Border Troops guard the longest frontier in the world, from the Baltic coast to the Pacific, from the Arctic tundra to the mountains of Central Asia. After the bloody clashes with China on the Ussuri in 1969, their importance is clearer than ever. Strengthening the border guards will keep foreign agents out, smugglers in check and Soviet citizens safely at home.

The leadership of the KGB has become convinced that the Americans are preparing a surprise nuclear attack. Operation RYaN, an acronym for 'nuclear missile attack' in Russian, orders every KGB and GRU station abroad to watch for warning signs: lights burning late at the Pentagon, blood banks filling up, officials cancelling their holidays. The hunt for the first strike may save the nation, or push the world to the brink.

Corruption has spread through the Party and the state like rot through timber. Ministers protect their clients, regional leaders run their territories as personal fiefdoms, and goods vanish from factories into the black market. A determined campaign of arrests and investigations would restore discipline, but it will make powerful enemies among a nomenklatura that has grown comfortable under the stability of cadres.

Since the days of Dzerzhinsky, the Chekists have called themselves the shield and the sword of the Party. Under this banner the KGB can bind its many tasks into a single purpose, from counter-intelligence at home to guarding the borders and watching for ideological subversion. A security service at the height of its power makes the Soviet state very difficult to undermine from within or without.

The Soviet Union is a federation of fifteen republics, each with its own Party, government and flag. Behind the slogans of the friendship of peoples lie real tensions: national elites seeking autonomy, Russians resentful of subsidising the periphery, and a population growing fastest in the south. Moscow must learn to manage the Union as carefully as it manages the economy.

Brezhnev's 'stability of cadres' has left powerful first secretaries in charge of the republics for years: Kunaev in Kazakhstan, Rashidov in Uzbekistan, Shcherbytsky in Ukraine. They deliver loyalty and plan figures, and in return Moscow leaves them largely alone. Should the Kremlin continue to trust these local barons, or send its own men to keep watch over them?

The bargain is simple: the republican leaders keep their territories quiet, vote with Brezhnev in the Politburo and meet their plans, at least on paper. In exchange Moscow asks few questions about how they run their domains. The Union will be calmer and more cohesive, even if corruption and nepotism flourish behind the facades of Tashkent, Alma-Ata and Baku.

Trust is good, but control is better. Moscow will place Russian second secretaries in every republican Party organisation, rotate officials between regions and break up the local networks that shield corrupt leaders. The republics will resent the outsiders, but no first secretary will ever again be able to treat his republic as a personal possession.

Ukraine is the second pillar of the Union, home to vital industries, rich farmland and a large and proud nation. Its first secretary, Petro Shelest, defends Ukrainian culture and the republic's economic interests, sometimes too openly for Moscow's liking. The Kremlin must decide whether to tolerate Shelest's course or replace it with something more reliably loyal.

What if Petro Shelest had kept his post? His book 'Our Soviet Ukraine' celebrates the republic's history and its Cossack traditions, and his leadership shields the Ukrainian language and intelligentsia. A Ukraine secure in its identity may prove a more willing partner in the Union, though some in Moscow fear it could also become a far more demanding one.

In 1972 Shelest is removed and Volodymyr Shcherbytsky, a close ally of Brezhnev, takes over in Kiev. Shelest's book is condemned as nationalist, and a wave of arrests sweeps through the Ukrainian intelligentsia while Russian gains ground in schools and publishing. Ukraine becomes a model of loyalty, but the resentment buried in those years does not simply disappear.

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are the most prosperous and Western-minded republics of the Union, with high living standards, a strong sense of national identity and long memories of independence. They can serve as a showcase of what socialism can achieve, or as a laboratory for deeper integration with the rest of the country. Moscow must choose how to treat its western frontier.

Let the Baltic republics be the shop window of socialism. Tallinn's designers, the fashion houses of Riga and the cafes of Vilnius can show visitors, and the rest of the Union, that Soviet life can be modern and stylish. Estonians already watch Finnish television across the gulf; allowing them a little more freedom may win more loyalty than any campaign of Russification.

New industrial combines in Riga and Tallinn need workers, and the Baltic republics cannot supply enough of them. Bringing in labour from Russia, Ukraine and Belorussia will boost production and tie the region more closely to the Union. Yet every new apartment block filled with Russian-speaking workers feeds the fear among Latvians and Estonians that they are becoming minorities in their own lands.

Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan form the southern frontier of the Union, a region of ancient nations, fierce pride and old rivalries. Their economies thrive on private plots and the shadow market as much as on the plan, and their Party bosses are among the most corrupt in the country. Bringing order to Transcaucasia will require both a firm hand and a careful touch.

In 1972 Eduard Shevardnadze, the Georgian minister of internal affairs, replaces the discredited Vasil Mzhavanadze as first secretary in Tbilisi. He launches a sweeping campaign against bribery and the black market, purging thousands of officials. Georgians are astonished, Moscow is impressed, and the ambitious new leader begins a career that may take him far beyond the Caucasus.

Heydar Aliyev, a career KGB officer, has led Azerbaijan since 1969. He presents himself as a scourge of corruption while building a network of loyal clans, and he flatters Brezhnev lavishly on every visit. Under his rule the oil industry of Baku is modernised and the republic reports spectacular growth. Backing Aliyev buys stability on the Caspian, at a price that is never written down.

The Armenians of Nagorno-Karabakh, an autonomous region inside Azerbaijan, have petitioned Moscow for decades to be transferred to Armenia, and each time the request is quietly buried. Granting it would satisfy Yerevan but enrage Baku; refusing it preserves the status quo while the grievance festers. Historically, this very question would begin to tear the Union apart in 1988.

In Central Asia, Kunaev in Kazakhstan and Rashidov in Uzbekistan rule with an almost feudal authority. Their republics deliver cotton, grain and unwavering loyalty, and in return Moscow tolerates their clans, their courts of flatterers and their creative accounting. The arrangement keeps the region calm, but the Kremlin knows less and less about what really happens in Tashkent and Alma-Ata.

Uzbekistan reports record cotton harvests year after year, and Moscow pays billions of roubles for them. But investigators suspect that much of this cotton exists only on paper, with the difference pocketed by a pyramid of officials reaching all the way to the top of the republic. Exposing the fraud would strike a mighty blow against corruption, but it will humiliate an entire republic.

More than a hundred languages are spoken across the Soviet Union, and the question of which should be taught in schools is never merely educational. Russian binds together the Union, the army and the economy, but the national languages carry the identity of each people. Moscow must decide how far to promote Russian and how much room to leave for the native tongues.

A decree of 1978 strengthens the teaching of Russian from the very first grade in every school of the Union, praising it as the language of inter-ethnic communication. Conscripts from Tashkent to Tallinn will understand their officers, and engineers can move freely between the republics. Yet when Georgia's language rights are threatened that same year, crowds fill the streets of Tbilisi in protest.

Rather than forcing Russian into every classroom, the Party could guarantee schooling in the native language of each republic, with Russian taught as a second tongue. National intelligentsias would welcome the gesture, and the friendship of peoples would sound less like Russification. The army complains that recruits arrive unable to follow orders, but loyalty freely given may be worth more.

The Union Treaty of 1922 bound the republics together, but the state it created is now groaning under the weight of national demands, economic strain and political doubt. If the bonds begin to weaken, Moscow must choose: renegotiate the Union as a voluntary federation of sovereign states, or hold it together through sheer force of will and arms.

A new treaty could transform the Soviet Union into a genuine federation of sovereign republics, with real powers over their economies, languages and cultures, united by a common defence, currency and foreign policy. The hardliners see it as the beginning of the end. The reformers answer that a union held together by consent is the only union that can truly last.

There will be no new treaty and no negotiation with nationalists. The Union was forged in revolution and war and will be preserved by the same means: the KGB will watch the national movements, the army will stand ready, and any first secretary who flirts with separatism will be removed. Order will be maintained, but at the cost of the goodwill of millions.

The Party has long proclaimed the emergence of a new historical community: the Soviet people, bound together not by blood or language but by shared ideals and a common future. With the Union secured, this promise may finally become reality, as Uzbeks, Ukrainians and Latvians come to see themselves as Soviet citizens first and foremost.

Guaranteed work, cheap bread, free healthcare and a separate apartment for every family: this is the promise of the Soviet way of life. For millions who remember the war and the crowded communal flats, these are the best years they have ever known. Celebrating these achievements reminds the people what they owe to socialism, and what they stand to lose.

Vodka is woven into every celebration, every bargain and every tragedy of Soviet life. Consumption keeps climbing year after year, and alcoholism fills the hospitals, empties the factories and shortens the lives of Soviet men. Yet the sale of alcohol also fills the state treasury. The Party must decide whether it can afford to fight the bottle, or afford not to.
