The state monopoly on vodka brings in a huge share of all retail revenue, money the budget simply cannot do without. Rather than fighting the national vice, the Ministry of Finance will quietly profit from it. Hospitals and factories will pay the price in absent workers and ruined health, but as long as the shelves are stocked, the people remain content.

In 1972 the Central Committee resolves to combat drunkenness and alcoholism, restricting opening hours, raising prices and cutting the production of strong spirits. Enforced seriously, the decree could save lives and lift labour productivity, though the treasury will lose a vital source of income. Many citizens will simply turn to home-distilled samogon, and their goodwill toward the Party may suffer.

From the Olympic podium to the ice hockey rink, the chessboard and the football pitch, Soviet athletes prove the strength of socialism to the whole world. Sports schools search for talent in every town and village, and champions become national heroes. Investing in sport costs little compared to missiles, yet every gold medal is a small victory in the Cold War.

In 1974 the International Olympic Committee awards the 1980 Summer Games to Moscow, the first Olympics ever to be held in a socialist country. New stadiums, hotels and an Olympic village must be built, and the capital polished for the eyes of the world. The Games promise a triumph of Soviet prestige, unless the West decides to stay away.

The cultural thaw of the Khrushchev years is long over, but it has never been fully reversed. Writers, filmmakers and theatre directors test the limits of what the censors will allow, and audiences flock to anything that hints at forbidden truths. The Party must decide whether to tighten its grip on culture or to permit a carefully managed openness.

Glavlit, the central censorship office, reviews every book, newspaper and film before it reaches the public. Under firm instructions from the ideological apparatus, it will continue to cut, delay and ban anything that strays from the Party line. Soviet culture will remain safely orthodox, while its most gifted artists either conform, fall silent or turn to samizdat.

Lyubimov's Taganka Theatre stages daring productions, Vysotsky's songs play on tape recorders in every apartment block, and Tarkovsky films masterpieces that the censors struggle to understand. What if the Party chose to tolerate rather than suppress them? A measure of cultural freedom could reconcile the intelligentsia with the state and show the world a more human face of socialism.

Despite decades of persecution, the Russian Orthodox Church endures, as do Muslim, Catholic, Baptist and Jewish communities across the Union. The Council for Religious Affairs keeps believers under close watch, and attending church is a risk for anyone with a career. The Party must decide whether to intensify the struggle against religion or to seek a quiet accommodation with it.

Religion is a relic of the past, destined to disappear as society advances toward communism. Lectures, museums of atheism and the Znanie Society will carry the scientific worldview into every town and village, while the authorities continue to restrict new parishes and the training of clergy. Believers will grow fewer in public, even if many continue to pray in private.

What if the Party sought a genuine partnership with the Moscow Patriarchate rather than merely tolerating it? Loosening the restrictions on parishes and seminaries could win the gratitude of millions of believers and turn the Church into an ally in patriotic and peace campaigns. Hardline ideologues are appalled, but the Church may prove a valuable pillar of stability.

Soviet women make up more than half of the workforce, serving as doctors, engineers and crane operators. Yet when their shift ends a second one begins: queues for groceries, cooking, laundry and childcare, with little help from husbands or the economy. Easing this double burden through more kindergartens, services and household goods would improve countless lives and keep women at work.

In Russia and the Baltic republics most families have one or two children, while in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan they have five or six. The demographic centre of the Union is shifting steadily southward, toward Central Asia and the Caucasus. Planners must adapt by building schools and jobs in the south, encouraging larger families in the north and preparing an army whose recruits speak less and less Russian.

Brezhnev's ideologists declare that the Soviet Union has reached the stage of 'developed socialism', a mature society on the road to communism, and the new constitution of 1977 enshrines the claim. If it can be made real, with rising living standards and a confident population, the socialist way of life may become an example the whole world wishes to follow.

Lenin's principle of peaceful coexistence holds that socialism and capitalism can compete without war. In the age of nuclear parity, the Kremlin sees a chance to turn the principle into practice through arms control talks, trade with the West and the recognition of the post-war order in Europe. Detente will not end the struggle between the systems, but it may move it to safer ground.

Chancellor Willy Brandt's new eastern policy offers an opportunity that seemed impossible only a few years ago. A treaty between the Soviet Union and West Germany would renounce the use of force and recognise the post-war borders of Europe, including the Oder-Neisse line. Moscow is ready to make the offer; Bonn must decide whether to sign it.

At the Twenty-Fourth Party Congress in the spring of 1971, Leonid Brezhnev unveils a Peace Programme that recasts Soviet foreign policy around peaceful coexistence. Recognition of Europe's post-war borders, arms limitation and expanded trade with the capitalist world are to secure what decades of confrontation could not. The treaty signed with Bonn in August 1970 already points the way; now the whole Politburo must commit to detente.

West Berlin remains the most dangerous flashpoint in Europe, an island of the West deep inside the German Democratic Republic. Ambassador Pyotr Abrasimov sits down with his American, British and French counterparts to settle access routes, transit rights and the city's ties to the Federal Republic. A Quadripartite Agreement would defuse a crisis that has flared repeatedly since 1948, but East Berlin fears that Moscow is trading away its interests for detente.

Since November 1969 Soviet and American delegations have been meeting in Helsinki and Vienna to discuss limits on strategic weapons. Vladimir Semyonov's team must reconcile the hopes of the Foreign Ministry with the deep suspicions of the General Staff and the defence industry. Now that rough parity with the United States is within reach, Moscow must decide whether to freeze the race through negotiation or press on towards outright strategic superiority.

In May 1972, beneath the chandeliers of the Kremlin, Leonid Brezhnev and Richard Nixon are ready to sign the first agreements limiting the nuclear arsenals of the superpowers. The Interim Agreement freezes the number of missile launchers, while the ABM Treaty restricts each side to minimal missile defences. For the marshals it is a constraint on Soviet power; for the Politburo it is formal recognition that the USSR stands as America's equal.

Marshal Andrei Grechko and the Central Committee's defence secretary Dmitry Ustinov argue that arms control merely freezes American advantages in technology. With a new generation of heavy missiles nearing deployment, they insist the Soviet Union can win the arms race outright if it keeps building. Abandoning the talks would delight the General Staff and the design bureaus, but it would also commit the economy to a ruinous competition with no end in sight.

No American president has ever made an official visit to Moscow. A summit with Richard Nixon would crown the policy of detente and could produce a joint declaration of Basic Principles governing relations between the two superpowers, pledging restraint and peaceful coexistence. Despite the American bombing of North Vietnam, Brezhnev is determined that the visit should go ahead, convinced that recognition as an equal is worth the indignation of Hanoi.

The Volga automobile plant at Togliatti, built with the help of Fiat, has shown what Western machinery and loans can achieve. Alexei Kosygin and the Ministry of Foreign Trade now seek credits from Western banks, licences and entire factories to modernise Soviet industry, paying with oil, gas and timber. The ideologues warn of dependence on capitalist creditors, but the planners see no faster way to close the technological gap.

Since de Gaulle's visit in 1966, France has been the Western power most willing to deal with Moscow on its own terms. President Georges Pompidou's visit in October 1970 offers the chance to deepen this special relationship through regular political consultations, joint research and industrial cooperation, from colour television to space science. A privileged partnership with Paris would show Washington that Western Europe need not follow American leadership in everything.

The first SALT agreements will expire in 1977, and a permanent treaty is needed to replace them. Meeting the new American president Gerald Ford near Vladivostok in November 1974, Brezhnev can agree on a framework of equal ceilings for strategic launchers and multiple warheads. The marshals grumble that American forward-based systems in Europe are left untouched, but a deal would keep detente alive after the fall of Nixon.

For a quarter of a century Moscow has sought formal recognition of the borders drawn in 1945. The Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, gathering thirty-five states in Helsinki, can finally deliver it. The price is the so-called Third Basket on human contacts, information and human rights. Gromyko considers it a harmless concession on paper, yet dissidents across the Union are already preparing to hold the Soviet state to its signature.

After years of haggling over warhead limits, cruise missiles and the Backfire bomber, a second strategic arms treaty is finally ready. In Vienna in June 1979, Brezhnev and Jimmy Carter can sign SALT II, setting equal limits on launchers and multiple warheads until 1985. The treaty would cap the arms race at a costly but stable level, provided the American Senate ever agrees to ratify it.

Detente is unravelling. Soviet involvement in Africa, the deployment of new SS-20 missiles in Europe and NATO's answer with Pershing and cruise missiles have poisoned relations with Washington. The Politburo must decide whether the policy of the Peace Programme can still be rescued through concessions, or whether the time has come to accept a renewed confrontation with the West.

Detente has brought recognition, trade and grain, and Moscow is not prepared to throw it away. Through new proposals on arms control, restraint in the Third World and personal letters to the American president, the Soviet leadership tries to rebuild trust before the hardliners in both capitals bury the policy for good. Such gestures cost prestige at home, and the generals will see them as weakness.

Washington has chosen confrontation, and Moscow will not be intimidated. The SS-20s stay in Europe, the military budget grows, and Soviet propaganda denounces the new American arms build-up as preparation for nuclear war. The years of summits and handshakes are over; the Soviet Union returns to the logic of the Cold War, convinced that only strength commands the respect of its adversaries.

Less than a year ago Soviet and Chinese soldiers fought pitched battles on Damansky Island in the Ussuri and at Tielieketi on the Xinjiang border. Beijing now calls the Soviet Union social-imperialist and its main enemy, while Moscow fears a nuclear-armed China of eight hundred million people along a frontier thousands of kilometres long. How to deal with Mao's China has become the most pressing security question facing the Politburo.

After Alexei Kosygin's hurried meeting with Zhou Enlai at Beijing airport in September 1969, both sides have agreed to talk. Since October, First Deputy Foreign Minister Vasily Kuznetsov has led a delegation in Beijing to negotiate the disputed border and avoid new clashes. Progress is slow and the rhetoric remains hostile, but every month of talks is a month without fighting on the Ussuri.

The General Staff, the Foreign Ministry and the International Department each offer a different answer to the Chinese challenge. Moscow can contain China with a wall of divisions and alliances, strike its nuclear programme before it matures, or seek a reconciliation that would reunite the two great communist powers. Each road carries its own risks, and the choice will shape Soviet policy in Asia for decades.

The Soviet Union will neither attack China nor bow to its demands. Instead, the frontier from the Pamirs to the Pacific is to become a defensive barrier, backed by a network of friendly states around China's periphery. Containment is expensive and slow, but it promises security without the risk of a nuclear war in Asia, and it leaves the door open for talks once Beijing becomes more reasonable.

Between 1969 and 1972 the Soviet forces facing China are to grow from a modest screen into a powerful front. New garrisons, airfields and depots are rising across the Trans-Baikal and Far Eastern Military Districts, while tank and motor-rifle divisions move east along the Trans-Siberian Railway. The buildup consumes enormous resources, but it ensures that the People's Liberation Army will never repeat Damansky on a larger scale.

Along the Amur and the Ussuri, where the border runs within sight of Chinese villages, the army is constructing fortified districts of bunkers, gun emplacements and dug-in tank turrets. Manned by machine-gun and artillery units, these defences are meant to blunt any Chinese offensive long enough for reserves to arrive from the west. Khabarovsk and Blagoveshchensk, both within artillery range of China, depend on them.

Mongolia guards the shortest route from northern China to Lake Baikal and the Trans-Siberian Railway. Under the treaty of 1966, Moscow can station the 39th Army in the country and turn the Mongolian People's Republic into a forward bastion against China. Yumjaagiin Tsedenbal's government is willing, but Ulaanbaatar expects economic aid in return for hosting Soviet tanks and airfields.

In June 1969 Leonid Brezhnev proposed a system of collective security in Asia, a vague idea that everyone in the region understood to be aimed at China. Reviving the proposal would bind India, Vietnam, Mongolia and Afghanistan more closely to Moscow and present the Soviet Union as the guarantor of peace in Asia. Beijing will denounce it as encirclement, but China's wary neighbours may find the offer attractive.

As the crisis in East Pakistan escalates and Washington moves closer to Beijing and Islamabad, Indira Gandhi's government seeks a reliable partner. A Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation, prepared by Andrei Gromyko and Swaran Singh, would make India the cornerstone of Soviet policy in South Asia and a counterweight to China. In return, Moscow must be ready to supply weapons and diplomatic cover should war break out.

Vietnam, increasingly at odds with Beijing, has become China's southern rival. A Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation with Hanoi would grant the Soviet Navy access to the great American-built base at Cam Ranh Bay and open a second front against China in the south. Yet the alliance could drag Moscow into a war over Cambodia, where Vietnam and China's protege Pol Pot are already clashing.

In 1969 Soviet diplomats quietly asked their American contacts how Washington would react to a strike on China's nuclear facilities. Some in the General Staff still believe that a single blow could destroy Mao's atomic programme before it can threaten Soviet cities. What if the option, never formally adopted, were taken seriously? The Politburo must decide whether to keep it on the table.

The planners of the General Staff draw up detailed options for a strike on the Chinese nuclear test site at Lop Nur and the weapons facilities around it. Missile brigades and long-range aviation are assigned targets, while ground forces prepare to exploit the chaos that would follow. The plan gives Moscow the means to topple the Maoist regime, but the decision to use it would be the gravest in Soviet history.

Orders are drafted for a strike at dawn: missiles and bombers against Lop Nur and China's nuclear infrastructure, tank armies in Mongolia and the Trans-Baikal ready to roll into Manchuria and Xinjiang. Moscow prepares to present the operation as a preventive measure against Maoist adventurism, but news of the preparations is already causing alarm in Washington, Delhi and Tokyo. Once the order is given, there is no way back.

What if the meeting between Kosygin and Zhou Enlai at Beijing airport in September 1969 had been a turning point rather than a mere ceasefire? An ideological truce, an end to the polemics between the two parties and a pullback of forces from the border could restore the alliance broken in the early 1960s. The hardliners in both capitals will resist, but a united communist world would transform the balance of the Cold War.

The bloody island of Damansky, which the Chinese call Zhenbao, lies on the Chinese side of the main channel of the Ussuri. Accepting the river's navigable channel as the border, as international practice suggests, would hand the island to China and remove the most visible symbol of the conflict. Historically the question was settled only in 1991; doing it now would show Beijing that Moscow is serious about peace.

Whether through strength or through compromise, the danger of a great war with China has receded. The divisions in the Far East can be held at a sustainable level, the frontier regions can turn to development, and the Baikal-Amur Mainline will one day connect Siberia's riches with the Pacific. For the first time since 1969, the Soviet Union can look east without fear.

Moscow speaks of a socialist commonwealth, a family of fraternal states bound together by Marxism-Leninism, the Warsaw Pact and Comecon. Behind the rhetoric lies a reality of Soviet garrisons in Central Europe, cheap raw materials flowing west and growing frustration in Warsaw, Budapest and Bucharest. Keeping the commonwealth united requires constant attention, generosity and, when necessary, pressure.

The tanks that rolled into Prague in August 1968 raised a question that still hangs over the Eastern bloc: how sovereign are the socialist states? Moscow can enshrine the right to intervene whenever socialism is threatened, or it can accept that each fraternal party must find its own way, with all the risks that entails. The answer will define relations with Eastern Europe for a generation.

In September 1968 Pravda declared that the sovereignty of each socialist country is limited by the interests of the socialist community as a whole. Making this principle the formal basis of bloc policy tells every party leader from East Berlin to Sofia that no one may leave the camp. Western governments will see it as proof that detente stops at the Elbe, but for Moscow the unity of the bloc comes first.

What if Moscow announced, twenty years early, that each socialist country may choose its own path? The Politburo could renounce the use of force against its allies and allow reformers like those of the Prague Spring to experiment freely. Eastern Europe would gain new legitimacy and the West would applaud, but the hardliners warn that once the doors are open, the whole bloc may walk through them.

At the Comecon session in Bucharest in July 1971, the member states are to adopt a Comprehensive Programme for socialist economic integration. Joint investment projects, coordinated five-year plans, specialisation of production and cooperation in science are meant to turn a loose trading club into an integrated economic bloc. Romania insists on its sovereignty, but most partners welcome Soviet resources and markets.

Soviet oil flows to Eastern Europe through the Druzhba pipeline at prices far below the world market. This subsidy keeps the economies of the fraternal states running and buys their loyalty, but every barrel sold cheaply in Leipzig or Bratislava is a barrel that could earn hard currency in Rotterdam. As world prices climb, the question of what fraternal oil should cost can no longer be avoided.

Moscow decides that the stability of its allies is worth more than hard currency. Oil and gas will continue to flow to Comecon partners at friendly prices, cushioning Poland and the German Democratic Republic from the shocks of the world economy. The Ministry of Finance counts the lost revenue, but the Politburo knows that a hungry, cold Eastern Europe would cost far more.

The Bucharest formula of 1975 tied Comecon oil prices to a moving average of world prices; what if Moscow went all the way? Charging the fraternal states the full market rate would bring substantial additional revenue and end the hidden subsidy to Eastern Europe. Warsaw, East Berlin and Prague will protest loudly, and their already strained economies may not survive the shock.

The gas fields of Orenburg could supply Eastern Europe for decades, if only a pipeline to the western border can be built. Moscow proposes that each Comecon partner construct its own section of the Soyuz line in exchange for guaranteed gas deliveries. The project would weld the bloc together with steel and gas, a monument to socialist economic integration stretching across the steppe and the Ukrainian plains.

Large joint manoeuvres demonstrate the unity and readiness of the Warsaw Pact. Exercises such as Brotherhood in Arms, held in the German Democratic Republic in 1970, and the Shield series bring together armies from the Baltic to the Black Sea under Soviet direction. Each exercise must be agreed with the allied governments, but the shared experience strengthens both the coalition and the Soviet Army itself.

The Unified Armed Forces of the Warsaw Pact are still more a coalition on paper than an integrated force. Under a forceful commander-in-chief such as Marshal Viktor Kulikov, a permanent staff, common doctrine and shared research could transform them into a single military machine. The allies will gain access to Soviet expertise, but they will also find their armies ever more closely bound to Moscow's plans.

In December 1970 sudden price increases just before Christmas drive the shipyard workers of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Szczecin into the streets. The militia opens fire, dozens are killed, and Władysław Gomułka falls, replaced by the Silesian party boss Edward Gierek. Moscow must decide how to handle Poland: rescue the new leadership with money and grain, or remind Warsaw firmly where its obligations lie.

Edward Gierek promises the Polish workers a better life, but he needs money and grain to deliver it. Moscow can extend credits, raw materials and food to stabilise his government and calm the shipyards. The help is expensive, and Gierek will soon be borrowing from Western banks as well, yet a stable Poland is the keystone of the Warsaw Pact and the corridor to the Soviet forces in Germany.

The Polish comrades have let the situation slip out of control, and Moscow will not reward failure. The Polish leadership is summoned to the Kremlin to hear unambiguous demands for ideological firmness, order in the shipyards and loyalty to the alliance. How Warsaw answers is up to the Poles, but every party leader in the bloc will understand the message.

Nicolae Ceaușescu refused to join the invasion of Czechoslovakia, recognised West Germany, kept relations with Israel and welcomed Richard Nixon to Bucharest in 1969. Romania remains a member of the Warsaw Pact and Comecon, yet it behaves more and more like a non-aligned state. Moscow must decide whether to tolerate this independent streak or to make an example of Bucharest.

Ceaușescu's independence is irritating, but Romania remains a one-party communist state with no intention of leaving the bloc. Moscow chooses to swallow its pride, keep the dialogue open and let Bucharest enjoy its moments on the world stage. Tolerance spares the alliance a damaging quarrel and frees the leadership to concentrate on more pressing matters.

Romania's flirtation with Washington and Beijing can no longer be tolerated. Moscow will freeze joint projects, cool party contacts and make clear to the other allies that independence has its price. The pressure may push Ceaușescu even closer to the West and China, but it will show the rest of the bloc exactly where the limits lie.

Since 1967 the Interkosmos programme has allowed Soviet allies to share in the conquest of space through joint satellites and scientific experiments. The next step is to fly guest cosmonauts from fraternal countries aboard Soyuz spacecraft to the Salyut stations. A Czechoslovak, Polish, East German, Cuban or Vietnamese cosmonaut in orbit would be a powerful symbol of socialist solidarity and of Soviet leadership in space.

What if the loose web of treaties binding the Eastern bloc were replaced by a formal Commonwealth of Socialist Nations? Permanent common institutions, coordinated planning and joint aid programmes could give the alliance a structure as solid as the European Community in the West. Smaller allies fear absorption into a Soviet superstate, but the advocates argue that only true integration can match the economic power of the capitalist world.

Lenin taught that the cause of socialism knows no borders, and the Soviet Union regards itself as the bulwark of national liberation movements around the world. Through the International Department of the Central Committee under Boris Ponomarev, Moscow supports communist parties, liberation fronts and progressive regimes in Asia, Africa and Latin America. Solidarity is a duty, but it is also a powerful instrument of Soviet influence.

Israeli deep-penetration raids are striking at the heart of Egypt, and Gamal Abdel Nasser flies secretly to Moscow to plead for help. Under Operation Kavkaz, an entire air defence division with modern surface-to-air missiles and squadrons of MiG-21s flown by Soviet pilots can be deployed along the Suez Canal. It would be one of the largest Soviet combat deployments outside the bloc, and a direct challenge to Israel and its American patrons.

After the death of Nasser in September 1970, Moscow is anxious to bind his successor Anwar Sadat to the Soviet camp. A Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation, signed in Cairo in May 1971, would formalise the presence of thousands of Soviet advisers and the flow of arms to the most important state in the Arab world. Sadat's loyalty is uncertain, but Egypt remains the key to Soviet influence in the Middle East.

North Vietnam's war against the United States and Saigon depends on Soviet surface-to-air missiles, MiG fighters, fuel and rice delivered through Haiphong and across China. Expanding this lifeline would strengthen Hanoi's defences against American bombing and secure Soviet influence over the Vietnamese communists, who are courted by Beijing as well. The supplies will anger Washington, but abandoning a fraternal party at war is unthinkable.

Cuba is the Soviet outpost in the Western Hemisphere, but its economy is reeling after the failed ten-million-ton sugar harvest of 1970. By buying Cuban sugar at preferential prices and supplying oil in return, Moscow can keep Fidel Castro's revolution afloat and bind the island to Comecon. The subsidy is expensive, but a socialist Cuba ninety miles from Florida is worth every rouble.

The Baathist regimes in Damascus and Baghdad are bitter rivals of each other, yet both are natural partners for Moscow. Iraq is ready to sign a Treaty of Friendship and needs Soviet help to nationalise its oil industry, while Hafez al-Assad's Syria seeks weapons and advisers to rebuild its army. Together they would give the Soviet Union a firm foothold in the Middle East, whatever happens in Cairo.

Founded in Moscow in 1960, the Peoples' Friendship University named after Patrice Lumumba educates thousands of students from Asia, Africa and Latin America. Expanding it would train a new generation of engineers, doctors and party cadres who return home with Soviet diplomas and, it is hoped, Soviet sympathies. Not every graduate becomes a friend of Moscow, but the investment in future elites pays off over decades.

From Egypt to Vietnam, Soviet officers train armies, operate radar stations and teach the use of modern weapons. A permanent corps of military advisers, organised through the Tenth Main Directorate of the General Staff, would make Soviet assistance more efficient and more influential. Advisers on the ground often achieve more than arms shipments alone, and they let Moscow know exactly what its partners are doing.

Every partner in the Third World asks for help, but Soviet resources are not unlimited. Moscow can build dams, steel mills and power stations as it did at Aswan and Bhilai, winning goodwill through visible development, or it can concentrate on weapons, which are cheaper to provide and buy influence with the generals who often hold real power. The choice will define the character of Soviet engagement in the developing world.

The Aswan High Dam remains the proudest symbol of Soviet friendship in the Third World. By expanding economic aid programmes, from the Euphrates dam in Syria to steelworks in India, Moscow can show that socialism brings not only weapons but development. Such projects take years and consume scarce resources, yet they leave lasting monuments and tie entire economies to Soviet technology and expertise.

Tanks, fighters and missiles are the Soviet Union's most sought-after exports. Selling them on generous credit terms, often never fully repaid, wins the gratitude of governments and armies across the Middle East, Africa and Asia. The defence industry welcomes the orders, and every customer becomes dependent on Soviet spare parts, ammunition and instructors for years to come.

As Portugal's empire collapses, the Marxist MPLA of Agostinho Neto fights rival movements backed by Zaire, South Africa and the United States for control of Angola. Fidel Castro is ready to send Cuban troops, but only Soviet aircraft and weapons can carry and equip them across the Atlantic. Supporting this bridge would establish a new socialist state in southern Africa, at the cost of further damage to detente.

In the Horn of Africa, Moscow has two clients who are about to go to war with each other. Siad Barre's Somalia hosts a Soviet naval facility at Berbera, while the revolutionary Derg in Ethiopia under Mengistu Haile Mariam proclaims Marxism-Leninism. When Somalia moves to seize the Ogaden, the Soviet Union will have to choose one side and lose the other.

Ethiopia, with its large population and revolutionary government, is the greater prize. Moscow can organise a massive airlift of weapons and send General Vasily Petrov to direct the defence of the Ogaden alongside Cuban brigades. The decision will cost the base at Berbera and the friendship of Somalia, but it could secure a loyal Marxist-Leninist ally on the Red Sea.

Somalia has been a faithful partner for years and hosts the valuable naval facility at Berbera. Continuing to arm Siad Barre's army would keep this foothold on the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, even as Somali forces advance into the Ogaden. Abandoning the revolutionaries in Addis Ababa would hurt Soviet prestige among African progressives, but a loyal ally in hand may be worth more than a promise.

In April 1978 the Saur Revolution brought the communist People's Democratic Party to power in Kabul, but its radical reforms have provoked rebellion across the country. In March 1979 an uprising in Herat killed Soviet advisers, and Nur Muhammad Taraki is begging for troops. The Politburo must decide whether to intervene directly or leave the Afghan comrades to fight their own war.

If the Afghan government formally asks for help, the Soviet Union can send a Limited Contingent of troops to secure the cities, roads and airfields while the Afghan army fights the rebels. Andropov, Ustinov and Gromyko believe a short intervention will stabilise the regime and keep Afghanistan out of American hands. The world will condemn the move, and no one can say how long the soldiers will have to stay.

In March 1979 Alexei Kosygin told Taraki on the telephone that Soviet troops could not replace the Afghan people in their own struggle. What if the leadership had held to his advice? Kabul would receive weapons, advisers and money, but not a single Soviet soldier. The Afghan communists will feel betrayed, yet the Soviet Union spares itself a war in the mountains that could last for years.

What if Moscow abandoned caution and openly embraced the role of vanguard of world revolution? Liberation movements from southern Africa to Central America would receive weapons, money and training without the restraint imposed by detente. The cost to the Soviet budget and to relations with the West would be immense, but the ideologues dream of a world where the correlation of forces has shifted decisively towards socialism.

British protection has ended, leaving the rulers responsible for the coast's external affairs and defence. Their separate courts and administrations must now decide how much authority to entrust to a common government.

The smaller emirates need roads, public services and dependable development finance. A common fund can direct projects towards settlements with the greatest needs and strengthen confidence in the union. Planning and supervising those works will require a continuing federal administration.
An agreement among the Trucial rulers offers a more manageable union, while Bahrain and Qatar pursue their own futures.
Bahrain and Qatar remain possible partners. Representation, the capital and their rulers’ sovereignty must be settled through agreement.

The rulers can ratify a provisional constitutional framework for common institutions. The settlement must define the responsibilities of the federation and the authority retained by each emirate. Its implementation will follow the division of powers agreed by the rulers.

All viable federal charters need common ministries and recognise the leading emirates. Prioritising entrenched emirate guarantees follows the historical bargain, while keeping federal coordination expensive.
Ministries already belong in the charter. A stronger federal mandate asks the rulers to delegate more authority than in the historical bargain, in exchange for clear limits and shared development.

The end of Britain's special treaty responsibilities leaves the coast to conduct its own foreign affairs and defence. The rulers can put their agreed constitutional settlement into effect and prepare to proclaim their union.

The rulers have agreed how their emirates will share authority, and British protection has ended. Proclaiming the United Arab Emirates gives the settlement a common name and establishes its federal offices. A federation must now reconcile the interests of the ruling houses with the responsibilities of an independent state.

Ras Al Khaimah's security concerns and claims to the Tunbs have complicated its place in the union. A settlement that recognises those concerns can bring its ruler and institutions into the federal bargain.

A consultative federal council can give the emirates a forum for public affairs while the rulers retain their constitutional authority. Recognising educational and civic associations under federal law gives their activities an accountable framework. Consultations and supervision require trained officials and a continuing federal administration.

Abu Dhabi uses the Bahraini dinar while the other emirates use the Qatar-Dubai riyal. A currency board and common dirham can simplify federal accounts and trade, provided the new monetary institutions earn confidence across the union.

The consultative council has given public affairs a federal forum. A further constitutional reform can open legal political competition and regular elections. The electorate will determine the governing coalition, while the ruling houses must accept a more uncertain political settlement.

The dynasty can turn personal access to the rulers into a durable federal bargain. Listening to local notables takes time and resources. Maintaining the rulers' confidence and clear lines of responsibility can help the union withstand a local succession crisis.
Abu Dhabi can spread oil-financed development beyond its own borders and make union valuable to the poorer emirates.
Dubai’s commercial institutions need room to operate. A bargain with its merchants attracts business while narrowing federal discretion.

Renewing the federal compact requires an agreed cabinet and a workable division of responsibilities between Abu Dhabi and Dubai. A Dubai-led ministry can strengthen confidence in the federal administration while the presidency remains a separate office.
Joint procurement and shared institutions can expand without abolishing the ruling houses. Consensus remains a real constraint.

The rulers can delegate clearer executive responsibilities to the presidency while maintaining their constitutional role. A stronger federal executive can carry decisions into effect more consistently, although emirates accustomed to managing their own affairs will resist the concentration of authority.
Clear obligations between court and ministry make the ruler’s promise more credible, at the price of maintaining a permanent federal apparatus.
A succession understood by the rulers protects the federation from becoming a contest over the whole state whenever one court changes hands.
A governing constitutional coalition can begin opening the institutions that the founding charter left under the rulers’ supervision.

The ruling houses can remain constitutional partners while a responsible cabinet directs ordinary administration. A clear division between court and ministry offers continuity, but limits the government's freedom to act alone.

A republican constitution can place federal authority in elected institutions. Civil guarantees and a professional administration can give the new government a dependable foundation, while the displacement of hereditary authority will unsettle established loyalties.
Published federal accounts allow deputies and merchants to judge how the new government uses public money.

Citizens need a durable stake in the new constitutional order. Reserving a larger share of employment and residency opportunities for them can strengthen support for reform while reducing the labour available to the trading cities.

Long-term residents have helped build the coast's commercial economy. More secure residency and advisory municipal participation can sustain that contribution, while placing wider obligations on local government.
Commercial and administrative courts need trained judges and enforceable jurisdiction if constitutional promises are to change everyday government.
Parliamentary oversight can outlive the first reforming cabinet if ministries accept regular scrutiny and an orderly transfer of office.
Arab nationalist ideas reached the coast through teachers, broadcasting and regional politics. A republican government would have to build institutions beyond those networks.
Teachers and civil administrators can define the republic through Arab public education and shared institutions rather than permanent military supervision.
A national command can provide discipline in a fragile republic. Its privileges impose a continuing cost and limit civilian authority.

A republic will inherit the rival offices and limited trained personnel of the ruling courts. A professional civil service can bring those administrations together, but its officials must be recruited, trained and paid.
A regional development compact offers teachers, training and a stronger Arab voice. Partners must agree to the obligations and retain their sovereignty.
Commercial independence can keep the republic from becoming a client of a larger Arab state, but it leaves defence more dependent on local resources.

A modest public industrial sector can broaden an economy built around oil receipts and commerce. The state will have to provide reliable power, skilled workers and sustained capital before new factories can meet that promise.
A settled division between cabinet, command and local government gives the republic a chance to survive its founders.
A left-led government must reconcile national sovereignty with an economy sustained by oil, merchants and a large expatriate workforce.
A communist cabinet can direct key enterprises toward a national plan, accepting the loss of private commercial initiative.
A non-aligned social government can leave the trading economy open while purchasing public services from its revenue.
Enforceable contracts and inspections can improve migrant workers’ bargaining position. Enforcement creates costs for employers and the state.
Residence-based access to basic services supports a stable workforce while greatly expanding the obligation of the small public administration.
Concentrating social entitlements on citizens builds a national constituency for reform, but leaves unequal access to public services.
Scholarships and technical institutes can supply planners and engineers without treating foreign advisers as a permanent substitute for local expertise.
A durable social settlement needs rules for funding, residency and public control that can survive more than one cabinet.

Sunni educational and charitable associations provide the reform movement with trusted local networks. Bringing those networks into government requires a settlement with merchants, the ruling families and institutions outside the movement.
Local charities can extend assistance through trusted institutions, while unequal provision makes federal oversight harder.
A common welfare administration gives reformers a national instrument but requires a larger and more expensive public service.

The coast needs professional skills as well as religious education. Reformers must decide how schools and training institutions can serve both purposes, and how much independence their teachers and associations retain.
A consultative civic pact preserves room for merchants and other associations, reducing the reform movement’s freedom to govern alone.
A stronger religious council can unify social policy while deterring some outside business and political cooperation.
Oil has made Abu Dhabi’s development possible, but contractual terms, technical expertise and ownership remain matters of negotiation.

Existing oil reserves need producing wells, gathering lines and trained crews before they can support the emirates’ ambitions. The first major capital programme expands Abu Dhabi’s modest operating capacity. Expanding oil operations draws labour and commerce towards the new industry, reducing the traditional coastal trades' contribution to household income.

A larger public equity share can bring more of the concession's income under the producing emirate's control. Foreign operators can remain technical partners, while the emirate assumes a greater share of the investment and operating risks.

Reliable technical services and experienced management are valuable to a small producing state. Stronger guarantees can secure that expertise, but leave a larger commercial margin with the partners and tie local operations more closely to them.

A second onshore programme extends producing fields and their pipelines. Its cost competes directly with schools, ports and the public budget, while the resulting receipts remain exposed to world oil prices. Expanding oil operations draws labour and commerce towards the new industry, reducing the traditional coastal trades' contribution to household income.

Offshore production requires platforms, subsea connections and marine support. Abu Dhabi and Dubai can both expand, but the programme commits a much larger sum than the first onshore wells. Expanding oil operations draws labour and commerce towards the new industry, reducing the traditional coastal trades' contribution to household income.

Further offshore expansion requires additional platforms, connections and marine support. Building on the first programme can raise operating capacity, but commits substantial capital that other parts of the federation also need. As the oil economy grows, crews and merchants find new work and the traditional coastal trades account for less of household income.
Professional administration can make the producing emirates’ oil arrangements more predictable while maintaining their separate ownership.

Abu Dhabi can turn exceptional oil receipts into a reserve and a professionally managed investment portfolio. Saving part of the windfall offers protection against future shocks while reducing the resources available for immediate development.
Using the windfall at home can accelerate physical development, while leaving fewer reserves for a downturn.

Public plans must remain affordable when the oil market turns. Reserves can support the budget; diversified earnings can reduce its dependence on exports. Budget reserves and clear spending priorities can protect essential administration when oil prices fall.

Long before oil exports, pearl divers, fishermen, boatbuilders and merchants earned their living along the coast. The great pearling seasons have faded, but fishing boats and dhow trading networks still sustain families. Better boats, handling and local markets can provide steadier livelihoods and reduce reliance on public assistance, even as the oil industry competes for crews and capital.

Reliable landing grounds, ice stores and fish markets can reduce spoilage and give crews a steadier return for their catch. A more secure household income eases demand for assistance. The works will also serve coastal traders, although administration and refrigeration bring continuing costs and oil development draws activity towards new industries.
A separate commercial zone can attract foreign firms with predictable rules while surrendering part of the local tax take.
Credit and contracts reserved for established local businesses can deepen national ownership, while limiting the scale of foreign participation.
Efficient customs and reliable connections matter as much as quays. The free zone needs a functioning transport economy around it.
A more disciplined local credit system can finance trade while requiring the public authorities to scrutinise business risk.
Reliable contracts can link Dubai’s ambitions to a wider federation while preserving the emirates’ distinct commercial jurisdictions.

Dubai's commercial air links need a larger airport, reliable ground services and connections to the port economy. A new runway and supporting facilities can bring passengers and high-value cargo to the coast, but their construction and operation require substantial funding and electricity.

Dubai's ports can support more than the movement of imported goods. Serviced industrial land, workshops and reliable utilities will give manufacturers a foothold beside the harbour, at the cost of a major capital commitment and greater demand for power and labour.

Services and industry can provide earnings beyond the producing fields. A broader economy will be better placed to absorb a fall in oil receipts, although its firms will remain exposed to regional insecurity and world markets.

Oil and gas revenues can finance an aluminium industry at Jebel Ali, turning imported alumina into metal for export. The smelter needs dependable electricity, cooling water, specialised equipment and trained crews. Its success would create a new industrial export, while tying a substantial part of the coast's power supply to continuous operation.

Construction across the emirates consumes steel brought through their ports. A state-backed rolling industry in Abu Dhabi can process imported billets and scrap into a domestic supply of finished steel. This accelerated industrial programme requires machinery, power and long-term working capital before it can compete with established foreign suppliers.

Many settlements still rely on a small number of teachers, medical staff and visiting services. District clinics, maternity care and new classrooms can help children survive and families remain in the towns. Keeping those services staffed will require a lasting commitment to health and education budgets.
Training nationals takes time but can reduce dependence on imported expertise and support a locally staffed administration.
International recruitment can relieve immediate shortages while increasing housing demand and the reliance on a mobile expatriate population.

Growing settlements cannot depend indefinitely on wells and irregular deliveries. Desalination, distribution pipes and sanitation can make larger towns viable and reduce disease, but the pumps and treatment works will consume power even when oil revenues fall.

Serviced neighbourhoods give citizen families room to grow without abandoning their ties to the emirates. Housing, schools and local facilities can strengthen the founding social bargain, while creating permanent obligations for the public budget.

The ports, building sites and industries depend on workers arriving from abroad. Permanent housing, clean water and clinics can turn crowded work camps into viable communities and sustain a much larger resident population. The emirates must fund the resulting health services and social infrastructure.
Universities and technical institutes can supply the skills a growing federation needs. Laboratories and teachers must be maintained after the opening ceremony.

A growing population needs reliable district health services, trained staff and an administration able to maintain them. Professional management can keep those institutions effective as the towns expand, although continuing care will remain a permanent public expense.
The end of British protection leaves a small population and distinct emirate forces facing powerful neighbours. Coordination matters before prestige purchases.
A common register of personnel, stores and contracts is the first step toward a force that the federation can actually sustain.
A shared chain of command can improve readiness, at the price of a larger standing federal organisation.
The emirates can retain local commands while standardising procedures. This protects autonomy but preserves duplication in personnel and administration.

Compatible depots, transport and communications can make a common command effective across the emirates. Reliable support reduces waste in the field, but requires trained personnel and continuing expenditure at home.
Standard equipment and training can make autonomous forces cooperate, even while their commanders remain answerable to different rulers.
A permanent staff can translate the federation’s limited resources into realistic operational plans.
Surveillance, air defence and maritime training address the coast’s vulnerabilities with a small professional force. Imported systems bring costs and external dependence.
A compact mobile land force can protect key routes and facilities, while consuming a larger share of the federation’s scarce personnel.
Maintenance, training and a realistic establishment matter more than a paper arsenal. The federation must be able to operate what it buys.

Independence requires a foreign service able to represent the federation and maintain regular contact with its neighbours. Professional diplomats can sustain those relationships and coordinate external policy, while a permanent ministry adds to the administrative budget. An invasion of Kuwait may require financial support, transit arrangements and preparations for a military contribution.
Missions and bilateral contacts allow the federation to work with Britain, Arab neighbours, Iran and both Cold War blocs without automatically joining any of them.
British and Western advisers can help sustain a professional force while maintaining an expensive reliance on imported equipment.
Buying and trading across blocs can reduce dependence on any single patron, at the price of a more complicated support system.

Training agreements can give local personnel access to experienced instructors and established procedures. Their value depends on clear obligations, sustained funding and skills that the federation can retain in its own forces.
Technical exchanges can support development while leaving the federation free to pursue its own diplomacy.

The Gulf monarchies share interests in consultation, trade and security, alongside disputes over borders and policy. Common standards and regular meetings can deepen cooperation while leaving each member responsible for its own commitments.
Abu Musa’s arrangement and the Tunbs dispute cannot be settled by the same formula. A negotiated accord may preserve trade while limiting immediate ambitions.
The federation can keep the islands at the centre of its diplomacy while accepting tension with a much stronger neighbour.
An Iraqi invasion of Kuwait would force the federation to weigh coalition support against the risks of exposure. Without that crisis, civil protection remains useful.

An invasion of Kuwait threatens the security of the Gulf and places its government under exceptional financial pressure. We can offer a contribution to support Kuwait, subject to its government's agreement. This financial commitment is separate from decisions on military access and participation in the war.

Kuwait may need access to the federation's ports and transport links during an invasion. Our government can offer transit arrangements to support its defence, subject to Kuwaiti agreement and the responsibilities of hosting foreign forces.

A military contribution to Kuwait's defence requires an explicit agreement over access, command and support. We can seek that agreement while retaining responsibility for our own troops and our decision to enter the war.

The seven rulers govern their own sheikhdoms, while Britain conducts their external relations and carries defence responsibilities. A common liaison office can make this divided arrangement work more effectively.
Some rulers would prefer continued British protection to facing stronger neighbours alone. London must decide whether it will revise its announced withdrawal policy and accept a renewed compact.

Britain has announced its withdrawal by the end of 1971. Local officials must organise records, train civil servants and prepare the departments that will assume the coast's new responsibilities. Staffing this work adds administrative expense; the trained civil service will remain after British protection ends.

A renewed compact gives the rulers time to strengthen their courts, customs offices and commercial administration. Shared institutions can make the coast easier to govern while Britain retains responsibility for external affairs and defence.

Independence transfers the burden of external affairs and defence to the coast. An orderly handover of responsibilities, stores and training arrangements will help the local administrations carry that burden.
Training teams and common equipment standards can strengthen the small local forces. Maintaining the relationship still requires a professional establishment and expenditure.
Predictable British-linked commercial arrangements can draw firms and expertise to the coast. The rulers must maintain oversight and accept the continuing limits of protection.
Independence need not sever the coast's British connections. A new friendship agreement can preserve consultation, technical advice and commercial links on terms accepted by both governments.

A continuing protection arrangement needs funding, reliable local institutions and an understood division of responsibility. It can offer stability and credit while leaving external sovereignty constrained.
Moscow and the fifteen republics pull in one direction: Gosplan's annual plan becomes a shared task. Whoever takes this focus takes it for the whole Union.
The planning committee no longer asks: it directs. Special tasks for single republics become routine.
Committees of People's Control in every ministry and every kolkhoz check the figures the republics report.
Pelshe's commission punishes on behalf of the Party itself - and the Party does not need to explain itself to the republics.
Republic against republic, factory against factory: the best of the plan carry the Transferable Red Banner.
Every factory has its pushers - men who know where to find cement, cables and a favour. The republics stop pretending they do not exist.
When the quarter ends, the factories storm: night shifts and Sunday shifts until the figures are met.
The best collectives promise more than Gosplan asked - and the newspapers print their names.
A wise director never reports his full capacity: next year's plan is calculated from this year's result.
The Party Congress adopts the directives of the Ninth Five-Year Plan (1971-1975) for the whole Union. Its watchword: prosperity.
The Union has fulfilled its plan in at least three years of this Five-Year Plan.
The Party Congress adopts the directives of the Tenth Five-Year Plan (1976-1980) for the whole Union. Its watchword: efficiency.
The Union has fulfilled its plan in at least three years of this Five-Year Plan.
The Party Congress adopts the directives of the Eleventh Five-Year Plan (1981-1985) for the whole Union. Its watchword: intensification.
The Union has fulfilled its plan in at least three years of this Five-Year Plan.
The Party Congress adopts the directives of the Twelfth Five-Year Plan (1986-1990) for the whole Union. Its watchword: acceleration.
The Union has fulfilled its plan in at least three years of this Five-Year Plan.

Ho Chi Minh's death has left the revolution with a shared legacy and several centres of authority. Le Duan, President Ton Duc Thang and Prime Minister Pham Van Dong must hold the institutions together through another difficult year.

Assign the next extraordinary cadre, salary and transport allocation to district reserve instructors. Local mobilisation will be better prepared, while provincial civilian offices must wait for their own expansion programme.

Assign the next extraordinary cadre, salary and transport allocation to provincial civil offices. Better local records and public services reduce administrative waste, while the reserve training network receives no equivalent expansion from this allocation.

A broader Front must offer rural representatives a practical role. Establish an advisory compact on farm inputs and local distribution, using their knowledge to improve deliveries while accepting that the Party cannot dictate every recommendation.

Sovereignty must be supported by the ability to keep workshops and defensive units supplied. Establish domestic spare part stocks, repair arrangements and alternative procurement contacts, accepting the cost of maintaining this independent organisation.
Administrative competence cannot be supplied by revolutionary credentials alone. Train cadres to investigate conditions, keep reliable accounts and deliver public services.
Mass organisations connect the state to villages, factories and neighbourhoods. Deepen that network while accepting the work required to maintain it.
War has displaced teachers and disrupted schooling without extinguishing the ambition to learn. Extend education beyond the better served towns and protect the next generation of technicians.
Women sustain production, public administration and family life under exceptional pressure. Wider participation must be accompanied by practical support rather than another unpaid obligation.
The National Assembly can become a more useful channel between policy and the people who live with it. Strengthening its work requires an administration capable of responding.
The cadre service must answer to a common chain of authority. Tighter discipline can improve execution, but it can also discourage honest disagreement.
Policy failures do not disappear when nobody dares to describe them. Protect criticism that exposes abuse while accepting a more contested political environment.
Provincial authorities know local shortages and productive possibilities better than distant offices. Give their councils a clearer place in the national programme.
Buddhist and Catholic communities are part of the nation, not a single political bloc. Negotiate practical protections for religious life and equal treatment before public authorities.
A durable charter must outlast the ambitions of its authors. Establish institutions that can carry public responsibilities through changes of leadership and government.
Le Duan places the struggle in the South at the centre of national strategy. The North must sustain that effort while living with the demands it makes on reconstruction.

Concentrate the next staff, reserve equipment and training allocation on a regular offensive. The main force gains the cohesion needed for a decisive campaign, while its supply commitment grows. Negotiations and local defence continue alongside this priority.

Concentrate the next staff and training allocation on staying power, protected routes and territorial defence. The army can sustain pressure with fewer supply demands, while a rapid offensive receives less planning attention. This course does not close the negotiating channel.
Bring the principal formations and their supporting production into a more concentrated effort. Farms and civilian workshops will feel the diversion of scarce resources.
Military pressure and negotiation can serve the same strategy. Prepare a diplomatic channel without assuming that the opposing governments will accept our terms.
Peace permits a congress to turn from the endurance of war to the shape of the national economy. The ambitions adopted here must still confront limited resources and administrative capacity.

Reserve the next industrial allocation for machine building, armament workshops and the technical knowledge needed to sustain them. More of the scarce capital stays in heavy production, leaving less for immediate agricultural improvement.

Direct the next reconstruction allocation towards food production and civilian works. Recovery must be visible in fields and ordinary workshops, even though the same investment cannot simultaneously expand the military production programme.
The northeastern industrial base can support a wider range of national production. Organise the planning and construction of a new combine rather than relying indefinitely on imported capacity.
Food supply and everyday goods determine whether recovery is felt outside the offices of the plan. Direct more of the programme towards those immediate needs.

The institutions of North and South cannot be joined by a proclamation alone. Where the country has actually been reunited, decide how quickly their administrations and economic arrangements should converge.
Rapid socialist transformation offers a clear political direction for the newly integrated economy. Its pace risks disruption where existing production and distribution cannot adjust.
A gradual transition can preserve working enterprises and local knowledge. It asks the revolutionary leadership to tolerate arrangements that do not yet match its final objectives.
Collective mastery places organised labour and state institutions at the centre of production. Making it effective requires more than slogans and additional administrative offices.
Household incentives can relieve pressure on food production without abandoning the socialist state. Such flexibility tests the authority of officials accustomed to uniform targets.
A unified socialist state must demonstrate that victory can become a sustainable civil order. Its social commitments will remain a claim on national resources.
Truong Chinh's authority rests on long service and the power of political doctrine. The plan must now be examined against the conditions it has actually produced.
Planning failures can be answered with firmer discipline and clearer obligations. That approach preserves central authority while narrowing the room for local initiative.
Economic evidence should be permitted to challenge established formulas. Send officials to learn why production and distribution fall short of their instructions.
Binding procurement targets offer the state more predictable deliveries. They can also weaken the incentive to produce beyond what households need for themselves.
A provincial inquiry must listen to producers rather than merely confirm reports already written in Hanoi. Its findings may reveal useful experiments and uncomfortable failures.
The congress documents must acknowledge the gap between intention and result. Prepare a reassessment that can give national renovation an intellectual and political foundation.
State subsidies protect expectations built over many years. Preserving them can cushion insecurity while committing the budget to continuing support.
Enterprise managers cannot be held responsible for results if every practical choice requires distant approval. Grant more autonomy and accept the uncertainty of restructuring.
Ration entitlements are a promise between the state and households under strain. Defending that promise must not conceal the weaknesses of the supply system behind it.
Selective price changes can reduce distortions without attempting every reform at once. Households and enterprises will still face a difficult adjustment.
Rectification should uncover administrative failure as well as punish misconduct. Honest review threatens networks that have learned to protect themselves.
Ideological guardianship can preserve a common political direction. It risks turning a necessary reassessment into another exercise in obedience.
Renovation requires permission to reconsider policies once presented as settled doctrine. Build that permission into the preparations for the next national programme.

District officials must be able to turn a national programme into budgets, supplies and working enterprises. Assign the next training allocation to practical administration and industrial management in the Party school network, while the specialist advisory staff receives no matching expansion.

The plan needs a specialist staff able to trace shortages through accounts, transport and prices. Assign the next training allocation to an economic and technical review team, while district Party schools continue without an equivalent expansion.
A handover can preserve continuity without denying the need for a new programme. Consult the existing leadership institutions and prepare an orderly succession.
Nguyen Van Linh presents renovation as a task of the Party itself. Economic change must confront entrenched interests without dissolving the authority expected to carry it through.

Direct the next agrarian renovation allocation towards household delivery contracts, accountable purchasing and the right to retain additional surplus. Cooperatives may still provide services, but this programme puts the new administrative effort behind household responsibility.

Direct the next agrarian renovation allocation towards shared equipment, technical staff and cooperative infrastructure. Household production continues, but the new funding strengthens common services and collective management rather than enlarging the household contract programme.
Expand the circulation of rural goods so that a productive harvest can reach buyers. Wider commodity trade also exposes households to movements in the market.
Tools, credit and shared equipment can make cooperative reform tangible. Their provision is a continuing commitment rather than a substitute for better incentives.
State enterprises need accounts that reveal costs and responsibilities. Begin separating an enterprise's productive performance from its access to political protection.
Price reform can be sequenced so that institutions have time to adjust. A slower transition places a heavier burden on coordination and supervision.
Blanket subsidies can no longer be treated as an unlimited promise. Their abrupt removal will expose enterprises and households to a painful transition.
Renovation needs a floor beneath those least able to absorb its costs. Protect basic consumption even where doing so slows fiscal adjustment.
Expansion without fiscal restraint risks reproducing the instability reform was meant to address. Accept a period of tighter spending and slower growth while restoring order.
Public criticism of abuse must reach beyond ceremonial self criticism. Expose practices that obstruct reform, even when influential cadres would prefer silence.
Economic renovation can proceed under a continued Party monopoly. Preserve that political boundary while changing the way the economy is managed.
Independent political organisation goes beyond consultation through the Front. Negotiate a new boundary of authority and accept a more fundamental challenge to the existing order.

Screen projects against the machinery, repairs and operating needs of domestic enterprises. Investment can proceed under continued Party rule; the question is how to use limited administrative capacity, not whether political pluralism is required for foreign capital.

Develop predictable approvals, project infrastructure and operating guarantees for investment partnerships. State oversight remains in place, while the programme commits more of the investment administration to supporting wider commercial access.
The socialist world cannot be assumed to remain a permanent source of support. Adapt renovation to a future in which Vietnam must rely on a wider range of economic relationships.
Vo Van Kiet's proposed national mandate puts practical administration ahead of rigid procedure. Begin with experiments that can demonstrate how production and distribution might work better.
Provincial initiative can solve problems before a national rule is ready. It also reduces the centre's control over the path of reform.
A coordinated national pilot can produce more comparable results. It requires a stronger apparatus to select projects, supervise them and evaluate their progress.
Food and manufactured goods must be able to move from producers to the cities. Remove practical obstacles without pretending that wider circulation is free of market risk.
Give priority projects an office responsible for delivery rather than another set of targets. Coordination itself must remain accountable for the resources it uses.
Reliable electricity determines whether workshops can make use of their labour and machinery. Prepare a period appropriate power project for the northern economy.

Allow enterprises to reinvest a larger share of operating earnings and remove unnecessary central processing. Their investment programme can move faster, but current tax receipts fall as more resources remain inside the firms.

Pool the next development allocation in the national treasury for coordinated infrastructure and priority works. Central direction can connect projects that individual enterprises cannot finance, at the expense of additional administration.
Local suppliers can reduce delays and connect workshops to a wider productive network. Give their development a place in the construction programme.
A working road spine binds production to distribution. Organise the recovery of northern links that have become an obstacle to everyday economic life.
Responsibility should remain attached to a named office when a project fails. Auditing delivery challenges administrative practices that benefit from ambiguity.
Small export experiments can test how Vietnamese producers meet outside demand. They also bring international fluctuations closer to the domestic economy.
A domestic supply chain offers resilience where imports are uncertain. Building it may require accepting a slower route to more efficient production.
Managers and technicians need opportunities to learn beyond the routines of command allocation. Invest in the skills required to operate the new productive arrangements.
A machine awaiting a minor imported component is a factory unable to work. Support local repair and spare parts workshops where domestic production is practical.
The plan should be judged by what reaches households and workshops. Keep the gains of successful experiments while funding the services needed to sustain them.

An autonomous Fatherland Front government would require a new political settlement. Give its constituent organisations a real mandate rather than treating their consultation as an endorsement already secured.

Give elected workplace representatives the leading role in allocating the next industrial management programme. Their knowledge can improve cooperation and civilian production, while consultation requires more administrative work. Technical specialists retain their ordinary advisory roles.

Give the next industrial management allocation to a specialist technical cabinet and its project staff. Construction and technical review can move more quickly, while maintaining qualified personnel requires a larger education commitment. Workplace representation remains part of ordinary administration.
Delegates who can be recalled must answer more frequently to their communities. That responsiveness changes the relationship between local representatives and the executive.
Public accounts make it harder to conceal the cost of a policy. Publication also exposes the government to challenges that closed administration can avoid.
The rural economy needs a compact that producers can regard as legitimate. Negotiate the relationship between procurement, household effort and public support.
Cooperative federations can pool resources without imposing one organisation on every village. Voluntary coordination demands patient administration.
Protected family holdings offer households greater security over their work. They narrow the space for officials to treat all rural activity as a planning instruction.
Village clinics turn a promise of social citizenship into a service people can use. Maintaining them requires staff, supplies and a recurring public commitment.
Small producers often lack the working capital to make use of their skills. Provide access to credit while accepting the task of supervising it responsibly.

Independent socialism needs productive competence as well as diplomatic declarations. Establish an industrial adaptation service for machinery and technical manuals, and connect it to a homeland defence programme that can function without surrendering control to a patron.
The socialist tradition contains voices that the existing order has excluded. Seek reconciliation with dissenters while accepting the political uncertainty of their return.
The Front can instead become a unified vanguard in its own right. Concentrating authority may preserve direction while limiting independent criticism.
Religious belief should not place a citizen outside the national compact. Translate accommodation into equal treatment by local institutions.
A common cadre service can hold the Front's different organisations together. Its scope must be supported by the administrative resources it demands.
A socialist national compact must reconcile participation with the obligations of government. Its stability depends on sustaining the services promised in its name.
An independent Democratic Party government would break with its historical role inside the communist led Front. Build a constitutional compact capable of giving that change a legitimate foundation.
Courts must be able to judge the use of public power without awaiting political permission. Independence requires institutions that can withstand pressure from the executive.
An emergency executive offers a more concentrated response to disorder. Its powers place the promised constitutional settlement under strain from the beginning.

Protect civic and professional associations so that citizens can organise, challenge waste and contribute to legislation. Their capacity strengthens constitutional government and public oversight, rather than turning political liberty into a substitute for laboratories or equipment.
Emergency powers need a defined purpose and a credible review. Without limits, temporary authority can become the normal condition of the republic.
Neither unrestricted private control nor comprehensive command offers an easy answer to recovery. Negotiate a mixed economy with public obligations and room for enterprise.
Open tenders can make public contracts answer to more than political connections. Transparency also removes instruments on which an executive may have relied.
National enterprises can preserve domestic control over important production. Protecting them may come at the expense of wider economic efficiency.
Small firms need secure rights before they can plan beyond immediate survival. Establish a legal framework capable of protecting those rights consistently.
A public technical college can widen access to the skills reconstruction requires. It will need a reliable education budget as well as buildings and instructors.
Citizens with different wartime loyalties must be able to live under the same civil order. Reconciliation cannot depend on permanent exclusion from public life.
Western guarantees might strengthen the government's international position. They also raise difficult questions about dependence and the conditions attached to outside support.
Constitutional government need not commit the republic to a strategic camp. A policy of armed neutrality demands a credible domestic basis for independence.
Trade can develop before a final strategic alignment is settled. Make practical economic contact possible without promising that outside governments will agree to every request.
A broad civilian coalition can protect constitutional government from a narrow factional contest. Its compromises will make executive decisions slower and more contested.
Government by consent depends on rules that remain credible when the incumbent loses. Negotiate guarantees that make peaceful political competition possible.
The northern Socialist Party would need a new mandate to govern independently of the Front's historical arrangements. Base that mandate on consent, public service and the rights of organised labour.
Independent unions can speak for workers beyond the priorities of a ministry or enterprise director. Their bargaining strength may challenge established production arrangements.
A pact between labour, management and the state can coordinate recovery. It requires institutions capable of mediating interests that do not naturally coincide.
Collective bargaining gives working conditions a place at the negotiating table. The process can protect social peace while slowing some adjustments in production.
Public arbitration offers a way to resolve labour disputes without suppressing them. A fair system requires expertise, time and a trusted administration.
Scientists and teachers belong at the centre of public reconstruction. Give their institutions resources adequate to the ambitions placed upon them.
Universal basic services can give social citizenship a meaning beyond income. Their continuing cost must be carried honestly in the public budget.
