Targeted provision can reach the poorest districts with fewer resources. It asks the state to identify needs and maintain access without turning assistance into patronage.
Housing cooperatives can combine public support with the organisation of residents. Their work remains a long term responsibility rather than a single construction announcement.
Rural health and literacy can widen the social foundations of recovery. Fund the local institutions that must deliver them through difficult conditions.
A social budget should show both the promises of government and the means available to honour them. Expose waste without hiding the real cost of public services.
Public ownership can preserve control over industries considered essential to national development. It does not remove the problems of management and productive efficiency.
A cooperative mixed economy can combine social ownership with a wider range of initiative. Its diversity requires a more capable framework of coordination.
Planning boards can bring elected representatives and producers into economic decisions. Their legitimacy depends on doing useful work rather than multiplying offices.
Small firms can coexist with cooperatives where their different strengths meet real demand. Wider exchange will also transmit more movement from the market.
A parliamentary social settlement must allow disagreement without abandoning public obligations. Its durability will be measured by how those obligations survive a change of government.

A VNQDD return to Hanoi would require a profound political rupture or a negotiated return from exile. Seek a republican mandate without pretending that nationalist factions have already become one movement.
The constitution should bind the president as firmly as it binds a political opponent. Establish legal limits that cannot be removed whenever the executive finds them inconvenient.
A strong presidency can impose direction on a divided nationalist coalition. That concentration of authority risks weakening the civil institutions the republic claims to defend.
National reconciliation requires terms on which former opponents can return to civil life. Offer conditional protection without erasing the memory of the conflict.
Rival armed factions cannot indefinitely remain governments within the government. Bring their integration under common authority while accepting the instability of the process.
Secure peasant holdings can give the republic a stronger rural foundation. A practical system of titles and dispute resolution must support that promise.
Protection can help domestic industry survive uncertain conditions. It can also shelter inefficient production and restrict access to more competitive suppliers.
A commercial republic would place more of recovery in the circulation of goods and enterprise. Its opportunities will depend increasingly on conditions beyond national control.
A national arsenal can reduce dependence on foreign military supply. Preparing its construction commits scarce capital to defence rather than civilian recovery.
Haiphong can serve as a centre for legitimate trade and commercial administration. Organise the institutions and construction required to make that role productive.
Religion, region and former allegiance must not determine who belongs to the republic. Turn the language of national unity into equal civil treatment.
Independence should not become a change from one foreign patron to another. Preserve room for national decision even where doing so limits easier economic opportunities.
External guarantees can support a vulnerable republic. Negotiate their terms rather than assuming that outside powers share every Vietnamese objective.
Citizen defence can connect sovereignty to a wider social responsibility. It also draws time and resources away from civil reconstruction.
Trade offers a route to development that military mobilisation cannot supply. Give commercial administration a stable place in national policy.
The republic must become more durable than the coalition that brought it to power. Seek institutions capable of surviving factional defeat without another rupture.

A provisional military council would replace the historical relationship between Party and army with a new concentration of power. Its first decisions must determine what the emergency is meant to achieve.
Professional service can offer a common standard where factions compete for influence. Its credibility depends on institutions that reward competence rather than loyalty alone.
A security directorate offers the council a firmer grip on opposition and administration. It also threatens the independent knowledge on which sound policy depends.
Officer standards should demand preparation as well as obedience. More professional training requires time that cannot also be spent on immediate expansion.
Screening the civil service can remove rivals but also deprive the state of experience. Recovery will suffer if political suspicion becomes a substitute for administration.
Civilian nationalists can supply expertise and a connection to political traditions outside the officer corps. Bringing them in will make the council's decisions more contested.
Defence industry can support the council's promise of security. Farms and the civilian economy will bear the opportunity cost of that priority.
Civil recovery offers a different basis for military legitimacy. Put reconstruction ahead of a rapid expansion in weapons production.
A dispersed military workshop can provide a more reliable repair and production base. Its construction must still be supported by the resources of the economy.
Demobilisation can return labour to civilian life and make public works possible. It also reduces the manpower held ready for military service.
Military enterprises should not be exempt from public accounting. Auditing them will challenge interests close to the council itself.
A permanent council would turn emergency authority into a governing institution. It must accept the long term political and intellectual costs of that choice.
A civilian transition needs a process that the armed forces cannot quietly reverse. Set the terms of a handover through negotiations with credible civilian representatives.
Armed neutrality promises to defend sovereignty without another patron's direction. Maintaining that posture can narrow the resources available for development.
A constituent assembly can give the next civil order a public foundation. Its disagreements are part of the transition rather than proof that transition has failed.
The provisional mandate must either become a defined institution or give way to a civilian order. End the uncertainty over who is entitled to govern and under which rules.

Bombing and interrupted supply have left workshops idle. Restore a working civilian production centre in Hanoi, put its machinery back into use and establish the base from which wider reconstruction can proceed.
Dispersed workshops are harder to neutralise in one attack. They also sacrifice some of the efficiency of production concentrated around a common infrastructure.
Industrial centres can bring labour, power and transport back into closer coordination. Concentration creates its own vulnerabilities and demands reliable supply.
Mobile crews can repair links that fixed offices are too slow to reach. Their labour must be drawn from other pressing tasks in the civilian economy.
Haiphong's productive role depends on usable power as well as access to the sea. Prepare the rehabilitation and construction needed to restore that foundation.
Northern districts cannot recover in isolation from one another. Reconnect the transport links on which production, food distribution and administration depend.
Capital goods promise a stronger productive base in the future. Giving them priority asks households to carry a heavier burden in the present.
Recovery must deliver goods that households need now. Place civilian consumption ahead of some demands for rapid military industrial expansion.

The northern workshop network must be able to repair and produce the equipment the army consumes. Equip a military production line within the reconstruction programme while the rest of the country continues to demand scarce machinery.

A working workshop is only the beginning. Expand the supply of tools, spare parts and trained supervisors needed by civilian construction, rather than forcing every project to compete for the same imported equipment.
Skilled workers and technicians are as necessary as machinery. Fund the training that allows restored facilities to produce reliably.
Domestic components can make essential production less vulnerable to an interrupted import. Their development may require accepting a slower rise in efficiency.
Specialist machinery can relieve constraints that domestic workshops cannot yet overcome. Access to it brings both opportunities and greater exposure to international conditions.
A repair depot can keep scarce equipment useful for longer. Its organisation requires staff, stocks and common technical standards.
Engineering contracts can bring knowledge that is difficult to acquire alone. Negotiate practical assistance without assuming that an invitation guarantees a partner.
Recovery has become more than the immediate repair of wartime damage. Consolidate the productive base while recognising the costs that a long conflict has left behind.
Food supply is a daily test of national resilience. Review procurement and distribution before a poor harvest or a broken transport link becomes a wider emergency.
Higher collective procurement targets can make deliveries to the state more predictable. They can also weaken incentives where households retain too little of their additional effort.
Household plots already have a place beside collective farming. Expand their incentives and productive role rather than treating every useful local practice as a deviation.
Irrigation work can make organised rural labour more productive. Prepare a district project that improves the agricultural base rather than merely increasing procurement demands.
Village producers need a practical route to buyers and supplies. Improve market access while maintaining the administrative work that makes exchange possible.
A grain reserve can cushion distribution when ordinary deliveries fail. Keeping it useful requires supervision, storage and a willingness to bear its cost.

Allocate the next rural investment programme to fertiliser, tools and repair capacity. Better inputs can raise yields without transferring still more labour into the fields, although imported supplies expose the programme to external disruption.

Allocate the next rural investment programme to organised labour, drainage and local access roads. It can proceed with fewer imported inputs, but the workers assigned to it cannot simultaneously fill the northern workshops.
Strengthen northern rice production through a new agricultural district. The project must be planned and built before its capacity can be relied upon.
Dykes and local roads protect the connection between the harvest and the population it must feed. Their maintenance is less spectacular than a new industrial target, but no less necessary.
Health and nutrition determine whether rural households can sustain their work. Extend practical provision while recognising its recurring demands on the state.

Use the next food security allocation to protect basic consumption and predictable prices. Broad support cushions households when distribution fails, while its administration must reach far beyond the most productive villages.

Use the next food security allocation to reward additional household deliveries. Contracted surplus can rebuild supplies and rural trade, but incomes become more exposed to prices and uneven market access.
A rural distribution service can bring essential goods closer to the people producing the harvest. Its reliability depends on resources as well as instructions.
A marketable surplus can improve the prospects of rural producers. The resulting trade also exposes them more directly to changing economic conditions.
Food security has improved through stronger production and distribution. Some expense and inefficiency will remain even after the worst shortages have been relieved.
The People's Army has accumulated experience under exceptional conditions. Review what that experience can teach without assuming that endurance removes the need for organisation and resources.
Local defence can use knowledge of terrain and dispersed organisation. It offers a different priority from concentrating resources in a larger military industrial effort.
Combined arms operations require coordination among forces with different demands. Their effectiveness depends on a supply system able to sustain the concentration.
A redundant network can keep supplies moving when one route fails. Building and maintaining it diverts resources from civil construction.
A professional general staff must turn experience into reliable planning. More demanding preparation will take longer than rapid mobilisation alone.
Hanoi and Haiphong require a more coherent air defence network. Prepare additional defensive installations without assuming that hardware can replace trained crews and organisation.
An affordable army must be matched to the resources the country can sustain. Reduce its demands even where that means holding fewer people ready for service.
Large mobilisation reserves preserve a capacity for prolonged war. Farms and rural households must live with the labour those reserves absorb.
Repair can keep scarce military equipment in use. Concentrating on existing systems also limits the resources available to investigate new ones.
Reserve cadres need training that can be repeated and passed on. The programme consumes time and labour that civilian reconstruction also requires.
The coastal approaches connect military security to trade and everyday supply. Organise a sustainable patrol programme suited to the country's resources.
Coastal defence offers practical protection before expensive naval prestige. Such concentration reinforces a more guarded relationship with the outside world.
A small fleet needs repair capacity before it can remain reliably at sea. Prepare a dockyard project that the country can sustain.
Civil defence and medical teams protect the ability of communities to endure disruption. Their work also requires a continuing social commitment.
A sustainable air force begins with trained crews and instructors. Give education and maintenance knowledge a place beside demands for additional aircraft.
Peace allows service personnel to return to civilian work and family life. Their settlement requires support, and demobilisation relinquishes part of the wartime recruitment advantage.
North and South remain separate political orders in a country whose future is contested. Military action, negotiation and the responsibilities of eventual peace must all be considered.

Concentrate additional staff work and supplies on battlefield pressure. Negotiations remain possible, but this allocation seeks leverage through the army and commits resources that cannot also enlarge the diplomatic effort.

Concentrate additional staff and political effort on a credible negotiating position. The armed struggle need not cease, but the delegation must be able to defend specific terms and maintain confidence that a settlement will be honoured.
The southern corridors must remain usable if military pressure is to be sustained. Their protection competes with the rebuilding of the civil economy.
Terms and guarantees have value only where the other parties are prepared to accept them. Exchange proposals while preserving a clear account of the responsibilities each government would assume.
The end of large scale fighting will not itself create a functioning civil settlement. Prepare the administrative and social work that must follow it.
Where the southern states are actually under our administration, a common framework can begin. Joining institutions after a long war will produce disruption before it produces coherence.
Peaceful coexistence would preserve two administrations while reducing the danger of renewed war. Such a settlement asks both governments to accept limits on their immediate objectives.
Southern recovery requires knowledge of existing production and distribution. Rebuilding should preserve what works while confronting the dislocation of national integration.
Families should not remain indefinitely separated by the political division. Organise channels of contact without pretending that trust can be restored by decree.
Citizenship must offer a future beyond permanent wartime labels. A sustainable civil order needs practical protection for people whose past does not fit one political narrative.
Security led screening places political control ahead of an open return to civil life. Exclusion and displacement will slow recovery and create further social obligations.
Conditional amnesty can bring former opponents back into productive and public life. The political leadership must accept the uncertainty that genuine reconciliation entails.
A common civil register can reduce administrative confusion. It must not conceal the insecurity created where people remain excluded from the settlement.
Displaced people and veterans need a route to stable homes and livelihoods. Resettlement is a public responsibility with costs that cannot be wished away.
A sustainable peace is measured by the society it permits to recover. Consolidate the settlement without treating military mobilisation as a permanent source of political purpose.
Chinese and Soviet assistance make possible an effort beyond the means of the domestic economy. Their rivalry gives Vietnam room to manoeuvre and reasons to guard its independence.
A deeper Soviet relationship can bring specialist knowledge and a more dependable channel of cooperation. It also ties national planning more closely to one outside partner.
Balancing Moscow and Beijing can preserve diplomatic room for manoeuvre. It requires careful administration of relationships whose priorities do not always coincide.
Soviet specialists can assist with problems that domestic institutions cannot yet solve alone. Their invitation requires agreement and practical preparation on both sides.
Vietnamese objectives cannot simply be delegated to either patron. Defend strategic autonomy even where it limits easier access to outside support.
Events in Laos and Cambodia affect security, supply and the prospects for peace. Maintain channels through which their governments can answer proposals in their own right.
Regional commitments can strengthen military cooperation while extending the burden on supply. Their terms must be accepted rather than presumed.
Restraint and withdrawal can reduce the demands of regional confrontation. They also require the leadership to temper expectations built around military pressure.
Northern defence must remain credible even during reconstruction. Preparing the frontier does not decide whether another government will choose confrontation.
Confidence building can make regional restraint more durable. It requires continuing diplomatic work rather than a declaration that old disputes have vanished.
Diplomatic isolation need not end every form of trade. Develop practical resilience while acknowledging the friction imposed by restricted access and uncertain partners.
Strategic self reliance can reduce vulnerability to pressure from outside. It may also mean accepting slower progress where domestic capabilities remain limited.
A controlled opening can connect the economy to a wider range of opportunities. The country will also experience more of the world's economic fluctuations.
Alternative suppliers can reduce the risk created by one interrupted relationship. Maintaining those connections brings its own costs of coordination.

Earlier normalisation would require the other governments to accept a different diplomatic course. Begin the negotiations without assuming that their sanctions or security policies have already changed.
The socialist world is changing, and established support cannot be assumed indefinitely. Prepare the institutions and relationships through which Vietnam can adapt.
The long war has bound local political cadres, village networks and regular formations into a single struggle. Preserve that experience as the army prepares for the campaigns still ahead.
Maintain contact with local institutions and southern allies. Communist revolutionary support is distinct from the general army programme.
Teach a regular army to operate in a dispersed war without treating militias as free equipment or manpower.
Rely on local initiative and political contact while accepting that decentralized command complicates major offensives.
Connect dispersed formations to a functioning staff and replacement system. The extra organization requires administrators.
Coordinate local political organization and the regular army. Both preparatory lines must be completed.
Make territorial defence and endurance the priority. This is useful during invasion, but gives up planning depth for a decisive offensive.
Concentrate the regular army for a prepared campaign. Supply demand rises and formations become harder to sustain.
Improve the army’s ability to preserve a territorial defence. The policy is not a damage bonus for an imaginary underground army.
Prepare the regular army for the current campaign, whether against South Vietnam or an invading force. Southern revolutionary support remains a separate optional action.
Turn the actual campaign experience into a doctrine lesson. A failed offensive does not receive a fabricated victory.
Use land adjudication, representation and civilian guarantees to address political grievances. FULRO is a conditional highland problem, not a label for all minorities.
Make intensive internal security deployment the first response. It offers organization while prolonging administrative and civilian burdens.
Fund schools, local administration and a credible land settlement. Services take resources before they yield political benefits.
Keep a forceful security programme under periodic review. More deployment does not remove the social causes of resistance.
Review the chosen local policy with representation from the affected population. Security and civilian guarantees remain distinct choices.
Retain a trained reserve for renewed danger. Civilian recovery continues to lose labour to defence.
Reduce the exceptional military commitment and direct labour towards production. Readiness grows more slowly.
Make retained readiness more sustainable through rotation. The reserve still carries an economic cost.
Support demobilized veterans and affected households. Productive recovery requires sustained public spending.
Preserve the doctrinal lessons without maintaining every temporary wartime measure indefinitely.
Conclude a programme of military learning and political recovery. Renewed war can reopen funded operational decisions without paying focus rewards twice.
Keep Cambodia’s sovereignty and changing political situation distinct from Vietnam’s own war. Cambodia is not an inevitable starting enemy.
Prepare a defined defensive plan for the southwestern frontier. Military preparation draws resources from reconstruction.
Organize relief and temporary administration for threatened communities. Protection requires public spending.
Unify the existing border staff and maintain a limited commitment. This is not an automatic invasion order.

The machinery of state has not kept pace with the times. A review of how we govern is overdue.
Foreign agents and domestic subversives demand a stronger security service.
Engineers, economists and planners replace party veterans in the ministries. Results will matter more than loyalty.
Only men we can trust will hold the levers of power, whatever their qualifications.
Every major camp receives a seat at the table. Unity has a price: endless negotiation.
A network of listening posts will monitor radio traffic along our borders.
An independent commission will investigate the ministries, the courts and the state companies.
Offices, licences and contracts reward those who stand by the government.
Overlapping ministries are merged and the provinces are reorganised.
The lessons of Algeria, Malaya and Vietnam are studied closely. Insurgents will find no safe ground.
The political police watch everyone. Few dare to speak openly, scientists included.
Censorship has been relaxed. New ideas circulate freely, including foreign ones.
Elections take place, but the result is never in doubt.
Power is concentrated in the capital. The provinces will follow its instructions.
The regions receive real authority over their own affairs.
Codebreakers and radio engineers form a directorate of their own.
Entrance examinations and fixed career paths will create a modern, professional administration.
Our institutions have weathered the storms of the decade. The state endures.
Parties that looked West in the 1970s sold membership of the prosperous \"free world\": Marshall-era trade, American credit and the European example.
Chambers of commerce and church lay groups carried Christian Democracy, and personal support groups (koenkai) carried Japan's LDP politicians; they bring calm and a base, but cost subsidies.
Watergate (1972-74) and the Pentagon Papers (1971) showed what an independent press could do: it spreads Western ideas fast and also exposes the government.
Portugal (1975-76) and Spain (1977) turned a democratic majority in the streets into a majority at the ballot box that the extremes could not overturn.
A new Western-oriented government arrives with a mandate: Brandt in 1969, Whitlam in 1972 and Suárez in 1977 all used their first year to push their programme.
Park Chung-hee, Suharto and the Shah justified personal rule by development: the leader stands above parties and answers for growth.
Decisions moved from parliament to the palace: Park's Blue House secretariat, Marcos in Malacañang and the Shah's court ran the state directly.
Korea's Economic Planning Board, Taiwan's CEPD and Indonesia's Bappenas gave a small team of technocrats direct access to the ruler.
Marcos proclaimed martial law in September 1972 (Proclamation 1081), closed Congress and the newspapers: calm streets, empty campuses, a growing constabulary.
Suharto's New Order won managed elections through Golkar (1971, 1977); the mandate on paper reassured donors, but patronage and campaign money had to be paid.
Korea and Taiwan tied credit and tax breaks to export performance, and Park reviewed the targets at monthly export promotion meetings; growth followed world demand - in both directions.
Korea's Heavy and Chemical Industry plan (1973), financed largely with foreign loans, and the Shah's oil-funded steel and petrochemical projects built heavy industry at speed.
The KCIA abducted Kim Dae-jung from Tokyo (1973) and the Emergency Decrees made criticism of the constitution a crime; the opposition was driven underground.

Korea's Yushin Constitution (1972) kept elections, but the president was chosen by the National Conference for Unification, a non-party body he chaired, and nominated a third of the Assembly: legality and an assured majority at once.
The Kaohsiung (1966) and Masan (1970) free export zones drew foreign assembly plants with tax holidays and cheap labour.
POSCO's Pohang steelworks (1973) and the Hyundai shipyard at Ulsan (1974) were built by state order, cheap credit and suppressed consumption.
\"Economy first\" was the official answer to every demand for freedom: Park and Suharto legitimised their rule through growth figures.
Double-digit growth became the regime's claim to rule: Korea grew about 10 % a year in the 1970s, Taiwan and Indonesia not far behind.
Korea's Saemaul Undong (1970) gave villages cement and steel for roads, roofs and irrigation, and tied the countryside to the president.
Korea's Homeland Reserve Forces (1968) and Taiwan's mobilisation laws put millions of citizens in reserve units and anti-communist drills.
Korea rotated some 320,000 troops through Vietnam (1964-73) and received American aid, weapons and procurement contracts in return - and American advice with them.
After the Nixon Doctrine (1969) and the US troop cuts, Korea's Yulgok plan (1974) and Taiwan built their own arms industries at their own expense.
National education charters, morning drills and anti-luxury campaigns preached hard work and order as patriotic duties.
Iran became the largest buyer of American arms in the 1970s and Korea levied a special defence tax (1975) to pay for its build-up: the strongman's army was his showcase.
At its height the developmental dictatorship fused party, planners and conglomerates into one machine for growth, as in Korea under Yushin or Taiwan in the 1970s.
Conservative governments promised competence rather than ideology: Heath announced a \"quiet revolution\" in 1970, while Pompidou (1969) and Fukuda (1976) presented themselves as sound managers.
Christian Democrats in Italy and Germany and the LDP in Japan saw themselves as the natural party of government, rooted in church, business and countryside.
Heath's 1970 White Paper on central government merged ministries into giant departments, and Barber's October 1970 package cut public spending to pay for lower income tax.
Gaullism concentrated power in the presidency and governed by decree and referendum; effective, but it alienated parliament and the unions.
The CDU/CSU union and the LDP's factions held liberals, farmers, Catholics and business together - at the price of endless bargaining.
The Selsdon programme (1970) promised to end subsidies to \"lame duck\" industries and cut public spending; the unions answered with strikes.
Heath nationalised the bankrupt Rolls-Royce (1971), then in his 1972 U-turn rescued Upper Clyde Shipbuilders and brought in an incomes policy to buy social peace.
De Gaulle and Pompidou went over the heads of the parties with referendums (1969, 1972) and television addresses to the nation.
West Germany's written coalition agreements (the first in 1961) and the LDP's factional quotas for cabinet posts kept multi-party and multi-faction governments together for years at a time.
Sound money as a programme: the Bundesbank's stability course and Fukuda's tight budget policy against the \"crazy prices\" of 1974 won the trust of bankers and savers.
Tanaka's Plan for Remodelling the Japanese Archipelago (1972) and the Tories' home-ownership drive built roads, towns and loyal voters.
Facing terrorism and strikes, conservatives ran on law and order: Nixon in 1968 and 1972, and the West German CDU/CSU, which pressed for ever tougher anti-terror laws in the 1970s.
The West German model of competition plus social insurance remained the reference point of every 1970s centre-right programme.
Italy's Christian Democrats campaigned to repeal divorce in the 1974 referendum and lost, 59 to 41 %; the stand rallied the devout but alienated the cities and the young.
Giscard d'Estaing lowered the voting age to 18 and legalised divorce by consent and abortion (1974-75), winning the young but angering the Church.
The CDU and the British Conservatives kept NATO at the centre: American technology and markets, alliance force goals to pay for.
Gaullist France left NATO's integrated command (1966) and built its own Mirage jets and AMX tanks: independent, respected and expensive.
Conservatives from Eden to Thatcher promised a \"property-owning democracy\": every homeowner and shareholder a stakeholder in order.
Whether in the alliance or alone, the centre right promised a defence strong enough to deter, and raised the budget to match.
The LDP governed Japan from 1955 to 1993 and Italy's Christian Democrats led every government from late 1945 to 1981: the right as the permanent establishment.
Liberals entered government as reformers: the FDP with Brandt (1969), Trudeau's Liberals (1968), D66 in the Netherlands (1973).
The social-liberal coalitions of the early 1970s drew up long reform lists for justice, education and the civil service.
After Nixon closed the gold window (1971) the Smithsonian pegs collapsed; from 1973 most Western currencies floated and capital controls began to fall (the US in 1974, Britain in 1979).

Trudeau's 1969 reform partly decriminalised homosexuality - \"there's no place for the state in the bedrooms of the nation\" - and liberals across Europe reformed criminal law; open societies are also open to rival ideas.
Liberal parties campaigned for proportional representation (the UK Liberals after February 1974): fairer seats, more stable consent, but coalition government.
The Tokyo Round (1973-79) cut industrial tariffs by a third; open economies grew with world trade and caught its shocks.
The FDP's Freiburg Theses (1971) demanded a liberalism of social reform: workers' share in capital, environmental protection, co-determination.
After Watergate the US strengthened its Freedom of Information Act (1974) over a presidential veto; officials and secret services lost their shield.
Britain (1969), West Germany (1970) and the US (26th Amendment, 1971) lowered the voting age to 18 and brought a new generation into the system.
London's Competition and Credit Control (1971) and the eurodollar boom freed the banks; credit grew fast, and the secondary banking crisis of 1973-75 followed.
West Germany's 624-Mark Act (1970) doubled state support for workers' savings and share schemes: wealth for employees through ownership rather than nationalisation.
With the reforms passed, liberals held the balance of power: the FDP decided who governed Bonn from 1969 to 1982.
Liberal economics promised growth from competition rather than plans, a theme that came to dominate Western economic policy by the end of the 1970s.
The US created the EPA and passed the Clean Air Act in 1970; West Germany's liberal interior ministry wrote the first environmental programme (1971).
The Open University (1971) and the wave of new German and Dutch universities opened higher education to the children of workers.
EFTA, the enlarged EEC (1973) and ASEAN's preferential trade (1977) opened neighbouring markets to industrial goods; farmers, who feared open competition, fought to keep their protection.
The Helsinki Final Act (1975) and Carter's human-rights policy (1977) made liberal values a foreign-policy tool; arms exporters lost customers.

\"Quality of life\" became a slogan of Western reformers in the early 1970s, from Bonn's social-liberal coalition to the new environmental groups: clean towns, public transport and leisure, not growth alone.
Liberal finance ministers bought precision instead of mass: guided anti-tank weapons and shoulder-fired missiles for a smaller, cheaper army.
Karl Popper's \"open society\" became the liberal creed of the Cold War: a state that can be criticised and corrected, prosperous because it is free.
Social democrats took power across the West around 1970: Brandt (1969), Kreisky (1970), Palme (1969), Whitlam (1972) - and raised social spending at once.
Brandt's 1969 government statement \"Mehr Demokratie wagen\" promised to open schools, workplaces and the state to participation.
Higher progressive taxes paid for the reform programmes: by the late 1970s Swedish and Danish tax revenues exceeded 40 % of GDP, among the highest in the OECD.
Britain's Social Contract (1974): the unions accepted wage restraint in return for social policy - and gained great influence over government policy.
Helmut Schmidt (1974-82) governed as a crisis manager rather than a party ideologue: efficient and trusted by business, suspected by the left.

West Germany's Codetermination Act (1976) gave employees half the supervisory board seats in firms with over 2,000 staff, with a shareholder casting vote; employers challenged it in the Constitutional Court and lost (1979).
Whitlam's Australia and Kreisky's \"Austro-Keynesianism\" ran deficits to keep demand and employment up after 1973.
Austria's Parity Commission let unions and employers settle wages and prices together; Kreisky's Austria had one of the lowest strike rates in the Western world.
Schmidt's \"Modell Deutschland\" (1976) steered the economy through the oil crisis with low inflation and international summitry.

Rudolf Meidner's plan, adopted by the LO unions in 1976, proposed union-run funds that would buy up Swedish firms out of profits; business mobilised against it, and only a diluted version passed in 1983.
Austria and Sweden kept unemployment at around 2 % through the 1970s with public works, training schemes and subsidised jobs.
Per Albin Hansson's folkhem (1928) - society as a good home for all - became shorthand for the Swedish welfare state and a model for social democrats elsewhere.
By the late 1970s the Nordic welfare states provided pensions, health care and childcare as universal, tax-funded public services.
Sweden (1962) and Britain (from 1965) replaced selective schools with comprehensives, and SPD-led German Länder opened Gesamtschulen, to open education to every class.
Canada's medicare covered every province by 1971, Australia launched Medibank (1975) and Italy its national health service (1978).

Brandt's Moscow and Warsaw treaties (1970) and the Basic Treaty (1972) accepted the post-war borders in return for trade, contacts and easier travel; critics said they legitimised the Eastern regimes.
Schmidt's 1977 London speech helped prompt NATO's double-track decision (1979): social democrats stood by the alliance against their own peace wing.
Separate taxation of spouses (Sweden 1971) and equal pay (Australia 1972) brought women into work and into the tax base; traditionalists, many in the churches, defended the single-breadwinner family.
The Palme Commission (1980-82) and the Socialist International argued that security could only be achieved together with the adversary, not against it.
The Scandinavian and Austrian model of high taxes, full employment and universal welfare was widely cited as a social model in the 1970s.
In the early 1970s the left was on the rise from Chile (Allende 1970) to Portugal (1974); communist and socialist parties grew wherever they could organise openly.

The Italian and French communist parties built their strength on factory cells, and Chile's \"cordones industriales\" (1972) organised whole industrial belts; employers lost control of the shop floor.
Party dailies such as L'Humanité and l'Unità sold hundreds of thousands of copies, and Radio Moscow and Radio Peking broadcast worldwide; the presses ran on subsidies.
By 1975 communist parties polled a third of the vote in Italy and were a leading force in Portugal's revolution; a mass movement makes the outlook hard to dislodge.

A new socialist government first fills the ministries and key posts with its own people, as Allende's Popular Unity cabinet (1970) and Vasco Gonçalves's provisional governments in Portugal (1974-75) did.
The ruling communist party places itself above the state: the party leads, the ministries execute, as most Soviet-type constitutions came to state outright.

After Khrushchev's fall (1964) the Soviet Presidium, renamed Politburo in 1966, ruled as a collective leadership around Brezhnev; the bloc parties copied the model of decisions taken in a closed circle.
The Soviet ninth five-year plan (1971-75) was the first to promise that consumer goods would grow faster than heavy industry.
Brezhnev's \"stability of cadres\", proclaimed after Khrushchev's constant reshuffles, left officials in post for decades; the apparatus was grateful and loyal, the economy slowly stagnated.
The Kosygin reform (1965) and Hungary's New Economic Mechanism (1968) gave enterprises profit targets and more freedom; the party conservatives saw their control slip.
Honecker's 1971 programme promised flats, subsidised prices and consumer goods (the 1973 housing programme); welfare bought loyalty and ran up a debt.
Soviet planning kept priority for \"Group A\" heavy industry and the defence sector under Dmitri Ustinov; consumer supply lagged while the arsenals grew.
Every important post from factory director to editor was filled from the party's nomenklatura lists; the system was reliable and slowly became a caste.

Under \"khozraschet\" (cost accounting) enterprises kept part of their profits for bonus and investment funds; Hungary's NEM went further, freeing many prices and ending compulsory plan targets for firms.
Gierek's Poland bought Western licences (Fiat cars, Massey Ferguson tractors) and whole plants on credit in the 1970s; modern factories rose and the foreign debt passed 20 billion dollars by 1980.
The Soviet VPK coordinated the defence ministries and gave them first call on steel, engineers and research institutes.
Each five-yearly party congress fixed the line for the next plan; the 24th CPSU Congress (1971) set the course of the decade.
Comecon's Complex Programme (1971) divided production between the member states through specialisation and joint projects such as the Soyuz gas pipeline, keeping most of their trade inside the bloc.
After 1969 Husák expelled or struck off hundreds of thousands of party members in Czechoslovakia and bought quiet with consumer goods; thousands of academics, writers and artists lost their posts.
Kádár's \"who is not against us is with us\" (1961) let Hungarians travel, read and trade a little; it was widely seen as the most liberal regime in the bloc and the most open to Western ideas.
Soviet arms, advisers and staff training tied the Warsaw Pact armies to Moscow after the 1969 reform of the Pact's joint command.
Détente brought Western grain, credits and technology to the East (Brandt's treaties 1970-72, Helsinki 1975), and with them Western ideas.
The Soviet constitution of 1977 (Article 6) and the GDR constitution of 1968 wrote the party's leading role into the basic law.
Warsaw Pact armies trained for a fast offensive war in Europe; large exercises such as \"Soyuz\" and \"Zapad\" (1981) tested the doctrine.
In 1971 Brezhnev declared the USSR a \"developed socialist society\": a mature, stable system that no longer needed upheaval, and slowly stopped changing.
The radical left hands authority to local communes and councils, as the Paris Commune ideal and Yugoslav \"social self-government\" promised.
Assemblies of delegates from factories and villages take the place of party parliaments, as in Yugoslavia's 1974 delegate system or the popular assemblies proposed in Portugal in 1975.
The 1975 land occupations in Portugal's Alentejo turned the great estates into collective farms run by the labourers.
Yugoslav workers' councils chose the managers and divided the income; the factories worked, but the centre lost its grip on decisions.
China's Cultural Revolution (1966-76) mobilised the young against \"revisionists\" in the party; it bred fervent loyalty to Mao but also violent purges, and schools and universities closed for years.
China's \"self-reliance\" (zili gengsheng) and Albania's isolation after 1978 made the economy hard to blockade but cut it off from foreign technology and trade.
Campaigns like \"Learn from Dazhai\" (1964-) and Cuba's ten-million-ton harvest (1970) threw whole populations at dams, terraces and canefields; much was built, much was wasted.
The 1974 Yugoslav constitution devolved power to the republics, communes and self-managed enterprises; investment no longer waited for Belgrade, though projects were often duplicated.
From 1968 some seventeen million Chinese urban youths were sent to the villages over a decade; fields gained hands, the universities lost a generation.
China's \"five small industries\" (1970) put steel, cement, fertiliser, machine and power plants in county after county; small, inefficient and independent.
Cuba's microbrigades (1970-) built housing with volunteer labour and Chinese water-conservancy campaigns dug canals by hand; the workplaces they left had to make up their output.
\"From the masses, to the masses\": the Maoist mass line made cadres live and work among the people they governed.
Guevara's \"new man\" and the Maoist campaigns replaced bonuses with honours and emulation; less went on consumer goods, but absenteeism spread (Cuba passed an anti-loafing law in 1971).
From 1967 Chinese \"three-in-one\" committees of soldiers, cadres and rebels replaced the party committees and governments of every province by 1968.
From 1968 over a million Chinese \"barefoot doctors\" and night schools brought basic medicine and reading to the villages at a fraction of the cost.
China and Cuba trained, armed and funded liberation movements in the 1960s-70s, from Africa to Latin America (Cuba in Angola, 1975).
Mao's \"people's war\" and Albania's bunker programme (1967-86, over 170,000 bunkers) prepared every village to resist an invasion.
The \"Serve the People\" and Lei Feng campaigns (1963-) held up selfless service as the model citizen of the new society.
People's militias armed the population on a mass scale: the Chinese militia counted tens of millions in the early 1970s.
The radical left promised a society without bosses or bureaucrats; where it governed, it built communes, councils and a deep suspicion of experts.
Mexico's PRI had ruled under various names since 1929 and Algeria's FLN since 1962: the party is the state, and the state hands out the jobs.
Dominant parties ruled in the name of a founding revolution (1910 in Mexico, 1954 in Algeria, 1952 in Egypt) and claimed its legitimacy for every new leader.
State firms such as Pemex, Sonatrach and Egypt's public sector companies were the backbone of the dominant-party economy.
The PRI organised society in sectors (CTM labour, CNC peasants, CNOP middle class): every group had a seat at the table and a share of the patronage.
In the 1970s planners and economists (\"técnicos\") gained ground against the old party bosses in Mexico and Algeria; efficiency rose, the old networks resented it.
On 24 February 1971 Algeria took 51 % of the French oil companies; Iraq (1972) and Venezuela (1976) followed. Revenue flowed home and foreign investors grew wary.
Sadat's Infitah (1974) and Mexico's border industry programme (1965) invited foreign investors with tax breaks; business boomed and the economy became exposed.
Fidel Velázquez's CTM delivered Mexican labour peace for decades in exchange for wages, housing funds (INFONAVIT 1972) and seats in Congress.
Algeria's Secretariat of Planning and Mexico's Ministry of Programming and Budget (1976) gave the technocrats their own power base.
Boumédiène spent the oil money on \"industrialising industries\": the El Hadjar steelworks, gas liquefaction and petrochemicals (plans 1970-77).
Egypt's Infitah brought joint ventures with Western and Gulf capital; when subsidies were cut the 1977 bread riots followed.
The PRI's outgoing president named his successor (the \"dedazo\", 1970 and 1976); the party closed ranks and the transfer of power stayed peaceful.
Echeverría's \"desarrollo compartido\" (1970-76) expanded state investment and social programmes to share the fruits of growth.
Cheap bread, fuel and staples through CONASUPO in Mexico and Egypt's ration system kept the cities quiet and the budget strained.

Algeria's Agrarian Revolution (1971) handed large estates to cooperatives against the landowners' resistance, and Tanzania's villagisation (1973-76) moved millions of peasants into Ujamaa villages, often by force.
Egypt (1971), India (1971), Iraq (1972) and Somalia (1974) signed friendship treaties with Moscow: arms and advisers in return for influence.
Sadat expelled the Soviet advisers in 1972 and courted Washington, and Algeria led the Non-Aligned Movement (1973): trade and favours from both sides, loyalty to neither.
Youth, women's and peasant unions of the ruling party (the FLN's UNJA, the ASU youth) reached into every village and school.
In Algeria, Egypt and Burma soldiers had made the regime (the Free Officers in 1952, Ne Win in 1962, Boumédiène in 1965); the dominant party kept the army inside the regime with budgets and honours.
The dominant parties defined success as development on their own terms: Mexico's \"stabilising development\" (1954-70) and Algeria's plans delivered long years of rapid growth.
Post-coup regimes governed through a Revolutionary Command Council - Egypt 1952, Iraq 1968, Libya 1969 - and paid the army first.
Egypt's Arab Socialist Union, Algeria's FLN and Somalia's Revolutionary Socialist Party (1976) channelled all politics into one organisation.
Land reform came early in the officers' revolutions: Egypt 1952, Iraq 1958 and 1970, Ethiopia's nationalisation of rural land in 1975.
Ba'athist Iraq after 1968 put party commissars into every unit and purged independent officers; the regime grew stable, the army less effective.
Libya's RCC (1969) and Ethiopia's Derg (1974) kept power with the officers themselves; uniforms ran ministries that civil servants had run before.
Iraq nationalised the Iraq Petroleum Company in June 1972 and Libya nationalised or took majority stakes in the foreign oil firms in 1971-74: a windfall, and Western capital grew wary.
Sadat's Infitah (1974) opened Egypt to Western and Gulf capital; the party left protested and liberal ideas returned with the investors.
After 1970 Assad and the Iraqi Ba'ath built parallel guard units and party cells in every barracks; neither regime fell to a coup again.
Libya's RCC spent oil money and the Derg Soviet credits on tanks and guns; by 1980 Ethiopia's army had grown into one of the largest in Africa.
Boumédiène's \"industrialising industries\" (1970-73 plan) put steel, petrochemicals and machinery under state companies such as Sonatrach and SNS.
Egypt's Law 43 of 1974 created free zones and joint ventures; Gulf and Western money arrived, and so did the swings of the world market.
Egypt's National Charter (1962), Syria's permanent constitution (1973) and Algeria's National Charter (1976) fixed the revolution in law.
Iraq's 1976-80 and Syria's 1976-80 plans poured the oil boom into factories, dams and roads.
Iraq's Popular Army (1970), Libya's People's Militia and the Derg's militias armed party loyalists as a counterweight to the regular officers.
Iraq's compulsory literacy campaign (1978-80) and Somalia's 1974 rural campaign after the new script taught millions to read, at the treasury's expense.
Iraq (1972), Somalia (1974) and Syria (1980) signed friendship treaties with Moscow: MiGs and T-62s on credit, and Soviet advisers in the staffs.
In July 1972 Sadat ordered out some 15,000-20,000 Soviet military advisers; Egyptians cheered, Washington and the Gulf took note, and the army trained without them.
Party unions, youth leagues and women's federations (the General Federation of Iraqi Women, 1969) tied every part of society to the regime.
After 1967 Egypt and Syria rebuilt their armies around missile air defence and anti-tank infantry, the forces that crossed the Suez Canal and attacked on the Golan in October 1973.
By the late 1970s the revolutions had become personal states: Gaddafi's Jamahiriya (1977), Assad's Syria, Saddam's presidency (1979).
The March 1979 referendum created an Islamic Republic with a broad coalition of clerics, liberals and the bazaar behind it.
The Assembly of Experts drafted a constitution joining an elected president and Majlis to clerical guardianship, approved by referendum in December 1979.
Baqir al-Sadr's Iqtisaduna (1961) set out an Islamic economy between capitalism and socialism; Iran replaced interest-based banking in 1983.
Grand Ayatollahs such as Shariatmadari wanted elected government with the clergy as advisers; in 1979-80 parties, papers and candidates still competed.
The Guardian Council (1980) checked every law against Islamic law and the constitution, giving the jurists a veto over the elected Majlis.
The Tehran bazaar financed the revolution and expected free trade, light taxes and the protection of private property in return.
The Foundation of the Oppressed (1979) took over the Pahlavi Foundation's assets to fund the poor, answering to no ministry.
Iran's first Majlis (1980) and the 1980 presidential election, won by a lay economist, showed a republic with real contests.
When the Guardian Council blocked the Majlis' land and labour laws, Khomeini created the Expediency Council in 1988 to settle such deadlocks.
Bazaar guilds and merchant networks close to the clergy controlled much of the import trade and informal credit, keeping goods moving through revolution and war.
The foundations ran hundreds of confiscated factories, hotels and farms and employed tens of thousands of the revolution's supporters.
Bazargan's government tried in 1979 to bring the neighbourhood revolutionary committees under the police and the courts.
Construction Jihad (1979) sent volunteers to build roads, wells and power lines in the villages the old regime had neglected.
Moderates pressed to reopen the universities closed in 1980 and to keep their secular faculty; they reopened in 1982-83.
The Ministry of Islamic Guidance (later Culture and Islamic Guidance) licensed books, films and newspapers, shaping public life through censorship rather than force.
\"Neither East nor West\" (1979) refused both blocs; the republic paid in lost trade and spare parts and built its own workshops instead.
Bazargan's government kept trade and diplomatic ties with the neighbours and even the West in 1979, until the hostage crisis ended the course.
Mosque associations, Islamic societies and charity funds gave the republic a social base that reached beyond the state.
Bazargan and Banisadr relied on the regular army rather than the new militias, and the regular army bore much of the early fighting after September 1980.
The republic's founding promise was justice for the mostaz'afin, the disinherited: subsidies, rural electrification and welfare paid by oil and the foundations.
Khomeini's 1970 lectures in Najaf argued that a just jurist must govern in the absence of the Imam; the 1979 constitution made it law.
The 1979 constitution placed the guardian jurist above president and Majlis, commanding the armed forces and appointing the top judges.
In June 1979 Iran nationalised all private banks and insurers, and then large industry, putting credit under revolutionary control.
The Revolutionary Guard Corps (May 1979) was built beside the distrusted regular army; the two competed for men, money and weapons all through the 1980s.
Dress codes, Islamic courts and the purge of secular officials (1980-81) remade public life; trade partners and the professional class drew back.
The Foundation of the Oppressed and other bonyads took over the old elite's confiscated assets and ran them largely tax-free and without public audit.
From 1980 the government rationed basic goods with coupons and fixed prices: the poor were fed, the bazaar was squeezed.
The Basij (1980) organised millions of volunteers - students, villagers, the elderly - and sent them to the front in the war with Iraq.
The Cultural Revolution Headquarters (1980) kept the universities closed until 1982-83 and rewrote curricula; councils kept watch over schools and media afterwards.
By the mid-1980s the Foundation of the Oppressed was one of the largest conglomerates in the Middle East: factories, shipping and real estate.
Under the US embargo (1979) the planners pushed self-sufficiency in food, spare parts and munitions, rebuilding plants foreign suppliers had serviced.
Revolutionary courts tried the old regime's officials and then the new regime's opponents, outside the ordinary judiciary.
The Martyrs' Foundation (1980) gave housing, pensions and university places to the families of the war dead, binding them to the state.
Neighbourhood committees (1979) policed morality and pursued opponents street by street until they were merged into the police in 1991.
Friday prayer leaders appointed in every city and state-funded seminaries carried the leadership's message into every neighbourhood.
Guards instructors went to Lebanon's Bekaa valley in 1982 and Tehran hosted Iraqi, Gulf and Afghan Shia exiles, at the price of regional isolation.
During the war Iran bought weapons from North Korea, China, Libya and - secretly - Israel and the United States (Iran-Contra, 1985-86): the front came before ideology.
After the 1981 bombings killed the president, the prime minister and dozens of officials, the regime built the security apparatus that broke the armed opposition.
The Defence Industries Organisation and the Guards' own workshops expanded production of rockets, mortars and small arms in the 1980s to outlast the embargo.
The 1979 constitution pledged support for the oppressed everywhere; Guards units abroad and allied movements made it policy, and the neighbours armed against it.
After 1967 the Islamic revival (al-sahwa) filled the space left by Arab nationalism; preachers, students and Gulf money spread it across the Muslim world.
The Muslim World League (1962) financed mosques, preachers and imams across Asia and Africa; the pulpit, more than the university, became the movement's school.

Islamic charities such as Egypt's al-Jam'iyya al-Shar'iyya or Kuwait's Social Reform Society ran clinics and schools the state could not provide, and answered to their own boards, not to the government.
By the late 1970s Islamist lists were winning student unions from Cairo to Kuala Lumpur, and in the 1980s Egypt's professional syndicates: the revival had become a mass movement.
Islamic governments of the period (Saudi Arabia, Pakistan after 1977, Sudan after 1983) claimed a religious mandate and governed largely by decree.
Saudi kings ruled as protectors of the faith; the alliance of the House of Saud with the Wahhabi scholars was the founding bargain of the state.
Faisal centralised power in the Royal Diwan and the Council of Ministers after replacing King Saud in 1964; princes held the key ministries.
Saudi Arabia upgraded its Central Planning Organisation (1965) to a Ministry of Planning in 1975 to spend the oil boom.
Faisal backed state girls' schools (1960) and introduced television (1965) despite clerical protest; modernisation came from the palace, and the ulema resented it.
The kingdom could also govern through the clerics: education, courts and morals stayed theirs in exchange for loyalty, at a cost to universities and science.
Under Yamani's \"participation\" (1972) the Gulf states bought into the foreign oil concessions step by step; revenues rose, and foreign capital grew wary.
After 1974 Saudi surpluses flowed into US Treasury bills and Western banks under a quiet agreement with Washington: high returns, tied to the Western market.
The first Saudi five-year plan (1970-75) built roads, power and industry with oil money; the second (1975-80) planned almost 142 billion dollars of spending.
The Committee for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice (the mutawwi'in) policed prayer times, dress and shops; merchants complained, but the streets stayed quiet.
SABIC (1976) and the new industrial cities of Jubail and Yanbu turned flared gas into petrochemicals owned by the state.
Kuwait's Fund for Future Generations and the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (both 1976) saved oil money abroad for the day the wells ran dry.
In 1971 the king founded the Council of Senior Scholars: the clerics gained an official voice, and the crown gained fatwas when it needed them.
The boom of 1974-81 brought cranes, contractors and more than a million foreign workers into the Gulf kingdoms.
After the Grand Mosque seizure of November 1979 the government gave the clerics more money, more control over schools and the closure of cinemas; public life grew more restrictive for a generation.
The tribal National Guard, trained by the American firm Vinnell from 1975, was expanded after the 1979 siege as the regime's main internal security force.
The US-Saudi Joint Commission (1974), F-15s (1978) and AWACS (1981) made Washington the kingdom's protector, and gave it a say in Riyadh.
Faisal championed the OIC (1969) and the Islamic Development Bank (agreed 1973), subsidised the frontline states and used the 1973 embargo: influence bought with money, at some risk.
By the early 1980s the monarchy had absorbed the shock of 1979 and the Shia unrest in the east; dissent went underground or abroad.
The Gulf monarchies spent billions on air bases, Hawk missiles and fighters in the 1970s; the air force was the prestige service of every royal family.
Faisal's pan-Islamism offered the Muslim world an alternative to Nasser's Arab socialism; it outlived him as the kingdom's foreign identity.
Islamising regimes began by proclaiming sharia the basis of law, as Zia did with the Hudood Ordinances in 1979 and Nimeiry in 1983; it rallied followers and alarmed neighbours and trade partners.
Zia replaced parliament with a nominated Majlis-e-Shura (1981): a consultative council of loyal notables and scholars instead of elected deputies.
Islamising states promised a treasury run on Islamic principles, on the model of the early bait al-mal, and an end to the corruption of the old order.

Pakistan's Federal Shariat Court (1980) and Sudan's emergency \"decisive justice\" courts (1983-84) gave religious law priority over civil law; the regimes gained authority while legal and academic debate narrowed.
Some regimes ruled through permanent mobilisation instead of courts, framing every policy as a struggle for the faith; the barracks grew and the shops emptied.
Pakistan's Zakat and Ushr Ordinance (1980) deducted 2.5 % from bank savings and a tithe on harvests to fund welfare; landowners and savers paid.
Pakistan (from 1981) and Sudan (1984) began moving banking to interest-free profit sharing; Gulf-backed Islamic banks welcomed it, Western lenders grew wary.
A ministry of religious affairs and endowments (awqaf) and Pakistan's Council of Islamic Ideology brought religious scholars into the administration of the state.
The Afghan war drew thousands of volunteers through Peshawar's service bureaus in the 1980s; they brought fighters and zeal, and foreign suspicion.
Pakistan created tens of thousands of local zakat committees that paid widows, orphans and students; the tithe on harvests funded village works.
Interest-free banks financed trade through mudaraba and musharaka partnerships; the first Islamic banks of the late 1970s grew fast on pious savings.
Rulers claiming religious authority expected the bay'ah, the oath of allegiance: Nimeiry styled himself imam in 1984, and Pakistan banned all political parties from 1979 to 1985.
The regime's economists promised a third way between capitalism and socialism, an economy of justice rather than growth.
Zia's education policy Islamised curricula and channelled zakat money to a fast-growing madrasa sector in the 1980s, while science teaching lost ground.
Zia kept civil courts, technocrats and the business class alongside the new religious institutions; stricter Islamists criticised the compromise, and the economy kept growing.
Saudi and Gulf money helped fund Pakistan's madrasas and the Afghan resistance in the 1980s, and Gulf preachers came with it.
Libya after 1969 expelled foreign bases, nationalised oil and declared an Islamic third way; independence came with isolation and sanctions.
Within a decade the Islamising states had reshaped public life: prayer at work, religious broadcasting and new laws on family and morals.
Islamising regimes put chaplains, prayer and religious instruction into the army; Zia made the Pakistani army the guardian of the ideology of the state.
The ideological state at its height: a single law, a single banner and a population mobilised for it, admired by its followers and isolated abroad.

The Lusaka summit (1970), attended by more than fifty states, revived the movement founded by Tito, Nasser and Nehru and made its summits a regular forum for countries that refused to choose between the blocs.

Bandung (1955) and the Algiers summit (1973) made non-alignment a diplomacy of conferences and joint demands; delegations, embassies and summits cost money, while both blocs offered aid to win the members over.

The Non-Aligned News Agencies Pool (1975, coordinated by Tanjug) and the call for a New World Information Order sought to end dependence on Western news agencies; Western governments and press groups attacked it as a licence for state control.

By the mid-1970s non-aligned states held a majority in the UN General Assembly and, with the Group of 77, pushed through the 1974 declaration on a New International Economic Order over Western objections.
Yugoslavia, India and Indonesia turned non-alignment, and Finland and Austria neutrality, from a slogan into an organising principle of the state.
Brotherhood movements argued that Islam and elections were compatible; where they could stand, as in Jordan or Kuwait, they won seats.
The Brotherhood was run by its Guidance Office under the General Guide; in power, the movement's leadership sat beside the cabinet.
The first International Conference on Islamic Economics (Mecca, 1976) gave the Islamic movement an economic vocabulary of zakat, honest trade and interest-free finance.
Jordan's Brotherhood worked within the parliamentary order and won 22 of 80 seats in 1989; coalition politics brought legitimacy and slow decisions.
Turabi's Islamic movement (from 1985 the National Islamic Front) built a disciplined organisation inside the Sudanese state after 1977; it worked, and the officers distrusted it.
Brotherhood clinics, schools and relief committees reached the poor quarters faster than the state; it cost money and earned loyalty.
Faisal Islamic Bank (Egypt and Sudan, 1977) collected the savings of the pious and of migrant workers in the Gulf; conventional banks lost deposits.
In 1987 the Egyptian Brotherhood ran in an Islamic Alliance with the Labour and Liberal parties and became the largest opposition bloc.
Sudanese Islamists took posts in the judiciary, the Islamic banks and the civil service in the early 1980s; the network ran the state, and patronage followed.
Community schools and literacy classes attached to mosques spread in the 1970s and 1980s, teaching reading and carrying the movement's message.
Islamic investment companies and merchant networks financed workshops, trade and housing with the savings of the faithful.
Sadat's releases (1971-75) and Nimeiry's national reconciliation (1977) ended years of persecution: for a time, the movement and the state made peace.
By the early 1980s Islamic banks and finance houses were a sector of their own from Khartoum to Kuala Lumpur.
Islamists in parliament pressed for bans on alcohol and stricter dress rules, as in Kuwait and in Egypt's sharia debates of the late 1970s; tourism and business interests resisted.
Islamist doctors, engineers and lawyers took over Egypt's professional syndicates in the 1980s, and ABIM organised Malaysia's graduates: a modern, educated Islam.
Millions of Egyptians, Sudanese and Jordanians worked in the Gulf after 1973; their remittances and Gulf donors helped fund the movement, and brought Gulf influence.
Through the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (1969) governments could mediate between Muslim states and stay outside both blocs; the generals found it soft.
The Islamic student associations of the 1970s produced a generation of pious professionals who carried the movement into the middle class.
The movement's international organisation, formalised in 1982, linked branches across the Arab world, Europe and Asia.
The movement's thinkers called it wasatiyya, the middle way between secularism and extremism: a pious, prosperous and electoral Islam.
Ne Win (1962), Mobutu (1965) and Suharto (1966-67) took power in non-aligned states and made their own office the only centre of power, backed by the army and the secret service.
Mobutu's single party (MPR, 1967) and Ne Win's Revolutionary Council (1962) concentrated every decision around the leader; ministers served at his pleasure.
Strongmen ran the economy through state firms answerable to the palace: Pertamina under Ibnu Sutowo, Gécamines in Zaire, the Burmese state corporations.

Mobutu renamed the country Zaire (1971) and himself Mobutu Sese Seko (1972), and his image opened the television news; the cult bound the nation to one man, while the patronage behind it hollowed out the state.

Yugoslavia's 1974 constitution set up a collective presidency and federal checks to take over after Tito; Franco's Organic Law of the State (1967) likewise laid down institutions meant to outlast him in Spain.
Zairianisation (1973) and Nigeria's Indigenisation Decree (1972) transferred foreign-owned firms or shares to nationals: a windfall for the regimes' clients, but foreign investors grew wary.
Suharto's IGGI consortium (1967) brought Western credit, while Tito drew IMF loans and Soviet trade at the same time; both regimes financed growth with borrowed money.
Yugoslavia's UDBA, Zaire's CND, Burma's Military Intelligence Service and Indonesia's Kopkamtib watched and detained opponents, and the UDBA also pursued émigrés abroad; student politics was curbed.

Franco's Cortes were chosen through family, municipality and syndicate; Suharto's Golkar, which won the 1971 election, organised civil servants, farmers and workers as \"functional groups\" instead of parties.

In Zaire the \"acquéreurs\" of the zairianised firms were mostly politicians, officers and regime insiders; many businesses soon failed, and from 1976 part of them was handed back to the former owners.
IGGI and World Bank credit financed Indonesia's Repelita plans from 1969: roads, ports, irrigation and fertiliser plants.

Burma's 1974 one-party constitution, Zaire's MPR and Indonesia's Golkar folded unions, youth and women's groups into one regime movement, while the old parties were banned or, in Indonesia (1973), forced to merge.
Indonesia's presidential instruction (Inpres) programmes, such as the primary-school drive of 1973, let the palace pay directly for schools, markets and clinics – and take the credit for them.
India's Emergency (1975-77) postponed elections and suspended civil liberties in the name of order; the jailed opposition united as the Janata Party and defeated the government in 1977.
Indonesia's P4 courses (1978) made civil servants and students study Pancasila; Mobutism and the \"Burmese Way to Socialism\" were taught the same way.
Yugoslavia flew American and then Soviet jets, and Mobutu was courted by Washington, Paris and Beijing at once: non-aligned strongmen took support from several sides and let foreign advisers in.
Mobutu's Division Spéciale Présidentielle (1985) and Syria's Defence Companies under Rifaat al-Assad (1971) were elite forces armed and paid by the regime, separate from the regular army.
Strongmen put officers and loyalists in charge of the provinces: military governors in Suharto's Indonesia, Mobutu's appointed regional commissioners, Ne Win's Security and Administrative Committees.
Yugoslavia and India flew Soviet MiG-21s alongside licence-built French helicopters (Gazelle, Alouette III) and used rival offers to bargain over price and licences.
Tito, a founder of the Non-Aligned Movement, took credits from both Washington and Moscow; Mobutu and Suharto stayed in power for over three decades by making themselves useful to outside patrons.
Switzerland and, after the 1955 State Treaty, Austria made permanent neutrality the core of national identity and a foundation of their economic success.
Switzerland's \"magic formula\" (1959) gave all four large parties seats in the Federal Council: consensus at home matched neutrality abroad.
The Swiss franc and the Austrian schilling (hard-currency policy from the 1970s) kept inflation below that of most of Western Europe through the oil shocks.
Sweden's totalförsvar and the Swiss militia army, planned to mobilise some 600,000 men within 48 hours, were meant to make an invasion too costly for either bloc.
Finland hosted the CSCE in Helsinki (1975), Austria built the UN City in Vienna (1979) and Switzerland offered its good offices: neutrality as a service both blocs needed.
Low-tax Swiss cantons such as Zug offered privileged rates to holding and domicile companies and drew in multinationals and commodity traders in the 1960s and 1970s.

Austria's Parity Commission (1957) negotiated wages and prices, and the Swiss labour peace agreement (1937) replaced strikes with bargaining: almost no strikes in the 1970s, bought with costly social compromises.
The Swiss shelter law of 1963 required shelters in new buildings, with the goal of a protected place for every resident; construction peaked in the mid-1970s at up to 400,000 places a year.
Banking secrecy (Swiss law of 1934) and neutrality made Zurich, Geneva and Vienna havens for capital from both blocs and the Third World, including flight capital and illicit funds.
Commodity traders and holding companies settled in low-tax neutral states in the 1970s (Marc Rich + Co. in Zug, 1974), paying their taxes there but bringing foreign interests with them.
Swiss machine tools, Swedish engineering (ASEA, SKF) and Austria's VOEST thrived on stable wages and long-term planning.
Swedish and Swiss doctrine held that neutrality was only credible if it was armed and economically independent; both blocs had to believe it.
Neutral Switzerland and Sweden had some of the highest incomes in Europe in the 1970s, and Austria was catching up fast.

The Schwarzenbach initiative against \"over-foreignisation\" won 46 % of the vote in 1970; the Federal Council had capped foreign labour with national quotas that year, and employers had to recruit fewer workers.

Sweden's 1975 immigrant policy gave foreign residents language courses and, from 1976, the vote in local elections; employers kept the labour they needed, and an anti-immigration group, Keep Sweden Swedish, formed in 1979.
Austria, Switzerland, Sweden and Finland signed free-trade agreements with the EEC in 1972-73 without joining it, and tied their markets to the West.
Finland's bilateral clearing trade with the USSR swapped ships and machinery for Soviet oil and cushioned the 1973 oil shock – at the price of Soviet influence (\"Finlandisation\").
Swiss voters decided the big questions by referendum – women's suffrage in 1971, the foreign-worker initiatives – which bound every camp to the result.
A neutral state could not rely on allied arsenals: Sweden built the Saab Viggen, Switzerland its own tanks and Oerlikon guns, Austria its Steyr vehicles.
By the late 1970s Switzerland and Sweden were the models of armed neutrality: rich, stable, defended by the whole nation and taken seriously by both blocs.
In much of Central America, in Lebanon and in the Philippines a few dozen landed and merchant families dominated 1970s politics through their own parties and networks of patrons.
El Salvador's \"fourteen families\", the Somozas in Nicaragua, a handful of zu'ama in Lebanon: politics was the business of a few houses.
A few trading families controlled imports, exports and banking in the Gulf, Lebanon and Central America, and governments depended on their goodwill.

Lebanon's National Pact (1943) divided offices among the confessional elites and Colombia's Sitges agreement (1957) between the two traditional parties: peace among the notables, but every decision needed all of them.
The Somozas ruled Nicaragua from 1936 to 1979 like a family firm: one house held the presidency, the National Guard and a large share of the country's land and industry.
In Marcos's Philippines state contracts, cheap credit and trading monopolies went to presidential cronies such as Eduardo Cojuangco (coconuts, later San Miguel beer) and Roberto Benedicto (sugar).
Coffee, sugar and cotton planters dominated Central American states; export taxes on the estates funded the state, while landless peasants worked them for low wages.

Colombia's National Front (1958-74) alternated the presidency between Liberals and Conservatives and split every office between them: it ended the partisan Violencia, but shut out other movements, some of which took up arms.
Nicaragua's Guardia Nacional was commanded by the Somoza family itself and served the dynasty rather than the state.
The Somozas, the Philippine Ayala and Lopez clans and Lebanese merchant houses turned land and trade fortunes into banks, utilities, property and industry.

Coffee, bananas, cotton and sugar earned most of Central America's export income in the 1970s, as sugar and coconut products did much of the Philippines'; the estate owners carried decisive political weight.
In El Salvador the coffee growers' associations and in Argentina the landowners' Sociedad Rural shaped economic policy, often more than parliament did.
The commodity boom of 1973-77 (sugar in 1974, coffee in 1976) filled the treasuries of the oligarchic states – for a while.
The Philippine land reform of 1972 (PD 27) covered only tenanted rice and corn land and spared the sugar and coconut estates: it gave some tenants land and angered the rice and corn landlords.
El Salvador's ORDEN and the Philippine Civilian Home Defence Forces (1976) armed loyal villagers against peasant organisers and rebels; their abuses fed the insurgencies that followed.
The Somozas and Central American planters relied on American aid, investors and the embassy's goodwill; the embassy expected to be heard in return.
Merchant oligarchies sold to whoever paid: Argentine grain went to the USSR during the 1980 US embargo, Lebanese and Gulf houses traded with both blocs.
In Lebanon, the Philippines and Central America oligarchic rule rested on clientelism: the patron found jobs, loans and doctors for his clients, and they voted as he told them.
Oligarch families kept their fortunes in Miami, Geneva and Panama; the connections brought foreign banks and cheap credit home.

At its height the oligarchic order looked unshakeable: the families held the land, the banks, the army and the vote – until the Sandinista revolution in Nicaragua and the coup and civil war in El Salvador (1979-80).
Hong Kong's Financial Secretary John Cowperthwaite (1961-71) kept the state small: low spending, no industrial subsidies or industrial policy, and minimal social welfare.
Hong Kong's Independent Commission Against Corruption (1974) broke up the police corruption syndicates within a few years; a small state depends on clean officials.

Financial Secretary Haddon-Cave (1971-81) called Hong Kong's doctrine \"positive non-interventionism\": the state set the framework and stayed out of the market unless intervention was clearly justified.

Colonial Hong Kong was run by appointed administrators, and Singapore by a technocratic cabinet facing no opposition in parliament (1968-81); decisions came fast, but the public had little say in them.

Classical liberals from Hayek (The Constitution of Liberty, 1960) to the US tax revolt (California's Proposition 13, 1978) wanted firm limits on taxing and spending; investors trusted the rules, the government lost room to act.
Hong Kong's standard tax rate of about 15 % on salaries and profits drew firms and capital from across the region, but left the treasury with less to spend.
Between 1974 and 1978 Chile returned or sold most of the firms taken over under Allende, raising revenue while the unions, already curbed by the junta, lost their strongest workplaces.
Hong Kong co-opted business and community leaders into hundreds of advisory boards instead of holding general elections (the \"administrative absorption of politics\", Ambrose King 1975).
