Hong Kong held the growth of public spending to the growth of the economy, and the 1970s American campaign for a balanced-budget amendment sought to write such a rule into the constitution.
Ireland's Shannon Free Zone (1959), Taiwan's Kaohsiung zone (1966) and South Korea's Masan (1970) drew foreign assemblers with tax holidays and duty-free ports, tying the economy to world demand.
Chile deregulated road transport and port labour from the late 1970s and sold its electricity and telephone companies in 1985-89; Japan broke up and privatised its national railways in 1987.
Robert Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) gave the minimal state its manifesto: courts, police and defence, and little else.
Hong Kong dropped its exchange controls in the early 1970s and Britain abolished its own in 1979: capital flowed in freely, and out again whenever the world market turned.

Milton Friedman proposed school vouchers in 1955, and Chile introduced vouchers and private health insurers (ISAPREs) in 1980-81: public spending fell, and critics pointed to a widening gap between rich and poor.
Friedman's negative income tax (1962) proposed replacing welfare offices with one cash payment; the US tested it in New Jersey (1968-72) and in Seattle and Denver during the 1970s.
Hong Kong and Singapore traded with both Cold War camps at once, from Western banks to Chinese and Soviet shipping, and felt every swing in world trade first.
Beirut until 1975 and the Bahamas, the Cayman Islands and Luxembourg prospered on bank secrecy and low taxes; foreign money also brought foreign influence and illicit funds.
Hong Kong's kaifong neighbourhood associations, clan societies and charities such as the Tung Wah hospitals carried much of the social work into the 1970s, with limited help from the state.
The Gates Commission (1970), with Milton Friedman as a member, recommended ending the US draft, which stopped in 1973: a smaller, professional force replaced the conscripts.
Hayek (Nobel 1974) and Friedman (Nobel 1976) gave free-market ideas new prestige, and Hong Kong's economy grew by about 9 % a year in real terms through the 1970s.
The Club of Rome's report (1972) sold millions of copies and turned \"limits to growth\" into a political programme; economists and industry attacked its forecasts from the start.
West Germany counted thousands of local citizens' initiatives (Bürgerinitiativen) by the mid-1970s, from Wyhl to Brokdorf; the green parties grew out of them.
The OECD adopted the polluter-pays principle in 1972, and Dutch (1970) and West German (1976) water-pollution levies made industry pay for its discharges while funding the clean-up.
The early West German Greens rotated their Bundestag deputies (from 1983), bound them to the party base and decided in open assemblies; the base trusted them, but decisions were slow.
The \"Realos\" around Joschka Fischer accepted ministries and coalitions (Hesse 1985) to get results, at the cost of bitter conflict with the party's radical wing.
Clean air and water laws (US 1970-72, Japan's \"Pollution Diet\" of 1970) protected health and farmland but slowed approval of new factories and dams.
After Wyhl (1975) and Zwentendorf (1978) the anti-nuclear movement became central to green politics; it bet on water, sun and wind instead of the atom.
Austria's Zwentendorf referendum (1978) stopped a finished nuclear plant, and Sweden voted on nuclear power in 1980: citizens could overrule government and industry.
Britain (1970), Japan (1971) and West Germany's Federal Environment Agency (1974) gave the environment its own ministry or agency, with real powers and a new bureaucracy.

India's Chipko movement (1973) defended village forests against commercial logging, Project Tiger (1973) created protected reserves, and the Forest Conservation Act (1980) curbed the clearing of forest land.
Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful (1973) and his Intermediate Technology group promoted small workshops and village power instead of giant plants.
Boulding's \"spaceship earth\" (1966), the first Earth Day (1970) and the UN Stockholm conference (1972) put ecology into schools and newspapers.
Amory Lovins' \"soft energy path\" (1976) answered the oil shock with efficiency and renewables instead of new oil and nuclear plants.
Gene Sharp's The Politics of Nonviolent Action (1973) inspired plans for defence by strikes and non-cooperation; the Danish, Dutch and Swedish governments commissioned studies of the idea.
Horst Afheldt's \"defensive defence\" (1976) wanted an army that could hold its own ground but threaten no one - dispersed light infantry with anti-tank weapons instead of tank divisions.

Latin America's Tlatelolco treaty (1967) banned nuclear weapons from the region, and New Zealand's nuclear-free policy (1984) closed its ports to nuclear-armed ships, straining its alliance with the United States.
The first fair-trade shops (1969-73), the call for a New International Economic Order (1974) and the Brandt Report (1980) pressed for fairer trade and more aid for the South - paid from the budget.

The \"Swords into Ploughshares\" badge of the East German church peace movement (1980-81) and the Euromissile protests (1981-83) brought millions onto the streets to demand disarmament and lower arms spending.
European green parties coordinated from 1979 and formed the Rainbow Group in the European Parliament (1984), spreading ideas and contacts across borders.
Herman Daly's Steady-State Economics (1977) gave the movement its economics, and Petra Kelly's West German Greens opposed the missiles of both blocs, protesting in East Berlin in 1983.
The Arusha Declaration (1967) promised a socialism neither copied from Moscow nor from Beijing, built on self-reliance and social spending.
Socialist charters such as Arusha (1967), Zambia's Mulungushi reforms (1968) and Guyana's Cooperative Republic (1970) turned party programmes into state doctrine.
India's Planning Commission (1950) and its five-year plans became a model for many non-aligned governments that wanted planning without Soviet control.
Tanzania (1965) and Zambia (1972) made the ruling party the only legal one: power and unity were secured, open debate and private business shrank.
Allende's Popular Unity (1970) and Sri Lanka's United Front (1970) governed as multi-party coalitions within parliamentary systems: broad alliances, constant bargaining.
Tanzania's Ujamaa policy (1967-76) moved millions of peasants into planned villages with communal plots; schools and water came closer, but forced villagisation (1973-76) disrupted farm output.
India nationalised its 14 largest banks in 1969 and Sri Lanka its company-owned plantations in 1975: credit was steered to state priorities, and foreign investors held back.
Tanzania's 1975 amendment declared party supremacy over the state, and party and state offices increasingly merged, which also bred patronage.
Allende's \"Chilean road to socialism\" (1970-73) kept parliament, courts and press, and Sri Lanka's United Front won and lost power at the ballot box.
Tanzania's adult literacy campaigns of the 1970s, organised in the villages by party and government, roughly doubled the share of adults who could read.
Indira Gandhi won the 1971 election on \"Garibi Hatao\" (abolish poverty): nationalised banks lent to farmers and small firms, and the state expanded public-sector plants and social programmes.
Youth leagues, women's unions and cooperative federations, such as TANU's Youth League, carried the programme into villages and workplaces.
By the late 1970s public-sector firms produced most of India's steel and power and much of its fertiliser, and played a similar role in many other non-aligned states.
Tanzania's National Service (JKT, compulsory for graduates from 1966) and the Zambia National Service (1971) sent young people to build roads and farms; Tanzanian students protested in 1966.
Tanzania's Musoma Resolution (1974) promised a primary school place for every child by 1977; enrolment nearly doubled within three years, and education spending rose sharply.

China built the TAZARA railway (1970-75) while Sweden and the other Nordic states became Tanzania's main donors; India took Soviet steel plants and American grain - and the influence that came with them.
The Group of 77 (1964) and the Arusha Programme for Collective Self-Reliance (1979) urged the South to trade with itself and depend less on donors.
Nyerere's \"Education for Self-Reliance\" (1967) wanted citizens who worked for the community; schools ran farms and workshops.
The UN declared a New International Economic Order in 1974, and Non-Aligned summits (Algiers 1973, Colombo 1976) made the South a voice in world politics.
Self-reliance (kujitegemea) was the stated goal of Nyerere's socialism: a mostly public economy meant to stand without either bloc, though Tanzania stayed heavily dependent on foreign aid.
Tito's break with Stalin (1948) and Romania's refusal to join the invasion of Czechoslovakia (1968) defined communist parties that took no orders from Moscow.
The Yugoslav party renamed itself a \"League\" (1952) to stress that it led society rather than administered it; its congresses set the line for the state.
Yugoslav \"social plans\" and Romanian five-year plans set investment priorities for the whole economy, outside Comecon's division of labour.

Yugoslav workers' councils (from 1950) helped choose managers and divided enterprise income, and the 1974 constitution and 1976 Associated Labour Act extended self-management across the whole economy.
After his 1971 visit to China and North Korea and the July Theses, Ceausescu centralised power and pushed heavy industry in Romania; culture and consumer goods suffered.
Romania joined the IMF and World Bank (1972) and Yugoslavia borrowed heavily from Western banks: new plants quickly, and a debt crisis in the 1980s.
Albania's 1976 constitution banned foreign credits and concessions; after the break with China (1978) it stood alone, shielded from outside pressure but cut off from foreign technology.
Yugoslavia's 1965 reform gave self-managed firms more freedom over prices, investment and foreign trade; Western credits and consumer goods followed, and so did exposure to world markets.
Romania's systematisation law (1974) planned to turn villages into agro-industrial towns; when the plan was revived in 1988, villages began to be razed and the programme drew international protest.
Dacia built Renaults under a 1966 licence, Zastava built Fiats and Oltcit (founded 1976) Citroëns; Western licences brought technology, paid for in hard currency.
Albania's Chinese-built Elbasan steel works (1970s) and Romania's Galati steel plant put steel, power and arms ahead of consumer goods.
The Romanian (1969) and Yugoslav (1974) tenth congresses confirmed their leaders' lines and filled the central committees with loyal cadres.
Yugoslavia grew by about 6 % a year in the 1970s and Romania, by official figures, even faster, turning both into industrial countries within a generation.
Yugoslavia's 1974 constitution gave its republics and provinces near-sovereign powers to keep the peace between its nations, weakening the centre.
Romania's Securitate and Albania's Sigurimi built dense informer networks and closely watched contacts with foreigners; the police budget grew and dissent was suppressed.
Tito co-founded the Non-Aligned Movement (Belgrade 1961) and was still its elder statesman at Havana (1979); summits, aid and prestige cost money.
Ceausescu hosted Nixon (1969), kept ties to Israel and West Germany and won US most-favoured-nation status (1975), opening Romania to Western partners and their influence.
Ceausescu's July Theses (1971) mixed communism with national pride and history; independent communist states leaned on patriotism to stay united.

Yugoslavia and Romania jointly developed the Orao/IAR-93 jet (first flight 1974), and Yugoslavia built the M-84 tank under Soviet licence and its own warships, to reduce their dependence on either bloc.
After 1968 Yugoslavia (law of 1969) and Romania organised the whole population for territorial war so that no bloc could occupy them as the Warsaw Pact had occupied Czechoslovakia.
Nationalist movements gained ground around 1970, from Turkey's Nationalist Movement Party (1969) to the Rhodesian Front's republic (1970) and Perón's return to Argentina (1973).
Mass leagues such as the Peronist Youth or Spain's Movimiento associations filled the streets with supporters, and with clashes.
Veterans' bodies (the Spanish Hermandad de Alféreces, the Portuguese Liga dos Combatentes) lent nationalism respectability, at the price of their pensions.
By the mid-1970s nationalists governed or shared power in Argentina, Rhodesia and Turkey (the 1975 Nationalist Front coalition), crowding out liberals and the left.
A nationalist government arrives with a mandate to act quickly, as Perón did with his 62 % in September 1973.
Populists came to power on personal popularity as much as on party machines: Perón won 62 % on his return in 1973.
Velasco Ibarra was president of Ecuador five times (1934-72), relying on radio speeches and rallies more than on any party.
Price controls on bread, fuel and rents were a common first measure of populist governments, as in Argentina in 1973.
Peronism rested on the CGT unions; social spending and union rights kept the base loyal and frightened investors.
George Wallace's campaigns and Nixon's 1969 \"silent majority\" speech courted the patriotic middle class against anti-war protesters and radicals.
Protection for national producers and limits on foreign capital (Argentina's 1973 foreign investment law) built at home but scared investors away.
Mogens Glistrup's Progress Party (Denmark 1973) won 16 % promising to abolish income tax and most of the bureaucracy.
The Peronist government's 1973 Pacto Social froze prices and wages by agreement of the CGT unions and the CGE employers: inflation fell for a year, then the pact broke down in 1974-75.
Populists campaigned against \"the establishment\": anti-corruption purges and back-tax drives against the old families followed.
State credit and \"buy national\" procurement grew domestic industry behind tariff walls, as across Latin America in the early 1970s.
Glistrup famously proposed replacing Denmark's defence with an answering machine; his party demanded deep cuts in both state staff and taxes.
Plebiscites and mass rallies rivalled parliament as a source of legitimacy, as in Perón's Plaza de Mayo addresses.
Populism lived on visible results for ordinary families: jobs, cheap goods and a rising standard of living.
\"Law and order\" was the theme of the Wallace and Nixon campaigns of 1968: more police, harder sentences, and a larger police bill.
\"Give me a balcony and I will be president,\" said Velasco Ibarra; charisma mobilised crowds but wore down institutions.
Perón's Tercera Posición - neither Washington nor Moscow - led Argentina to trade with the Eastern bloc and to grant Cuba a credit of 1.2 billion dollars for Argentine goods in 1973-74.
Turkey's Demirel and other anti-communist populists traded loyalty to the West for American aid and equipment.
Peronism called itself a movement, not a party: unions, youth and women's branches all answered to the leader.
Populists promised the army respect and the nation pride, as Perón did in courting the armed forces after his 1973 return.
At its height a populist government claimed to have renewed the nation itself, as Peronism did in its \"Argentina Potencia\" programme.
The regime presents itself as a national revolution against party politics and class war, as the Estado Novo did.
Spain's Movimiento Nacional and Portugal's União Nacional (Acção Nacional Popular from 1970) were the only legal parties.
Isolated regimes learned to live with embargoes: Rhodesia withstood UN sanctions after 1966 through import substitution and trade via South Africa.
The Falangist \"bunker\" of 1973-75 insisted on the Movimiento's primacy over reformist ministers; ideology rose and administration slowed.
From 1957 Franco handed the economy to Opus Dei technocrats (López Rodó, Ullastres); growth came, the old guard lost ground.
The Estado Novo's corporations united employers and workers under state arbitration; strikes were banned.
Portugal spent around 40 % of its budget on the colonial wars (1961-74); four years of service became normal.
The Frente de Juventudes and the Mocidade Portuguesa organised youth in camps, parades and pre-military training.
Spain's three Development Plans (1964-75) steered investment into growth poles and infrastructure.
Spain's compulsory Organización Sindical bound workers and owners into one syndicate per branch and enforced labour peace by law, until clandestine Workers' Commissions spread in the 1960s.
Wartime regimes built their own arsenals: Portugal's Braço de Prata arsenal and Rhodesia's sanctions-era workshops armed the troops.
Spain's Organic Law of the State (1967) codified the regime's institutions so that it could outlive its founder.
Spain's \"miracle\" (1959-74) gave the regime its strongest argument: dams, factories and tourism instead of the hunger years.
Prior censorship (Portugal's Exame Prévio, Spain before 1966) kept dissent out of print and much literature and scholarship with it.
Fraga's Press Law (1966) and Caetano's \"evolution in continuity\" opened the regime to Europe, and to its critics.
Portugal in Africa and the Rhodesian bush war (escalating from 1972) made counter-insurgency the army's school, and drained the treasury.
Spain rented bases to the US (1953, renewed 1970) and Portugal kept the Azores in NATO: aid and arms for American influence.
Spain's \"25 Years of Peace\" campaign (1964) presented order and stability as the regime's gift to a war-scarred generation.
Staff colleges and NATO courses produced professional officers who later led or accepted the transitions in Portugal and Spain.
The regime's founding myth of national greatness, kept alive in parades and schoolbooks until its end in 1974-75.
A junta first secures the barracks with larger budgets and privileges for the officer corps, as in Greece after 1967 or Chile after 1973.
Coups from Greece (1967) to Chile (1973) and Turkey (1980) opened with numbered radio communiqués; parliament was dissolved and the parties suspended or banned soon after.
Most juntas appointed civilian economists under a general: Roberto Campos in Brazil, Martínez de Hoz in Argentina, the ODEPLAN team in Chile.

Nigeria's military government (1975-79) set a timetable for civilian rule and Ghana's AFRC (1979) kept the scheduled elections; the promise bought calm and foreign goodwill but let the parties recover.
Brazil (1964-85) and Chile (1973-90) turned the coup into a regime with its own constitution; the universities and the middle class paid with their freedoms.
Chile's 1975 \"shock treatment\" (Sergio de Castro and other Chicago-trained economists) sold state firms and opened the economy; wages and unions bore the cost.
Brazil's \"economic miracle\" (1968-73) and Velasco's Peru built state industries with foreign loans; growth was real and so was the debt that came due in the 1980s.
After the 1973 elections the Turkish army stepped back but kept its voice in the National Security Council as guardian of the state; the officers lost office but kept their prestige.
Brazil's Escola Superior de Guerra taught that the enemy was internal; the Southern Cone juntas adopted versions of the doctrine and the police budget grew with it.
Between 1974 and 1978 Chile returned or sold off most of the several hundred firms taken over under Allende, cutting state losses and raising some revenue.
Brazil's Embraer (1969) and Argentina's Fabricaciones Militares put officers in charge of steel, aircraft and arms plants.
Juntas governed through numbered decree-laws (Chile's junta issued some 3,500 by 1980): fast, but without the consent parliament had provided.
Juntas justified themselves by results: while the economy grew, the barracks and the middle class stayed loyal.
Operation Condor (1975) linked the Southern Cone secret services to pursue opponents across borders; over such abuses the US Congress cut military aid to Chile (1976) and Argentina (1978).
Peruvian, Thai and Indonesian (dwifungsi) officers built roads, schools and clinics in the countryside to win the villages; the troops trained less.
US military aid and IMET training (F-5 fighters, Huey helicopters) equipped most anti-communist juntas, along with American influence over their officers.

After the US human-rights embargoes, and Brazil's 1977 break with US military aid, the juntas bought from France and Israel and built their own weapons (Brazil's Engesa, Chile's FAMAE): independent but expensive.
Once the insurgency was broken the regime declared victory and lifted the state of siege, as Chile's junta did in March 1978, replacing it with a state of emergency.
The juntas spent their money on the forces that kept them in power: Argentina's junta bought Israeli and French jets and German-designed tanks and warships between 1976 and 1982.
At its height the military state ran ministries, governorships and state firms through serving officers, as in Brazil under Médici or Argentina under the Proceso.
Monarchies drew legitimacy from dynasty and nation alike, as Jordan's Hashemites and Morocco's Alaouites did.
The kings of Morocco, Jordan and Nepal appointed and dismissed governments at will under their constitutions.
Planning bodies answering to the throne set the economic course above party politics, as Iran's Plan and Budget Organisation did under the Shah.
Thailand's king backed the students and a new constitution in October 1973; Juan Carlos did the same in Spain after 1975.
Hassan II's 1970 constitution and Nepal's panchayat kept power with the king - and Haile Selassie's refusal to share it ended in 1974.
Iran's White Revolution (from 1963) gave land to peasants and sent a literacy corps to the villages; landlords and clergy turned against the Shah.
Royal holdings and court favourites ran key businesses, from Iran's Pahlavi Foundation to Morocco's palace-linked firms: dependable, and dependent on patronage.
Spain's Constitution of 1978 made the crown the guarantor of democracy and bound the army to it.
After the coup attempts of Skhirat (1971) and the 1972 attack on his jet, Hassan II took personal command of the armed forces and tightened his palace security.
Thailand's royal development projects (from 1969) built dams, roads and model farms in the poorest provinces.
Morocco's Moroccanisation decree (1973) forced foreign firms to sell majorities to nationals - many of them close to the palace.
Royal courts (Morocco's royal cabinet, Jordan's Royal Hashemite Court) worked beside the government and kept the notables in line.
The oil and phosphate booms of 1973-74 let monarchies fund palaces, subsidies and loyal middle classes.
Hassan II ruled as Amir al-Mu'minin and Thailand's king as patron of Buddhism: faith anchored the throne, not the laboratories.
The Shah's court pushed women's rights (Family Protection Law 1967) and Western education, and alienated the clergy.
Under the Nixon Doctrine (1969-72) Iran and Saudi Arabia bought American jets and tanks as the Gulf's \"twin pillars\", and hosted American advisers.
The Green March of 1975 rallied every Moroccan party behind the king on a national claim, and strained relations abroad.
The Persepolis celebrations of 1971 dazzled the world's leaders, and their cost was remembered at home.
Royal armies were the throne's last line: Jordan's army, heir to the Arab Legion, decided the Black September conflict of 1970 in the king's favour.
Hussein survived Black September, Hassan two coups and Bhumibol 1973 - the monarchies that adapted outlasted the decade.
The world is divided between two camps. We must decide where we stand.
Our embassies are understaffed and our diplomats untrained. That ends now.
Good relations start with trade. Our neighbours are our natural partners.
Parliament, the press and the officer corps argue over the nation's defence.
Every nation must find its place in the Cold War. Ours is still undecided.
War between the blocs would destroy us all. Coexistence is the only sane policy.
Threats must be met before they reach our borders.
Washington, London and Paris offer capital, technology and protection.
Moscow supports the struggle against imperialism with weapons, credit and advisers.
Peking shows that a peasant nation can build socialism by its own strength.
We will not choose between the two blocs. The spirit of Bandung guides us.
Neither Washington nor Moscow will decide our fate. The nation comes first.
Bunkers, tank traps and shelters will make any invasion costly.
The army is the school of the nation.
Western banks and companies are invited to invest, and they will expect a return.
Soviet officers will train our army, and they will report to Moscow.
An economy built on our own strength is hard to blockade.
Our neutrality is our shield. We join no alliance and host no foreign bases.
The people must be ready to defend the nation at any moment.
Factories, not tanks, will make us strong.
We have not forgotten what was taken from us.
Radio stations, scholarships and friendship societies carry our ideas abroad, at a price.
In the General Assembly every nation has one vote, and ours will be heard.
We will mediate between the blocs and lower the temperature of the Cold War.
Only those willing to go to the brink are taken seriously.
Market, plan or something in between: the most important decision of the decade.
Prices are freed, licences abolished and private enterprise encouraged.
The state guides, private enterprise produces, and the unions have a say.
Our creditors are willing to talk. Better terms now will save us later.
The plan builds quickly, but without competition productivity lags and foreign capital stays away.
The countryside feeds the nation and deserves our support.
Tax breaks and guarantees will bring foreign capital into the country.
A modern stock exchange will channel savings into industry.
State and business pursue common targets.
A few large companies will carry the flag on world markets.
Banks, mines and heavy industry pass into the hands of the people.
A state planning committee will draw up the five-year plans.
The great estates are broken up and the land is given to those who till it.
New seeds, fertiliser and irrigation can double our harvests.
Hundreds of exemptions are abolished. Fewer taxes, but everyone pays.
Duty-free zones near our ports will attract assembly plants for the world market.
Employers and unions negotiate wages and working conditions at one table.
Private plots are merged into collective farms. The village will feed the factory.
Small farmers join cooperatives to share machines, seed and credit.
Modern farms produce for the market.
Growth rates that astonish the world: this is our economic miracle.
Pension funds will invest in the country's future and secure old age.
The mixed economy delivers: rising wages, full shops and social peace.
Steel, cement and machines: the foundations of a socialist economy.
Our fields will feed the nation and its neighbours.
Roads, railways and power lines will tie the nation together.
The railway remains the backbone of a modern economy.
Modern highways will connect our cities.
An army without fuel is no army. We will build national fuel depots.
Millions are moving from the villages to the cities. They need homes and work.
Power lines reach the countryside.
Larger reserves will protect us from embargoes and price shocks.
The state will lead the economy to modernity.
We must produce what we need ourselves.
Our mines and wells hold untapped wealth.
Domestic production replaces imports.
Careful budget measures will put growth on a solid footing.
More hands in more factories.
Better tools and better training make every worker count.
High tariffs and import quotas protect our young industries.
Our products will compete on the world market, and we will feel its swings.
Textiles, shoes and household goods: industry begins with the consumer.
The workers are the strength of the nation.
A modern state needs steel and heavy machinery.
Our industry is hungry for power. Where will it come from?
Foreign cars will show our engineers what is possible.
Old arsenals are refitted for modern weapons.
State contracts will modernise the arms industry.
Synthetic fuel makes us less dependent on imported oil.
Great dams will tame our rivers and light our cities.
Coal and oil are proven, cheap and available.
The atom will power our cities. Atoms for peace.
Our own car factories will employ thousands.
Arms makers and shipyards are combined into one defence industry.
Wars around the world create demand. Our factories will supply it.
Modern turbines get more power out of every ton of coal.
Our first nuclear power station goes on line.
Transistors and computers are the industries of tomorrow.
Standard conversion kits allow factories to switch production quickly.
A robust grid keeps the lights on even under strain.
High-voltage lines carry power across the country with fewer losses.
Shopkeepers, clerks and engineers want a share of the growing prosperity.
Every child must learn to read and write.
Faith gives the people strength in uncertain times.
The state belongs to all citizens, whatever their faith.
The old families still hold much of the nation's wealth.
Students and teachers go to the villages to teach every adult to read.
Free schooling opens the door to advancement.
Traditional values are upheld.

Spain enters the new decade under a ruler who can no longer personally supervise every ministry, faction and security organ. Franco remains the source of authority, but his declining health is turning every appointment and public appearance into part of the succession struggle.

The MATESA export-credit scandal has exposed fraud, ministerial patronage and a widening breach between technocrats and old Falangists. Reopening the files will not cleanse the regime quietly, but it will reveal who still controls the state.

Falangist veterans, security officials and uncompromising Francoists reject any opening that could dismantle the victory of 1939. Their support offers discipline now and a dangerous claim on the succession later.
A limited investigation can sacrifice compromised officials without placing the entire regime on trial. The Aperturistas will gain room to argue that reform is the only way to preserve order.
The state can close ranks, suppress the most damaging evidence and move on. Stability bought through concealment will deepen corruption and convince the Bunker that pressure always works.

Juan Carlos was designated Franco's successor in 1969. We must now harden that settlement into an operative chain of authority, reassuring monarchists without allowing the prince to become an independent center of power.

The Movimiento Nacional remains the regime's only legal political framework. Renewed appointments, patronage and ideological discipline will make it a weapon in the coming struggle rather than a ceremonial shell.

Reformist officials believe limited pluralism and European integration can protect the state from revolutionary rupture. Giving them access will weaken the old guard and create expectations that cannot easily be withdrawn.

The military trial of ETA defendants has become an international test of the regime. Confirming death sentences would satisfy the hardliners; clemency would reduce foreign pressure while revealing the limits of repression.

Juan Carlos must learn the armed forces, the ministries and the unwritten limits of Francoist power. Whether he becomes custodian or reformer will depend on the allies he gathers before the throne is vacant.

Police intelligence and the political-security services will receive wider surveillance authority against ETA, clandestine parties and dissident labor networks. The state will see more, but govern through fear more openly.

Carefully selected associations, restrained press latitude and administrative reform can widen participation without immediately legalizing opposition parties. The opening may stabilize succession, or teach society to demand more.

As his physical command fades, Franco increasingly falls back on the conspiratorial anti-Masonic and antisemitic language of the regime's formative years. Broadcasting that rhetoric will mobilize loyalists at a severe diplomatic cost.

The Organic Law created a legal distinction between head of state and head of government. Making that separation real will allow a prime minister to manage daily rule while Franco remains the ultimate source of legitimacy.

Suspended guarantees and expanded police powers can impose calm on universities, factories and the Basque provinces. This is continuity through coercion, and every month of it narrows the regime's peaceful exits.

Admiral Luis Carrero Blanco will become President of the Government, translating Franco's personal authority into institutional continuity. His appointment strengthens the Bunker while placing the entire succession project on one man.

ETA is preparing an attack on Carrero Blanco. Changing routes, penetrating safehouses and hardening his convoy may save the architect of continuity, but overt precautions are costly and politically embarrassing.

Operation Ogre has settled the fate of Carrero Blanco, but not the regime he was meant to preserve. The final cabinet of Franco's lifetime must govern through weakening personal authority while reformists, hardliners and the designated heir prepare for the inevitable vacancy.

Arias Navarro's programme promises political associations and limited participation without abandoning the Fundamental Laws. Its ambiguity may briefly unite reformers and loyalists, but it cannot satisfy both.
The public campaign by Giron and the old guard threatens even the narrowest opening. Isolating its organisers will give Arias room to proceed while sharpening the Bunker's hostility.
The Bunker can be reassured with protected offices, firm limits on political association and renewed commitments to the Movement. Reform will survive, but only within a much narrower corridor.
Franco's illness has placed Juan Carlos in temporary command of the state. The prince can use this rehearsal to learn the machinery of power and establish direct ties to ministers and commanders.

The Green March and competing Moroccan and Mauritanian claims have made Spain's hold on Western Sahara untenable without escalation. Madrid must choose between an orderly withdrawal and a costly colonial stand.
The Generalissimo is dead. The institutions he balanced against one another must now function without the final arbiter who created them.
State mourning will give the armed forces, the Movement and the court a brief common ritual. Beneath the ceremony, every faction is counting loyalties.
Law names an heir, the Falange claims a revolution and the old institutions demand continuity. Spain must decide which meaning of Francoism, if any, will survive Franco.
The Bourbon restoration will proceed under Juan Carlos I. His crown can preserve legal continuity while opening a path toward political reform, provided the armed forces accept the pace of change.
The old shirts will reject both Bourbon restoration and parliamentary liberalization. The Movement will claim the state in the name of the National-Syndicalist revolution.

Neither a reforming monarchy nor a Falangist revolution will be allowed to endanger the state. A regency-backed executive will preserve the institutions, police powers and hierarchy of late Francoism.

Juan Carlos must rule beyond the coalition that placed him on the throne. Presenting the Crown as an institution for every Spaniard will give reformists political cover without immediately breaking legal continuity.

Entrenched ministers, Movement officials and security hardliners can obstruct every reform from inside the state. Removing them will weaken the Bunker, but it will also unsettle the institutions on which the new monarchy still depends.

The old Cortes will be asked to authorize its own replacement through law and referendum. Reform from within the inherited legal order offers a peaceful bridge to representative government, though failure would expose the Crown to both opposition and reaction.

A broad amnesty will release political prisoners and allow exiles to return, removing one of the opposition's central demands. It also asks victims and institutions of the old order to accept a difficult legal compromise.

The Movimiento Nacional can no longer remain the compulsory political structure of the state. Its political organs will be extinguished, its public functions absorbed by the administration and its monopoly brought to an end.

A representative system requires genuine competitors. Conservatives, liberals, socialists and communists will be permitted to organize openly, accepting short-term polarization in exchange for a legitimate political arena.

Universal, direct and secret elections will choose new Cortes. Adolfo Suarez and the democratic center must now seek authority from the electorate rather than from the institutions of the former regime.

Government, trade unions, employers and democratic parties will share the burden of fighting inflation and stabilising the transition. Wage restraint and fiscal reform can buy peace, but only at real social cost.
Josep Tarradellas can return from exile to head a provisional Generalitat. Restoring Catalonia's historic institution will channel regional demands into negotiation rather than rupture.

A parliamentary monarchy, popular sovereignty and constitutional rights will replace the Fundamental Laws of Francoism. Ratification will complete the legal transformation of Spain and bind the Crown to democratic government.

Constitutional autonomy will be extended through negotiated statutes and elected regional institutions. Decentralisation can integrate Spain's nationalities and regions, but uneven expectations will persist.

Spain applied to join the European Communities in 1977. The constitutional settlement now allows Madrid to deepen negotiations, align national institutions with European standards and make democratic consolidation part of the accession process.

Lieutenant Colonel Tejero's seizure of the Cortes has exposed the transition's most dangerous fault line. The response of the Crown and high command will determine whether constitutional government survives the night.
Juan Carlos will publicly order the armed forces to obey the constitutional authorities. A clear defence of legality can break the coup while binding the Crown's legitimacy to democracy.

Peaceful alternation in office and the acceptance of electoral defeat will prove that the constitutional order no longer depends on one government or one king. The transition can finally become ordinary democratic politics.
The emergency logic of the Transition has run its course. Spain will now be governed through durable parties, regular elections and competing cabinet programmes.
Santiago Carrillo will seek a parliamentary mandate for a specifically Spanish road to socialism: pluralist, constitutional and independent of Moscow.
The PCE will bind itself openly to competitive elections, civil rights and peaceful transfers of power, closing the door on one-party rule.
A new democratic labour settlement will strengthen collective bargaining and social protection while preserving the constitutional order.
Worker participation, cooperative credit and municipal enterprise can broaden ownership without placing the entire economy under central state management.
Energy, transport and other strategic industries will be placed under public ownership to secure national productive capacity.
Spain will pursue strategic autonomy, cooperation with its Iberian and Mediterranean neighbours and freedom from automatic bloc discipline.
The Eurocommunist project will be consolidated through elections, social administration and pluralist institutions rather than revolutionary dictatorship.
A broad electoral mandate gives Felipe González the authority to modernise Spain while expanding social protection and civilian control.
Obsolete industries must be restructured and new investment directed toward sectors capable of competing in an integrated European economy.
Democratic legitimacy will be reinforced through broader social insurance, public healthcare and a permanent partnership with organised labour.
Appointments, planning and internal security will be subordinated unambiguously to the elected government.
Spain will confirm its Atlantic commitments while using membership to professionalise its armed forces and deepen ties with Western democracies.
The government will honour its commitment to strategic restraint and allow the electorate to decide Spain's relationship with NATO.
Spain will combine competitive industry, capable public services and parliamentary government in a durable social-democratic settlement.
Adolfo Suárez will rebuild the reformist centre as an independent liberal force after the fragmentation of the UCD coalition.
The liberal centre will restrain the security state and make individual rights the test of democratic consolidation.
Deregulation, lighter taxation and modern offices will help commerce and professional services become engines of growth.
Investment from the established Western economies can accelerate Spain's modernisation and bind its young democracy to Europe.
Commercial links with Portugal, France and Italy will make Spain a natural bridge between Western Europe and the Mediterranean.
The CDS will become a stable governing institution rather than another temporary vehicle of the Transition.
Manuel Fraga will organise the democratic right around constitutional order, competent administration and Atlantic cooperation.
Professional revenue collection and clearer accounts will strengthen the state without another nominal tax increase.
Regional self-government will be consolidated within a common constitutional framework acceptable to the democratic centre-right.
Employers and organised labour will share the costs of modernising Spanish industry under a conservative government.
Spain's democratic right will anchor the country in Atlantic security cooperation and the project of European integration.
A durable parliamentary majority will allow the centre-right to govern efficiently without reopening the constitutional settlement.
Spain's democratic settlement and years of institutional convergence have prepared the country to enter the European Communities as a full member.
Giron's assault on reform has rallied the Bunker and forced Arias to retreat. The regime will present immobility as fidelity, closing the narrow opening before it can become a precedent.

Jose Utrera Molina will turn the Secretariat-General of the Movement into the directing office of the Falangist state. His appointment joins the old guard's programme to a functioning party bureaucracy.
The Bourbon succession may proceed only if the king accepts the political supremacy of the Movement. The Crown will provide continuity and ceremony without acquiring an independent mandate.

Opus Dei administrators and market-oriented officials are blamed for corruption, social dislocation and ideological drift. Removing them will place economic policy back under reliable political command.
No National-Syndicalist restoration can survive without the officer corps. Promotions, commands and guarantees of military privilege will bind the armed forces to the new order.

Veterans, youth organizations and provincial Falangist networks will return to public life. Their discipline can intimidate opponents and fill the streets, but their methods will deepen social tension.
The 1938 labour charter will again define work as a duty regulated through the state rather than a field of free bargaining. Social guarantees will be paired with compulsory discipline.

Schools, universities and youth organisations will be reorganised around service, hierarchy and national-syndicalist doctrine. The regime seeks a generation that inherited loyalty instead of merely submitting to it.
Workers and employers will be incorporated into state-supervised organisations by branch of production. Class conflict is to be administered inside the regime, not represented by independent unions.
Import substitution, public investment and national control of strategic sectors will reduce exposure to foreign pressure. Independence will come at the cost of efficiency and access to capital.

Spain will reject both liberal capitalism and Marxist planning in favour of corporatist direction, worker participation and strategic ownership. The model promises national solidarity but depends on coercive coordination.

Political, economic and military institutions will be subordinated to a permanent National-Syndicalist order. The Falange will claim that Franco's compromise has finally given way to its unfinished revolution.
The monarchy will remain as a source of legal continuity and ceremonial unity, while real authority rests with the Movement. The king will reign only so long as he does not govern.
Spain will reject both Bourbon legitimacy and parliamentary sovereignty. Authority will derive from the national community, its syndicates and the state built by the Falange.
Appointments, unions, youth organisations and the Cortes will be brought under a single Movement hierarchy. The distinction between party and state will become largely formal.
The Regency Council will convert temporary authority into a disciplined executive. Carrero Blanco, if he survived, or Carlos Arias Navarro will govern in the name of institutional continuity.

Juan Carlos will be crowned only after an unequivocal commitment to the victory of 18 July and the Fundamental Principles of the Movement. Succession will preserve the regime rather than reinterpret it.

Carlos Arias Navarro will remain President of the Government and guardian of Franco's institutional legacy. Continuity and a narrow administrative opening will take precedence over constitutional reform.
Limited political associations may operate inside the Movement, but independent parties will remain prohibited. Controlled competition can refresh the regime without conceding popular sovereignty.
The armed forces remain the final guarantor of the order created in 1939. Renewed command oaths and institutional privileges will ensure that no reformist coalition can bypass them.

Market-oriented administrators will remain in office to protect growth, investment and the machinery of government. Their expertise is useful so long as political authority remains beyond their reach.
The technocrats will carry the late Franco-era development plans into a new investment cycle, expanding productive capacity without opening the political system.

The monarchy will preserve Franco's Fundamental Laws, military guarantees and controlled representation rather than introduce parliamentary sovereignty. Royal authority will modernise the regime without democratising it.
ETA's campaign will be met with special courts, expanded intelligence powers and reinforced deployments in the north. Security may improve, but collective pressure will deepen political estrangement.

The American base agreements will be renewed in exchange for military assistance, investment and diplomatic recognition. Strategic partnership offers the regime external legitimacy without requiring political convergence.

The Cortes will continue to represent families, municipalities and syndicates rather than competing parties. Consultation will be permitted, but sovereignty will remain with the institutions of the regime.

Press latitude, administrative consultation and restricted associations can be offered without submitting the executive to a national vote. The opening is intended to absorb pressure, not transfer power.
A council of senior officers and trusted civilians will assume emergency authority to prevent both revolution and uncontrolled reform. Its mandate will be temporary in law and indefinite in practice.
The founder is gone, but his institutional order can endure through bureaucracy, security power and military guardianship. Personal dictatorship will become an impersonal authoritarian state.

Iraq's attack on Kuwait threatens the sovereignty of the Gulf's states and the order on which their security depends. We will seek authority to use American military power to reverse the conquest, while leaving the commitment of forces in the hands of Washington and its coalition partners.

The forces needed to defend the Gulf must reach the region before they can influence events there. We will approach friendly governments about staging rights and prepare the supply arrangements on which any sustained American deployment will depend.

A response to the conquest of Kuwait will carry greater weight if regional and international governments accept a common purpose. We will seek their cooperation and negotiate the commitments they are willing to make, knowing that political endorsement alone does not place their forces under American command.

Iraq's northern parties possess their own ambitions, grievances and memories of outside intervention. Opening channels to them will clarify what they seek from Washington and what they can undertake themselves. Public encouragement must be weighed against the consequences for people who may act upon it.
Open separate channels to the Kurdish parties. Their priorities and rivalries remain distinct.

Our mandate in the Gulf is strongest when its objectives remain clear. We will concentrate on Kuwait's restoration and organize a disciplined humanitarian effort, accepting that restraint leaves Washington with less influence over the struggle for power inside Iraq.

Iraqi Kurdish leaders may provide a local counterweight to Baghdad, but their military position cannot be sustained by American declarations alone. We will offer arms and continuing support on terms that the local administrations can accept, committing resources to a conflict whose end Washington cannot dictate.

Relief and protection in northern Iraq depend on supply routes through neighboring states. We will negotiate access with governments whose own interests in the Kurdish question may differ sharply from ours. Their cooperation must be maintained rather than taken for granted.

Fighting and displacement in the north have left communities beyond the reach of dependable public services. An American relief effort can keep essential supplies moving and help damaged infrastructure recover, provided neighboring governments allow the necessary routes to remain open.

A protected relief area requires more than a declaration. We will support the logistics of an accessible northern refuge, while recognizing that the security of its inhabitants still depends on the forces present and the willingness of outside governments to remain involved.

American and cooperating air forces can make attacks on the northern communities more difficult. We will prepare interception, air-superiority and liaison arrangements from consenting bases. The commitment must be sustained by actual aircraft and the governments willing to host them.

Local councils and party administrations must provide more than military leadership if the north is to recover. We will support representative institutions and a functioning regional budget, while allowing the Kurdish parties to negotiate their own relationship and priorities.

An agreement with Baghdad could turn an uncertain refuge into recognized self-government within Iraq. We will seek terms that protect regional budgets and local security, and support reconstruction only once the governments concerned accept and uphold the settlement.

The regional administrations may be unable to secure dependable guarantees from Baghdad. An external American commitment would strengthen their defence, but would also leave Washington responsible for a costly undertaking that Iraq's government continues to contest.

Northern recovery needs roads, functioning administration and an economy able to support returning families. We will negotiate assistance with the local authorities and support practical reconstruction, whether their security rests on an accepted Iraqi settlement or a continuing external commitment.
